stories.title: Crowded political landscape leaves Quebec voters lukewarm as election nears
stories.summary: Five parties are likely to win seats, but none has attained a critical mass of support in lead-up to Oct. 5
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Voters in Quebec are facing an almost unprecedented array of choices in this fall’s election, but amid the noise and bluster of a crowded field, they have yet to fall in love with any of their options.

On Oct. 5, Quebeckers will select from five major political parties who are all likely to win at least a handful of seats in the province’s National Assembly. It should be an embarrassment of riches, but voters seem unable to muster much enthusiasm for anything on the menu.

The Parti Québécois is favoured to win the most seats, but is hamstrung by its promise to hold a referendum on Quebec sovereignty that most people don’t want. The Coalition Avenir Québec is weighed down by the baggage of eight years in power. The opposition Liberals are stubbornly unpopular among francophones.

When the CAQ formed its first government in 2018, promising a new brand of nationalism that didn’t include a referendum on separation, it blew up a political landscape that had been defined for decades by the debate over sovereignty. Eight years on, the electoral battlefield is littered with shrapnel from that explosion.

The result is five parties that all cater to subsets of the Quebec electorate. But none of those parties has so far proved capable of seducing a critical mass of voters in a campaign that feels strangely stagnant.

Each of the five contenders has a core of loyal support, often concentrated in certain regions. Sovereigntists mostly vote for the PQ. Anglophones (largely in and around Montreal) consistently support the Liberals. The CAQ is the party of choice for older francophones who don’t want a referendum. Urban progressives support Québec solidaire, a left-leaning sovereigntist party, while the Conservatives have a strong base among right-leaning voters around Quebec City.

But with all five parties polling below 30 per cent, two- and three-way races are playing out in ridings across the province. The three leading parties – the PQ, CAQ and Liberals – are all within a few points of each other, while roughly 40 per cent of voters still say their choice isn’t locked in.

On a doorstep in the Quebec City suburb of Charlesbourg, PQ candidate Gabriel Coulombe recently made his pitch to a couple who said they haven’t made up their minds about which way to vote.

“The goods were not delivered” under the CAQ government, Mr. Coulombe told the couple.

But Gilles Simard and Sylvie Dinel were unconvinced. They later told The Globe and Mail they have no interest in the sovereignty referendum promised by PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, which would be the province’s third vote on the question of whether Quebec should remain in Canada.

Ms. Dinel said she’s thinking about voting for the Quebec Conservatives, a relatively new party projected to win seats for the first time this year. She voted for the CAQ four years ago, but they made some “bad choices,” she said.

Mr. Simard seemed more inclined to give the CAQ another chance, though he didn’t offer the party a ringing endorsement. Leader Christine Fréchette “is already in place,” he said. “There won’t be a bunch of surprises.”

The riding of Charlesbourg voted solidly CAQ in the last two elections. But as voters seek change this time around, the campaign is a tight three-way race between the PQ, the CAQ and the Conservatives.

“It’s the kind of election that could be decided by a few hundred or a few dozen votes,” Mr. Coulombe said in an interview.

Quebeckers have once before elected members of five parties to the provincial legislature, back in 1976. That election was an inflection point for the province, said Youri Rivest, co-founder of polling firm Synopsis Recherche. That year, René Lévesque led the Parti Québécois to form its first government, while the once-powerful Union Nationale won seats for the last time. Two of the other parties were bit players that dissolved not long after.

This time, Mr. Rivest said, the five parties competing for votes are the result of a “fragmentation of the sociopolitical values of Quebeckers.” After decades of elections fought between the sovereigntist Parti Québécois and the federalist Liberals, the CAQ in 2018 suddenly made it possible to vote on other issues.

“There was a very strong tension between federalists and sovereigntists,” he said. “But once you remove that tension, it reveals another axis – one that’s left-right.”

Québec solidaire, the left-leaning party, won 10 seats for the first time in 2018. The Conservatives claimed nearly 13 per cent of the vote four years ago, but won no seats.

Evelyne Brie, an assistant professor of political science at Université de Montréal, said the regionalization of politics is not unique to Quebec, and is partly driven by the rise of alternative media.

“It’s possible to get information from media outlets that are very specialized,” she said. “This creates echo chambers.”

Two weeks ahead of election day, none of the leaders has managed to trigger one of the waves of popular sentiment for which Quebec is known, and the result on Oct. 5 will most likely be a minority government. With the electorate so fragmented, polls have shown little movement since the early days of the campaign.

In Charlesbourg, that suits some voters just fine. In a campaign that has lacked much sizzle, there is at least some genuine excitement here about the prospect of a Conservative caucus in the National Assembly. Leader Éric Duhaime has campaigned mostly in the Quebec City region, and is hoping to hold the balance of power.

His candidate in the suburban riding is 23-year-old Eloïse Coulombe – no relation of the PQ candidate. While door-knocking one evening this month, Ms. Coulombe was stopped on the sidewalk by Réjean Laliberté, an older voter who wanted to show his support.

“I’m fed up with having the same old people in government squandering our money,” he later told The Globe. If the Conservatives form an opposition party, he added, “I’ll be the happiest man in the world.”

Across the street, a woman opened her door to call out to Ms. Coulombe. “Bravo!” she shouted. “We’re voting for you!”

A poised and articulate university student, Ms. Coulombe embodies Mr. Duhaime’s reinvention of his party. Four years ago, the Conservative leader drummed up support by railing against pandemic public-health restrictions. Today, he has recast his party as a sober watchdog fighting to protect taxpayers from state profligacy. He has proposed major tax cuts and more private health care.

Prof. Brie said it’s a “nice problem” to have a proliferation of parties that resonate with certain segments of the population. “That’s actually healthy for a democracy,” she said.

But in a province where political movements ebb and flow, it remains to be seen whether such a congested playing field can last. Four years ago, the PQ was on the verge of extinction when it won just three seats in the legislature. Earlier this year, the CAQ was about to be wiped out. Both have made unlikely comebacks.

“Something is going to be reconfigured,” said Mr. Rivest. “The system isn’t designed to handle this.”

But with all five parties polling below 30 per cent, two- and three-way races are playing out in ridings across the province. The three leading parties – the PQ, CAQ and Liberals – are all within a few points of each other, while roughly 40 per cent of voters still say their choice isn’t locked in.
On a doorstep in the Quebec City suburb of Charlesbourg, PQ candidate Gabriel Coulombe recently made his pitch to a couple who said they haven’t made up their minds about which way to vote.
“The goods were not delivered” under the CAQ government, Mr. Coulombe told the couple.

content_blocks.caption: Mr. Coulombe campaigns in Charlesbourg. While favoured to win the most seats, the PQ is hamstrung by its promise to hold a sovereignty referendum. Renaud Philippe/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: But Gilles Simard and Sylvie Dinel were unconvinced. They later told The Globe and Mail they have no interest in the sovereignty referendum promised by PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, which would be the province’s third vote on the question of whether Quebec should remain in Canada.

Ms. Dinel said she’s thinking about voting for the Quebec Conservatives, a relatively new party projected to win seats for the first time this year. She voted for the CAQ four years ago, but they made some “bad choices,” she said.

Mr. Simard seemed more inclined to give the CAQ another chance, though he didn’t offer the party a ringing endorsement. Leader Christine Fréchette “is already in place,” he said. “There won’t be a bunch of surprises.”

The riding of Charlesbourg voted solidly CAQ in the last two elections. But as voters seek change this time around, the campaign is a tight three-way race between the PQ, the CAQ and the Conservatives.
“It’s the kind of election that could be decided by a few hundred or a few dozen votes,” Mr. Coulombe said in an interview.

Quebeckers have once before elected members of five parties to the provincial legislature, back in 1976. That election was an inflection point for the province, said Youri Rivest, co-founder of polling firm Synopsis Recherche. That year, René Lévesque led the Parti Québécois to form its first government, while the once-powerful Union Nationale won seats for the last time. Two of the other parties were bit players that dissolved not long after.

content_blocks.caption: René Lévesque, shown in 1983, was the first premier from the Parti Québécois. The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: This time, Mr. Rivest said, the five parties competing for votes are the result of a “fragmentation of the sociopolitical values of Quebeckers.” After decades of elections fought between the sovereigntist Parti Québécois and the federalist Liberals, the CAQ in 2018 suddenly made it possible to vote on other issues.
“There was a very strong tension between federalists and sovereigntists,” he said. “But once you remove that tension, it reveals another axis – one that’s left-right.”
Québec solidaire, the left-leaning party, won 10 seats for the first time in 2018. The Conservatives claimed nearly 13 per cent of the vote four years ago, but won no seats.

Evelyne Brie, an assistant professor of political science at Université de Montréal, said the regionalization of politics is not unique to Quebec, and is partly driven by the rise of alternative media.
“It’s possible to get information from media outlets that are very specialized,” she said. “This creates echo chambers.”

Two weeks ahead of election day, none of the leaders has managed to trigger one of the waves of popular sentiment for which Quebec is known, and the result on Oct. 5 will most likely be a minority government. With the electorate so fragmented, polls have shown little movement since the early days of the campaign.

In Charlesbourg, that suits some voters just fine. In a campaign that has lacked much sizzle, there is at least some genuine excitement here about the prospect of a Conservative caucus in the National Assembly. Leader Éric Duhaime has campaigned mostly in the Quebec City region, and is hoping to hold the balance of power.

His candidate in the suburban riding is 23-year-old Eloïse Coulombe – no relation of the PQ candidate. While door-knocking one evening this month, Ms. Coulombe was stopped on the sidewalk by Réjean Laliberté, an older voter who wanted to show his support.

“I’m fed up with having the same old people in government squandering our money,” he later told The Globe. If the Conservatives form an opposition party, he added, “I’ll be the happiest man in the world.”

content_blocks.caption: University student Eloïse Coulombe is the Conservative candidate in Charlesbourg. Renaud Philippe/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: Across the street, a woman opened her door to call out to Ms. Coulombe. “Bravo!” she shouted. “We’re voting for you!”

A poised and articulate university student, Ms. Coulombe embodies Mr. Duhaime’s reinvention of his party. Four years ago, the Conservative leader drummed up support by railing against pandemic public-health restrictions. Today, he has recast his party as a sober watchdog fighting to protect taxpayers from state profligacy. He has proposed major tax cuts and more private health care.
Prof. Brie said it’s a “nice problem” to have a proliferation of parties that resonate with certain segments of the population. “That’s actually healthy for a democracy,” she said.

But in a province where political movements ebb and flow, it remains to be seen whether such a congested playing field can last. Four years ago, the PQ was on the verge of extinction when it won just three seats in the legislature. Earlier this year, the CAQ was about to be wiped out. Both have made unlikely comebacks.
“Something is going to be reconfigured,” said Mr. Rivest. “The system isn’t designed to handle this.”

stories.title: Heritage Property tax relief approved by city committee, long road ahead to creation
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London City Council's Planning and Environment Committee took a step toward the potential creation of a tax discount program to help property owners pay for the upkeep of historic buildings, Monday.
· Posted: Sep 22, 2026 5:14 AM EDT | Last Updated: 43 minutes ago

The five-person committee voted unanimously to have a recommendation to implement such a program brought to the next council for consideration during the creation of the city's 2027-2031 strategic plan and next multi-year budgeting process.
While the committee voted in favour of moving closer to the creation of an eventual program, there's little information on what it might look like and what the impact would be on taxpayers.
A long-defunct pilot program to offer tax refunds to heritage property owners previously existed in the city from 2007 to 2010.
Under the previous program, owners of eligible properties entered agreements with the city that ensured the property was maintained.

In exchange, the city offered up to 40 per cent off the tax bill for the property up to $3,000 for multi-residential properties. For apartment, commercial and mixed-use buildings, the tax break was up to 20 per cent to a maximum of $5,000.
Annual funding for the program per year was capped at $50,000 and applications were first-come, first-served.
In a report to the planning committee, city staff noted that program was well-liked and used by landowners, despite ultimately not being renewed when it expired in 2010.
Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis, who sits on the committee as deputy chair, expressed concern over the lack of a concrete vision for what the program might look like.
Lewis suggested a model similar to what Collingwood, Ont., uses, which is similar to London's previous program.

"What I'm really looking for is the preservation and maintenance agreement, and a recommendation on a budget allocation," said Lewis. "It might not be $50,000, but a recommendation based on the number of heritage designations we have."
Differing from London's previous program, the Collingwood model offers a flat 20 per cent reduction across all types of heritage properties.

Members of the committee agreed municipal staff should be required to include a recommendation for a model based on Collingwood's approach when the matter is brought before the next council during budgeting.
With the planning committee's approval, the prospect of creating a heritage property tax relief program in London must still be approved by the entirety of City Council before moving forward.
Council meets Wednesday.

stories.title: Traffic, transit and affordability top issues in London's Ward 8 election race
stories.summary: Traffic, transit and affordability top issues in London's Ward 8 election race CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: 3 candidates are vying to represent the west London ward at city hall
Traffic, transit and the rising cost of living are among the issues shaping the race for London's Ward 8, where three candidates are vying for a seat on city council.
Incumbent Coun. Steve Lehman is seeking a third term, while Coralia Tudor and Osam Ali are challenging him in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The candidates say residents have raised broader city issues, including property taxes, affordability, homelessness and addiction, while also pointing to concerns closer to home, from traffic and transit to residential development and road safety.
Here's what the candidates say they would focus on if elected.
Lehman was first elected to Council in 2018, and won a second term in 2022.
He said he's seeking another term because there is "still work to be done for Ward 8 and the city" and he is eager to continue it.
For Lehman, traffic is one of the most pressing issues facing the rapidly growing west end.
"We've seen a bottleneck in the north-south," he said. "We've seen Wonderland come to almost a standstill every day from Spring Bank up to Sarnia Road, and that's pushed traffic over to Hyde Park."
Lehman said he worked to have the widening of Wonderland Road included again in the city's Master Mobility Plan. He wants to continue pushing for the project if he is re-elected.

He has also been in contact with Ontario's Transportation Minister Rob Flack over bringing an extension of Highway 402 up to the north end of the city, to help people get down to the 401 without clogging inner-city roads.
"We have an opportunity right now on the west side of London before it is all developed," he said.
"Now is the time to act, and I'm not thinking about the next five years, I'm thinking about the next 20 years for London."
Tudor is a former educator and paralegal who said she now works in philanthropy and volunteers with a number of community organizations.
She said she decided to run because she believes the city could be doing better on a number of issues.
"I'm seeing a lot of things that I don't like happening in our city, things that I think we could be doing better and I want to make that change," she said.
Transit is one of the issues she said she hears about most from Ward 8 residents.
Tudor said some routes don't work well for people trying to travel within the west end or get to Western University.
"The number one joke I get from residents is 'well, I suppose transit is so bad everyone's just had to buy their kids a car,'" she said. "But that's not a good answer, right?"
Tudor said she would redesign routes around where people actually need to travel. She also wants to see more bus stops designed so buses can pull out of traffic while passengers board and exit.
She said that could improve both transit service and traffic flow.
Residential infill is also an issue Tudor wants to address, she said, adding that residents are concerned about high-density developments.
"It's not that people are opposed to apartments per se, but heights are being changed, volumes are being exceeded for what the capacity is able to hold on those streets," she said.

A 20-year resident of London, Ali has lived in Ward 8 for five years. With a PhD in software engineering, he has worked for London Health Sciences Centre for 18 years, and teaches at Fanshawe College.
Ali previously ran in the 2018 election for Ward 8, capturing around six per cent of the vote.
One of the big concerns he hears from voters is that City Hall is not responsive enough. He said it can take weeks for people to get a response to emails.

He also wants to see more support for small businesses in the area. There is a Business Improvement Area (BIA) for Hyde Park, but that only extends about one block into Ward 8, with the majority of the BIA situated in neighbouring Ward 7.
Ali also has concerns about road safety in the area, pointing to a lack of sidewalks in the Hunt Club neighbourhood, and to Hyde Park Road, where he said accidents have become frequent.
"When I talk to the residents over there, they complain that the city is not doing a good job," he said. "For example, with speeding on Hyde Park, or the same area getting hit three times with cars."
Londoners will head to the polls to elect a mayor and council on Oct. 26.

Traffic, transit and the rising cost of living are among the issues shaping the race for London's Ward 8, where three candidates are vying for a seat on city council.

Incumbent Coun. Steve Lehman is seeking a third term, while Coralia Tudor and Osam Ali are challenging him in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The candidates say residents have raised broader city issues, including property taxes, affordability, homelessness and addiction, while also pointing to concerns closer to home, from traffic and transit to residential development and road safety.

Here's what the candidates say they would focus on if elected.

Lehman was first elected to Council in 2018, and won a second term in 2022.

He said he's seeking another term because there is "still work to be done for Ward 8 and the city" and he is eager to continue it.

For Lehman, traffic is one of the most pressing issues facing the rapidly growing west end.

"We've seen a bottleneck in the north-south," he said. "We've seen Wonderland come to almost a standstill every day from Spring Bank up to Sarnia Road, and that's pushed traffic over to Hyde Park."

Lehman said he worked to have the widening of Wonderland Road included again in the city's Master Mobility Plan. He wants to continue pushing for the project if he is re-elected.

He has also been in contact with Ontario's Transportation Minister Rob Flack over bringing an extension of Highway 402 up to the north end of the city, to help people get down to the 401 without clogging inner-city roads.

"We have an opportunity right now on the west side of London before it is all developed," he said.

"Now is the time to act, and I'm not thinking about the next five years, I'm thinking about the next 20 years for London."

Tudor is a former educator and paralegal who said she now works in philanthropy and volunteers with a number of community organizations.

She said she decided to run because she believes the city could be doing better on a number of issues.

"I'm seeing a lot of things that I don't like happening in our city, things that I think we could be doing better and I want to make that change," she said.

Transit is one of the issues she said she hears about most from Ward 8 residents.

Tudor said some routes don't work well for people trying to travel within the west end or get to Western University.

"The number one joke I get from residents is 'well, I suppose transit is so bad everyone's just had to buy their kids a car,'" she said. "But that's not a good answer, right?"

Tudor said she would redesign routes around where people actually need to travel. She also wants to see more bus stops designed so buses can pull out of traffic while passengers board and exit.

She said that could improve both transit service and traffic flow.

Residential infill is also an issue Tudor wants to address, she said, adding that residents are concerned about high-density developments.

"It's not that people are opposed to apartments per se, but heights are being changed, volumes are being exceeded for what the capacity is able to hold on those streets," she said.

A 20-year resident of London, Ali has lived in Ward 8 for five years. With a PhD in software engineering, he has worked for London Health Sciences Centre for 18 years, and teaches at Fanshawe College.

Ali previously ran in the 2018 election for Ward 8, capturing around six per cent of the vote.

One of the big concerns he hears from voters is that City Hall is not responsive enough. He said it can take weeks for people to get a response to emails.

He also wants to see more support for small businesses in the area. There is a Business Improvement Area (BIA) for Hyde Park, but that only extends about one block into Ward 8, with the majority of the BIA situated in neighbouring Ward 7.

Ali also has concerns about road safety in the area, pointing to a lack of sidewalks in the Hunt Club neighbourhood, and to Hyde Park Road, where he said accidents have become frequent.

"When I talk to the residents over there, they complain that the city is not doing a good job," he said. "For example, with speeding on Hyde Park, or the same area getting hit three times with cars."

Londoners will head to the polls to elect a mayor and council on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Families of first-degree murder victims call for parole reform
stories.summary: Victims' families are calling for parole reforms, urging changes to Canada's justice system.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Toronto - “We’re talking about a guy who walked over, put the gun to my brother’s head, and pulled the goddamn trigger,” said Cody Baylis, as he gestures to his own head, his hand mimicking the gun that killed his brother.

It was June 1994. Baylis was in Florida when he learned that his big brother, Toronto Police Constable Todd Baylis had been shot and killed on the job. Todd was just 25 years old at the time and had been chasing after a suspected drug dealer who pulled out a gun and opened fire, shooting him in the head.

Clinton Gayle was found guilty of first-degree murder and attempted murder for shooting Baylis’ partner who survived. Gayle was sentenced to life in prison with no chance at parole for 25 years.

The Baylis family now must appear at a parole hearing every two years. They’ve already had to attend four separate parole reviews.

Speaking to CTV News from his home in Brampton, Ont., Baylis shared his mounting frustration after having to attend yet another hearing this past July, reliving the trauma of losing his brother.

“2019, 2021, 2024, 2026. We’ll have to go back in 2027 or 2028, it’s ridiculous,” said Baylis.

Gayle and others facing life sentences can request a parole hearing every two years, once the initial 25 years of their sentence has been served.

CTV News has obtained a copy of a letter written by the Toronto Police Association, requesting that the federal government increase the time between parole hearings from “five to seven years” and allow judges the power to impose “parole ineligibility periods for up to 35 years” for those convicted of first-degree murder.

This coming January, serial rapist and killer Paul Bernardo will have his fourth parole hearing.

“It’s just pure entertainment for him. He has no remorse,” said trial lawyer Tim Danson.

Danson represents the families of victims Leslie Mahaffy and Kristen French, who were both murdered by Bernardo. He attends each parole hearing pro bono, to support the Mahaffy and French families.

He still sees a “sadistic, sexual psychopath” in Paul Bernado.

“When he’s asked during a parole review why he would carry out these horrific attacks on these teenage girls he answers by saying ‘well, they weren’t doing what I told them,’” Danson said.

“He answers these questions like you and I would talk about the weather.”

Danson says the French, Mahaffy and Baylis families are all asking for parole reform, and they believe that Canada’s worst convicted killers shouldn’t be allowed to traumatize a family every two years.

Our justice system shouldn’t be one size fits all, we’re not talking about someone “stealing candy from a candy store” said Baylis.

“It’s horrific what the justice system does to victims’ families. They drag us through this process, and I find myself asking why. Well, I’ll tell you, it’s because a killer’s rights are more important that mine, my dead brother’s, yours, or anybody else’s.”

The Toronto Police Association’s letter, sent to multiple members of parliament, says in part that the federal government “committed to us earlier this year that this issue would be addressed in the fall. We are now two weeks into September, and with the latest news about Paul Bernardo, the issue could not be more urgent.”

The Department of Justice has not responded to a request for comment.

stories.title: Canadian airports can anchor a global infrastructure champion
stories.summary: Ottawa decision to sell concessions in four major domestic hubs promises to be a win for passengers and taxpayers
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
If you are reading this while killing time waiting for a flight in one of Canada’s major airports, you are sitting in what should be the country’s next global corporate champion.

The federal government’s long-overdue decision to sell concessions in four major domestic hubs – Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal – promises to be a win for passengers and taxpayers. After years of analysis paralysis, Prime Minister Mark Carney has an opportunity to improve the passenger experience while raising billions of dollars.

The ultimate goal in this exercise, clearly visible to a Prime Minister who started his career as a Goldman Sachs banker advising governments on privatizations, should be creating a private-sector operator of Canadian airports that does business around the world.

At least one domestic pension fund, Montreal-based PSP Investments, is already well down this runway.

In June, months before Mr. Carney announced plans to sell airport concessions at last Tuesday’s Canada Investment Summit, Montreal-based consultant Fethi Chebil published a sector study that started with a metaphysical question for the government.

“What is an airport for? An asset to sell, or a tool to build a national operator?” Dr. Chebil said in his June report.

For governments, Dr. Chebil concluded that launching a business beats selling a few terminals. To support his argument, Dr. Chebil pointed to the success that Canada’s largest pension funds have enjoyed internationally as owners of airport operators, and the virtues of this model for frequent flyers.

The poster child for airport operators globally is PSP, which pays for the retirements of soldiers, Mounties and civil servants. The $321-billion fund manager has built a global business that should serve as a road map for Canadian airport ownership.

In 2013, PSP acquired a collection of European airports from a German infrastructure fund for €1.1-billion. The wholly owned subsidiary, branded as AviAlliance, now operates seven facilities in Scotland, Germany, England and Puerto Rico.

AviAlliance is the largest holding in a PSP infrastructure portfolio that handily beat performance benchmarks over the past decade.

AviAlliance airports also charge travellers less for food, beverages and fees than Canadian airports, according to Dr. Chebil’s research. Domestic airports operate as non-profit, debt-funded Crown corporations, a cumbersome, only-in-Canada ownership approach devised in 1992. Dr. Chebil said in his report: “The 1992 structure is not delivering lower costs to users.”

Private airport owners would create more opportunities for travellers to drop stupid amounts of money on cucumber-lined Hendrick’s martinis or Rolex watches. That’s discretionary consumer spending. Want to curtail the cost of a trip? Avoid airport restaurants and retailers.

The experience in Europe and Australia, where governments sold airport concessions, is to keep costs down by regulating fees on monopoly services such as baggage handling or aeronautical services including navigation. Governments use the same approach to ensure pipeline operators and electrical utilities don’t gouge consumers.

In 2016, former federal finance minister Bill Morneau launched an economic review that said selling airports was among the best options for a government that needed to find money for infrastructure projects. A decade later, Mr. Carney is following through.

For insight into how the Prime Minister thinks about finance, recall Mr. Carney’s pointed criticism of the billions in “dead money” on corporate balance sheets back in 2012, when he was governor of the Bank of Canada.

In a Q&A after a speech to the Canadian Auto Workers union, the then-central banker took CEOs and boards to task for being excessively cautious by sitting on cash, rather than investing in growth or returning money to shareholders.

There is a straight line from what Governor Carney said about dead money years ago to what Prime Minister Carney announced on airports last week.

Last Tuesday, in his opening speech at the investment summit, Mr. Carney said by selling airport concessions, while retaining ownership of the assets, “we will unlock their true value, by bringing in new capital and expertise into their operations and growth.”

“We will reinvest the tens of billions of dollars of capital we raise into the infrastructure that Canada needs,” the Prime Minister said.

Airports represent dead money on the federal government’s balance sheet. Selling concessions to operate Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal’s terminals can make flying more pleasant, without boosting the cost of travel.

And placing the country’s four major airports in the proven hands of a fund manager such as PSP could create a global champion in a critical infrastructure sector.

stories.title: Ontario hospitals ordered to improve detection protocols for sepsis
stories.summary: Several sepsis-related deaths in the province in recent years, including that of a 16-year-old, have sparked public outcry
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Hospitals in Canada’s most populous province will be required by Ontario Health to establish protocols by early next year to identify and respond to sepsis, which can be fatal if patients do not receive timely medical intervention.

A copy of a clinical memorandum, sent in the spring and obtained by The Globe and Mail, details how Ontario Health, a government agency designed to modernize the health care system, is working to set consistent provincial expectations for how hospitals respond to potential cases of sepsis. The new protocols must be in place by March, 2027, according to the memorandum.

There have been several sepsis-related deaths in Ontario hospitals in recent years that have sparked public outcry, including that of 16-year-old Finlay van der Werken . In February, 2024, he waited more than eight hours in an Oakville, Ont., emergency department to be seen by a doctor before he died of sepsis and pneumonia.

Sepsis is when the body kicks into overdrive in response to an infection. If it is not recognized early, it can lead to shock, organ failure and death. As of 2020, it was estimated 75,000 cases of sepsis occur every year in Canada, leading to 18,000 deaths .

The clinical memorandum, dated April 20, pegs the cost of sepsis to Ontario’s health care system to be more than $1-billion a year. The document, sent to chief medical executives and hospitals in the province, said institutions must have sepsis screening or warning mechanisms in place for inpatient units by March 31, 2027.

“Hospitals can fulfill this requirement by using a health information system (HIS) with an integrated early warning system or by implementing a routine screening process – either on paper or electronically – for acutely ill, high-risk patients,” it said.

The document also cites strong evidence that early identification and timely sepsis treatment improves patient outcomes, but that benefits can only be achieved when protocols are embedded in workflows and consistent.

Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said the provincial government is working to promote standardized practices and clinical awareness.

“As per the Minister’s direction, Ontario Health has convened an expert panel of leading clinicians to review currently established sepsis guidelines and opportunities for improvement,” she said in an e-mail.

Last October, the van der Werken family met with Ms. Jones to call for changes to how emergency care is delivered in Ontario, including standardized maximum ER wait times for vulnerable pediatric patients.

The circumstances of Finlay’s death will be the subject of a future discretionary coroner’s inquest , but a date has not been set.

Ontario resident, Gurinder Sidhu, has also called for reforms to ensure early intervention and treatment of sepsis. He says his wife, Ravinder, with whom he has three children, developed postpartum sepsis that caused organ failure and led to her death in June, 2025.

Kassandra Costabile is also pushing for accountability following her sister’s death, which she believes was preventable. Rheanna Laderoute died in February, 2022, after showing signs of septic shock following an abortion.

Last October, Nova Scotia rolled out a provincewide approach that authorized emergency room nurses to administer antibiotics and IV fluids to anyone suspected of having sepsis.

The measure was applauded by advocates who want the approach expanded to other provinces and territories.

Nova Scotia’s changes were implemented following several prominent sepsis cases that resulted in legal action.

For its action plan, the provincial health authority drew lessons from NHS Scotland, the publicly funded health care system in that country, and the B.C. Sepsis Network, a clinician initiative in that province.

In New York State, sepsis detection regulations in place for the past 13 years have been credited with saving tens of thousands of lives . They include strict timelines for interventions, including early delivery of antibiotics.

The measures, known as Rory’s Regulations, were put in place after the April 1, 2012, death of 12-year-old Rory Staunton, who had undiagnosed and untreated sepsis. His parents, Ciaran and Orlaith Staunton, founded the U.S. advocacy organization, End Sepsis , the year of his death.

In a recent interview, Ms. Staunton said she has spoken with the van der Werken family and that she was heartbroken to learn Finlay waited so long before being seen by a doctor.

Finlay and Rory’s deaths were preventable, she said.

“I think it’s about time Canada got their act together. What’s stopping them?”

The document also cites strong evidence that early identification and timely sepsis treatment improves patient outcomes, but that benefits can only be achieved when protocols are embedded in workflows and consistent.
Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said the provincial government is working to promote standardized practices and clinical awareness.

“As per the Minister’s direction, Ontario Health has convened an expert panel of leading clinicians to review currently established sepsis guidelines and opportunities for improvement,” she said in an e-mail.

Last October, the van der Werken family met with Ms. Jones to call for changes to how emergency care is delivered in Ontario, including standardized maximum ER wait times for vulnerable pediatric patients.

content_blocks.text: The circumstances of Finlay’s death will be the subject of a future discretionary coroner’s inquest , but a date has not been set.
content_blocks.html: The circumstances of Finlay’s death will be the subject of a future discretionary coroner’s inquest, but a date has not been set.

content_blocks.text: Ontario resident, Gurinder Sidhu, has also called for reforms to ensure early intervention and treatment of sepsis. He says his wife, Ravinder, with whom he has three children, developed postpartum sepsis that caused organ failure and led to her death in June, 2025.

content_blocks.text: Kassandra Costabile is also pushing for accountability following her sister’s death, which she believes was preventable. Rheanna Laderoute died in February, 2022, after showing signs of septic shock following an abortion.
content_blocks.html: Kassandra Costabile is also pushing for accountability following her sister’s death, which she believes was preventable. Rheanna Laderoute died in February, 2022, after showing signs of septic shock following an abortion.

content_blocks.text: Last October, Nova Scotia rolled out a provincewide approach that authorized emergency room nurses to administer antibiotics and IV fluids to anyone suspected of having sepsis.
The measure was applauded by advocates who want the approach expanded to other provinces and territories.
Nova Scotia’s changes were implemented following several prominent sepsis cases that resulted in legal action.

For its action plan, the provincial health authority drew lessons from NHS Scotland, the publicly funded health care system in that country, and the B.C. Sepsis Network, a clinician initiative in that province.

In New York State, sepsis detection regulations in place for the past 13 years have been credited with saving tens of thousands of lives . They include strict timelines for interventions, including early delivery of antibiotics.
content_blocks.html: In New York State, sepsis detection regulations in place for the past 13 years have been credited with saving tens of thousands of lives. They include strict timelines for interventions, including early delivery of antibiotics.

content_blocks.text: The measures, known as Rory’s Regulations, were put in place after the April 1, 2012, death of 12-year-old Rory Staunton, who had undiagnosed and untreated sepsis. His parents, Ciaran and Orlaith Staunton, founded the U.S. advocacy organization, End Sepsis , the year of his death.

His parents, Ciaran and Orlaith Staunton, founded the U.S. advocacy organization, End Sepsis, the year of his death.

content_blocks.text: In a recent interview, Ms. Staunton said she has spoken with the van der Werken family and that she was heartbroken to learn Finlay waited so long before being seen by a doctor.
Finlay and Rory’s deaths were preventable, she said.
“I think it’s about time Canada got their act together. What’s stopping them?”

ByJacques Gallant Courts and Justice Reporter

Ontario’s patient ombudsman says stories of people being held in isolation for years at the province’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital are “deeply troubling,” as his office considers what actions it may take.

Craig Thompson has been “closely following” the Star’s investigation into the use of long-term seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene, said a statement from his office.

“The patient experiences being shared are deeply troubling. All patients should receive safe and appropriate mental health care consistent with recognized, evidence-informed approaches,” said the statement.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Image 10Image 11Image 12Image 13

“We are always assessing what actions the office may take that are consistent with our legislative mandate. To maintain the integrity of our investigations, we do not generally comment on current or potential investigations.”

Should Thompson launch an investigation, it wouldn’t be the first.

Jake Gordon is being released from seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care. His mom credits the Star’s investigation for the change.

Concerns about prolonged isolation were being flagged more than 40 years ago at Waypoint’s predecessor facility, the Star has learned. That year, an outside expert panel found that putting a patient in seclusion beyond even 24 hours should be treated as an “extraordinary” event.

The “excessive” use of seclusion is “blatantly unethical as well as untherapeutic,” said a report prepared at the time for the Ministry of Health.

The patient ombudsman — an independent office that takes patient complaints about Ontario health institutions— can commence an investigation based on a complaint or on its own initiative, but the probe is done behind closed doors and usually only the findings and recommendations are released to the public.

Lawyer Anita Szigeti, an expert on mental health law who has several clients in seclusion at Waypoint and who has written to Thompson directly, said she was pleased with his response, while reiterating that there still needs to be an independent and public investigation.

“It signals to me that the issue is on their radar,” she said of the patient ombudsman. “They’re following it, and they’re thoughtfully considering what they can do.”

The Star’s investigation has revealed that Waypoint is keeping seriously mentally ill patients in seclusion for years — 20 years and counting in the case of Camelott Hamblett— despite its own policy stipulating that seclusion should be the option of last resort to deal with a patient who poses an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others. It’s also supposed to be used for as brief a time as possible.

Leading experts have described the hospital’s practice as “egregious,” “abusive,” unlike anything seen in other North American hospitals, and akin to torture.

Seclusion means locking a psychiatric patient up alone in a room.

Waypoint policies say it's a last resort, to be used for as brief a time as possible, with a patient who poses an imminent risk.

Waypoint has been keeping some patients in seclusion for years on end; forCamelott Hamblett, it's been 20 years.

Leading experts have described Waypoint's practices as “abusive” and unlike anything seen in other North American facilities.

Waypoint says it is following a set of best practices called the Six Core Strategies to reduce seclusion.[](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/ontario-hospital-ceo-says-shes-adopted-the-best-strategies-to-end-years-long-patient-isolation-thats-clearly-not-true-the-strategies-creators-say/article_b5aabff7-c847-4b09-8985-09cfd3a5fbdf.html "https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/ontario-hospital-ceo-says-shes-adopted-the-best-strategies-to-end-years-long-patient-isolation-thats-clearly-not-true-the-strategies-creators-say/article_b5aabff7-c847-4b09-8985-09cfd3a5fbdf.html")

The first of the six says the hospital CEO must be directly involved in the day-to-day use of seclusion.

Waypoint CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji has told the Star she will not do that, saying it would be inappropriate.

Warnings about “unethical” long-term seclusion at Waypoint and its predecessor, Oak Ridge, go back to at least 1984.

In 2019, a former Waypoint psychiatrist warned the Ford government the hospital's practices are "horrific" — but the Ministry of Health took no further action.

An independent report in the case of Andrew Azevedo found patients are being kept in conditionsakin to the UN definition of torture.

That assessment also found the hospital routinely does not meet its own standards, including failing to give secluded patients two hours outside their rooms each day.

Waypoint has refused to divulge how many patients are in long-term seclusion.

More than 40 years before the latest controversy, a panel made up of outside psychiatrists, lawyers and other experts were tasked with conducting a review of the operations at Oak Ridge, the maximum-security division of what was then the Penetanguishene Mental Health Centre. Oak Ridge was later demolished, and the current facility on the site was renamed Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in 2011.

The probe in 1984 was sparked by concerns about staffing levels, the provision of therapeutic services and patients complaining their rights were being violated. The panel, chaired by forensic psychiatrist Dr. Stephen Hucker, provided dozens of recommendations.

The panel’s report is found within thousands of pages filed as part of a proposed class-action lawsuit against Waypoint by Toronto firm Rochon Genova. The courts declined to certify the matter as a class-action, finding that seclusion is an individualized process and patients alleging wrongdoing would have to bring individual claims.

The panel was alarmed to learn that patients in Oak Ridge’s behaviour therapy unit— which housed people exhibiting “dangerous behaviours”— were sometimes being secluded for days.

Patients inside a hallway at the old Oak Ridge maximum-security facility in a 1987 file photo.

Frank Lennon/Toronto Star

The panel learned that a patient could be secluded for five days for: fighting or trying to fight with staff, possessing a dangerous weapon or making a serious escape attempt. Three days of seclusion could be ordered if the patient was hoarding medication, destroying property or trying to fight with another patient. It was unclear to the panel why assaulting a patient could get someone less time in seclusion than for assaulting a staff member.

“Seclusion for such long periods is extremely hard to justify,” says the panel’s report. “It is questionable whether the lengthy periods of seclusion are more effective as behavioural modifiers than shorter periods.”

The panel said it was “strongly of the view” that a 24-hour period in seclusion should be the “absolute outer limit” based on “what is fair, reasonable, and humane.”

Seclusion beyond 24 hours “might be possible only under extraordinary circumstances,” the panel said, but recommended that it only be done with the approval of the hospital administrator, who should also review all instances of seclusion throughout Oak Ridge at least monthly.

There’s no mention in the report about patients being secluded for years, as is the case now, more than 40 years later. Some of the report’s language mirrors the Six Core Strategies, the internationally recognized best practices to reduce the use of seclusion that Waypoint has said it is implementing, but the strategies’ creators believe otherwise.

The first strategy is that the CEO should be involved in daily seclusion decisions, but Waypoint CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji has told the Star that would be inappropriate, citing unspecified provincial legislation.

Many of the expert panel’s members have since died. Hucker, the chairperson, declined to comment, citing the passage of time.

Szigeti said that the patient ombudsman’s response is stronger “than anything we’ve heard from government or organizations with any oversight role.” And it calls into question what other bodies could be doing.

The class action documents also include a 2001 “snapshot” review of seclusion and restraint across the province, conducted by the Psychiatric Patient Advocate Office (PPAO), a branch of the Ministry of Health. The advocate office is meant to protect the rights of patients. It doesn’t have the power to change a doctor’s order, but it has local offices in all of Ontario’s psychiatric hospitals to help patients resolve concerns with hospital staff or find lawyers.

The office spoke with 44 patients in 2001 and 17 staff members, almost all nurses. Half of the patients indicated there had been no confrontation with another person before they were secluded or restrained, and they were unaware of what was required of them to be released. A physician assessed the patient in person prior to ordering seclusion or restraint in about half of the cases reviewed, while only a third of those orders specified a length of time.

The review proposed 23 “best practices,” emphasizing proactive planning,explaining to patients the specific behaviours required to be released from seclusion, and staff training in de-escalation techniques, crisis intervention, and supportive psychotherapy.

“Whereas the risks of seclusion and restraint have been well established, the benefits remain uncertain,” the review said, encouraging the hospitals to move toward “treatment in a restraint-free environment.”

Twenty-five years later, the PPAO declined to comment on the ongoing use of seclusion at Waypoint and whether the office plans to launch another review. An unsigned email from the office said to contact the Ministry of Health’s communications branch, which subsequently did not respond; the Ministry of Health has never responded to any of the Star’s questions regarding seclusion at Waypoint.

In 2001,the advocate office was described as an “arm’s-length program” of the ministry. Its website now says it is“part of” the ministry.

Szigeti said long-term seclusion is “exactly the kind of issue where I should think the PPAO would play a leadership role,”and so their silence is concerning, she said.

Questions have also been raised about whether the office is being kept in the dark about the number of patients in seclusion.An independent assessment prepared by corrections expert Andrea Monteiro in the case of Andrew Azevedo— who has been held in seclusion for five years at Waypoint— noted that his family said in May of this year that Waypoint had never told them about the existence of the advocate office.

Monteiro found no record in Azevedo’s file that Waypoint ever notified the PPAO when his seclusion was repeatedly extended.

This despite the fact that the PPAO told the ministry as far back as 2019 that Waypoint was notifying them when a patient was placed in seclusion, according to documents filed in the proposed class-action.The ministry was conducting a probe at the time after concerns about long-term isolation had been raised by two Waypoint psychiatrists. Ministry officials also spoke by phone to one Waypoint vice-president who assured them there were policies in place to reduce people's time in seclusion.

The ministry officials concluded that the concerns about seclusion were not corroborated based on the information they received from Waypoint— information that was “supported by the PPAO,” says a memo to then-assistant deputy health minister Tim Hadwen in April 2019.

“It appears that Waypoint has policies and procedures in place to support quality clinical care and oversight,” the memo states. “No further action is needed.”

stories.title: Family remembers Darius MacDougall one year after disappearance
stories.summary: A year after his disappearance, the family of Darius MacDougall still returns to the campsite where he was last seen, hoping answers will one day come to light.
stories.author: Justin Sibbet
stories.content:
On Sept. 21, 2025, six-year-old Darius MacDougall vanished from a public camping area near the Alberta-British Columbia border in the Crowsnest Pass.

Almost at once, police, search and rescue crews and other first responders began a full-scale search of the mountainous terrain in an effort to find Darius.

Now, one year later, with no answers, Darius’ family has returned to that camping spot, holding out hope that he is still out there, somewhere.

“Darius, we still love you, miss you. We’re never going to stop searching for you, buddy,” said Leslie Tallmadge, Darius’ grandfather. “I come here and I walk and I look, (I’d) look anywhere for you.”

The search effort was extensive, with drones, dogs, helicopters and hundreds of crew members, including specialized teams such as underwater divers, all taking part in the hopes of finding Darius.

After more than a week, RCMP called the search off.

On Monday, one year after Darius went missing, officers released a statement saying they haven’t stopped their investigation.

“The Alberta RCMP recognizes that Darius’ disappearance continues to weigh heavily on his family and those who know and love him. The passage of time does not lessen the importance of finding answers, and investigators remain committed to pursuing information that may help bring clarity to what happened to Darius.”

They say investigators remain focused on reviewing information, pursuing viable leads and identifying any information that may help provide answers about Darius’ disappearance.

“To date, RCMP has received just over 70 tips from the public regarding this investigation, and every tip was fully investigated. Unfortunately, none have led to finding Darius. However, we will continue to investigate.”

For Darius’ family, the concern is that he was never lost in the mountains, but kidnapped instead.

“Somebody had to have taken him. There’s just been too many people out here, too many searches not to find anything. To me, somebody as come and taken him,” said Tina Herron, Darius’ grandmother.

Tallmadge agrees, believing search crews exhausting all efforts should have yielded results.

“11 days straight with 200 plus searchers every day — there’s no way we missed anything,” said Tallmadge.

At the time, RCMP said there was no evidence of a kidnapping and an Amber Alert was never issued, something that has never sat well with Herron.

“No matter who it is, it’s a child. They should have an Amber Alert, whether it meets the criteria or not, he should have it.”

A few days after Darius went missing, a Change.org petition was started to change how Amber Alerts are issued.

As of Monday, it has more than 20,000 signatures.

Darius would be seven years old now and his family is still urging anyone with any information to contact RCMP.

“If you see something or you know something, call the police. He’s out there somewhere. If you see him, call the police,” said Tallmadge.

RCMP have the same public message.

“The Alberta RCMP continues to encourage anyone who may have information about Darius’ disappearance or whereabouts to come forward. You can contact the Crowsnest Pass RCMP at 403-562-2866. Information that may seem insignificant could be important to the investigation, and investigators will assess any new information provided.”

On Tuesday evening, a candlelight vigil will be held at Lethbridge City Hall to bring greater awareness to the ongoing search efforts for Darius MacDougall.

stories.title: RCMP has pulled resources from Air India bombing investigation, victims’ families say
stories.summary: Only one person was ever convicted in connection with the 1985 terrorist attack, which remains the deadliest in Canadian history
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
The head of the group that represents the families of the victims of the 1985 Air India bombing says the RCMP has pulled back resources dedicated to investigating the deadliest terrorist attack in Canadian history.

Deepak Khandelwal, whose two siblings, Chandra and Manju, died in the bombing, said the RCMP told victims’ families in a Sept. 12 meeting in Toronto that investigators had exhausted all angles, and the investigation is considered “inactive.”

Only one person was ever convicted in connection with the bombing, bomb maker Inderjit Singh Reyat, who pleaded guilty to manslaughter in 2003. Trials for two British Columbia men allegedly tied to the explosion ended in acquittals.

Mr. Khandelwal said in an interview that he is “disappointed, angry, upset.”

“But not surprised, because they have let us down for 41 years, and this is just the next step in it.”

Federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said in a statement to The Globe and Mail that the RCMP have told Ottawa that the investigation “remains open.”

“This is not a closed matter. Should new, credible information or evidence come forward, it will be assessed and investigated and may lead to further investigative steps,” Mr. Anandasangaree said. His office did not immediately respond to follow-up questions asking for specifics on what resources remain actively committed to the investigation.

The RCMP did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Khandelwal was a first-year university student from Saskatoon when he flew across the Atlantic with his father to identify the bodies of his older sisters. He is now head of the Air India Flight 182 Victims Families Association. “They don’t close a file, but inactive means there’s no resources assigned to it,” he said of the RCMP.

Since the meeting with police earlier this month, families of some victims have sent letters to Prime Minister Mark Carney and the RCMP accusing investigators of failing to look into every possibility.

Sudha Berry, whose 16-year-old brother was killed on the flight, wrote in her letter to Mr. Carney and the RCMP that the trust victims’ families placed in Canadian institutions has been “betrayed repeatedly.”

“While we acknowledge that there are many activities that you undertake that we will never be aware of and that there are many dedicated officers who have devoted their careers to the investigation, the fact remains that the results have been less than satisfactory,” Ms. Berry wrote.

It has been more than 41 years since Air India Flight 182 departed Montreal’s international airport en route to Delhi and was destroyed by a bomb in midair as it flew near the coast of Ireland. All 329 passengers, most of them Canadian, were killed in the June 23, 1985, bombing.

Authorities believe Sikh extremists fighting for independence from India planted the bomb on the plane, which crashed in the Atlantic Ocean near Ireland’s southern coast.

A public inquiry into the subsequent investigation found “a cascading series of errors” by the RCMP, CSIS and the federal government, according to the inquiry’s 2010 final report.

Recently, families of victims have been waiting for Ottawa to release the scattered pieces of airplane fuselage from storage in B.C., held under lock-and-key because of the investigation.

Many of the families living in Canada have received the belongings of victims that were collected in the wreckage, Mr. Khandelwal said. But only some of the families in the U.S. and India have received the belongings of their loved ones, he said.

Mr. Khandelwal said he and the families were blindsided by the RCMP’s decision. The RCMP’s invitation to the Sept. 12 meeting, reviewed by The Globe, said it would be providing an update on the status of the investigation, “including an outline of future steps.”

The RCMP’s communication with families in recent years has slowed to a drip, Mr. Khandelwal said.

He said families requested a meeting with RCMP investigators in June 2025 when, days before the attack’s 40th anniversary, Mounties told media that a suspect known as “Mr. X” had died before facing charges . RCMP said the individual was believed to have helped test a bomb before the attack.

Mr. Khandelwal said families learned of the revelations through media reports and requested a meeting shortly after. He said the meeting didn’t happen until the RCMP summoned families for the update earlier this month in Toronto.

His message to the RCMP is simple: continue the investigation.

“I just think they need to keep the investigation going. They need to be transparent with the family members in whatever confidential way, and they have to commit to being a little bit more regular in communicating with families,” he said.

stories.title: BC Conservatives regroup as several ex-MLAs return to caucus in wake of leader’s resignation
stories.summary: Opposition party attempts to bolster its ranks ahead of possible snap election
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Some dissident MLAs are rejoining the BC Conservatives as the province’s Opposition attempts to bolster its ranks ahead of a possible snap election and just a day after its leader resigned.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s announcement Sunday that she was stepping down as leader because of “infighting” prompted the return of some party members who had left the caucus over her leadership. On Monday, the party announced that Scott McInnis, Trevor Halford, Claire Rattée, John Rustad and Linda Hepner are once again Conservatives.

Speculation that NDP Premier David Eby would call an election two years early dramatically ramped up last week. Mr. Eby has said he has warned Elections BC and his caucus to be “election ready” amid disruptions posed by the U.S. trade war.

His government has made a flurry of announcements in recent days, including last week pausing an expansion to the provincial sales tax and on Monday reversing an earlier halt to long-promised expanded services at Burnaby Hospital.

On Monday, Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim urged the NDP government not to call an early vote until after provincewide municipal elections on Oct. 17, which he said deserve the “full, undivided attention” of residents.

Mr. Rustad, who returned to the Conservatives Monday after being expelled from caucus last Friday, said they have had unity talks with CentreBC, a party of eight MLAs who were formerly Conservatives. He himself is a long-time MLA who led the Conservatives from a fringe party to within a hair of winning the previous provincial election in 2024 before being ousted as leader.

“The province cannot afford two opposition parties while [Premier] David Eby measures the timing of an election,” he said in a news release.

He stated the chances of a merger are high, but neither the Conservatives nor CentreBC would confirm any efforts to coalesce centre-right politicians into one party.

Mr. Rustad said he would not impose his vision on the renewed party, and he advised former BC Liberal premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell to follow his example. He identified both of them as among the ”players" trying to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and said they should realize that “their time is over.”

The caucus of B.C.’s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election after Ms. Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of the vote happening while the Opposition has no permanent leader.

Mr. Rustad said he accepted an offer to rejoin the Conservatives because he believes in Lorne Doerkson, their new interim leader. Mr. Doerkson was first elected to represent a riding in the Interior in 2020 for the BC Liberal Party, which later rebranded itself as BC United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives and was re-elected in 2024.

Mr. Doerkson is expected to speak to reporters for his first time as party leader on Tuesday.

Ms. Findlay said Sunday that she would remain the Conservative candidate for a by-election this Saturday in Abbotsford-Mission. But a snap provincial election called before then would override that.

Her resignation as leader followed weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, with the defection or expulsion of 13 MLAs, including Mr. Rustad.

He said Monday that he asked Ms. Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”

The next day, he said, he got a text from her expelling him, but 15 minutes later that was rescinded. On Friday, he was once again told he was out.

Ms. Findlay’s departure prompted the NDP caucus to meet on Sunday night, according to an e-mail from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators on Sunday, instead of just those on the government benches.

“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the e-mail obtained by The Canadian Press said.

The message said the meeting was to “discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Mr. Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

In a question-and-answer period with Union of BC Municipalities conference delegates after Mr. Eby’s keynote address last week, the Premier ducked questions about an early election call.

Conference delegates on Wednesday had passed an emergency resolution urging Mr. Eby to hold off on calling an election until after October’s municipal votes, to avoid interfering with local campaigns.

Mr. Eby told the crowd he understood the anxiety that duelling elections could create and that he would take the resolution and its concerns seriously.

B.C. Attorney-General Niki Sharma was asked at an unrelated news conference Monday whether it was ethical to call an election with the Opposition in such disarray. She declined to answer the question directly after being asked twice.

“If the Premier decided to do an election call, he will do so by recommending that to the Lieutenant-Governor in accordance with our Constitution and all the laws,” she said.

Ross Pink, a professor of political science at Kwantlen Polytechnic University, said the Opposition should appoint a new leader as soon as possible, adding campaign debates have frequently catapulted lesser-known political leaders toward wider electoral victories.

The professor, who has run a mentorship program for the past five years pairing Kwantlen students with provincial and federal politicians for four-month stints, said Mr. Eby’s election calculus could reap huge rewards or backfire immensely.

“Politics really is always about opportunity and timing,” Prof. Pink said.

With a report from The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: The caucus of B.C.’s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election after Ms. Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of the vote happening while the Opposition has no permanent leader.

Mr. Rustad said he accepted an offer to rejoin the Conservatives because he believes in Lorne Doerkson, their new interim leader. Mr. Doerkson was first elected to represent a riding in the Interior in 2020 for the BC Liberal Party, which later rebranded itself as BC United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives and was re-elected in 2024.
Mr. Doerkson is expected to speak to reporters for his first time as party leader on Tuesday.
Ms. Findlay said Sunday that she would remain the Conservative candidate for a by-election this Saturday in Abbotsford-Mission. But a snap provincial election called before then would override that.
content_blocks.html: Ms. Findlay said Sunday that she would remain the Conservative candidate for a by-election this Saturday in Abbotsford-Mission. But a snap provincial election called before then would override that.

content_blocks.text: Her resignation as leader followed weeks of upheaval in the Conservative caucus, with the defection or expulsion of 13 MLAs, including Mr. Rustad.
He said Monday that he asked Ms. Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”
The next day, he said, he got a text from her expelling him, but 15 minutes later that was rescinded. On Friday, he was once again told he was out.

Ms. Findlay’s departure prompted the NDP caucus to meet on Sunday night, according to an e-mail from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators on Sunday, instead of just those on the government benches.
“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the e-mail obtained by The Canadian Press said.

The message said the meeting was to “discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Mr. Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.
In a question-and-answer period with Union of BC Municipalities conference delegates after Mr. Eby’s keynote address last week, the Premier ducked questions about an early election call.

Conference delegates on Wednesday had passed an emergency resolution urging Mr. Eby to hold off on calling an election until after October’s municipal votes, to avoid interfering with local campaigns.
Mr. Eby told the crowd he understood the anxiety that duelling elections could create and that he would take the resolution and its concerns seriously.

B.C. Attorney-General Niki Sharma was asked at an unrelated news conference Monday whether it was ethical to call an election with the Opposition in such disarray. She declined to answer the question directly after being asked twice.
“If the Premier decided to do an election call, he will do so by recommending that to the Lieutenant-Governor in accordance with our Constitution and all the laws,” she said.

Ross Pink, a professor of political science at Kwantlen Polytechnic University, said the Opposition should appoint a new leader as soon as possible, adding campaign debates have frequently catapulted lesser-known political leaders toward wider electoral victories.

The professor, who has run a mentorship program for the past five years pairing Kwantlen students with provincial and federal politicians for four-month stints, said Mr. Eby’s election calculus could reap huge rewards or backfire immensely.
“Politics really is always about opportunity and timing,” Prof. Pink said.

stories.title: Ontario to standardize trucker training after audit flagged widespread issues
stories.summary: Large trucks accounted for 12 per cent of all fatal collisions between 2019 and 2023, according to Auditor-General’s report
stories.author: Sara Mojtehedzadeh
stories.content:
The Ontario government says it will standardize commercial truck driver training in the wake of a scathing Auditor-General report that identified widespread issues with instruction and licensing in the province.

Ontario will work with industry stakeholders to develop a new curriculum aimed at strengthening road safety, Minister of Transportation Prabmeet Sarkaria said on Monday. But some representatives of the trucking industry say additional measures are required to address their concerns with training and oversight of commercial truck drivers.

The announcement follows a May report from provincial Auditor-General Shelley Spence, which found some private career colleges in Ontario were accrediting drivers without the minimum training requirements, and in some cases had altered student records to falsify their qualifications.

Currently, aspiring commercial truck drivers in Ontario must complete mandatory entry-level training, which consists of a minimum of 103.5 hours of instruction. Private career colleges must submit their curriculum details for approval to the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security to ensure they meet provincial standards.

The Transport Ministry said that under the new approach schools will be required to follow a standardized curriculum that will include “more than 103 hours of clear, robust and consistent training.” The plan is expected to be implemented by early 2027, after consultation with industry stakeholders.

While large trucks represent about 3 per cent of all vehicles on provincial roads, they accounted for 12 per cent of all fatal collisions between 2019 and 2023, Ms. Spence’s report noted. Truck driver violations in Ontario have also spiked in recent years. For example, between 2020 and 2024, the percentage of truck drivers found in violation of rules requiring them to keep daily vehicle inspection logs increased by 135 per cent.

It is not clear how the new curriculum proposals will differ from the province’s existing practices, but the province said it is considering additional training subjects such as fatigue management and rural driving.

Rolf VanderZwaag, one of the architects of Ontario’s mandatory entry-level training standards, which were implemented in 2017, said the essential driving skills program he helped develop is “effectively a standardized curriculum.”

“Most Ontario schools already use it,” said Mr. VanderZwaag, who is the CEO of Techni-Com Inc., which produces compliance and training products for the trucking industry.

Mike Millian, president of the Private Motor Truck Council of Canada, a national association representing companies with in-house commercial trucking fleets, said any improvement in training standards are welcome.

However, additional reforms are urgently needed to address industry’s concerns around training and oversight, he said.

“Having a standardized curriculum is not what our key issue is. Our key issue is people aren’t following the curriculums that they’re submitting,” he said.

Around one quarter of the 216 private colleges offering truck driver training in the province had never been inspected by the provincial colleges ministry, the report found – noting the ministry employed just eight inspectors to audit all 595 private colleges in Ontario.

As part of the research conducted for the May report, Ms. Spence’s office sent students undercover to five unnamed private colleges and found that some students were not taught the required elements of truck driving, including reverse parking and emergency stopping.

As previously reported by The Globe, industry groups have called on the province to overhaul training and licensing procedures, and for the Transport Ministry to take full carriage of the file from the Ministry of Colleges and Universities.

The Private Motor Truck Council of Canada has called for more inspections at private career colleges and heftier fines for those who fail to meet provincial training standards for truck drivers.

Currently, private career colleges face fines of between $250 and $1,000 for first offences, according to the Auditor-General report.

In its statement Monday, the Transport Ministry said it was introducing a dedicated integrity manager for truck driver testing across the province and weekly reviews of commercial driver training schools.

The Professional Truck Training Alliance of Canada (PTTAC), which advocates for progress in education and training in the transportation sector, has also called for numerous reforms, including stricter screening of aspiring drivers’ criminal record and driver abstracts. The organization has also advocated for testing instructors to be equipped with body cameras as a fraud prevention tactic, and has called for dual-facing cameras to be required in training vehicles.

“We want to continue to see improvement, but at the end of the day, regulation and compliance without any enforcement falls on deaf ears,” said Kim Richardson, a senior adviser to PTTAC.

The Private Motor Truck Council’s Mr. Millian said any improvements to the provincial curriculum must include more one-on-one training time for drivers.

“The key area that we see as an issue in the industry is people’s ability to back up the vehicle and operate the truck safely up and down the highway,” he said.

After completing entry-level training, aspiring drivers must take road exams at DriveTest centres. These are run by a third-party provider, Serco, for the Transport Ministry.

As previously reported by The Globe, five employees of driver-licensing centres in Ontario were also charged earlier this year with allegedly accepting bribes to manipulate the results of commercial truck-driving tests.

Mr. Millian says Serco’s Brampton, Ont. testing campus already employs two integrity officers to prevent cheating on road tests.

“We have seen some increases in enforcement, which is welcome,” he said. “But we need to go further.”
