stories.title: Fourth Marineland whale dies after relocation, third at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago
stories.summary: A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health after arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday. The park said 26-year-old Osiris died Monday morning. The female beluga was one of 10 that came to Shedd from Marineland, the shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, […]
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Posted September 21, 2026 10:16 pm.

A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health after arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday.

The park said 26-year-old Osiris died Monday morning. The female beluga was one of 10 that came to Shedd from Marineland, the shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont.

It was part of the world’s biggest collective move of captive whales.Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its animals.

Over a series of moves beginning in July,Marineland moved 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums abroad: Shedd in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio and San Diego, Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.

Osiris was “not a consistent eater” but had improved recently after receiving fluids and medication, Shedd said.

“Our care team observed sudden changes this morning in both Osiris’s behaviour and respiratory patterns,” Shedd said in a statement.

“Respiratory rates are one of many measures we track closely and continuously, as changes can signal that an animal May need additional support. The team moved Osiris to the medical habitat, so immediate care could be provided if needed. Her condition declined rapidly, and Osiris passed away despite lifesaving efforts by our veterinary and animal care teams.”

The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.

Two other Marineland whales, Rain and Peekachu, died at Shedd within weeks of the move. One longtime Shedd resident beluga, Beethoven, also recently died.

All are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.

Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic last week.

The whales were cleared by veterinarians at Marineland and the other parks to move and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also signed off on the relocation.

Last week, Shedd said it is concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord.

“Secord has not yet been consistently taking in the amount of food teams would like to see, even as they try different feeding approaches and offer different types of herring to gauge her preference,” Shedd said in a blog post last week.

Marineland originally sought to move the whales to China after securing a deal to sell all 30 of its belugas to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, which has a Guinness Book of World Record for the largest aquarium in the world.

Thompson blocked that move, saying it was not in the best interest of the whales and inconsistent with a 2019 federal law. That law banned whale and dolphin captivity, but grandfathered in Marineland’s whales. It also banned breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its whales by sex. And the law banned performances.

Marineland turned to an American-led consortium to house the world’s biggest pod of captive belugas, but they needed five aquariums to house them all.

There are no breeding or performing restrictions at belugas’ new homes.

Marineland’s whales had struggled in recent years. Nineteen belugas and one killer whale died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

The park blames some of those deaths on the new federal laws.

Sources have said Marineland, which is about a kilometre from Horseshoe Falls, has been sold on the condition that all animals are gone.

Several hundred deer remain.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Over a series of moves beginning in July,Marineland moved 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums abroad: Shedd in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio and San Diego, Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.
Osiris was “not a consistent eater” but had improved recently after receiving fluids and medication, Shedd said.
“Our care team observed sudden changes this morning in both Osiris’s behaviour and respiratory patterns,” Shedd said in a statement.

“Respiratory rates are one of many measures we track closely and continuously, as changes can signal that an animal May need additional support. The team moved Osiris to the medical habitat, so immediate care could be provided if needed. Her condition declined rapidly, and Osiris passed away despite lifesaving efforts by our veterinary and animal care teams.”
The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.
Two other Marineland whales, Rain and Peekachu, died at Shedd within weeks of the move. One longtime Shedd resident beluga, Beethoven, also recently died.
All are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.
Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic last week.
The whales were cleared by veterinarians at Marineland and the other parks to move and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also signed off on the relocation.
Last week, Shedd said it is concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord.

“Secord has not yet been consistently taking in the amount of food teams would like to see, even as they try different feeding approaches and offer different types of herring to gauge her preference,” Shedd said in a blog post last week.

Marineland originally sought to move the whales to China after securing a deal to sell all 30 of its belugas to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, which has a Guinness Book of World Record for the largest aquarium in the world.

Thompson blocked that move, saying it was not in the best interest of the whales and inconsistent with a 2019 federal law. That law banned whale and dolphin captivity, but grandfathered in Marineland’s whales. It also banned breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its whales by sex. And the law banned performances.
Marineland turned to an American-led consortium to house the world’s biggest pod of captive belugas, but they needed five aquariums to house them all.
There are no breeding or performing restrictions at belugas’ new homes.
Marineland’s whales had struggled in recent years. Nineteen belugas and one killer whale died at the park between 2019 and 2025.
The park blames some of those deaths on the new federal laws.
Sources have said Marineland, which is about a kilometre from Horseshoe Falls, has been sold on the condition that all animals are gone.
Several hundred deer remain.

stories.title: After Belleville, Ont., shooting, a look at recent violent incidents near synagogues
stories.summary: Ontario’s police watchdog is investigating after a 29-year-old man allegedly opened fire at a constable stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday night. The resulting shootout left both the suspect and the officer with serious injuries and sparked widespread condemnation from political leaders. Police have declined to comment on a possibl…
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s police watchdog is investigating after a 29-year-old man allegedly opened fire at a constable stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., ON Sunday night. The resulting shootout left both the suspect and the officer with serious injuries and sparked widespread condemnation from political leaders. Police have declined to comment on a possible motive in the attack.

Here are some other violent incidents that have taken place at or near Canadian synagogues and Jewish institutions in the last few years.

June 2026: Police are called for a fire at Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom in Westmount, Que., ON the island of Montreal. The synagogue’s rabbi said at the time the fire appeared to have been triggered by a Molotov cocktail tossed at a window. A 38-year-old man is arrested and was expected to face charges.

April and May 2026: A man in Toronto allegedly carries out two assaults against members of the Jewish community using a gel blaster imitation gun. One of the incidents takes place outside the Congregation Chasidei Bobov synagogue. The 18-year-old suspect is charged with assault with a weapon and possessing a weapon for a dangerous purpose.

March 2026: Two Toronto-area synagogues, the Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto synagogue in Vaughan, Ont., and Shaarei Shomayim synagogue in Toronto’s north end, are damaged by gunfire overnight. No injuries are reported. Over the following months, police arrest three suspects aged 17, 18 and 23 and charge them with several offences. York regional police said last month they are no longer seeking suspects, but the investigation is ongoing.

December 2024: A Montreal-area synagogue, Congregation Beth Tikvah in Dollard-des-Ormeaux, Que., is firebombed, causing minor damage to the building and the nearby offices of a Jewish community group. Months later, police arrest a 19-year-old man and charge him with arson and other offences.

December 2024: A Jewish girls’ school in Toronto’s north end is damaged in an overnight shooting. Police said the suspects were allegedly seen shooting from inside a vehicle before fleeing. They said Bais Chaya Mushka in North York had also been the target of two similar shootings in October and May of that year.

May 2024: The front door of the Schara Tzedeck synagogue in Vancouver is charred in an alleged arson. No one is injured.

May 2024: Bullet holes are found in the front of a Montreal building housing a Jewish school, Belz, and the Young Israel of Montreal synagogue.

November 2023: Montreal police find bullet holes in the door of the Yeshiva Gedola school and bullet casings on the ground. Police said a suspect had been seen firing a weapon at the school before taking off in a vehicle. A 20-year-old man is arrested months later and charged with offences including discharging a firearm and vehicle theft.

November 2023: The front door of the Congregation Beth Tikvah synagogue and the back door of the nearby Jewish organization Federation CJA office in a Montreal suburb are damaged in two overnight firebombings. The buildings were empty at the time.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Danielle Smith denies watering down government messaging on independence question
stories.summary: Alberta Premier disputes social media post by UCP president which claims she is trying to appear neutral
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Monday reiterated her position that the province should remain in Canada, even as her United Conservative Party grapples with an internal fight over separatism and a constituency association openly called for a leadership review.

On Monday, Ms. Smith disputed a social media post by UCP president Rob Smith, in which he claimed that she watered down the government’s messaging around the upcoming independence question in a bid to appear neutral.

On Oct. 19, Alberta voters will pick between two options: remain in Canada, or begin working toward holding a second, binding secession vote.

Ms. Smith made her comments days after the UCP’s Highwood constituency association – her former riding – voted to challenge her leadership, with one prominent separatist citing the Premier’s pro-Canada position as the motivating factor.

“The fact of the matter is, you always do have alternative voices in every political party. You’ve got to listen to them, you’ve got to respect them – but in the end, we make decisions based on the things that we can agree on,” Ms. Smith said at an unrelated news conference.

The Alberta premier told a virtual assembly discussing the province's future in Canada that a lot of Albertans are angry, but it would be a mistake to separate now that progress is being made with Prime Minister Mark Carney on Sept. 19.

The Canadian Press

The Premier referenced Alberta’s long-standing grievances with Ottawa, but stood by her support for a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada,” nodding to the UCP’s founding principles that pledged a commitment to the federation. At a public forum on separation over the weekend, Ms. Smith choked back tears while recounting a historic list of frustrations with Ottawa.

“I’m not a neutral party, and I believe that we should remain, and I believe that we should do everything we can to address the things that are causing grievances,” she said on Monday.

Support for separation in Alberta, estimated to be between 25 and 30 per cent, has remained steady for years. But a large segment of UCP members, pegged by some pollsters to make up about half the party’s membership, support independence.

The Highwood constituency association’s vote is the first time since becoming UCP Leader in 2022 that Ms. Smith has faced formal dissatisfaction over her leadership from within party ranks. At her last leadership review in November, 2024, Ms. Smith received 91 per cent support from party members.

A leadership review would only be triggered if at least 21 of the party’s 87 constituency associations vote for holding a special meeting on Ms. Smith’s future.

The Highwood association’s president, Helen Holder, also sits on the UCP provincial board as vice-president of fundraising. Ms. Holder declined to comment.

RJ Sigurdson, the party’s MLA for Highwood, pledged his support to Ms. Smith in an e-mailed statement, writing that the constituency association “does not reflect the views of my constituents broadly.”

Ms. Smith’s office did not respond to e-mailed questions, including whether the Premier feels it’s appropriate for Ms. Holder to remain on the party board.

UCP spokesperson Dave Prisco, in a statement, pointed to Ms. Smith’s 2024 leadership review and the party’s fundraising strength as evidence that most UCP members support her. Mr. Prisco did not address Ms. Holder’s involvement in the vote.

“You only see results like that when you have a strong leader with overwhelming support,” Mr. Prisco wrote.

Tanya Clemens, a leader with the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide and a Highwood UCP member, linked her endorsement of a leadership review to what she described as Ms. Smith’s “adversarial role” toward independence.

But her vote doesn’t mean she wants Ms. Smith “gone,” she said in a video posted to social media.

Divisions around separatism have wrought tensions within the UCP and, at times, put party leadership at odds with the Premier. On Monday night, UCP board members Samantha Steinke and Brad LaForge were scheduled to appear at a Calgary event with prominent separatist leaders Mitch Sylvestre, Jeffrey Rath and Cory Morgan. Neither Ms. Steinke nor Mr. LaForge responded to a request for comment.

Ms. Smith’s government has budgeted $4-million to advertise ahead of the referendum, prompting questions around fairness from both separatist and federalist groups hamstrung by strict spending limits.

Mr. Smith, the party president, attempted to address those concerns to party members over the weekend in a social media post where he claimed that the Premier “assured” him that the government’s advertising around the independence question would be “as NEUTRAL as possible.”

“I’ve heard some of these ads, and I believe what the Premier told me,” wrote Mr. Smith, who has no relation to the Premier.

Asked at the Monday news conference whether she told him the government would be neutral on the separation question, the Premier said: “That’s not true.”

The two have previously clashed over the UCP’s stance on separatism. In May, Mr. Smith told The Globe and Mail that the party would be neutral on the issue ahead of the referendum , and he believed the majority of UCP members will vote against remaining in Canada.

The next day, Ms. Smith said the party supports Alberta staying in Canada, saying she holds the final word on the UCP’s stance.

stories.title: Bear cub rescued from Okanagan Lake faces uncertain future
stories.summary: However, at an estimated 30 pounds, wildlife experts say the young bear faces significant challenges heading into winter with the odds of survival not in its favour.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik, Amy Judd
stories.content:
A dramatic rescue unfolded in the middle of Okanagan Lake when a family boating near Vernon came across a young bear struggling to stay afloat.

Christina Zamniuk and her family jumped into action after spotting the cub in the water on Saturday, Sept. 12.

“He was struggling to stay above the water,” Zamniuk said. “His little nose was going under, he was blowing bubbles, his back legs were not moving anymore.”

The family managed to get the bear onto their boat and safely out of the water.

They affectionately named the cub Boo Boo.

But what happened after the rescue has raised concerns for Zamniuk.

She says the family was surprised when conservation officers did not attend in person. Instead, they were advised over the phone to push the bear off the boat once they reached shore.

“They told us just to shove him off the boat. We didn’t want to do it,” Zamniuk said. “The fact that the conservation officers were just like, well, you know, we have to trap him, and we don’t know if we can do anything, and just let him go. He’ll be fine.”

Reluctantly, the family followed the advice and released Boo Boo near the shoreline.

The cub was seen heading into the woods.

However, at an estimated 30 pounds, wildlife experts say the young bear faces significant challenges heading into winter with the odds of survival not in its favour.

“Very slim,” said Angelika Langen of the Northern Lights Wildlife Society.

“There’s still some time for it to gain weight for the winter, but normally we say they should have at least 50 pounds. If it’s a small cub, 50 pounds can sustain them through hibernation. Thirty pounds will not be able to do that.”

The Northern Lights Wildlife Society has sent a team to the area where the cub was released near the Chief Saddlemen Road in the Parker Cove area off of Westside Road near Vernon.

They are hoping to capture it and bring it into shelter for the winter before releasing it.

When asked why conservation officers did not pick up the cub after it was rescued from the water, the ministry responsible said it wasn’t a public safety issue.

However, Zamniuk says she feels conflicted about pushing the bear cub off the boat and hoping he makes it on his own.

“I don’t know if that doesn’t sit that well with me,” she said.

“And I can’t stop thinking about him.”

stories.title: Major language school Ilac closes abruptly after filing for bankruptcy, stranding hundreds of students
stories.summary: Sudden shutdown leaves at least 1,362 students in limbo, with some at risk of losing thousands of dollars in prepaid fees and accommodations
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
When Berta Alonso received an e-mail on Friday from the International Language Academy of Canada telling her the school had filed for bankruptcy and was closing immediately, she figured she had been hacked.

The 18-year-old student from Barcelona was two weeks away from completing a marketing diploma at ILAC’s Vancouver campus. She couldn’t fathom that ILAC, one of the largest private language-instruction schools in the country, would file for bankruptcy and shutter without warning, stranding at least 1,362 students studying in Toronto and Vancouver. Some are at risk of losing accommodations and work permits tied to ILAC.

“Everybody thought that it was fake because it was, like, a crazy thing that no one expected,” Ms. Alonso said. “I was so scared and frustrated.”

The sudden closing of ILAC is the most recent fallout from the federal government’s U-turn on international student policy, even though many of ILAC’s students were in Canada on visitor’s visas, rather than study permits, according to Languages Canada. The organization represents private English and French language schools nationwide.

When the federal government began imposing restrictions on student visas and postgraduate work permits in early 2024, private schools that taught Canada’s two official languages to people from overseas saw demand dwindle. The number of students learning English or French as a second language at a private school has fallen nearly in half since 2019, down to 81,636 students last year from 150,112 in 2019, according to Languages Canada .

Less than a week before ILAC closed, EC English, an international language school with campuses in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, abruptly shut its doors as well. That closing affected 471 students across the country.

“Canada’s linguistic infrastructure is disappearing, and without it, we actually can’t build,” said Gonzalo Peralta, executive director of Languages Canada. “It should be part of the talent strategy for Canada’s future.”

Mr. Peralta said other language schools have closed since Ottawa reined in the international student program. It did so in response to public concerns that a surge in temporary residents had made housing, entry-level jobs and other resources harder for Canadians to access.

But previous shutdowns were orderly, he added. “What is really concerning right now is that we have these two large schools that have closed in a disorderly fashion, without assuming the responsibility for the students.”

Bankruptcy documents obtained by The Globe and Mail show ILAC had just over $1-million in cash on hand, plus $6.9-million in securities. The company had just over $135-million in liabilities when it filed for bankruptcy on Friday.

ILAC chief executive officer John DeFranco informed staff of the closing in a brief video call at 4:15 p.m. ET on Friday, according to a student-services worker who had been with the company for four years.

The Globe has agreed not to name the former employee because he hopes to keep working at language schools and fears that speaking out will hurt his career prospects.

Before their e-mail and internal messaging access was cut off, ILAC staff scrambled to share personal phone numbers with co-workers who had become like family, he said. Teachers who had developed curriculum rushed to print copies before the printers were shut off.

“Everybody who worked at ILAC did not know this was going to happen, and are horrified that it did,” he said, adding staff had just welcomed a fresh crop of overseas students to an ILAC high school in Toronto a few weeks ago. Friday was parent-teacher interview day.

Before the shutdown, ILAC ran traditional language classes in person and online, a diploma-granting career college and private high schools in Vancouver and Toronto. It also had long-standing partnerships, known as pathways programs , with dozens of publicly funded colleges and universities that helped students improve their French or English before starting postsecondary programs.

In 2019, ONCAP, the mid-market private equity platform of Onex Corp., acquired a majority stake in ILAC Education Group in partnership with ILAC’s founders and management.

One of those founders, Jonathan Kolber, wrote on LinkedIn on Monday that he left ILAC’s board a year and a half ago because of differences with the company’s new CEO.

He wrote that the closing was a surprise to everyone at ILAC, “and the hardest part is the sales team are being accused of knowing. Please know they were lied to until the last moment. They were promised ILAC would never go bankrupt. They were told to sell to clients right until the end.”

Mr. Kolber did not respond to an interview request.

Mr. DeFranco, the CEO of ILAC, told The Globe by e-mail: “Limits on international students mean fewer people can access the education and opportunities we were built to provide. We know how difficult this is for our students and staff. We are working closely with regulators to ensure students receive the support they need during this transition, and are doing everything we can to minimize impacts on our students, employees, and partners.”

Adam Shantz, a managing partner at ONCAP, added in a separate e-mailed statement that “sector-wide limits on admissions for international students have negatively impacted every language school in the country, including ILAC.”

Mr. Peralta said Languages Canada and its other member schools have promised to place every student whose education was disrupted by the EC Canada and ILAC closings in a Canadian language program as soon as possible at no charge.

But some students risk losing the thousands of dollars they paid to ILAC for accommodations and other services beyond tuition.

Annabel Wittan, a 19-year-old student from Berlin, said she paid ILAC about $11,000 for three months of English classes plus shared accommodations in residence in Burnaby, B.C. She moved in less than a week before receiving the same e-mail as Ms. Alonso informing her that ILAC was closing immediately.

“I have to move out or pay again because we don’t get the money back,” she said.

stories.title: London Airport offers sunny destinations for winter travellers, including stops in U.S. despite trade war
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/1HUUGAxpz08 As the seasons change and the temperature decreases, birds flying south for the w...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
As the seasons change and the temperature decreases, birds flying south for the winter will become a common sight for people in and around London. Some people even follow them down as well, flying off to somewhere warm and sunny to wait out the cold and return for the spring.

But for some, the choice of where they might go may have changed.

The London International Airport released its winter sun flight schedule on Friday, Sept. 18, featuring a large list of destinations including Cancun, Mexico, Orlando, Fla. and Montego Bay, Jamaica, as well as locales in the Dominican Republic, among others.

“We’ve been [to Jamaica] before and it’s a nice place,” said John Smith, a resident of Comox, B.C. who was flying out of London to Toronto. “We would like to go back.”

Janet Benoit from Calgary and Sarah Mann from Edmonton, respectively, both considered Mexico to be their destination of choice if they were to fly south for the winter.

The locations that Londoners wanted to go to weren’t the only ones on their mind. When asked about where they’d want to travel, Smith, Benoit and Mann all had the same answer, one that speaks to the larger ongoing trend of Canadian tourism to the United States declining because of the ongoing trade war: “Anywhere but the U.S.”

“I don’t feel safe leaving Canada going to the United States,” said Benoit, with Mann adding that she had stopped flights to the United States that she was supposed to be on.

A copy of the London Airport’s winter sun flight schedule. Airport staff expect all of the venues to be popular, even with the trade war causing a decline in Canada-U.S. tourism. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

The winter sun flight list has two American destinations on its list: Orlando and Fort Lauterdale, both in Fla.

“They’re both booked fully going and coming,” said ACE (Airport Comfort Enhancer) staff member Corinna Rogers, adding that every option on the winter flight schedule is equally popular. “I find it goes on right up until the very end.”

Rogers said that in her experience, flights to the United States out of London have declined on a casual basis, but that American holiday destinations still have things that travellers find appealing.

“Fort Lauterdale for the kids,” she said. “They like to go to Orlando, they want the beaches and stuff like that.”

Rogers also said that even while people may think about the trade war, they will take flights to the United States for the benefit of their friends and families.

Wendy Joanasie, a Londoner waiting on a flight to Toronto, cited Hawaii as her travel destination of choice.

“I haven’t thought about it, but if I was going to [fly south], I would go,” she said.

Ultimately, Rogers highlighted that the Orlando and Fort Lauterdale destinations are still just two of several options for Londoners to choose from.

“It just gives them an opportunity to make the decision for themselves.”

The flights are offered in partnership with with Porter Airlines, Air Transat, WestJet and Sunwing Vacations, and the travel destinations are:

Nine flights weekly to Cancun, Mexico

Three flights weekly to Orlando, Fla.

Four flights weekly to Fort Lauderdale, Fla.

Three flights weekly to Montego Bay, Jamaica

Two flights weekly to Punta Cana, Dominican Republic

Weekly service to Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic

Janet Benoit from Calgary and Sarah Mann from Edmonton, respectively, both considered Mexico to be their destination of choice if they were to fly south for the winter.

The locations that Londoners wanted to go to weren’t the only ones on their mind. When asked about where they’d want to travel, Smith, Benoit and Mann all had the same answer, one that speaks to the larger ongoing trend of Canadian tourism to the United States declining because of the ongoing trade war: “Anywhere but the U.S.”
“I don’t feel safe leaving Canada going to the United States,” said Benoit, with Mann adding that she had stopped flights to the United States that she was supposed to be on.

A copy of the London Airport’s winter sun flight schedule. Airport staff expect all of the venues to be popular, even with the trade war causing a decline in Canada-U.S. tourism. Photo by: Curtis Stokman
The winter sun flight list has two American destinations on its list: Orlando and Fort Lauterdale, both in Fla.

“They’re both booked fully going and coming,” said ACE (Airport Comfort Enhancer) staff member Corinna Rogers, adding that every option on the winter flight schedule is equally popular. “I find it goes on right up until the very end.”

Rogers said that in her experience, flights to the United States out of London have declined on a casual basis, but that American holiday destinations still have things that travellers find appealing.
“Fort Lauterdale for the kids,” she said. “They like to go to Orlando, they want the beaches and stuff like that.”
Rogers also said that even while people may think about the trade war, they will take flights to the United States for the benefit of their friends and families.
Wendy Joanasie, a Londoner waiting on a flight to Toronto, cited Hawaii as her travel destination of choice.
“I haven’t thought about it, but if I was going to [fly south], I would go,” she said.
Ultimately, Rogers highlighted that the Orlando and Fort Lauterdale destinations are still just two of several options for Londoners to choose from.
“It just gives them an opportunity to make the decision for themselves.”
The flights are offered in partnership with with Porter Airlines, Air Transat, WestJet and Sunwing Vacations, and the travel destinations are:
Nine flights weekly to Cancun, Mexico
Three flights weekly to Orlando, Fla.
Four flights weekly to Fort Lauderdale, Fla.
Three flights weekly to Montego Bay, Jamaica
Two flights weekly to Punta Cana, Dominican Republic
Weekly service to Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic

stories.title: Feds approve FortisBC's Tilbury LNG expansion under 'one project, one review'
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government has approved expansion of the Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C., saying potential adverse effects are justified by the project's benefits.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The federal government has approved expansion of the Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C., saying potential adverse effects are justified by the project’s benefits.

Sept. 21, 2026

DD[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/feds-approve-fortisbc-s-tilbury-lng-expansion-under-one-project-one-review/article_9df82a3f-1564-5b0f-b7cf-701c411382e1.html)

By The Canadian Press

Monday’s approval under the “one project, one review” principle came immediately after the B.C. government issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC for the project on Tilbury Island in the Fraser River.

The province says the project could generate 6,200 full-time-equivalent years of employment during construction and 100 permanent jobs, and contribute up to $1.7 billion to provincial GDP during construction.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Wheel It Studios: how a mobile recording studio is reshaping Toronto's music scene

Federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin says in a statement the project shows how to “create jobs and grow the economy while protecting the environment and advancing reconciliation.”

The project involves adding a large new storage tank and equipment to produce up to 7,700 tonnes of liquefied natural gas per day.

But it has faced opposition from within the B.C. government, with Kelly Greene, minister of emergency management and climate readiness, saying in July she was “disappointed” by FortisBC’s decision to move forward with the project, citing safety concerns.

“For months, I have listened to safety concerns from people in my community. I raised those issues with government at every opportunity. I am disappointed with FortisBC’s decision, as I know many of those I represent will be,” she said at the time.

Greene said her opposition had remained unchanged since before she was elected to the legislature, while NDP Premier David Eby said his government has a “big tent,” which allowed Greene to criticize the plan.

Federal Energy Minister Tim Hodgson called the approval “a step forward in our mission to get major nation-building projects built faster.”

“Today’s approval of the Tilbury Phase 2 LNG expansion project will power BC Ferries with cleaner fuel, strengthen Canada’s energy security and create economic opportunities for British Columbians,” he said on social media on Monday.

The B.C. government had touted the expansion as helping meet rising demand for LNG at the Port of Vancouver and improving access to fuel for vessels that travel the coast and across the Pacific.

The province said in a statement on Monday that the environmental assessment certificate included “18 legally binding conditions related to air quality, wildlife protection, greenhouse-gas reduction, health and emergency planning, and ongoing monitoring of impacts to First Nations.”

It said the Environmental Assessment Office sought consensus with 12 Indigenous nations, while 13 other Indigenous groups were informed of key milestones.

The assessment process was initiated in February 2020, but the province said it was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic, and FortisBC submitted a revised application in February 2026.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Forever Canadian officially becomes third-party advertiser in upcoming Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Forever Canadian will officially participate in the campaign as a third-party advertiser despite being registered as one with Elections Alberta since June.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Forever Canadian has announced it will shift direction with just weeks until Albertans head to the polls, and encourage voters to choose to remain in Canada, despite criticism that the group has been campaigning this entire time.

The group’s founder and former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk said Monday that Forever Canadian will pivot from promoting national unity to officially become a third-party advertiser to campaign for Alberta remaining in Canada.

“We will be imploring that every eligible voter votes in this particular election, and checks off option 1, that is option A, on question 10 for Alberta to remain in Canada,” Lukaszuk said.

Question 10 on the upcoming referendum ballot asks if Alberta should remain a province of Canada, or if the Government of Alberta should commence the legal process to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

The move comes as the group has been crisscrossing the province for more than than a year handing out more than 80,000 lawn signs and hosting events, including a weekend concert in Calgary to support Canadian unity.

Lukaszuk formed Forever Canadian in July 2025 to petition Albertans to remain in Canada, which gathered 404,293 verified signatures.

However, Lukaszuk has maintained he wanted MLAs to vote on the matter in the legislature rather than a referendum.

With weeks to go until Albertans head to the polls, Lukaszuk said the group had to “shift gears” due to concerns around voter apathy.

“This is not the time for complacency. Voter turnout is the most important thing at this time and we have learned what happens when voters are complacent,” he told reporters. “It is imperative during this most important vote, that I think any of us will participate in our lifetime, to not assume anything and come out and vote.”

To do that, Lukaszuk said, Forever Canadian must act as a third-party advertiser despite being registered as one with Elections Alberta since June 8.

2:07 Forever Canadian says books are clean as Danielle Smith questions 3rd-party finances

“The difference between what they have been doing and what they’re about to do is probably going to be difficult for most people to discern,” said Lori Williams, an associate professor of policy studies at Mount-Royal University in Calgary.

Third party advertisers are subject to stringent regulations like a $607,000 spending limit as well as weekly donation disclosures.

Lukaszuk told reporters Forever Canadian will be filing its financials “moving forward,” but not since it registered as a third-party advertiser.

Cory Morgan, who founded the pro-separation third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence, has accused Forever Canadian of not following the regulations since the campaign period began.

“Mr Lukaszuk has been playing pretty cute with the wordage of the legislation and definitely at the least has been violating the spirit of the legislation of disclosure and campaign limits throughout this thing,” Morgan told Global News. “Claiming he’s not campaigning while he has a campaign office, while he has a campaign bus and while he puts out campaign signs.”

According to Elections Alberta, Forever Canadian “had not engaged in referendum advertising,” which it said “must relate to a specific referendum question, must be advertising (meaning paid) and must attempt to persuade an elector to vote in a particular way with respect to that referendum question.”

Forever Canadian has raised $0 as of Sept. 17, according to the Elections Alberta website.

“We’ve gotta know how much did you raise and where did it come from because, let’s quit pretending, he’s been participating in a campaign for months,” Morgan said.

In an interview with Global News, Stephen Carter, the founder of Alberta’s Voice, welcomed Forever Canadian into the pro-federalist campaign.

However, Carter noted the importance that all third-party advertisers follow the regulations laid out in the legislation.

“We don’t want to give that excuse to Danielle Smith, the second that this campaign becomes something that wasn’t official or where the rules weren’t followed, it gives her the opportunity to open this door again and have another referendum,” Carter said.

According to Lukaszuk, Forever Canadian has complied with the legislation as the campaign “up to now was not a referendum campaign in the view of Elections Alberta.”

stories.title: Massive 30-foot basking shark stuns onlookers in Nova Scotia
stories.summary: A massive 30-foot basking shark, one of the world's largest fish, cruised among boats in Halifax's Bedford Basin Friday and Saturday, drawing crowds of astonished spectators.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
A rare visit from one of the ocean’s largest fish turned heads in Nova Scotia over the weekend, as a basking shark estimated to be about 30 feet long cruised among boats and drew dozens of onlookers to the waterfront in Halifax’s Bedford Basin.

Video shared on social media Friday and Saturday showed the massive shark swimming near the surface, its dorsal and tail fins breaking the water as it moved through the northwestern end of the Halifax harbour.

The sighting quickly became the talk of the area, attracting spectators to the Bedford Basin Yacht Club in hopes of catching a glimpse of the giant fish.

“As we were driving along the shoreline we saw a fin. I screamed ‘Shark!’ to the girls and we pulled over and we ran down to the dock to get a closer look,” said Christie Wisener, who witnessed the animal Friday evening.

Her daughter, Sydney Wisener, described the encounter as exciting. “It was splashing me. I was very excited to see it,” she told Global News.

David Hamilton, a member of the Bedford Basin Yacht Club, said he and his son went to the marina hoping to spot the shark after hearing reports about it. About 10 minutes after arriving, Hamilton said he noticed the animal’s large dorsal fin cutting through the water.

“All of a sudden we had 30 kids and adults at the end of the dock watching this shark swim around,” he said. “It was three or four feet away from us. It was pretty daunting to see something that large.”

Hamilton said the shark spent time weaving among boats in the marina. “It had come right up and it was doing loops,” he said. “And then you just see the thing come by, and it was super ominous as it just cruised by. There’s the head, there’s the dorsal fin, there’s the tail.”

Another witness, David Rankin, compared the animal to the famous shark from the movie Jaws . “The shark is so big-looking, like the mechanical shark in Jaws,” he said. “It almost seemed to want to play with us. It seemed like it knew we were there and kept coming in.”

2:06 Vancouver Island diver captures rare shark encounter

Despite its imposing size, experts say basking sharks pose no threat to humans.

“They’re a filter-feeder,” said Fred Whoriskey, a biology professor at Dalhousie University. “In many respects, you could consider them a gentle giant. There’s no reason to panic when you see one of these.”

The basking shark is the second-largest fish in the world, reaching lengths of up to 12 metres. It feeds on plankton and is commonly found along Atlantic Canada’s coastline during the summer months.

Tonya Wimmer, co-executive director and conservation director with the Marine Animal Response Society, said the organization received a call about the shark through its incident reporting hotline on Friday.

While basking sharks are native to Atlantic Canadian waters, she said seeing one so deep inside Bedford Basin is exceptionally rare.

“We certainly do get reports of basking sharks around Nova Scotia and even in some coastal areas, but in the very back of the Bedford Basin? That was a new one for us,” Wimmer said.

2:43 ‘I’ll be staying out the water’: Australian locals avoid water after 4 shark attacks in 2 days

Whoriskey said it is uncommon to find a basking shark inside a harbour and suggested the animal may have entered the area while searching for food or had become disoriented in shallow waters.

“My guess is that this is a very lost basking shark,” he said. “It somehow got itself into a constricted area and it is really confused and doesn’t know how to get out.”

Wimmer called the encounter a “pretty spectacular sight” and said it was encouraging to see people observing the shark from a safe distance. “It was great to see people were watching from shore, they were watching from the wharf and no one was in the water trying to approach,” she told Global News.

The Atlantic population of basking sharks has been listed as a species of special concern by the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada since 2009. Scientists say much remains unknown about the species, including where the sharks spend the winter after leaving coastal waters.

For many of the people who gathered along the basin this weekend, however, the encounter was simply a memorable reminder of the marine life found off Nova Scotia’s shores.

“It just made us really appreciate Nova Scotia and all that we have in this beautiful province and in our oceans here,” said Christie Wisener.

–with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Origin of destructive B.C. wildfire remains under investigation: police
stories.summary: Penticton - Police say they are continuing to work with wildfire personnel and others on a multi-agency investigation into the origin of the Bald Range fire, which destroyed or damaged about 150 properties in British Columbia's south Okanagan last month.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
PENTICTON - Police say they are continuing to work with wildfire personnel and others on a multi-agency investigation into the origin of the Bald Range fire, which destroyed or damaged about 150 properties in British Columbia’s south Okanagan last month.

Sept. 21, 2026

By The Canadian Press

RCMP in Penticton, B.C., issued a brief statement Monday saying members of the RCMP forensic identification section, wildfire personnel, the Office of the Fire Commissioner and others have completed an assessment of the area.

But the Mounties didn’t elaborate further, only saying the probe continues.

They say investigators are looking to speak with anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity or seen people or vehicles in the area of Princeton-Summerland Road and Bathville Road, including the Crump and Trout Creek recreation sites, around the time of the blaze that exploded within hours of its discovery on Aug. 7.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Police say they are particularly interested in reviewing any video footage or photographs captured in the area that afternoon and evening.

The Bald Range blaze forced some 20,000 people out of their homes as it raced toward Summerland, B.C., where it damaged or destroyed about 40 properties after razing about 110 structures in and around the small community of Faulder.

RCMP have said an 80-year-old woman died suddenly while she was fleeing her home west of Summerland, about 400 kilometres northeast of Vancouver.

The fire’s explosive growth prompted B.C. officials to declare a state of provincial emergency that lasted nearly three weeks, ending on Aug. 28.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

They say investigators are looking to speak with anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity or seen people or vehicles in the area of Princeton-Summerland Road and Bathville Road, including the Crump and Trout Creek recreation sites, around the time of the blaze that exploded within hours of its discovery on Aug. 7.

Police say they are particularly interested in reviewing any video footage or photographs captured in the area that afternoon and evening.

The Bald Range blaze forced some 20,000 people out of their homes as it raced toward Summerland, B.C., where it damaged or destroyed about 40 properties after razing about 110 structures in and around the small community of Faulder.
RCMP have said an 80-year-old woman died suddenly while she was fleeing her home west of Summerland, about 400 kilometres northeast of Vancouver.
The fire’s explosive growth prompted B.C. officials to declare a state of provincial emergency that lasted nearly three weeks, ending on Aug. 28.

stories.title: Popular hair product recalled across Canada
stories.summary: More than 90,000 units of Schwarzkopf Professional Osis Grip Mousse have been recalled in Canada over a packaging issue that could cause the container to burst.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
More than 90,000 units of a popular hair product have been recalled in Canada.

According to a Health Canada notice on September 21, the recall affects the 6.76-fluid-ounce (200-millilitre) Schwarzkopf Professional Osis Grip Mousse, sold between November 2023 and June 2026. The product was manufactured in Hungary.

The notice says the recalled product has packaging issues that can cause it to leak when the container is under pressure.

“The leakage and resulting pressure May cause the package to burst, which could result in injury or property damage,” it adds.

As of Sept. 18, the company had received one report of an incident in Canada, but Health Canada said there had been no reports of injuries.

The recall affects the following 25 batches:

2901x4577n, 2901x4578n, 290265p91o, 290665q30o, 290855n31o, 290866r38p, 290994281n, 291046l06p, 291174w17n, 291435h76o, 291435h77o, 291455n33o, 291515a59o, 291515a99o, 291515b01o, 291555n33o, 291615b01o, 291616b68p, 291716b69p, 291825e960, 291925e96o, 292015b73o, 2928y538bo, 2928y539bo and 293066u32p.

Consumers should immediately stop using the recalled product and return it to the place of purchase for a refund.

Consumers can also contact the company’s consumer support at skpcanada-support@henkel.com . Health Canada also advises consumers to report any health or safety incidents involving the product through its Consumer Product Incident Report Form .

The recall follows a similar action by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Aug. 11, where the product was distributed across 12 states.

stories.title: Five people fined for illegal shellfish harvesting on Vancouver Island
stories.summary: Campbell River - Five people have been fined a combined $19,000 after harvesting shellfish from a contaminated area on Vancouver Island.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Fisheries and Oceans Canada says officers were patrolling in late June when they came across people harvesting shellfish from an area in Campbell River, B.C., that was closed under the Canadian Shellfish Sanitation Program.

The department says shellfish harvested from closed areas can contain contaminants, bacteria, viruses or biotoxins that aren’t visible and can cause illness or death.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Wheel It Studios: how a mobile recording studio is reshaping Toronto's music scene

It says harvesting from those areas also puts the public at risk, threatens sustainable fisheries and disadvantages harvesters who comply with the law.

Besides being fined, three of the people were also convicted of licence violations and one of providing a false statement to a fishery officer.

The department says officers seized more than 130 Pacific oysters and some mussels and Manila clams, with all live shellfish returned to the harvest site.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

stories.title: How B.C. Conservatives went from 44 seats to a party in turmoil
stories.summary: Just two years ago, B.C.’s Conservatives appeared to be on the verge of taking power. Now, it's fighting for political survival after a damaging exodus.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – Just two years ago, B.C.’s Conservatives appeared to be on the verge of taking power.

John Rustad led the party to 44 seats in the 2024 provincial election, just three seats short of the Ndp’s 47 seat majority. It was the Conservatives’ strongest showing in decades, a coalition of moderates and the more socially conservative, moving the party from the political fringe into the province’s official opposition.

Now, the party is fighting for its political survival after a damaging exodus.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned as Conservative leader Sunday after less than four months on the job, following weeks of defections, expulsions and internal fighting that have divided the right.

MLA Lorne Doerkson was appointed interim leader Monday with Premier David Eby’s NDP poised to call an early election.

The turmoil is not simply the result of Findlay’s divisive leadership.

University of British Columbia political scientist Stewart Prest says the Conservatives are dealing with a deeper debate over what the party should actually represent.

“There is more that divides these two groups in many ways on some crucial questions than what brings them together,” Prest told CTV News Monday.

The Conservatives’ rise and the first cracks

The modern Conservative resurgence in B.C. began under Rustad, who joined the party in 2023 and helped turn it into the primary alternative to the NDP.

The party absorbed much of the vote that for decades went to the B.C. Liberals, who had unsuccessfully rebranded as B.C. United, then suspended its campaign during the 2024 election.

Leader Kevin Falcon urged supporters to back the Conservatives as several B.C. United MLAs crossed the floor to run for Rustad’s party.

Despite its stunning success, the patchwork Conservative caucus contained a wide range of political views and the tension became too difficult for Rustad to manage.

By December 2025, several Conservative MLAs had signed a letter calling for Rustad to resign. The party’s board attempted to remove Rustad after he initially refused to leave.

Rustad resigned the following day saying he wanted to avoid a civil war within the party.

Findlay takes the reins post-Rustad

The party chose Findlay as its new leader in May 2026, but just barely. She won after a four-round leadership contest, receiving 51 per cent of the vote.

Findlay appealed to the right, promising a government guided by faith, family, and freedom.

But the new leader quickly faced resistance from members of her caucus. Beginning in August, MLAs announced they were leaving, with several citing concerns about Findlay’s leadership and the direction of the party.

“She said it’s my way or the highway. And a lot of members of her caucus chose the highway,” said University of British Columbia political scientist Hamish Telford.

By the middle of September, a total of 13 MLAs had exited or been kicked out of caucus.

Eight of them joined CentreBC, a party formed in 2025 that is now being led by Kamloops Centre MLA Peter Milobar, who left the Conservatives in mid-August.

CentreBC is now the B.C. legislature’s third-largest party. Milobar has said it intends to run candidates in all 93 ridings if an early election is called.

The divide May be bigger than Findlay

In the wake of Findlay’s departure, politicians on both sides say the door is open to a dialogue on reuniting the right.

Prest describes the current Conservative movement as two distinct factions: a more centrist group represented by CentreBC and a Conservative Party that has moved further to the right.

For more moderate voters, he said, some of the positions associated with Findlay and her supporters May be difficult to reconcile with their own political views.

“It would take a special kind of politician to find a way to bring those two groups together,” Prest said.

Telford doesn’t see the two merging. “I think in the short term at least, we’re going to have sort of two centre-right parties, competing against each other. And that’s why the NDP wants to call this election and take advantage of it.”

That creates a new political problem for the right: voters who once had essentially one major alternative to the NDP could soon have two.

What is at stake for Eby

That division could have immediate consequences if Eby calls an election.

The premier has repeatedly said his government and Elections B.C. need to be ready for an election, while declining to announce when or if one will happen. The NDP currently holds a one-seat majority.

A provincial election would also overlap with B.C.’s municipal election campaign, which is already underway ahead of voting Oct. 17. Local government representatives have criticized the possibility of an early provincial vote.

For the Conservatives, an election would come with the party still led on an interim basis and without a permanent leader.

For that reason, Telford says an election call could be seen as dirty pool. “There’s long been a sort of a gentlemen’s understanding or agreement in Canadian politics that you don’t call an election when the official opposition party is without a leader,” he said.

Prest said the government could benefit from Conservative disorganization, but an early election could also remind voters that the NDP has chosen to seek a new mandate only two years after winning one.

“The NDP could run the risk of looking very much focused on their own interests, rather than voters’ interests,” Prest said.

stories.title: Fourth Marineland whale dies after relocation from Niagara Falls park
stories.summary: Osiris, a 26-year-old beluga, has died at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A fourth whale that was moved out of Marineland in July has died after struggling with its health after arriving at her new home in Chicago, Shedd Aquarium said Monday.

The park said 26-year-old Osiris died Monday morning. The female beluga was one of 10 that came to Shedd from Marineland, the shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ont.

It was part of the world’s biggest collective move of captive whales. Marineland had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its animals.

Over a series of moves beginning in July, Marineland moved 30 belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums abroad: Shedd in Chicago, SeaWorld locations in San Antonio and San Diego, Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta and Oceanografic Valencia in Spain.

Osiris was “not a consistent eater” but had improved recently after receiving fluids and medication, Shedd said.

“Our care team observed sudden changes this morning in both Osiris’s behaviour and respiratory patterns,” Shedd said in a statement.

“Respiratory rates are one of many measures we track closely and continuously, as changes can signal that an animal may need additional support. The team moved Osiris to the medical habitat, so immediate care could be provided if needed. Her condition declined rapidly, and Osiris passed away despite life-saving efforts by our veterinary and animal care teams.”

The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.

Two other Marineland whales, Rain and Peekachu, died at Shedd within weeks of the move. One longtime Shedd resident beluga, Beethoven, also recently died.

All are being investigated, but the results have not yet returned, Shedd said.

Another Marineland beluga, Jelly Bean, died at Oceanografic last week.

The whales were cleared by veterinarians at Marineland and the other parks to move and Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also signed off on the relocation.

Last week, Shedd said it is concerned about the health of another recently moved whale, Secord.

“Secord has not yet been consistently taking in the amount of food teams would like to see, even as they try different feeding approaches and offer different types of herring to gauge her preference,” Shedd said in a blog post last week.

Marineland originally sought to move the whales to China after securing a deal to sell all 30 of its belugas to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, which has a Guinness Book of World Record for the largest aquarium in the world.

Thompson blocked that move, saying it was not in the best interest of the whales and inconsistent with a 2019 federal law. That law banned whale and dolphin captivity, but grandfathered in Marineland’s whales. It also banned breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its whales by sex. And the law banned performances.

Marineland turned to an American-led consortium to house the world’s biggest pod of captive belugas, but they needed five aquariums to house them all.

There are no breeding or performing restrictions at belugas’ new homes.

Marineland’s whales had struggled in recent years. Nineteen belugas and one killer whale died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

The park blames some of those deaths on the new federal laws.

Sources have said Marineland, which is about a kilometre from Horseshoe Falls, has been sold on the condition that all animals are gone.

Several hundred deer remain.

The park will conduct a necropsy to try to better understand what happened.

There are no breeding or performing restrictions at belugas’ new homes.

stories.title: Funeral for London woman at the centre of second-degree murder investigation to be held Saturday
stories.summary: Near a seasonal scarecrow out front of a townhome at 685 Chelton Road in London sits several floral bouquets.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Near a seasonal scarecrow out front of a townhome at 685 Chelton Road in London sits several floral bouquets.

Each was placed by passersby, wanting to express grief for a mother who died in what police called a “violent incident” last week.

Authorities have not named the victim, but multiple social media posts and online fundraisers confirmed she is Raman Devi, a mother of two young children.

London Police began a femicide investigation after the arrest of 41-year-old Mandeep Singh at the home in the Summerside neighbourhood on Sept. 15.

Officers arrived to find a woman with life-threatening injuries. She was rushed to hospital, where she died.

Off camera Monday, a neighbour recalled a disturbing scene, telling CTV News they witnessed children being hurriedly carried out of the family home by a grandmother moments after the incident.

Singh faces a second-degree murder count .

But should the police femicide investigation lead to an automatic first-degree murder charge, there would also be a minimum 25-year sentence if convicted.

Police have said there are “indications that it (the investigation) could meet the threshold” for femicide.

Meanwhile, two separate online fundraisers in Raman Devi’s name have already raised more than $30,000.

One of the fundraisers is endorsed by the London Sikh Society.

In a telephone call, its president Hakikat Singh Gill said he is grateful for the support offered by the local community.

He also stated his organization is working with Raman Devi’s family members, including her children.

Gill added a funeral for her will be held on Saturday, Sept. 26 at 1 p.m. at Forest Lawn Funeral Chapel on Dundas Street East.

stories.title: Punk Rock Flea Market celebrates 10th anniversary
stories.summary: London's Punk Rock Flea Market (Prfm) is celebrating its 10th anniversary. The event, which runs from this Thu...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
London’s Punk Rock Flea Market (Prfm) is celebrating its 10th anniversary. The event, which runs from this Thursday to Saturday, is expected to take over Dundas Place and Downtown London with live music, vendors, and skateboarders. But for the organizers, it’s more than just punk rock.

“We’re really talking about the local arts and culture, but the name Punk Rock Flea Market, that’s our roots, that kind of DIY ethos, but we kind of wrapped our arms around any of the local artists and community members and musicians.” Said Julie and Shayna, two of the co-organizers of Prfm. “We started in 2016, when we saw a gap in events of this sort, to gather alternative makers and small businesses, that didn’t really have a place to sell their wares at traditional pop-up markets.”

London is itself recognized as a Unesco City of Music. The organizers say they’re proud to be apart of London’s rich history of music. “[We] think that the designation really helps to uplift artists in terms of export opportunities, and it also helps put us on the map as a city of importance, musically in Canada.”

“London has a pretty vibrant punk culture, it has a history of punk culture”, said Adi Berardini, editor-in-chief of Femme Art Review, a publication providing space for Lgbtq+ and women’s voices to reflect on art. She went on to emphasize the importance of events like Prfm. “In a more conservative city like London, I think it’s important to have these events, because we have to continue to work against the grain as well, and create space for those who are alternative and part of the punk scene.”

Punk Rock Flea Market begins Thursday night and runs until Saturday. You can find more info on their Instagram .

stories.title: Pharmacy treatments for Lyme disease cut N.S. emergency visits in half: study
stories.summary: Blacklegged tick bites can lead to Lyme disease, as well as Anaplasmosis, Babesiosis and Powassan virus though Nova Scotia has not seen Powassan cases so far.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The number of Nova Scotians visiting the emergency department for treatment of tick bites dropped by about half after the province gave pharmacists permission in 2021 to assess and provide preventative Lyme disease treatment, a new study has found.

The study, published Monday in the Canadian Pharmacies Journal, showed pharmacists are able to examine a suspected bite and if confirmed to be from a tick that can transmit Lyme disease , prescribe the standard oral treatment called doxycycline to limit the risk of it developing.

Emily Black, lead supervising author of the study and acting director of the College of Pharmacy at Dalhousie University, said it’s a sign of improvements in the system.

“It really shows that people want other options for access for things like tick bites. They really don’t want to be sitting in the emergency department,” she said. “But I also think it suggests or shows that they really value the care that pharmacists can provide and really trust their assessment and ability to do that.”

The study looked at patient cases of tick bites reported at three Nova Scotia emergency departments in the 16 months before and 16 months after the August 2021 change.

Before implementation, there were a total of 617 visits for tick bites. Once pharmacists could assess the bites, the study found 402 people visited an emergency department during a period of 16 months after the change. When compared to the overall emergency department volume in each 16-month period, the study showed the rate of tick-bite visits was cut roughly in half.

2:09 New tick-borne illness on the rise in Canada

By expanding tick treatments to pharmacies, the Pharmacy Association of Nova Scotia says people can get help faster.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

“We really don’t want people with minor ailments, things that they categorize in the ER as level four or level five, we don’t want those in the ER, we want them being taken care of in the community,” said Allison Bodnar, CEO of the association.

In the latest quarter, from April to June, Bodnar said pharmacists in the province assessed more than 8,000 tick bites. She stressed it shows how prevalent the issue of tick bites has become in Nova Scotia.

Nova Scotians can typically book a same-day or following day appointment online as opposed to driving to the hospital and waiting hours to be seen. Treatment for tickborne illnesses must be administered within 72 hours to limit the risk of their development.

“Their community pharmacy may be a lot closer for them to their home and a lot easier to access than, say, driving to an emergency department,” Black said. “It gives them more timely accesss as well, where they may not be able to get in to see their primary care provider.”

Pharmacists are becoming a primary source for Lyme disease treatment in Nova Scotia, a separate study showed.

A 2024 study in the Canadian Pharmacists Journal, which Black was also a part of, found pharmacists prescribed 61.3 per cent of all single-dose doxycycline prescriptions following the province giving them prescribing authority.

Even though a high number of people are turning to pharmacists for Lyme disease treatment, Black said more work can still be done.

“There’s still a lot of people out there who maybe don’t know about the service,” Black said. “I think there’s work to do in terms of increasing awareness around what can be offered in community settings and the different health-care providers that can offer that.”

Nova Scotia has high rates of Lyme disease, the provincial government said in a bulletin last year. It said the province is also seeing more cases of Anaplasmosis and a few cases of Babesiosis, two other tick-borne illnesses. While Powassan virus is another known tick-borne illness, there are no known cases in the province.

stories.title: Civilian schools are training the air force’s next generation of technicians for the first time
stories.summary: Demand for professionals who certify whether an aircraft is fit to fly surges as Ottawa focuses its defence modernization efforts
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
The Royal Canadian Air Force is outsourcing its aircraft technician training for the first time, as demand for the professionals who certify whether an aircraft is fit to fly surges amid modernization efforts.

Nearly 200 RCAF members are learning how to be aircraft technicians at civilian schools while the air force’s own academy in Borden, Ont., runs at full capacity. The inaugural students under this initiative began classes in July.

It’s a first for the air force, after the Canadian Forces , more broadly, has been outsourcing training for decades with professions such as construction engineers.

“We have a number of new and extremely modern and complex aircraft coming online, and we need to stand ready and have our technicians ready when these platforms arrive at the operational units,” said Lieutenant-Colonel Meagan McGrath, a staff officer who leads the outsourced training initiative for the RCAF’s Air Maintenance Branch. “There’s no time to waste here.”

The air force has secured standing offers from 10 civilian schools across the country to train aircraft technicians, allowing it to increase its pace of graduation as it experiences a growth in enrolment. Not all 10 currently have RCAF members studying at them. One of the busier schools is the British Columbia Institute for Technology (BCIT), where 84 of the approximately 190 RCAF members in the Force’s program are enrolled.

On a Monday afternoon in early September, students in uniform stood attentively, listening to their professor talk about aircraft wiring at BCIT’s aerospace campus near the Vancouver International Airport. In a classroom close by, their civilian colleagues did much the same, learning everything from how to repair fuselages made with composite materials to what the inside of an airplane wheel looks like.

The two cohorts will study the same Transport Canada-certified curriculum over the next several months, but with two very different outcomes. One will finish their program and enter the job market, likely looking for work in the commercial aviation sector. The other will either finish and travel to their posted unit to learn more about the military aircraft fleets they’ve been assigned to or return to base for further training.

The air force began looking into outsourcing training for these technicians in the fall of 2024, shortly after publishing its training modernization strategy in the spring.

This was also around the time when the military branch decided it would aim to train its aircraft technicians to national standards, such as Transport Canada’s, and work with schools whose curriculum abides by these standards, Lt.-Col. McGrath said.

“It’s part of the modernization effort. There’s a standard that exists. Let’s reach towards it,” she said.

Aircraft technicians are critical to an aircraft being deemed safe to fly. It’s their name on the line if anything goes wrong, said Gerry Egan, associate dean of aerospace at BCIT.

“The buck stops with that individual and the team of individuals making that aircraft safe for flight, and then they hand it off to the flight crew and say, ‘Here’s your aircraft,’” said Mr. Egan, a former aircraft maintenance engineer himself.

There are three main categories that aircraft technicians can specialize in at BCIT: structures, electronics – also called avionics – and maintenance. Those specializing in structures are responsible for maintaining and repairing parts of the aircraft such as the fuselage, wings and tail. Those specializing in avionics are responsible for all of the electrical systems, including navigation and communication. And those specializing in maintenance are the “jack or jill of all trades,” said Mr. Egan, meaning they’re the ones responsible for the certification of an aircraft after it has undergone any type of repair or routine maintenance. Thus, they have to know a little bit of everything.

While the RCAF has different professional titles for each of the three aforementioned technician categories, they’re consistent with what the military employs.

The maintenance, repair and overhaul work these technicians perform is highlighted as a key capability by Ottawa’s new Defence Industrial Strategy, which was released earlier this year, as well as the Department of National Defence’s 2026-27 departmental plan. In this plan, Ottawa highlights the modernization of aerospace maintenance technician training as one of the air force’s priorities for the current fiscal year.

Across the country from BCIT, Nova Scotia Community College has a heavy military presence on its campus too. The school has been working with the Forces for decades, including on its outsourced training for construction-related courses.

The college is also training aircraft technicians for the RCAF, but this time through a different military education program called the Non-Commissioned Member Subsidized Training and Education Plan. This program offers full-time paid education at certain Canadian schools to either civilians looking to join the Forces, or non-commissioned members who are already enrolled but want to become experts in their field.

Andrew Lafford, vice-president of academics at the college, said he’s noticed an increase recently in the number of students in uniform on campus in tandem with an increase in the number of training contracts the school is working with the Forces on.

Back at BCIT, the school is preparing to launch its first 18-week full-time program in May dedicated to teaching people how to build, repair, fly and collect data with drones. Through informal discussions, Mr. Egan said he’s gleaned the military is keen to learn more about it, as they, too, are having to navigate new training for autonomous systems.

The scope of the modernization effort that the air force is currently undertaking is the greatest since the Second World War, said Lt.-Col. McGrath.

“It’s really a moment in time, and I think we’ve grasped very quickly that we need to adjust to accommodate this moment and to find solutions.”

stories.title: $16 million housing project unveiled in Walkerton for low to moderate income earners
stories.summary: Ground has officially been broken on a new housing project in Bruce County.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Ground has officially been broken on a new housing project in Bruce County.

“This fills a really important piece of the housing puzzle, that subsidized county housing provided by the Bruce County Housing Corporation. It meets the needs of some people who really need help finding homes in our community,” said Bruce County Warden Luke Charbonneau.

The $16 million project, located in Walkerton, will be a mix of 41 affordable and market rate units. Tenants will be selected from Bruce County’s community housing waitlist, which is more than 800 people long.

“41 units isn’t solving that problem, but it’s one project at a time, one unit at a time, until we meet that need,” said Charbonneau.

Brockton’s Mayor calls the new housing project “workforce” housing, geared towards existing, and possibly new, low to middle income earners.

“For example, there is great demand at our hospitals and long term care homes, for personal support workers (PSW). They might make a salary in the range of $28 an hour. If that’s the only source of income they have, they are definitely under stress with rent. And this type of project will be geared towards that person. So, a PSW who lands a job at Bruce Lea Haven Long Term Care Home for example, could apply to the county to be on the waiting list, and at that income level, they could qualify for a subsidized rent in this building,” said Brockton Mayor Chris Peabody.

The mix of tenants concerns Walkerton business owner, Darren Holm. He believes those already on Bruce County’s nearly 1000 person community housing waitlist, should be first in line, for the new Bruce County housing project, expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

“What happens to the people that are indeed challenged and are vulnerable, that have been on the list for multiple years? Are they passed over for this new population of residents?” questioned Holm.

Bruce County didn’t provide the break down of how many units in the new Eastridge Community Housing Project would be affordable, and how many would be market-rate, or how tenants would be selected.

Peabody says nearby this new project, 70 housing units are currently being constructed, a portion of which will be affordable, and a handful of units in the existing apartments in the Eastridge development are subsidized by the county as well.

“We know there’s the need, and this isn’t the only solution. There have been other solutions we’re working on,” he said.

“We’re a growing community. Every one of the municipalities in Bruce County is slated to grow. So, we have more and more people moving here wanting to live here. And we need to find places for them to be. Ultimately, we want this county to be a place where anybody can find a place to live,” said Charbonneau.

Bruce Power has contributed $1 million towards the Eastridge Community Housing project. The Ontario government is also covering a multimillion-dollar portion of the construction costs. Brockton donated the land. Bruce County will build, and operate the housing complex.

“It would just be really nice to have some clear cut answers on who’s paying for it, who’s going to live there, and how the whole economics of it works out. How much we as taxpayers are going to be on the hook for the initial buildout, and the ongoing operations of it,” said Holm.
