stories.title: SIU investigating shooting near Belleville synagogue on Yom Kippur
stories.summary: Man and police officer injured after exchange of gunfire
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi
stories.content:
A shooting at a small synagogue on a residential street in Belleville, Ont., left a police officer in critical condition and bullet holes in the building’s stained-glass windows as worshippers gathered on Sunday night to mark Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish calendar.

A 29-year-old man armed with a shotgun opened fire on a policeman stationed outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue around 7:10 p.m., initiating a shootout, said Kristy Denette, spokeswoman for the Special Investigations Unit. The agency handles cases involving Ontario police that result in death or serious injury.

The suspect was also injured and is in hospital in life-threatening condition, according to the SIU. The officer, Constable Jeff Smith of the Belleville Police Service, is in critical but stable condition. A second officer also fired their weapon, Ms. Denette said.

“There are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me, and some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot-out windows, that sort of thing,” she told reporters. “So it would have been quite the scene.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney and other politicians condemned the shooting as an attack on the Jewish community. Canada has seen an increase in violence targeting Jewish institutions in recent months, including attacks at synagogues, schools and businesses. Many institutions have ramped up security for the high holidays. Police have so far not commented on a specific motive for the attack in Belleville.

Unlike most of the other attacks, which have targeted Jewish institutions in large urban areas, Sunday’s shooting occurred at a synagogue with a tiny congregation in a small city. The Sons of Jacob has a membership of roughly 35 families and doesn’t even have a part-time rabbi.

“Who would think it would happen here, of all places?” Norm Weddum, president of the congregation, said in an interview.

Less than half an hour before the attack, Mr. Weddum said hello to Constable Smith, who was stationed in the synagogue’s parking lot in an unmarked vehicle, and thanked him for his work.

Mr. Weddum said shooting erupted outside the synagogue as about 25 worshippers were milling around, about to begin evening prayers. He yelled at the crowd to take cover in the building’s sanctuary. Then, about 20 shots were fired through the synagogue’s front stained-glass windows, he said.

“All hell broke loose at that point,” he said. “We’re all crouched down. The glass is breaking.”

Among the crowd was Mary Cohen, the congregation’s treasurer, who dropped to the floor and then hid behind some curtains with her husband.

“It’s our most holy holiday of the year, and to experience something like that on this kind of a day, it’s a trauma to all the members,” she said.

Mr. Weddum credited Constable Smith with preventing a tragedy.

“If that officer had not been there, I probably wouldn’t be talking to you right now. Simple as that,” he said, adding, “That officer, he saved everyone’s lives in that building.”

Belleville Police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks said Constable Smith is recovering in intensive care. He is part of the emergency response unit and a 12-year member of the police force.

“While he continues to face a significant road to recovery, his condition has stabilized, and we remain hopeful and encouraged by his progress,” she said.

Deputy Chief Meeks identified the suspect as Sean Ward, 29, of Quinte West, Ont.

Ms. Denette of the SIU said the suspect was critically injured in the shootout and had no vital signs, “but was sort of brought back to life, so to speak.”

The scene was cordoned off with yellow police tape Monday as police scoured the area for evidence. Ammunition casings and what appeared to be a long gun were still visible on the pavement, as were several vehicles with what looked like bullet scars and broken glass.

Scott Granville, who lives around the corner from the synagogue, was out for a walk Sunday evening when he heard an explosion of gunfire. He said he heard between 20 and 30 shots exchanged in a relatively short time.

“I knew right away that it was a shootout, not just shots, because there were different calibres. You could tell there were different guns going off,” Mr. Granville said.

Melissa Walker was working in her front yard on Victoria Street about a block away when she heard the gunfire and approached to see what was happening. She saw a gunman in a white T-shirt crouched low at the side of a vehicle, she said, as police fired at him from their location nearer to the synagogue.

“I saw him get shot,” Ms. Walker said.

“The closer I went, shots were still ringing out, and my body just told me not to go further.”

Then police pulled up and shouted at the suspect to get down, she said. At that point he was already down and looked to have been hit multiple times, she said. Then the officers kicked away what appeared to be a long gun, she added.

Darren Millar, who also lives nearby, said he was just around the corner sitting on his porch when he heard gunfire.

“I heard three loud explosions. I guess it was a shotgun, but it sounded like a bomb or a grenade or something. It was really loud. It was louder than any gun I’ve ever heard,” he said.

About 30 seconds after the shooting stopped, he jumped in his vehicle and drove down the street toward the synagogue. His dash cam captured the scene as three officers ran toward the suspect and two others stood over him as he lay on the ground.

Mr. Weddum said he sees the attack as targeting the Jewish community.

“We view it as a hate crime,” he said. “I mean, you know, a guy shows up on a Sunday, walking towards a synagogue that is packed due to the high holiday services, carrying a rifle. Now he is not out for a Sunday stroll.”

Deputy Chief Meeks said there was no threat to public safety but added that police have increased patrols in Belleville and are working closely with community leaders.

“Let me be very clear – antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community. Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones or participating in community life,” she told reporters.

A national-security source told The Globe and Mail that the RCMP-led Integrated National Security Enforcement Team, which oversees terrorism investigations, was not involved in the Belleville investigation as of Monday. However, the source said the Ontario Provincial Police’s Provincial Anti-Terrorism Section is assisting. The Globe is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

“Jewish people must be able to worship safely. To live free, open, proud Jewish lives,” he said in a statement on Monday. “Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford paid tribute to the officer injured in the shooting, calling him a hero who “stopped a tragedy.”

“I find it disgusting, someone would go into a synagogue, or potentially go into a synagogue, on Yom Kippur or any day, or any place of worship, it’s disgusting,” Mr. Ford told reporters at Queen’s Park on Monday.

He also said the suspect should face consequences: “Whoever the assailant was needs to be charged, and I don’t care if he’s in the hospital or not. Unacceptable.”

SIU investigators are canvassing for witnesses and plan to review footage from officers’ body-worn cameras and vehicles. Ms. Denette said the team expects to spend two days processing the scene.

“It’s quite a complex scene and there’s a lot of cartridge cases to collect,” she said. “There’s multiple firearms. There’s a number of vehicles that are involved.”

Meanwhile, police in Durham Region said Monday that they charged a 19-year-old man with making threats motivated by hate for alleged online posts about carrying out a shooting at an area synagogue.

With reports from Laura Stone, Mercedes Stephenson and Tu Thanh Ha

stories.title: House of Commons is back as Liberals vow ‘significant’ legislation coming
stories.summary: Government House leader Steven MacKinnon has promised "significant" economic legislation will become the "centrepiece" of the fall sitting of Parliament.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Members of Parliament return from their summer break Monday, with the economy and trade partnerships in centre-focus after the trade war with the United States dramatically escalated over the summer months.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says his Liberal government will introduce some of the most consequential legislation in decades this sitting.

Government House leader Steven MacKinnon has promised “significant” economic legislation will become the “centrepiece” of the fall sitting of Parliament.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne is poised to introduce a fresh bill to extend relief for the excise tax on fuel and has a fall budget in the works as well.

2:22 Liberals to propose major labour code changes

The Liberals are surging ahead in the polls and command a majority in the House of Commons.

That follows a string of floor-crossers and byelections over the past year that pushed the Liberals out of a shaky minority into a thin majority of 173 seats, That has left the opposition parties smarting with less control over the parliamentary agenda and slumped in the polls.

There are six vacant seats which will require byelections in the coming months.

2:02 Carney rallies Liberal caucus in Ottawa after fruitful Europe trip

Conservative stalwart Larry Brock resigned his seat in the Brantford-Brant riding last week to return to his former career as a Crown prosecutor.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also held a campaign-style rally in Brantford, Ont., in the riding, just west of Hamilton on Sunday. Poilievre announced Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis will be the party’s candidate in the byelection, which has yet to be called.

New Democrats were significantly reduced in number in the last election and party leader Avi Lewis remains without a seat in the House. They return to Ottawa without longtime MP Alexandre Boulerice, who stepped down to run for a provincial seat in the Quebec election.

It leaves the NDP with just five MPs in the House.

The Liberals have had high-profile resignations of their own, most notably Steven Guilbeault. He resigned in August citing frustration with the Liberal party’s pivot under Carney’s leadership on energy and environmental policies.

Ottawa took more steps over the summer toward making a new West Coast pipeline possible. Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced in July they worked out an arrangement to support a future pipeline to the southern B.C. coast under a private-public partnership.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s White House has meantime cranked up trade pressure on Canada and continued to threaten its sovereignty. Trump has threatened that he will escalate his deepening trade war by the end of the year with additional tariffs on steel and autos if the two sides can’t reach an agreement.

That, after Canada’s negotiating team walked away from a potential deal with the White House in August at the 11th hour, saying that what was on the table was a bad deal for Canada.

The trade conflict escalated, with Trump imposing another volley of tariffs and threatening even more, while Canada imposed its own counter-tariffs. Trump has also since responded by attempting to rebrand Lake Ontario as Lake America and to cut off certain Canadian imports to the United States.

Carney has meantime been traversing the world at an aggressive pace as he seeks to quickly deepen ties with and attract investment from countries outside of the United States.

1:33 Conservative caucus shows signs of division as B.C. meetings wrap

In the past week alone, Carney attended the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, where he delivered a major speech after the president of the European Commission said she would like to see Canada become an “associate member” of the EU. He squeezed in a quick jaunt to the U.K. on that trip for a bilateral visit with Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Carney also hosted a major investment summit in Toronto, where he won accolades from former prime minister Stephen Harper.

Carney nodded to the intense pace he’s working at while addressing his caucus on Friday, when he noticed he misspoke during his speech, saying “seven weeks” instead of “days.”

“It felt like seven weeks, but it was seven days. But this is the pace we need,” Carney said.

Carney will be in New York for meetings around the United Nations this week, though he is not scheduled to address the General Assembly.

He is expected to have more travel in the fall months, with several summits on the horizon.

Critics caution new legislation could threaten the right to strike.

MacKinnon, Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu and Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc are scheduled to hold a joint press conference on the bill after it’s introduced later today.

On Saturday Hajdu said the goal is to “reduce” the number of times the government intervenes in the collective bargaining process and MacKinnon said the goal is to make it “easier” to reach an agreement.

MacKinnon told CBC News there are “too many” lockouts, strikes and threats of job action and that it “harms” investment and employment.

Labour leaders, including the heads of Unifor and Canadian Labour Congress, have said any measure that restricts workers’ ability to strike weakens their rights and strips bargaining power.

Trump has threatened that he will escalate his deepening trade war by the end of the year with additional tariffs on steel and autos if the two sides can’t reach an agreement.
That, after Canada’s negotiating team walked away from a potential deal with the White House in August at the 11th hour, saying that what was on the table was a bad deal for Canada.

The trade conflict escalated, with Trump imposing another volley of tariffs and threatening even more, while Canada imposed its own counter-tariffs. Trump has also since responded by attempting to rebrand Lake Ontario as Lake America and to cut off certain Canadian imports to the United States.
Carney has meantime been traversing the world at an aggressive pace as he seeks to quickly deepen ties with and attract investment from countries outside of the United States.

In the past week alone, Carney attended the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, where he delivered a major speech after the president of the European Commission said she would like to see Canada become an “associate member” of the EU. He squeezed in a quick jaunt to the U.K. on that trip for a bilateral visit with Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Carney also hosted a major investment summit in Toronto, where he won accolades from former prime minister Stephen Harper.
Carney nodded to the intense pace he’s working at while addressing his caucus on Friday, when he noticed he misspoke during his speech, saying “seven weeks” instead of “days.”
“It felt like seven weeks, but it was seven days. But this is the pace we need,” Carney said.
Carney will be in New York for meetings around the United Nations this week, though he is not scheduled to address the General Assembly.
He is expected to have more travel in the fall months, with several summits on the horizon.
Critics caution new legislation could threaten the right to strike.
MacKinnon, Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu and Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc are scheduled to hold a joint press conference on the bill after it’s introduced later today.

On Saturday Hajdu said the goal is to “reduce” the number of times the government intervenes in the collective bargaining process and MacKinnon said the goal is to make it “easier” to reach an agreement.
MacKinnon told CBC News there are “too many” lockouts, strikes and threats of job action and that it “harms” investment and employment.
Labour leaders, including the heads of Unifor and Canadian Labour Congress, have said any measure that restricts workers’ ability to strike weakens their rights and strips bargaining power.

stories.title: ‘Stitched it back’: Edmonton event where locals mend clothes promotes sustainability
stories.summary: Pearce Carpenter says fixing the holes in the black balloon bottoms they bought from an Edmonton thrift store is their way of tackling fast fashion.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Pearce Carpenter says fixing the holes in the black balloon bottoms they bought from an Edmonton thrift store is their way of tackling fast fashion.

“There is so much textile waste in the world, so if we just fix old clothes, like holes in the crotch areas of pants, it’s one little quiet act of rebellion,” said Carpenter, who uses they and them pronouns, while stitching over the part of the pants where two holes once were.

“Crotches wear out so quickly in pants just from rubbing your thighs.”

Before they started stitching, they said they lengthened the pants by cutting them near the ankles, adding a blue-coloured fabric with yellow squares and threading the ends back on.

“It’s such a fun way to add creativity to your wardrobe.”

Carpenter was among dozens who spent a part of their Saturday fixing old and beloved items at a clothing mending event at the University of Alberta called Human Ecology Clothing Repair Café.

Samantha Barrios Mendoza, a psychology student and event co-ordinator, said the gathering has been happening monthly for the last five years during the school year.

But the number of attendees has grown in the last year or so, likely due to the affordability crisis.

“I think people are starting to become more interested in learning how to mend because things are a little tight right now,” said Barrios Mendoza, as the sound of sewing machines and classical music hummed behind her.

“Why buy something new with hard-earned money when you can just repair something you love?”

Barrios Mendoza said many attendees believe repairing clothes can also reduce the environmental impact of fast fashion.

Fast fashion describes clothing produced quickly with cheap materials that copies popular styles from major fashion labels and designers. In recent years, fast fashion manufacturers have come under intensifying pressure to reduce their contributions to climate change.

The United Nations Environment Programme estimates that each year, the world generates fabric waste at a rate equivalent to a garbage truck’s worth being dumped or incinerated every second.

“There are new items and fabrics being pumped out every day in the fashion industry,” Barrios Mendoza said.

“So not buying new clothes and repairing is taking action for sustainability.”

Barrios Mendoza said that while repairing clothing does not reverse the climate crisis, it means a lot to the people who do it.

She said a woman once added floral trinkets to her wedding dress, and a mother used fabric she had kept since her kids were infants to make aprons for them after they grew up and moved away.

“People have made memories through mending,” Barrios Mendoza said.

Attendees are provided with needles, threads, fabrics and ribbons, as well as drinks and snacks.

Experts also attend some events to teach new repair methods.

Most of the mending consists of fixing holes.

“We also do a little bit of resizing. People will bring in their skirts or their shirts, and they’ll bring them down a size or up a size, or they’ll turn some fabric into a bag,” Barrios Mendoza said.

She said she got into mending when she was a teen.

“I have a bag that I’ve had for 15 years, and hole after hole, straps falling down, I’ve just stitched it back together,” she said.

The stitches remind her of how much she has improved her mending skills over the years.

“Now it has patches and little stitch marks, and I can see where I started learning how to sew and then how the stitch marks got more even.

“The bag is now a piece of me.”

Tacjana Maj-Pfleger, another event attendee, said she takes pride in the things she has fixed.

“I have this ethos where good clothing doesn’t have to be new clothing,” she said, while sewing fabrics onto the back of an old denim jacket to make it thicker.

“I’m fairly poor, honestly, but also, fast fashion is terrible.”

stories.title: Buyers trim $19,000 off price of Etobicoke waterfront condo
stories.summary: Unit features a kitchen with an island and quartz countertops, as well as two full bathrooms and a laundry closet
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
15 Legion Rd., No. 504, Toronto

Asking price: $759,000 (July, 2026)

Selling price: $740,000 (August, 2026)

Previous selling price: $709,000 (May, 2021); $560,000 (July, 2017); $338,000 (July, 2014); $291,002 (December, 2011)

Taxes: $3,250 (2025)

Days on the market: 12

Buyers’ agent: Ira Jelinek, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

Buyers looking for a home close to the Etobicoke waterfront were drawn to this two-bedroom, corner unit with 937 square feet of living space at Beyond the Sea, a multi-tower community on Mimico Creek and across the street from Humber Bay Park West on Lake Ontario.

“There was definitely supply to choose from, but this was the one they wanted,” said the buyers’ agent, Ira Jelinek.

“They were looking for something with more space than the standard condo, and this definitely has more space.”

The buyers spent days negotiating for a reduced sale price for the home listed in July with an asking price of $759,000. The parties signed off on a $740,000 deal in August.

“Generally, with the uncertainty of the market with tariffs, it’s a good time to be a buyer,” Mr. Jelinek said.

“Buyers definitely have some more leverage now.”

This 15-year-old unit has wall-to-wall windows in both bedrooms and two sets of sliding doors to a wraparound balcony from the living and dining area.

There is a kitchen with an island and quartz countertops, as well as two full bathrooms and a laundry closet.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $1,011 cover heating and water. Common areas include a kids’ playroom, a party room, a gym, an indoor pool, and a rooftop deck with barbecue areas.

“The wraparound balcony is a nice feature to have,” Mr. Jelinek said.

stories.title: SIU to provide update on shooting near synagogue in Belleville, Ont.
stories.summary: Ontario's police watchdog is expected to provide an update this morning following an exchange of gunfire near a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., that left a man and a police officer injured on Sunday night.
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press
stories.content:
BELLEVILLE - A man armed with a shotgun allegedly opened fire at a police officer stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., on Sunday night, triggering a shootout that left him and the officer seriously injured, Ontario’s police watchdog said Monday.

The shooting took place at the start of Yom Kippur as people gathered inside the Sons of Jacob synagogue to observe the holiest day on the Jewish calendar, prompting police in other Canadian cities to increase patrols around synagogues and other places of worship.

Kristy Denette, a spokesperson for the Special Investigations Unit, said dozens of shots were exchanged, leaving nearby vehicles and homes riddled with holes. There was no forensic confirmation Monday morning as to whether the synagogue was hit, she said.

Ontario's police watchdog says a man armed with a shotgun opened fire at a police officer stationed outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., on Sunday night, triggering a shootout that left both seriously injured. The shooting took place as people gathered inside the synagogue to observe Yom Kippur. (Sept. 21, 2026)

The suspect came within about half a block of the synagogue, Denette said at a news conference.

The initial gunfire exchange involved a Belleville police officer and a 29-year-old man, and a second officer opened fire afterward, Denette said, adding the agency’s investigators are securing video from body-worn cameras to get a better sense of the sequence of events.

The man was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and the police officer was in hospital in critical but stable condition, the SIU said.

Belleville police Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks identified the alleged shooter as Sean Ward, of the nearby city of Quinte West, and the officer as Const. Jeff Smith, who has been with the force for nearly 13 years.

“We are incredibly grateful for the community and the outpouring of support we have received from our community and policing partners from across the province,” Meeks said at the news conference.

“I also want to acknowledge the significant impact this incident has had on Belleville’s Jewish community. We recognize the concern and uncertainty many may be feeling, particularly given that this occurred near the Sons of Jacob synagogue during one of the holiest days in the Jewish faith.”

A police officer and a man were wounded in an exchange of gunfire Sunday near a synagogue in Ontario as members of the Jewish community marked Yom Kippur, authorities said. (Sept. 21, 2026)

The deputy chief did not speak to a possible motive in the shooting. When asked whether police were operating under the assumption that the suspect was trying to get inside the synagogue, Meeks said she could not provide any further information on the investigation.

Shortly afterward, Denette was asked whether there was any evidence it was a “terrorist attack aimed at the Jewish community.”

“I’d be speculating, but I mean I think that common sense would say that probably was the case,” she said before adding that aspect of the incident is not the SIU’s jurisdiction.

“I want to be clear, the Special Investigations Unit has a limited mandate and our mandate is to criminally investigate the actions of a police officer.”

Witnesses described a chaotic and frightening scene as gunshots rang out shortly after 7 p.m. on Sunday.

Douglas Lobel, who was inside the synagogue, said the gunfire exchange “seemed like an eternity.”

“It probably went on for about two, maybe three minutes at the most and after that, the shooting stopped, so we just kind of stayed in the building, waiting for some type of instructions,” he said.

Lobel said at some point a police officer came into the lobby and shouted: “Is anybody hurt?”

No one was injured and the group of about two dozen people inside the synagogue was told to stay put while police tended to the injured officer, Lobel said.

“This officer was a hero who saved our lives,” he said, noting the synagogue had requested police presence outside the building due to security concerns. “If this officer wasn’t there, I don’t know what could have happened.”

Lobel said the congregants remained in the synagogue and prayed until they were eventually escorted out of the building and into a city bus that took them to a police station.

Heather Moon, who lives near the synagogue, said she had just put her younger child to bed when she heard multiple shots.

“I thought it was a car backfiring and it was not,” she said Monday. “It was very, very scary.”

Moon said she heard “probably” 25 to 30 shots as she recorded video.

“It was like boom, boom, boom, and then bang – and those ones you could feel in your chest, like they just shook you,” she said.

Sons of Jacob synagogue president Norman Weddum said in a statement to community members on social media that all services scheduled for Yom Kippur have been cancelled.

The shooting drew widespread condemnation from community and political leaders.

On X, Prime Minister Mark Carney wrote: “Canada’s government will do everything in our power to support law enforcement in ensuring that the perpetrator is held accountable to the fullest extent of the law.”

Premier Doug Ford said in his own post that he was “disgusted” by the shooting.

“My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear,” he wrote on X.

Federal Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre also condemned the shooting, saying that Jewish Canadians must be able to feel safe in their communities.

The Belleville police deputy chief said the force has stepped up patrols across the city, including around places of worship.

“Let me be very clear: antisemitism, hate and violence have no place in our community,” Meeks said. “Every person deserves to feel safe when attending a place of worship, gathering with loved ones or participating in community life.”

Toronto police said that while there’s no known threat to local synagogues, they are increasing patrols out of an abundance of caution. Police forces in other parts of Ontario and in Winnipeg have issued similar statements.

The shooting comes after a string of violent incidents that have taken place at or near Canadian synagogues and Jewish institutions in the last few years, including shots fired overnight at synagogues in Toronto and Vaughan, Ont., last spring.

Durham regional police also said Monday that they have arrested a 19-year-old man who threatened to carry out a shooting at a synagogue in the region.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

—With files from Maan Alhmidi and Paola Loriggio in Toronto

stories.title: Vigil to mark 1 year since Nooran Rezayi shot and killed by police in Longueuil
stories.summary: An evening vigil is being held in Longueuil to mark one year since 15-year-old Nooran Rezayi was shot and killed by a local police officer.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
An evening vigil is being held in Longueuil to mark one year since 15-year-old Nooran Rezayi was shot and killed by a local police officer.

Rezayi was killed after police responded to a 911 call reporting a group of allegedly armed youths on Montreal’s South Shore.

Quebec’s police watchdog later said the only firearm seized at the scene belonged to the officer who shot Rezayi.

The watchdog submitted its investigation report to Quebec prosecutors in March, who will determine whether charges should be laid.

Rezayi’s family is expected to attend the vigil and has invited members of the public to join them in honouring his life.

The vigil is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. outside a Longueuil police station before continuing to the intersection where Rezayi was killed.

Six members of Rezayi’s family have filed a $2.2 million civil suit against the City of Longueuil and its police force.

In a separate investigation into the events preceding Rezayi’s death, Montreal police announced charges against 11 young people in late June.

But in August, the prosecution stayed the charges after obtaining new evidence that raised what it described as a complex legal issue.

The case has also prompted a separate administrative investigation into the Longueuil police service over its handling of the aftermath of the shooting.

stories.title: Phrasing of questions in Alberta referendum could have major impact on results: poll
stories.summary: Many Albertans would have different answers if the upcoming referendum questions were to be worded differently, a new survey found.
stories.author: Devon Dekuyper
stories.content:
Many Albertans would have different answers if next month’s referendum questions were to be worded differently, a new survey found.

In an experiment conducted by the Angus Reid Institute, poll results were collected for the 10 existing referendum questions as they will appear on the ballot, and compared with results for the same questions, but phrased according to Angus Reid’s own best practices for polling.

The results showed Albertans’ answers would vary significantly, depending on exactly how the question is asked.

An earlier survey by Angus Reid found one in five Albertans (21 per cent) described them as difficult to understand, while 34 per cent said the questions are very clear, and 43 per cent described them as mostly clear.

“When you think about what one-fifth of the voting population of Alberta would look like, you’re already into potentially hundreds of thousands of potential voters,” said Shachi Kurl, president of Angus Reid.

When separated by age demographic, the data show more than a third of those aged 18-34 found the questions confusing or difficult to understand.

“When you’ve got a third of young Albertans throwing up their hands and saying this is either mostly or completely difficult to follow . . . I think there are big concerns about, first of all, are they going to vote, and do they feel confident in what exactly they’re casting a ballot around?” Kurl said.

With that in mind, Angus Reid researchers sought to find out how Albertans would respond if the questions were posed according to standard polling methodology.

The first question on the referendum, for example, asks Albertans, “Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?”

When polled, 62 per cent of participants answered “yes,” 33 per cent answered “no,” and five per cent were unsure.

The existing phrasing asks Albertans multiple questions at once: whether the province should take increased control of immigration, whether immigration levels should be decreased, whether economic migration should be prioritized, and whether Albertans should have first priority for jobs.

When asked each sub-question individually, 56 per cent of those surveyed felt immigration to Alberta should be reduced, while only 46 per cent felt that people already living in Alberta should be given greater priority for new employment opportunities.

Overall, however, 80 per cent of participants disagreed with at least one of the original question’s elements.

“When you’re asking a double- or a triple-barreled question, it certainly leaves room for doubt as to what part of the question people are responding to or answering,” Kurl said.

Mount Royal University political scientist Lori Williams said she’s found many people are “just completely overwhelmed” by the wording of the questions.

“The first four questions are very complex and difficult to understand,” she said. “That first question has four questions in it. Two of the (other) questions contradict one another . . . There’s questions within questions within questions.

“It essentially gives the government both control in terms of the question it asks, and control in terms of how it interprets the results,” she said.

Looking at question eight, which asks Albertans, “Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?” — those polled were split, with 44 per cent answering “yes” and 44 per cent answering “no.”

However, 58 per cent said they felt provinces receiving federal funding should generally be required to meet the conditions attached to that funding, and 52 per cent said the federal government should be able to reduce or withhold the funding if conditions are not met.

“We didn’t actually even test all of the official ballot questions because some of them were written fairly clearly,” Kurl said.

“But we certainly wanted to better understand and disaggregate some of the most obvious examples of questions that did not read as particularly clear in terms of what people were answering.”

The first survey, which asked about the referendum questions as they are written on the ballot, was conducted from Aug. 10 to 13.

The second survey, which parsed out various aspects of the questions, was conducted from Aug. 26 to Sept. 1. Each surveyed a randomized sample of around 1,000 Canadian adults who are residents of Alberta.

Angus Reid notes a margin of error of ±3 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: Four Ontario nuclear reactors taken off-line ahead of Pickering station’s refurbishment
stories.summary: Work expected to take units out of service for a decade and extend the plant’s life by up to 38 years
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
An Ontario nuclear plant is beginning a massive refurbishment project today, as Premier Doug Ford’s government looks to lean heavily on nuclear energy to serve the province’s growing electricity needs.

Four reactors at Pickering Nuclear Generating Station are starting to come off-line so they can be refurbished at an estimated cost of $26.8-billion , with the actual refurbishment work set to start in January.

The project is expected to take the units out of service for about a decade and would extend the nuclear plant’s life by up to 38 years, producing enough electricity to power 2.2 million homes.

The work includes replacing 1,520 fuel channels, 48 boilers and building a 1.5-kilometre deep-water intake.

Energy Minister Stephen Lecce is touting that the project will support 30,500 jobs, with the vast majority of the costs staying in Ontario.

Environmental Defence has expressed concerns that taking Pickering’s reactors off-line for most of the next decade will increase the province’s already-growing reliance on natural gas to generate electricity, driving up greenhouse gas emissions.

stories.title: $1.5M gift to King’s University College funds classroom upgrades, student learning
stories.summary: King’s University College is set to receive a $1.5-million estate gift - the largest single donation in the institution’s history, to support classroom renewal projects and expand experiential learning opportunities for students.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
King’s University College is set to receive a $1.5-million estate gift from alumnus Frank Schlichtherle, the largest single donation in the institution’s history, to support classroom renewal projects and expand experiential learning opportunities for students.

The gift from Schlichtherle, a 1962 graduate of King’s, will fund modernization of learning spaces across campus, including a classroom that will be named in his honour. It will also establish an endowed experiential learning award to help a student access a global learning opportunity that might otherwise be financially out of reach.

King’s announced the donation as it continues efforts to upgrade teaching and learning spaces. A recently renovated classroom in Wemple Hall, funded through donor support, is among the projects already completed.

The college said Schlichtherle’s contribution will help advance broader renewal plans, including proposed upgrades to Wemple Hall’s east wing. Concept designs envision brighter classrooms with increased natural light, updated furnishings and new spaces for students to meet and collaborate.

“More than half a century after graduating, Frank Schlichtherle’s extraordinary gift will transform classrooms and gathering places into modern, accessible and inclusive spaces for students to learn and thrive,” King’s president Robert Ventresca said in a statement.

Ventresca said the donation will also help expand access to experiential learning opportunities for future students.

Schlichtherle graduated from King’s in 1962 and spent his career teaching history at Cayuga and Caledonia high schools before retiring in 1996. According to the college, he began supporting King’s in 1988 and remained a yearly donor for decades.

“For Frank, this is a crowning moment, a chance to give back to the place that helped shape who he became,” said Terra Ahrens, executive director of foundation, alumni and development at King’s. “More than 60 years after graduating, his connection to King’s continues through a gift that reflects both his lifelong commitment to education and his belief in the transformative power of the student experience.”

The college said the donation will create new capacity to update campus learning spaces while helping students participate in international and experiential learning programs.

stories.title: Morning Update: Euro visions and Parliament’s return
stories.summary: Also in today’s edition: Okanagan’s summer lookback, and art for the season ahead
stories.author: Sierra Bein
stories.content:
Good morning. On the eve of Parliament’s return, Ottawa met once more with our close friends in Europe. More on that below, along with climate change in the Okanagan Valley and AI in the military.

Canada and France will start sharing space-launch systems and satellite data reception facilities, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced after a meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saint-Pierre and Miquelon yesterday.

The big picture: Carney and Macron chose to meet on the archipelago of nearly 6,000 French citizens located 25 kilometres off Newfoundland’s Burin Peninsula as a show of solidarity and confirmation of sovereignty in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s aggression.

Up next: The two leaders are both headed to New York this week for United Nations General Assembly sessions.

Shannon Proudfoot : Canadian pride and rage in the face of tariff madness

Andrew Coyne : We may look back on this as the week Canada began to take its fate into its own hands

James Bradshaw : Carney’s investment summit attracted ‘all the right people.’ Will it bear fruit?

Paul Waldie : Carney, other Western leaders pleased with deal between U.S., Denmark and Greenland

Reading this online? Start your morning with context and insight on the day's biggest stories, in your inbox every weekday.

Investigations into a series of shootings in Toronto have been stymied because a key cellphone that was seized in connection with the case is running on a privacy-focused operating system and investigators have so far been unable to unlock the device, according to a police source.

The details: The phone operates on a little-known and highly secure operating system called GrapheneOS, reputed to be one of the most difficult systems to penetrate, the source said. It’s available for users to download and install for free, based on the Android Open Source Project. It was created by Toronto programmer Daniel Micay.

The federal government plans to kick off Monday’s return of parliamentary sittings with the introduction of major legislation targeting project approvals and Canada’s labour laws. The Canadian Labour Congress has already expressed concern with some of the proposals, which they say would limit bargaining power and encourage federal intervention to end strikes and lockouts.

What else: Another government bill that could be introduced will enable the extension of the federal gas tax break. MPs and senators will also debate several bills still making their way through Parliament, most notably the lawful access bill, C-22 .

Kerry-Lynne Findlay has resigned as leader of the Conservative Party of BC less than four months after taking the helm, ending a brief and tumultuous tenure beset by controversy, an exodus of MLAs and escalating internal opposition to her leadership.

The context: As of last night, 13 MLAs had departed since she became leader: 10 who quit, including Surrey-Serpentine River’s Linda Hepner, who left the party caucus earlier that day, and three whom Findlay removed. A 14th MLA, Reann Gasper, had given up her seat in Abbotsford-Mission to allow Findlay to run.

After a summer of fire in B.C.’s Okanagan Valley, weary locals are rethinking their way of life – or choosing to leave. The very climate that once made the the valley fruitful is now beginning to undermine both its bounty and its appeal. Devastating events once considered exceptional are now simply part of the region’s new reality.

What’s next: The defining season of the region is becoming harder to count on. The valley is gaining heat but losing water, gaining growing days but losing certainty about what crops will actually make it through to harvest. But it’s more than smoke and wildfires: Deep freezes have wiped out entire peach, nectarine and cherry crops, and, in some cases, entire vineyards.

Our arts team has collected all the best entertainment for the season. stories.title: Police investigate reports of missing election signs in Lambton County
stories.summary: Police say the unauthorized removal, damage or tampering of election signs could result in charges under the Criminal Code of Canada.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Lambton County OPP is reminding residents to respect election signs as municipalities across Ontario prepare for municipal elections on Oct. 26.

Police say the unauthorized removal, damage or tampering of election signs could result in charges under the Criminal Code of Canada.

The reminder comes after Lambton County OPP received complaints about election signs being removed without authorization in communities across the county.

OPP is asking anyone with information about the theft or damage of election signs to contact the Lambton County detachment at 1-888-310-1122.

Those wishing to remain anonymous can contact Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477) or submit a tip online through Sarnia-Lambton Crime Stoppers. Police note tipsters May be eligible for a cash reward of up to $2,000.

Municipal elections are scheduled to be held across Ontario on Oct. 26.

stories.title: Probes into Toronto’s shooter-for-hire network thwarted by impenetrable phone, police source says
stories.summary: Key cellphone seized in connection with the case runs on privacy-focused operating system, investigators so far unable to unlock it
stories.author: Joe Friesen, Robyn Doolittle
stories.content:
Investigations into a series of shootings in Toronto have been stymied because a key cellphone that was seized in connection with the case is running on a privacy-focused operating system and investigators have so far been unable to unlock the device, according to a police source.

Police believe the cellphone may contain communications and other data that could point to those responsible for ordering the shootings, including the March attack on the U.S. consulate, the source added.

In June, police launched a series of raids in response to the attack, as well as others on synagogues and local businesses in Toronto. An officer was killed in those operations and several suspects were arrested.

The phone operates on a little-known and highly secure operating system called GrapheneOS , reputed to be one of the most difficult to penetrate in the world, the source said. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source, who is not authorized to discuss the case.

GrapheneOS is available for users to download and install for free and is based on the Android Open Source Project, which allows developers to modify elements of the basic Android framework. GrapheneOS was created by Toronto programmer Daniel Micay.

The police theory is that these shootings, which targeted buildings, businesses and other property, are the work of a loose network of mercenary gunmen unconnected to their targets, hired like gig workers via encrypted messages.

While GrapheneOS represents a uniquely difficult challenge for law enforcement, security features built into other technology also pose a serious problem. Newly released models of the iPhone, for example, can be complicated for investigators to crack, as are messaging apps such as Signal and WhatsApp, which offer users encryption and auto-delete functions.

The Toronto Police Service said that while it cannot comment on the status of a particular forensic examination, its officers are seeing encrypted technology used to plan a range of criminal activity.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw has publicly expressed his support for new federal legislation currently before Parliament, Bill C-22, that in his view would assist investigators who encounter encrypted information.

The controversial bill would force electronic service providers to facilitate the interception of data to help police and intelligence services with investigations. But it has been opposed by tech companies and advocates for civil liberties.

“As criminals increasingly use encrypted technology to facilitate serious criminal activity, law enforcement needs the appropriate lawful tools to keep pace,” said Stephanie Sayer, a Toronto police spokesperson.

The GrapheneOS project said in a statement issued through its lawyers that, like any technology, it can be used for legitimate purposes or be misused by those involved in criminal activity. The project condemns all acts of violence, it said.

It also said it has not received any kind of request for assistance from a Canadian police force in recent months. If it were to receive such a request, the operating system is designed to make that type of assistance impossible, according to its statement.

“GrapheneOS is designed such that the project cannot bypass its own security protections. There are no backdoors, master keys, or remote access capabilities,” the statement said.

“This is a deliberate architectural choice: security that relies on the benevolence of the developer is not security at all.”

Experts say police are now able to crack many of the most popular cellphone configurations, thanks largely to the help of companies that specialize in digital forensics.

But GrapheneOS appears to be a different case.

It bills itself as a privacy- and security-focused operating system designed to protect against data theft, surveillance and security vulnerabilities. It has been praised by Edward Snowden, the former government contractor who revealed U.S. mass surveillance capabilities and was later charged with espionage.

Mr. Micay, who declined an interview request but responded to questions through his lawyer, started work in this domain more than a decade ago when he was 20 years old.

He eventually co-founded a company called Copperhead along with two others that later dissolved in a legal dispute that’s still before Ontario’s Superior Court. But the project continues as GrapheneOS, which is a registered non-profit in Canada.

GrapheneOS has about 350,000 to 400,000 users, according to its website, compared with the billion or more people using Apple’s standard iPhone operating system.

It’s funded by donations, which it says have been substantial, according to a post on its website earlier this year connected to a WIRED magazine article about the legal fight over Copperhead. The same post said that Mr. Micay’s income comes solely from sponsors on the GitHub platform, and that the GrapheneOS Foundation “is a non-profit and no one is getting rich from it.”

Mr. Micay said in court documents that he still contributes to the project but stepped down from the lead-developer role in 2023. The GrapheneOS Foundation lists Mr. Micay as a director, with a registered office address in Toronto.

In its statement to The Globe, GrapheneOS said its system, like other operating systems, has protections against unauthorized access.

“In cases where individuals are attempting to access a device without the owner’s PIN or password, operating systems have no way of knowing whether an ‘unauthorized’ access attempt is valid,” the statement said. “The project does not distinguish between ‘good’ and ‘bad’ actors, because such distinctions are inherently subjective and subject to abuse.”

The tradeoff to using this kind of high-security operating system is that it’s less convenient, so few people do it, said David Lie, a professor of computer and electrical engineering at the University of Toronto. But Prof. Lie said there’s no legal prohibition against using a privacy-focused operating system, and in some cases, it may be essential for political dissidents, activists and journalists.

Last year, an American political activist who had GrapheneOS installed on his phone was stopped at a U.S. border entry point. He was asked to provide the code to unlock the device and instead provided what’s known as a duress PIN, which triggered a mechanism that wiped his phone clean. He has since been charged with destroying property to prevent seizure.

GrapheneOS issued a post on social media earlier this year defending the duress PIN, which it described as one relatively minor feature in its suite of defences.

“GrapheneOS is completely legal. We have no obligation to weaken any of the security protections it provides,” the post said. “Laws attempting to make it illegal or require weakening the security would be unconstitutional.”

Bill Budington, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an organization that defends civil liberties in the digital sphere, said GrapheneOS’s effectiveness stems from the decision to treat any function that might compromise security as an opt-in choice for users.

“They’ve prioritized fixing areas of the operating system that will increase what’s called your attack surface, the places where an attacker can gain access to your device,” Mr. Budington said.

Mr. Budington said GrapheneOS is portrayed at times as a tool that appeals to bad actors, but that’s not accurate, in his view.

“There are a number of reasons why someone might want to use GrapheneOS rather than the base Android, and it has nothing at all to do with whether they’re committing crimes,” Mr. Budington said. “There are plenty of people using these operating systems because they don’t want [to give away] access to their devices.”

The technology’s appeal to criminal groups contributed to the breakdown of the Copperhead company in 2018, according to an affidavit filed by Mr. Micay.

He said his former business partner, James Donaldson, “decided to pursue business deals with criminal organizations.” The affidavit names a Canadian company called Phantom Secure, whose CEO was sentenced in the U.S. to nine years in prison for selling supposedly secure cellphones to transnational drug cartels.

Mr. Micay says in the court documents that he was uncomfortable with the proposals, which included making changes to the operating system’s security protocols and initiating remote updating systems that would allow third parties to have access to users’ phones.

He instead chose to delete part of the company’s technology to protect its users from interference from criminal organizations, the documents state. He subsequently ended his relationship with Mr. Donaldson, who is not connected to the GrapheneOS project.

Mr. Donaldson and Copperhead reject that version of events and said in their filings that they never pursued business deals with criminal organizations. They said the business relationship broke down because of Mr. Micay’s “belligerence and refusal to deal with Mr. Donaldson.”

Canadian authorities have long sought a law that would force electronic service providers to grant access to data in a timely manner, a provision some have compared to requiring an open electronic backdoor. Bill C-22, currently before Parliament, may finally grant law enforcement much of what they have been seeking. But how to strike a balance on privacy and security is the subject of intense debate.

Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto called the bill’s data-retention requirements, which would mandate electronic service providers keep detailed data of nearly every Canadian for a year, revealing their movements and who they contacted, “almost certainly unconstitutional.”

Major tech companies such as Signal, which provides secure messaging, and DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused search engine, have said they would withdraw from Canada if they were forced to reveal or retain user data that compromises users’ privacy.

Although it was once difficult for law enforcement to search locked cellphones, it’s now relatively routine, said Alain Filotto, a retired RCMP officer who now runs a digital-forensics company in B.C.

He said there are two major software companies that supply digital-forensic solutions to police: Cellebrite, with headquarters in Virginia, and Magnet Forensics, based in Waterloo, Ont.

“They can pretty much unlock any phone,” Mr. Filotto said.

Neither Cellebrite nor Magnet Forensics would comment on whether it has ever succeeded in extracting digital data from a phone running GrapheneOS.

The RCMP and the FBI also declined to comment on that question.

GrapheneOS is available for users to download and install for free and is based on the Android Open Source Project, which allows developers to modify elements of the basic Android framework. GrapheneOS was created by Toronto programmer Daniel Micay.

The police theory is that these shootings, which targeted buildings, businesses and other property, are the work of a loose network of mercenary gunmen unconnected to their targets, hired like gig workers via encrypted messages.

While GrapheneOS represents a uniquely difficult challenge for law enforcement, security features built into other technology also pose a serious problem. Newly released models of the iPhone, for example, can be complicated for investigators to crack, as are messaging apps such as Signal and WhatsApp, which offer users encryption and auto-delete functions.

The Toronto Police Service said that while it cannot comment on the status of a particular forensic examination, its officers are seeing encrypted technology used to plan a range of criminal activity.

Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw has publicly expressed his support for new federal legislation currently before Parliament, Bill C-22, that in his view would assist investigators who encounter encrypted information.

The controversial bill would force electronic service providers to facilitate the interception of data to help police and intelligence services with investigations. But it has been opposed by tech companies and advocates for civil liberties.

“As criminals increasingly use encrypted technology to facilitate serious criminal activity, law enforcement needs the appropriate lawful tools to keep pace,” said Stephanie Sayer, a Toronto police spokesperson.

The GrapheneOS project said in a statement issued through its lawyers that, like any technology, it can be used for legitimate purposes or be misused by those involved in criminal activity. The project condemns all acts of violence, it said.

It also said it has not received any kind of request for assistance from a Canadian police force in recent months. If it were to receive such a request, the operating system is designed to make that type of assistance impossible, according to its statement.
“GrapheneOS is designed such that the project cannot bypass its own security protections. There are no backdoors, master keys, or remote access capabilities,” the statement said.
“This is a deliberate architectural choice: security that relies on the benevolence of the developer is not security at all.”
Experts say police are now able to crack many of the most popular cellphone configurations, thanks largely to the help of companies that specialize in digital forensics.
But GrapheneOS appears to be a different case.

It bills itself as a privacy- and security-focused operating system designed to protect against data theft, surveillance and security vulnerabilities. It has been praised by Edward Snowden, the former government contractor who revealed U.S. mass surveillance capabilities and was later charged with espionage.
Mr. Micay, who declined an interview request but responded to questions through his lawyer, started work in this domain more than a decade ago when he was 20 years old.

He eventually co-founded a company called Copperhead along with two others that later dissolved in a legal dispute that’s still before Ontario’s Superior Court. But the project continues as GrapheneOS, which is a registered non-profit in Canada.
GrapheneOS has about 350,000 to 400,000 users, according to its website, compared with the billion or more people using Apple’s standard iPhone operating system.

It’s funded by donations, which it says have been substantial, according to a post on its website earlier this year connected to a WIRED magazine article about the legal fight over Copperhead. The same post said that Mr. Micay’s income comes solely from sponsors on the GitHub platform, and that the GrapheneOS Foundation “is a non-profit and no one is getting rich from it.”

Mr. Micay said in court documents that he still contributes to the project but stepped down from the lead-developer role in 2023. The GrapheneOS Foundation lists Mr. Micay as a director, with a registered office address in Toronto.
In its statement to The Globe, GrapheneOS said its system, like other operating systems, has protections against unauthorized access.

“In cases where individuals are attempting to access a device without the owner’s PIN or password, operating systems have no way of knowing whether an ‘unauthorized’ access attempt is valid,” the statement said. “The project does not distinguish between ‘good’ and ‘bad’ actors, because such distinctions are inherently subjective and subject to abuse.”

The tradeoff to using this kind of high-security operating system is that it’s less convenient, so few people do it, said David Lie, a professor of computer and electrical engineering at the University of Toronto. But Prof. Lie said there’s no legal prohibition against using a privacy-focused operating system, and in some cases, it may be essential for political dissidents, activists and journalists.

Last year, an American political activist who had GrapheneOS installed on his phone was stopped at a U.S. border entry point. He was asked to provide the code to unlock the device and instead provided what’s known as a duress PIN, which triggered a mechanism that wiped his phone clean. He has since been charged with destroying property to prevent seizure.
GrapheneOS issued a post on social media earlier this year defending the duress PIN, which it described as one relatively minor feature in its suite of defences.

“GrapheneOS is completely legal. We have no obligation to weaken any of the security protections it provides,” the post said. “Laws attempting to make it illegal or require weakening the security would be unconstitutional.”

Bill Budington, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, an organization that defends civil liberties in the digital sphere, said GrapheneOS’s effectiveness stems from the decision to treat any function that might compromise security as an opt-in choice for users.
“They’ve prioritized fixing areas of the operating system that will increase what’s called your attack surface, the places where an attacker can gain access to your device,” Mr. Budington said.
Mr. Budington said GrapheneOS is portrayed at times as a tool that appeals to bad actors, but that’s not accurate, in his view.

“There are a number of reasons why someone might want to use GrapheneOS rather than the base Android, and it has nothing at all to do with whether they’re committing crimes,” Mr. Budington said. “There are plenty of people using these operating systems because they don’t want [to give away] access to their devices.”
The technology’s appeal to criminal groups contributed to the breakdown of the Copperhead company in 2018, according to an affidavit filed by Mr. Micay.

He said his former business partner, James Donaldson, “decided to pursue business deals with criminal organizations.” The affidavit names a Canadian company called Phantom Secure, whose CEO was sentenced in the U.S. to nine years in prison for selling supposedly secure cellphones to transnational drug cartels.

Mr. Micay says in the court documents that he was uncomfortable with the proposals, which included making changes to the operating system’s security protocols and initiating remote updating systems that would allow third parties to have access to users’ phones.

He instead chose to delete part of the company’s technology to protect its users from interference from criminal organizations, the documents state. He subsequently ended his relationship with Mr. Donaldson, who is not connected to the GrapheneOS project.

Mr. Donaldson and Copperhead reject that version of events and said in their filings that they never pursued business deals with criminal organizations. They said the business relationship broke down because of Mr. Micay’s “belligerence and refusal to deal with Mr. Donaldson.”

Canadian authorities have long sought a law that would force electronic service providers to grant access to data in a timely manner, a provision some have compared to requiring an open electronic backdoor. Bill C-22, currently before Parliament, may finally grant law enforcement much of what they have been seeking. But how to strike a balance on privacy and security is the subject of intense debate.

Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto called the bill’s data-retention requirements, which would mandate electronic service providers keep detailed data of nearly every Canadian for a year, revealing their movements and who they contacted, “almost certainly unconstitutional.”

Major tech companies such as Signal, which provides secure messaging, and DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused search engine, have said they would withdraw from Canada if they were forced to reveal or retain user data that compromises users’ privacy.

Although it was once difficult for law enforcement to search locked cellphones, it’s now relatively routine, said Alain Filotto, a retired RCMP officer who now runs a digital-forensics company in B.C.
He said there are two major software companies that supply digital-forensic solutions to police: Cellebrite, with headquarters in Virginia, and Magnet Forensics, based in Waterloo, Ont.
“They can pretty much unlock any phone,” Mr. Filotto said.
Neither Cellebrite nor Magnet Forensics would comment on whether it has ever succeeded in extracting digital data from a phone running GrapheneOS.
The RCMP and the FBI also declined to comment on that question.
With research by Stephanie Chambers

stories.title: Here's how Buy Canadian scanner apps did on identifying food origins
stories.summary: Smartphone apps promising to help shoppers identify Canadian groceries have popped up since the onset of trade tensions with the United States last year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Smartphone apps promising to help shoppers identify Canadian groceries have popped up since the onset of trade tensions with the United States last year.

But how do these apps compare?

After reviewing more than a dozen options, The Canadian Press chose three apps to use on a variety of common grocery items.

Here are the results delivered by Buy Beaver, O SCANada and Maple Scan:

Pied-Mont Dora strawberry jam

Buy Beaver: The jam jar received a full score of 100 because it is manufactured in Quebec. The app didn’t provide information about the parent company or source of ingredients.

Buy Beaver rates items on a scale of zero to 100, which it says is based on the company’s manufacturing location, ingredient sources and the location of its parent company.

O SCANada: Dora was labelled as “Canadian-owned,” as it is a Canadian family-owned food manufacturer headquartered in Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que. It didn’t specify the origin of ingredients used to make the jam, which it said was not publicly disclosed.

Maple Scan: Pied-Mont Dora was identified as a Quebec-based company, labelling it as both made and packaged in Canada. It also offers the company’s history, highlighting its Canadian roots.

Kraft peanut butter

Buy Beaver: It scored zero because Kraft Heinz Co. is headquartered in the U.S. The app didn’t recognize its Canadian manufacturing location or source of ingredients.

O SCANada: The app said the product is “not Canadian-owned,” but correctly identified its manufacturing location in Mont-Royal, Que. Meanwhile, ingredient origins aren’t specified. “Origin of peanuts is not publicly disclosed,” the scan found.

Maple Scan: The PB was labelled as both made and manufactured in Canada.

Redpath granulated sugar

Buy Beaver: The sugar scored 70 for being a subsidiary of American Sugar Refining Inc., which it has been since 2007. The app said its manufacturing location is in Canada and that most of its ingredients are Canadian.

Though refined and packaged by Redpath, the majority of sugar cane used in Canadian sugar production is imported in bulk from tropical regions in South and Central America, according to the Canadian Sugar Institute, since Canada’s climate is not suitable for growing sugar cane.

O SCANada: The app called the product “not Canadian-owned,” correctly noting Redpath is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based company. The country of origin for sugar cane was not disclosed. It called the product “not Canadian-owned.”

Maple Scan: The sugar was called a product of Canada, made in Canada and packaged domestically. The app said the manufacturer is based in Ontario and identified American Sugar Refining as its parent company.

French’s tomato ketchup

Buy Beaver: The ketchup earned a score of 70 out of 100, with the app identifying the U.S.-based McCormick & Co. as its owner (McCormick Canada brought its French’s ketchup production in-house in 2021). Manufacturing locations were listed as Canada and Baltimore, Md. It said the ingredients were “100 per cent Canadian.”

O SCANada: The product was labelled “not Canadian-owned,” but knew that its manufacturing plant is in London, Ont. and made with Canadian tomatoes sourced from Ontario growers.

Maple Scan: The app said it is not a product of Canada, but is made in Canada with 100 per cent Canadian tomatoes, and is bottled in Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Base Line Road East to close for underground servicing work
stories.summary: A signed detour will direct traffic along High Street, Emery Street East and Ridout Street South.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A stretch of Base Line Road East will be closed for several days beginning Monday as crews complete underground servicing work in the area.

The City of London says Base Line Road East will be closed between High Street and Ridout Street South from Sept. 21 until approximately Sept. 24. The work involves connecting water, storm sewer and sanitary sewer services to a nearby property.

A signed detour will direct traffic along High Street, Emery Street East and Ridout Street South.

The south sidewalk within the construction zone will also be closed. Access to nearby homes will be maintained throughout the project, according to the city.

Some London Transit Commission routes will be affected by the closure. Transit riders are encouraged to check the LTC website for updated route and schedule information.

The work is taking place near the Wellington Gateway Phase 2A and 2B construction area. Motorists should expect delays and changing traffic conditions and are advised to follow posted detour signs.

stories.title: Ottawa building sovereign AI ecosystem for Canadian defence operations
stories.summary: Called the MAIple Stack, the initiative was launched last year, but few details have been released publicly about what it entails
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Canada is partnering with domestic artificial-intelligence technologies to enhance military operations, the Department of National Defence says, as the use of AI and data sovereignty become increasingly vital to national security and modern warfare.

Called the MAIple Stack, the initiative was launched last year, but few details have been released publicly about what it entails.

Through questions submitted to DND over the summer, The Globe and Mail has learned that MAIple Stack is bringing together a suite of sovereign AI technologies from Canadian companies for use in defence operations.

In a statement provided to The Globe, DND spokesperson Kened Sadiku said: “Ultimately, the initiative is intended to support [Canadian Armed Forces] personnel who operate in complex, data-rich environments, to improve situational awareness, and support faster, better-informed decision-making.”

He added that “Any companies that are involved with the MAIple Initiative at this time have been chosen through a lens of expanding Canada’s burgeoning sovereign AI ecosystem, ensuring partnerships with Canadian technology companies and alignment with the Defence Industrial Strategy.”

MAIple Stack represents a first step in assessing how the department, as well as the Forces, can implement future Canadian AI capabilities, he said.

AI is rapidly changing the way wars are fought. Militaries employing drones or sensors, for example, might use AI to help analyze and dissect the data collected by these devices. The technology is also being developed to speed up the pace of making decisions in military operations, as well as to create lifelike training simulations for soldiers away from the battlefield.

In recognition of this, the Armed Forces and DND released a 32-page AI Strategy in 2024 committing themselves to becoming “AI enabled” by 2030.

Despite the involvement of a handful of Canadian companies, Ottawa has offered little information about MAIple Stack’s function or importance. In response to a request for an interview about the initiative, the federal government initially agreed but later backed out, citing concerns over national security.

Ottawa answered an initial list of questions sent by The Globe but did not respond to a second set asking for further details, such as funding or examples of use in operations.

In the 2026-27 DND departmental plan, with a $33.5-million “seed investment,” a “key initiative” around the use of sovereign AI technology is cited as being tested in military deployments.

The AI initiative is being introduced through a phased approach, which the federal government said includes experimentation, integration into its operations and “lessons learned.” Canadian defence tech companies have previously asked for more opportunities to test their products with the Forces and make changes based on feedback, rather than trying to fit a one-time set of criteria for procurements.

“The ecosystem is designed to evolve as the Canadian AI industry grows and diversifies its capabilities,” he wrote.

stories.title: Carney eyes UN reform in New York, unclear whether he’ll meet Trump at Unga
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s attempt to bring Canada closer to Europe and strengthen ties with countries around the world will continue this week in U.S. President Donald Trump’s hometown, as he attends the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.
stories.author: Jeremie Charron, Mike Le Couteur
stories.content:
Ottawa - Prime Minister Mark Carney’s attempt to bring Canada closer to Europe and strengthen ties with countries around the world will continue this week in U.S. President Donald Trump’s hometown, as he attends the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (Unga) in New York City.

Senior government officials who briefed reporters ahead of the trip said Carney will meet with world leaders and business leaders, but it’s unclear if the prime minister and American president will meet on the sidelines of Unga.

As some world leaders, like Trump, move away from multilateralism, one of the things Carney will focus on is reform of the United Nations and selection of the organization’s next secretary-general. Antonio Guterres is in his second and final five-year term as head of the UN, which comes to a close at the end of this year.

“At a moment when the international order is being remade, Canada intends to help shape it,” Carney said in a statement ahead of the trip. “At the General Assembly, we will sit down with partners old and new, defend the rules that protect our sovereignty, and turn co-operation into real opportunity for Canadian workers and businesses.”

Senior government officials added that the prime minister will “call for concrete progress on UN reform efforts, so the organization remains relevant in this new context.” Officials noted that Carney wants to see reform that “helps the UN continue to be efficient and relevant in this period of significant global change.”

Part of that change has seen the Trump administration withdraw the U.S. from multiple UN agencies and organizations, like the World Health Organization and the cultural agency Unesco.

During a nearly one-hour speech at the General Assembly in 2025, during which the teleprompter stopped working, Trump railed against the UN and openly questioned the effectiveness of the organization, arguing it failed to serve U.S. interests.

“What is the purpose of the United Nations? The UN has such tremendous potential ... but it’s not even coming close to living up to that potential,” Trump said. Later, when meeting face-to-face with Guterres, Trump told the secretary-general, “our country is behind the United Nations 100 per cent.”

Advancing a two-state solution in the Middle East

On Tuesday, Carney is expected to co-host an event with France and the United Kingdom on the two-state solution, a year after the three countries recognized an independent Palestinian state at the General Assembly.

Last year, Canada recognized the state of Palestine as part of a co-ordinated international effort which Canadian officials said was to “preserve the viability of a two-state solution.”

That support came after the Palestinian Authority committed to advance governance reforms, pursue demilitarization and hold local elections.

Canadian officials told reporters these meetings will be an opportunity for nations to continue showing support for the two-state solution while looking at the implementation of key priorities and progress that has been made.

Face to Face with Trump

The Unga in New York will also mark the first time Prime Minister Carney and President Trump will be face-to-face since trade talks between the two countries fell apart.

After a caucus retreat on Parliament Hill Saturday, the prime minister was asked directly whether he has plans to meet with Trump in New York.

“We’ll meet with lots of leaders in New York,” said the prime minister, offering no definitive answer.

The question of a meeting in the Big Apple between the two leaders, or even with anyone from the U.S. administration, was also raised during a technical briefing with reporters ahead of Carney’s visit.

“Nothing is confirmed right now,” said a senior government official speaking on a not-for-attribution basis.

Meanwhile, Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum said last week that her country is getting closer to a deal with Trump, and hopes to reach a deal soon.

Asked Saturday about what that could mean for Canada, the prime minister responded that “it means we’re a sovereign country.”
