stories.title: B.C. Conservatives' Findlay resigns; interim leader named ahead of potential election
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia's political landscape continues to shift, with Kerry-Lynne Findlay stepping down as the leader of B-C's Conservatives Sunday, and the party's board of directors appointing MLA Lorne Doerkson as interim leader hours later.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - After weeks of defections, expulsions and ugly infighting that reduced the British Columbia Conservative caucus by more than a third, the official Opposition’s legislative ranks are growing again.

The party’s new interim leader, Lorne Doerkson — who was appointed Sunday after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay — has moved swiftly to restore five legislators to the caucus amid the prospect of an early election.

Former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford, and legislators Linda Hepner, Scott McInnis and Claire Rattée are all back in.

The party has been announcing the returns on social media on Monday under the slogan “Conservatives unite against the NDP.”

The appeal to unity comes after the tumultuous reign of Findlay, who had expelled Rustad, Halford and Rattée on Friday, with Hepner quitting early Sunday.

They were among 13 Conservatives who resigned or were evicted from the caucus since August, during upheaval centred on Findlay’s leadership and what some called “ideological purity tests.”

Findlay was narrowly chosen as leader in May, running on a platform of “faith, family and freedom.”

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were “obviously lots of people” in B.C. who don’t know Doerkson, a Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a “quality individual” and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.

“I am returning to do the work, not to run the next chapter from the outside,” Rustad later said on social media.

“If the new leadership wants my help, they will have it. I will not force my old vision onto them.”

Rustad said talks between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party — which now houses eight former Conservative MLAs — should succeed and the province “cannot afford two opposition parties” with an election on the cards.

But while the theme of the day was unity, there were still some recriminations.

Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to “let politics go.”

He said Clark and Campbell were among the “players” trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that “their time is over.”

“That May mean time is over for me, too. I don’t know,” said Rustad, adding that “it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside.”

Clark swiftly clapped back.

“John! Pull yourself together man,” she said on social media.

Clark had earlier said in an interview that different factions on the right in B.C. needed to come together, to resolve this “chaotic” moment.

The former BC Liberal premier said she had been fielding calls all day on the way forward.

“I’m reminding them all, that we all used to work together, and we can all do that again,” she said, calling the prospect of an election call less than two years into Premier David Eby’s mandate “absolutely unheard of and it is a disgrace.”

She said she was not playing matchmaker between Opposition factions.

“I’m not deeply involved in negotiations or anything of that nature. I am just sitting by my phone...(we) absolutely cannot afford another four years of this absolutely terrible government.”

Rustad — who said his “time as leader is over” but not his service to the province — said “high level” unity talks underway between the Conservatives and CentreBC had a 95 per cent chance of success.

The legislature’s updated party standings are 47 for the NDP — giving them a one-seat majority — with 29 Conservatives, two Greens, two vacancies, and 15 Independents, including those joining CentreBC.

The developments come after the caucus of B.C.‘s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.

An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad said there was a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives. He was reelected in 2024.

Rustad also provided a timeline of the chaos that preceded his short-lived expulsion from the Conservatives on Friday.

He said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”

The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.

But on Friday Rustad was told he was out.

Speculation about a snap election being called intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham would not be running for a sixth term.

NDP MLAs had met the previous night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.

“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

It went on to say the meeting was to “to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.

The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.

Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be “election ready.”

McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay’s leadership.

He said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return “home” came at a critical time for the province, and he rejected the need for “ideological purity tests.”

No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a “big tent party,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Rustad said talks between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party — which now houses eight former Conservative MLAs — should succeed and the province “cannot afford two opposition parties” with an election on the cards.
But while the theme of the day was unity, there were still some recriminations.
Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to “let politics go.”
He said Clark and Campbell were among the “players” trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that “their time is over.”
“That May mean time is over for me, too. I don’t know,” said Rustad, adding that “it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside.”
Clark swiftly clapped back.
“John! Pull yourself together man,” she said on social media.
Clark had earlier said in an interview that different factions on the right in B.C. needed to come together, to resolve this “chaotic” moment.
The former BC Liberal premier said she had been fielding calls all day on the way forward.

“I’m reminding them all, that we all used to work together, and we can all do that again,” she said, calling the prospect of an election call less than two years into Premier David Eby’s mandate “absolutely unheard of and it is a disgrace.”
She said she was not playing matchmaker between Opposition factions.
“I’m not deeply involved in negotiations or anything of that nature. I am just sitting by my phone...(we) absolutely cannot afford another four years of this absolutely terrible government.”
Rustad — who said his “time as leader is over” but not his service to the province — said “high level” unity talks underway between the Conservatives and CentreBC had a 95 per cent chance of success.

The legislature’s updated party standings are 47 for the NDP — giving them a one-seat majority — with 29 Conservatives, two Greens, two vacancies, and 15 Independents, including those joining CentreBC.

The developments come after the caucus of B.C.‘s governing NDP met Sunday night to discuss a potential early election in light of Findlay’s resignation, raising the prospect of voters going to the polls while the Opposition has no fixed candidate to become premier.
An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad said there was a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives. He was reelected in 2024.
Rustad also provided a timeline of the chaos that preceded his short-lived expulsion from the Conservatives on Friday.
He said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”
The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.
But on Friday Rustad was told he was out.
Speculation about a snap election being called intensified Monday when the NDP announced that cabinet minister Lana Popham would not be running for a sixth term.

NDP MLAs had met the previous night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.
“I’m sure you’ve seen by now, but KLF has resigned as leader of the BC Conservatives,” the email obtained by The Canadian Press said.

It went on to say the meeting was to “to discuss and hear from Cheryl and her team,” an apparent reference to Cheryl Oates, Eby’s former chief of staff, who has been appointed to manage the NDP campaign for the next election, whenever it is held.
The Canadian Press briefly attended the meeting, along with at least two Conservative legislators, before being asked to leave.
Eby said last week that he told his legislators they need to be “election ready.”
McInnis, who represents Columbia River-Revelstoke, had quit the Conservative caucus on Sept. 2, saying he did not agree with the direction of Findlay’s leadership.
He said in a statement on Monday that the opportunity to return “home” came at a critical time for the province, and he rejected the need for “ideological purity tests.”
No party had ever defeated the B.C. NDP without being a “big tent party,” he said.

stories.title: NDP meets on election prospects as B.C. Conservatives name Doerkson interim leader
stories.summary: Victoria — The caucus of British Columbia's governing NDP has met to discuss a potential early election after the resignation of Opposition B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:

The party’s new interim leader, Lorne Doerkson — who was appointed Sunday after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay — has moved swiftly to restore five legislators to the caucus amid the prospect of an early election.

Former leader John Rustad, former interim leader Trevor Halford, and legislators Linda Hepner, Scott McInnis and Claire Rattée are all back in.

The party has been announcing the returns on social media on Monday under the slogan “Conservatives unite against the NDP.”

The appeal to unity comes after the tumultuous reign of Findlay, who had expelled Rustad, Halford and Rattée on Friday, with Hepner quitting early Sunday.

They were among 13 Conservatives who resigned or were evicted from the caucus since August, during upheaval centred on Findlay’s leadership and what some called “ideological purity tests.”

Findlay was narrowly chosen as leader in May, running on a platform of “faith, family and freedom.”

Rustad told a news conference at the legislature that there were “obviously lots of people” in B.C. who don’t know Doerkson, a Cariboo-Chilcotin legislator, but he called Doerkson a “quality individual” and said he would be happy to have him lead the party into an election if he wanted.

“I am returning to do the work, not to run the next chapter from the outside,” Rustad later said on social media.

“If the new leadership wants my help, they will have it. I will not force my old vision onto them.”

Rustad said talks between the Conservatives and the breakaway CentreBC party — which now houses eight former Conservative MLAs — should succeed and the province “cannot afford two opposition parties” with an election on the cards.

But while the theme of the day was unity, there were still some recriminations.

Rustad said of speculation about the future of the Conservatives that people like former premiers Christy Clark and Gordon Campbell needed to “let politics go.”

He said Clark and Campbell were among the “players” trying now to manoeuvre what he called the centre right, and they should realize that “their time is over.”

“That may mean time is over for me, too. I don’t know,” said Rustad, adding that “it is time for that older generation of politicians to step aside.”

Clark swiftly clapped back.

“John! Pull yourself together man,” she said on social media.

Clark had earlier said in an interview that different factions on the right in B.C. needed to come together, to resolve this “chaotic” moment.

The former BC Liberal premier said she had been fielding calls all day on the way forward.

“I’m reminding them all, that we all used to work together, and we can all do that again,” she said, calling the prospect of an election call less than two years into Premier David Eby’s mandate “absolutely unheard of and it is a disgrace.”

She said she was not playing matchmaker between Opposition factions.

“I’m not deeply involved in negotiations or anything of that nature. I am just sitting by my phone…(we) absolutely cannot afford another four years of this absolutely terrible government.”

Rustad — who said his “time as leader is over” but not his service to the province — said “high level” unity talks underway between the Conservatives and CentreBC had a 95 per cent chance of success.

The legislature’s updated party standings are 47 for the NDP — giving them a one-seat majority — with 29 Conservatives, two Greens, two vacancies, and 15 Independents, including those joining CentreBC.

An interim leader is prohibited by the Conservative constitution from seeking the party leadership on a permanent basis, but Rustad said there was a way for Doerkson to become premier.

Doerkson was first elected in the riding of Cariboo—Chilcotin in 2020 as a member of the BC Liberal party, which rebranded as B.C. United, before he crossed the floor to join the Conservatives. He was reelected in 2024.

He said he asked Findlay to step down last Wednesday at a caucus meeting, where there was “emotion and frustration around the table.”

The next day he got a text from Findlay expelling him. Fifteen minutes later that was rescinded.

NDP MLAs had met the previous night to discuss Findlay’s departure, according to an email from party staff that was inadvertently sent to all legislators, instead of just those on the government benches.

MONTREAL - Leaders of Quebec’s political parties on Monday ruled out forming alliances with their opponents to govern, as polls point to a possible minority outcome with two weeks to go before the Oct. 5 provincial election.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said he’s not looking at forming an alliance with the Quebec Conservatives, or any other party, as opponents continued to try to paint his party and Éric Duhaime’s with the same brush.

stories.title: Montreal city council to debate bylaw banning insults against municipal employees
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal city council is set to debate a proposed bylaw this week that could ban people from insulting municipal employees, including police officers.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.scrape_error: 429 Client Error: Too Many Requests for url: https://www.thestar.com/news/canada/quebec/montreal-city-council-to-debate-bylaw-banning-insults-against-municipal-employees/article_de999693-d7c2-52d0-aa05-999fc8d05597.html
paragraphs: MONTREAL - Montreal city council has adopted a bylaw to ban people from insulting police officers and other municipal employees.
The debate over the rule lasted over half an hour, with the official opposition saying the proposed bylaw was “half-baked.” It was adopted with 35 voting in favour and 25 opposed.
“We are being asked to vote now and consult later,” said Marie Plourde, leader of the official opposition.
Under the bylaw, residents who insult city staff would face fines between $300 and $1,000 for a first offence. Subsequent offences could result in fines up to $2,000.
City officials have not said when they will implement the bylaw.

Yves Francoeur, head of the police brotherhood, has said his union’s members have been pushing for such a bylaw for years. But lawyers and civil rights groups worry the bylaw could infringe on the constitutional right to freedom of expression.
Other municipalities in the province, including Quebec City, Laval, Longueuil and Sherbrooke, already have similar bylaws.
The Canadian Press reported in June that some of these municipalities have issued thousands of fines over the past six years.
“Giving the middle finger, it’s not what will give you a ticket,” the mayor said before the council meeting. “Let’s just be honest. There’s bigger issues in terms of the attitude of some citizens.”
The new Montreal bylaw would ban insults, harassment, threats, abuse and intimidation, as well as offensive and aggressive behaviour.
It also includes provisions saying city employees could refuse to provide services to someone who misbehaves. However, the bylaw doesn’t define what could be construed as an insult.
City councillor Carla Beauvais heavily criticized the administration for not providing clear definitions. She also questioned the lack of public consultations.

“A threat can be proven. An offensive word is felt. And how a person feels can vary from one person to another. So where does the offence begin? Where does permissible anger end? The text doesn’t say,” said Beauvais.
She cited various decisions from the Quebec City municipal court in which judges could not agree on what constitutes an insult, raising concerns that the rule will cause a backlog at the courthouse.

Opposition councillor Martine Musau Muele added that council was asked to vote on the rule without adequate information. She said the documents councillors received did not provide statistics and reports to support the need for the bylaw.
She also said the city did not conduct any risk assessment or prove that the measures under the Criminal Code are insufficient to deal with belligerent residents.

“Citizens are extremely concerned. People do not understand the reasoning of the administration. What led you to decide that today, with everything going on, that this is the most optimal move?” Muele said. “This is a draft, not a proposal.”

The two councillors also raised concerns around giving police more powers while public trust is fragile. In June, Montreal police disbanded a night patrol unit in the multicultural neighbourhood of Montréal-Nord over allegations of racism and misconduct.

During council, Martinez Ferrada acknowledged that “there will be more questions around this bylaw in the coming months” but insisted the administration “needed to act.” She said the administration would make reports publicly available.

She said she “understands the concerns,” and “shares some of them.” However, she said incidents of inappropriate behaviour have increased dramatically and are harming city employees, and making it more difficult to recruit new employees.

“We are simply saying that there is a line between challenging an institution and engaging in behaviour that is inappropriate toward the people who work for it,” said the mayor. “The thousands of women and men who work every day to serve Montreal have the right to protection from their employer, which is us.”
She noted that women are most often the target of disrespectful behaviour and listed misogynistic insults she said employees commonly receive.

The debate around banning insults in Montreal resurfaced in March, after videos of a man insulting a police officer with misogynistic comments went viral. The man was charged in July with defamatory libel under the Criminal Code and had pleaded not guilty.
However, critics have said the bylaw could hinder de-escalation efforts and harm those who are victims of racial profiling, in crisis, or experiencing homelessness.

Four community organizations sent the mayor a letter on Sept. 17 expressing their concerns. These organizations include rights and freedom advocacy groups, a legal clinic and an anti-racism group based in the borough of Montréal-Nord, where the police patrol unit was disbanded.

“The proposed regulation does not merely prohibit violent behaviour or conduct that threatens physical integrity, which is already prohibited by the Criminal Code,” the four organizations wrote in a joint letter. “It bans expressions that are not threatening simply because they are likely to cause discomfort, for example, ‘offensive’ behaviour.’”
They also argued the rules could be applied arbitrarily because it would be left to police officers’ discretion to issue fines.
Another lawyer, Sibel Ataogul, has proposed offering free legal help to citizens contesting the bylaw.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

stories.title: Vigil to mark one year since Nooran Rezayi shot and killed by police in Longueuil
stories.summary: Longueuil - An evening vigil is being held in Longueuil to mark one year since 15-year-old Nooran Rezayi was shot and killed by a local police officer.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux The Canadian Press
stories.content:
LONGUEUIL - It took about 20 minutes for a procession of mourners to walk from a police station in Longueuil, Que., to the location where 15-year-old Nooran Rezayi was killed.

A year earlier, surveillance video released by his family’s lawyers appeared to show Rezayi was shot within seconds of police arriving at the scene.

When the group of about a dozen people reached the site Monday evening, Rezayi’s mother, Fahima Rezayi, clutched a small framed photograph of her son and screamed: “Justice for my son.”

The crowd then fell quiet for a minute of silence at the place where the teenager was killed on Sept. 21, 2025.

The vigil brought family, friends and supporters together on Montreal’s South Shore to mark a year without him — and a year spent waiting to learn whether the police officer who shot him will face criminal charges.

Many of those gathered outside the police station in Longueuil’s Saint-Hubert borough were dressed in black. Conversations were subdued, often little more than whispers, as the family stood together before beginning the walk.

Rezayi’s relatives occasionally embraced one another and wore white T-shirts bearing a photograph of the teenager smiling and giving a thumbs-up, alongside the words “Justice for Nooran.”

Nearby, several young people stood apart from the crowd wearing masks with messages calling for justice.

One person carried a sign reading “Nooran means light.” Another read “Forever 15.” Behind them, a large banner called for an end to police violence.

Rezayi’s sister, Frozan Rezayi, struggled through tears as she described her brother as “the light of our home, of our days,” and said he would remain the light of their hearts.

“He was a son, a brother, a cousin, a friend, a nephew, a child,” she told the crowd. “A child who brought joy everywhere he went.”

She remembered a teenager who liked making people laugh and smile, and who had dreams, plans and years of life still ahead of him.

“How has it already been a year since they took my brother’s life? And there are still no answers,” she said.

A year after Rezayi’s death, the central question for his family remains unresolved: whether the officer who shot him will face criminal charges.

Rezayi was killed after Longueuil police responded to a 911 call reporting a group of allegedly armed youths in a residential neighbourhood in Saint-Hubert.

Quebec’s police watchdog, the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes, later said the only firearm seized at the scene belonged to the officer who shot Rezayi. Investigators also seized a baseball bat, a backpack and ski masks.

The police watchdog completed its investigation in March and submitted its report to Quebec prosecutors, who must determine whether criminal charges should be laid.

Speaking at the vigil, family lawyer Fernando Belton said the lack of answers a year after the shooting has left Rezayi’s relatives living with uncertainty.

Belton told the crowd that the young people had been sitting on a sidewalk with their phones when police arrived and that Rezayi was shot within seconds. “Today, it is time to say: enough,” he said.

Belton said Rezayi’s death has also left other young people wondering about their own safety during encounters with police. “I think of every one of these young people who ask themselves, ‘Will I be next?’” he said.

He also spoke of parents fearing for their children when they leave home.

“I think of the mothers who have to send their child to school and who are forced to tell them, ‘Please, my boy, come back. Come back alive,’” Belton said.

He told Rezayi’s relatives their legal team would continue seeking answers. “We’re going to fight until the end to get justice for Nooran,” he said.

The shooting has led to several parallel proceedings. Six members of Rezayi’s family have filed a $2.2-million civil lawsuit against the City of Longueuil and its police force. The lawsuit alleges officers used unreasonable and disproportionate force. The allegations have not been tested in court.

The Quebec government has also launched an administrative investigation into the Longueuil police service over its actions following the shooting.

The police watchdog was notified of the shooting one hour and 36 minutes after it occurred. Documents released by Longueuil Mayor Catherine Fournier also indicated that Longueuil officers continued questioning witnesses at the scene.

Longueuil police have maintained their actions and the delay were justified under the circumstances.

Meanwhile, Montreal police conducted a separate criminal investigation into the alleged events preceding Rezayi’s death.

Eleven young people were charged in June, but prosecutors stayed the proceedings in August after obtaining new evidence that raised what they described as a complex legal issue. None of the charges involved possession of a firearm or harm to another person.

As the vigil returned to the place where her brother died, Frozan Rezayi urged those around her to keep saying his name.

“We are here to speak for Nooran, so that he is remembered,” she said. “So that his name continues to be heard.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

— with files from Erika Morris and Morgan Lowrie in Montreal

stories.title: Police officer injured after Yom Kippur shooting at Belleville synagogue
stories.summary: Shots went through stained glass windows, but the building wasn't breached
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
A Belleville, Ont., police officer is in critical but stable condition today after being shot while exchanging gunfire with a shooter outside a synagogue where worshipers had gathered to mark Yom Kippur on Sunday evening.

In a Monday press conference near the scene outside Sons of Jacob Congregation in the city’s east end, Belleville Police Service deputy chief Sheri Meeks said Const. Jeff Smith, a 13-year officer, has a long recovery ahead, but they are “encouraged by his progress.”

The suspected shooter, meanwhile, was identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward of nearby Quinte West, who is in life-threatening condition, according to the province’s Special Investigations Unit (SIU) spokesperson Kristy Denette.

“It’s my understanding that he was very critical and was (vital signs absent), but was sort of brought back to life, so to speak,” she said, noting he sustained “multiple strikes from the officer.”

It’s unclear what charges he might face and Meeks said Belleville police would not release any further information while SIU investigates.

Denette said preliminary evidence suggests Ward arrived in a black pickup truck just after 7 p.m. with a shotgun, which he fired at Smith, who was already on the scene in an unmarked police vehicle. Smith returned fire and was joined by another responding officer who also fired at Ward, who was struck.

As they continue to gather body-cam and police vehicle camera footage, Denette said it’s too early to determine the exact sequence of events.

“I don’t have a sense of timing right now, but what I can tell you is there are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me,” she said.

'Bang! Bang! Bang!': Confusion, gunshots during Yom Kippur service at Belleville synagogue

Police officer shot outside Belleville synagogue identified, faces 'significant road to recovery'

“And some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot-out windows, that sort of thing. So it would have been quite the scene indeed.”

Denette couldn’t confirm if the synagogue was damaged, but synagogue president Doug Weddum told National Post that stained glass windows decorating the outside were peppered with bullets.

The SIU spokesperson also couldn’t confirm if the place of worship was the target of the attack and refused to speculate, but said “common sense would say that probably was the case.”

Still, Denette stressed that the civilian-led SIU’s legislative mandate is to investigate police officers who have discharged their weapons in the line of duty, not Ward’s alleged crime.

A security guard on site identified only as Mike told The Intelligencer the first shot sounded like it came from a “heavy rifle” and was met with rounds from a smaller gun.

“Sitting there, we hear, ‘Pop! Pop! Pop!’ We don’t know if there’s only one shooter,” congregant Doug Lobel told National Post. “For me the biggest concern was … are they going to get into the building?”

The roughly 25 congregants took cover on the floor until police came in to sweep the building, after which they went to the police station by bus and returned home later. The synagogue has cancelled all remaining Yom Kippur day services and will advise when they will resume.

Tactical officers, aerial drones to scan neighbourhood backyards, and an armoured vehicle were dispatched during Belleville police’s initial response, according to The Intelligencer.

Neighbourhood resident Scott Granville posted a video to X that he said was recorded “about a half a block away after the majority of the gunfire.”

“I was a half a block away so heard but did not see the event,” he wrote. “I was close enough to worry about stray bullets though especially with the houses nearby.”

Denette said 20 to 30 gunshots “would be a fair estimate” based on early evidence.

A heavy police presence remained outside the synagogue on Monday, one which Denette said would remain for a couple of days.

“It’s quite a complex scene and there are a lot of cartridge cases to collect,” she explained. Reaction to another shooting incident near an Ontario synagogue was swift and widespread.

Premier Doug Ford said he “was disgusted” and expected all responsible to be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.

“My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear,” he said on social media.

“My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones. We owe an immense debt of gratitude to this brave officer and to all the first responders who acted so quickly to keep the community safe.”

Multiple synagogues in Ontario, specifically the Greater Toronto Area, have been targeted in shooting attacks in recent years as antisemitism grows in Canada. This March, three separate GTA synagogues were hit by gunfire within five days — Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto in Thornhill and North York’s Temle Emanu-el and Shaarei Shomayim. York Regional Police have charged three suspects in connection with a pair of the shootings.

John Fraser, a Liberal MPP in Ottawa, called it “a horrific act of antisemitic violence.”

The Jewish community is on high alert as they mark the holiest day of the year. Police forces had announced security plans for the Jewish holidays amid a wave of antisemitism.

“For years we have seen a growing number of Jewish centres targeted by gunfire,” said Fraser. “It was only a matter of time before someone was brazen enough to do something like this.”

Toronto Police Services said in a statement on X that it was not aware of any threats or connection to Toronto, but would still increase “visibility and patrols and synagogues and other places of worship out of an abundance of caution.”

“Our thoughts are with the Belleville police officer who was injured and their loved ones and colleagues.”

Police in York Region north of Toronto, about 180 kilometres away, said it understood the Belleville incident would ​cause concern in its jurisdiction, and they remain in contact with their “faith partners.”

“Our officers will continue to be visible in the areas where people gather to worship,” it said in a statement.
paragraphs: A Belleville, Ont., police officer is in critical but stable condition today after being shot while exchanging gunfire with a shooter outside a synagogue where worshipers had gathered to mark Yom Kippur on Sunday evening.

In a Monday press conference near the scene outside Sons of Jacob Congregation in the city’s east end, Belleville Police Service deputy chief Sheri Meeks said Const. Jeff Smith, a 13-year officer, has a long recovery ahead, but they are “encouraged by his progress.”

The suspected shooter, meanwhile, was identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward of nearby Quinte West, who is in life-threatening condition, according to the province’s Special Investigations Unit (SIU) spokesperson Kristy Denette.
“It’s my understanding that he was very critical and was (vital signs absent), but was sort of brought back to life, so to speak,” she said, noting he sustained “multiple strikes from the officer.”
It’s unclear what charges he might face and Meeks said Belleville police would not release any further information while SIU investigates.

Denette said preliminary evidence suggests Ward arrived in a black pickup truck just after 7 p.m. with a shotgun, which he fired at Smith, who was already on the scene in an unmarked police vehicle. Smith returned fire and was joined by another responding officer who also fired at Ward, who was struck.
As they continue to gather body-cam and police vehicle camera footage, Denette said it’s too early to determine the exact sequence of events.
“I don’t have a sense of timing right now, but what I can tell you is there are dozens of bullet holes in the street behind me,” she said.
'Bang! Bang! Bang!': Confusion, gunshots during Yom Kippur service at Belleville synagogue
Police officer shot outside Belleville synagogue identified, faces 'significant road to recovery'
“And some homes have been hit and there are some vehicles with shot-out windows, that sort of thing. So it would have been quite the scene indeed.”
Denette couldn’t confirm if the synagogue was damaged, but synagogue president Doug Weddum told National Post that stained glass windows decorating the outside were peppered with bullets.
The SIU spokesperson also couldn’t confirm if the place of worship was the target of the attack and refused to speculate, but said “common sense would say that probably was the case.”
Still, Denette stressed that the civilian-led SIU’s legislative mandate is to investigate police officers who have discharged their weapons in the line of duty, not Ward’s alleged crime.
A security guard on site identified only as Mike told The Intelligencer the first shot sounded like it came from a “heavy rifle” and was met with rounds from a smaller gun.

“Sitting there, we hear, ‘Pop! Pop! Pop!’ We don’t know if there’s only one shooter,” congregant Doug Lobel told National Post. “For me the biggest concern was … are they going to get into the building?”

The roughly 25 congregants took cover on the floor until police came in to sweep the building, after which they went to the police station by bus and returned home later. The synagogue has cancelled all remaining Yom Kippur day services and will advise when they will resume.
Tactical officers, aerial drones to scan neighbourhood backyards, and an armoured vehicle were dispatched during Belleville police’s initial response, according to The Intelligencer.
Neighbourhood resident Scott Granville posted a video to X that he said was recorded “about a half a block away after the majority of the gunfire.”
“I was a half a block away so heard but did not see the event,” he wrote. “I was close enough to worry about stray bullets though especially with the houses nearby.”
Denette said 20 to 30 gunshots “would be a fair estimate” based on early evidence.
A heavy police presence remained outside the synagogue on Monday, one which Denette said would remain for a couple of days.
“It’s quite a complex scene and there are a lot of cartridge cases to collect,” she explained. Reaction to another shooting incident near an Ontario synagogue was swift and widespread.
Premier Doug Ford said he “was disgusted” and expected all responsible to be prosecuted to the full extent of the law.
“My thoughts are with the Jewish community in Belleville and across Ontario, who have every right to gather and worship safely and without fear,” he said on social media.

“My thoughts are also with the police officer who was shot, along with their family and loved ones. We owe an immense debt of gratitude to this brave officer and to all the first responders who acted so quickly to keep the community safe.”

Multiple synagogues in Ontario, specifically the Greater Toronto Area, have been targeted in shooting attacks in recent years as antisemitism grows in Canada. This March, three separate GTA synagogues were hit by gunfire within five days — Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto in Thornhill and North York’s Temle Emanu-el and Shaarei Shomayim. York Regional Police have charged three suspects in connection with a pair of the shootings.
John Fraser, a Liberal MPP in Ottawa, called it “a horrific act of antisemitic violence.”
The Jewish community is on high alert as they mark the holiest day of the year. Police forces had announced security plans for the Jewish holidays amid a wave of antisemitism.
“For years we have seen a growing number of Jewish centres targeted by gunfire,” said Fraser. “It was only a matter of time before someone was brazen enough to do something like this.”

Toronto Police Services said in a statement on X that it was not aware of any threats or connection to Toronto, but would still increase “visibility and patrols and synagogues and other places of worship out of an abundance of caution.”
“Our thoughts are with the Belleville police officer who was injured and their loved ones and colleagues.”

Police in York Region north of Toronto, about 180 kilometres away, said it understood the Belleville incident would ​cause concern in its jurisdiction, and they remain in contact with their “faith partners.”
“Our officers will continue to be visible in the areas where people gather to worship,” it said in a statement.

stories.title: Shooting near Belleville synagogue leaves two injured, including police officer
stories.summary: The incident occurred at 7:10 p.m. in the area of Bleecker and Victoria avenues, leaving an individual and Belleville officer injured after an exchange of gunfire, police say.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin
stories.content:
A shooting near a Belleville, Ont., synagogue left a police officer injured Sunday night as many were gathering to observe Yom Kippur.

An officer encountered an individual at about 7:10 p.m. in the area of Bleecker and Victoria avenues , the Belleville Police Service said in a news release .

Both were injured and transported to the hospital, police added.

Officers noted that there was no further threat to public safety, but advised the public to avoid the area.

Belleville police notified Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, which later said it invoked its mandate “following an exchange of gunfire near the Sons of Jacob synagogue.”

The SIU said Monday morning that a spokesperson would provide an update from the area at about 11 a.m.

The watchdog is called to investigate the conduct of officers in Ontario when police interactions may have resulted in death, serious injury, a firearm discharge or sexual assault.

Toronto police have increased patrols at synagogues and other places of worship “out of an abundance of caution,” they posted on social media Sunday night, adding that there’s no known threat to Toronto.

“I’m disgusted by the shooting that took place outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville earlier this evening as Jewish community members gathered to mark Yom Kippur,” Ford wrote. “I expect that all those responsible are arrested and prosecuted to the full extent of the law.”

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow issued a statement regarding the need for increased security for Jewish communities following the incident.

“Jewish Torontonians should not need police presence to observe Yom Kippur, or to simply live their day-to-day lives,” she s aid on social media Sunday night.

She also added that “no expense will be spared” in keeping the community safe amid rising antisemitism.

Ottawa South MPP John Fraser called the shooting at a place of worship “cowardly and disgusting.”

Fraser also said no one at the synagogue was injured.

stories.title: A modern B.C. cabin invites you to gather and enjoy the view – preferably with a glass of wine
stories.summary: In B.C. wine country, a contemporary cabin invites you to pour a glass and enjoy the view
stories.author: Matthew Hague
stories.content:
In B.C. wine country, a contemporary cabin invites you to pour a glass and enjoy the view

Every three to four weeks, Carey Doberstein, a political science professor, and Jesse Goodwin, a physician, make a five-hour trek from their condo in Vancouver to their cabin in the Okanagan. They love when their friends come along, spending a week or two enjoying the charms of the area. “We bike around to different wineries,” Doberstein says.

“We like independent places such as Daydreamer,” Goodwin says. “Their sparkling shiraz is a favourite.”

The cabin itself, on a hillside near the town of Naramata, is relatively compact. It has about 120 square metres of living space on one level, including three small bedrooms. “We didn’t want the bedrooms to be large,” Goodwin says. “It’s not about coming here and spending time alone in your room. It’s about gathering together or going outside.”

Just over half the floor plan, about 70 square metres, is a communal great room combining kitchen, dining and living areas. It’s flanked on two sides by large terraces that, in good weather, double the space to socialize, chat and sip wine. To the east, there is a secluded courtyard with a fire pit. To the west, a balcony with expansive views of Okanagan Lake and the surrounding mountains.

The cabin was designed by Sanders Green, a local architecture firm co-founded by Warren Sanders, a childhood friend of Doberstein, and Will Green. “Warren and Will really thought about how the sun moves throughout the day,” Doberstein says. “The courtyard is better in the mornings, before the sun rises over the mountains, or later in the evening, when the sun is setting on the other side of the house.”

Both terraces are connected to the great room by floor-to-ceiling, sliding glass doors. “That way we never lose sight of one of the best features of the house,” Doberstein says. “Even in the back courtyard, we can look through the house and out the other side. We always see the vineyards and the lake.”

The interiors accentuate the vista. The ceiling tilts up toward the lake, allowing for larger windows to the west, essentially turning the centre of the home into a giant viewfinder. The room is a relatively narrow five metres deep but about three times as long. “We really focused on the proportions of that room,” Sanders says. “We didn’t want it to be too wide, or the overhangs too large, to pull anyone too far from the landscape.”

For the furniture and decor, Doberstein and Goodwin worked with Brittany McMullen of Third Street Studio, who also designed the couple’s city place. “The goal was to kind of keep things low and lounge-y, so we weren’t obstructing sight lines to the mountains,” McMullen says. “I also wanted to keep the palette low key. It’s a cabin. A lot of the colours were inspired by the surrounding nature.”

Throughout, natural woods such as white oak cabinets and cedar ceilings create a sense of warmth. Organic materials, including a wool area rug from Vancouver’s Solari, add texture. Although there is a desk tucked in one corner – “it’s a place to park a laptop and get things done as needed,” McMullen says – the overall vibe is restful, rustic and unplugged.

The same is true on the exterior, where everything is elemental. The cabin is wrapped in charred cedar, a rot and insect-resistant cladding, and rests on walls of hand-placed stones that were found on the site. “I think in the Okanagan there’s so much pressure to build the biggest thing possible,” Sanders says. “Our approach here was to really respect the site and reflect the people who live there.”

After Doberstein and Goodwin moved into their cabin, McMullen felt there was something missing in the dining area. “They entertain often,” she says. “So why not a fun bar cart?” She picked the Arcade Bar Cart, a Deco-inspired option from Canadian brand Gus Modern.

For their finishes, Doberstein and Goodwin wanted low maintenance options. In the kitchen, Sanders Green selected a backsplash that looks like travertine, a stain-prone stone, but is actually Dekton, an engineered Spanish product that doesn’t mark, even when doused in red wine.

paragraphs: In B.C. wine country, a contemporary cabin invites you to pour a glass and enjoy the view

Every three to four weeks, Carey Doberstein, a political science professor, and Jesse Goodwin, a physician, make a five-hour trek from their condo in Vancouver to their cabin in the Okanagan. They love when their friends come along, spending a week or two enjoying the charms of the area. “We bike around to different wineries,” Doberstein says.
“We like independent places such as Daydreamer,” Goodwin says. “Their sparkling shiraz is a favourite.”

The cabin itself, on a hillside near the town of Naramata, is relatively compact. It has about 120 square metres of living space on one level, including three small bedrooms. “We didn’t want the bedrooms to be large,” Goodwin says. “It’s not about coming here and spending time alone in your room. It’s about gathering together or going outside.”

Just over half the floor plan, about 70 square metres, is a communal great room combining kitchen, dining and living areas. It’s flanked on two sides by large terraces that, in good weather, double the space to socialize, chat and sip wine. To the east, there is a secluded courtyard with a fire pit. To the west, a balcony with expansive views of Okanagan Lake and the surrounding mountains.

The cabin was designed by Sanders Green, a local architecture firm co-founded by Warren Sanders, a childhood friend of Doberstein, and Will Green. “Warren and Will really thought about how the sun moves throughout the day,” Doberstein says. “The courtyard is better in the mornings, before the sun rises over the mountains, or later in the evening, when the sun is setting on the other side of the house.”

Both terraces are connected to the great room by floor-to-ceiling, sliding glass doors. “That way we never lose sight of one of the best features of the house,” Doberstein says. “Even in the back courtyard, we can look through the house and out the other side. We always see the vineyards and the lake.”

The interiors accentuate the vista. The ceiling tilts up toward the lake, allowing for larger windows to the west, essentially turning the centre of the home into a giant viewfinder. The room is a relatively narrow five metres deep but about three times as long. “We really focused on the proportions of that room,” Sanders says. “We didn’t want it to be too wide, or the overhangs too large, to pull anyone too far from the landscape.”

For the furniture and decor, Doberstein and Goodwin worked with Brittany McMullen of Third Street Studio, who also designed the couple’s city place. “The goal was to kind of keep things low and lounge-y, so we weren’t obstructing sight lines to the mountains,” McMullen says. “I also wanted to keep the palette low key. It’s a cabin. A lot of the colours were inspired by the surrounding nature.”

Throughout, natural woods such as white oak cabinets and cedar ceilings create a sense of warmth. Organic materials, including a wool area rug from Vancouver’s Solari, add texture. Although there is a desk tucked in one corner – “it’s a place to park a laptop and get things done as needed,” McMullen says – the overall vibe is restful, rustic and unplugged.

The same is true on the exterior, where everything is elemental. The cabin is wrapped in charred cedar, a rot and insect-resistant cladding, and rests on walls of hand-placed stones that were found on the site. “I think in the Okanagan there’s so much pressure to build the biggest thing possible,” Sanders says. “Our approach here was to really respect the site and reflect the people who live there.”

After Doberstein and Goodwin moved into their cabin, McMullen felt there was something missing in the dining area. “They entertain often,” she says. “So why not a fun bar cart?” She picked the Arcade Bar Cart, a Deco-inspired option from Canadian brand Gus Modern.

Because the layout of the great room is unique, McMullen ordered a custom rug from the Vancouver store Salari. To compliment the natural palette of the space, she picked the Beat Moda D 129/61, which incorporates brown, beige and rust tones.
The dining chairs, from Canadian brand Sundays, are called Tuck because the armrests slide neatly under a standard-height dining table. The low profile helps maintain clean sight lines.
The blackened oak of the Tangerine stools by New Zealand brand Resident at the kitchen island echoes the unique, charred cladding that wraps the outside of the house.

stories.title: I visited Kalamazoo to find out why people in Michigan wanted to celebrate Canada.
stories.summary: As Donald Trump insults Canada, a festival in Kalamazoo, Michigan, celebrates the deep connections and shared culture between the two countries.
stories.author: Francine Kopun
stories.content:
KALAMAZOO, MICH. — While U.S. President Donald Trump was insulting Canadians, a Kalamazoo woman in white work boots with red maple leaves on the toes was feverishly plotting to celebrate them, which is why, on one of the last nights of summer, Rush lyrics could be heard slipping down the stairs of a live music venue onto the treed pedestrian mall of this Midwestern city.

Upstairs, locals were rocking out to a local band, Rock RX, along with organizers of the fourth annual Can-Am Peace Jam , a celebration of Canadian culture meant to repair the fraying bonds of friendship between two countries that have been kindred neighbours for more than 150 years, north and south of a border that used to feel nominal.

A festival born from frustration

Many of the people in this town of roughly 73,000, like Channon Russette-Mondoux, the woman in the maple leaf work boots, have strong connections to Canada, often through marriage. Russette-Mondoux was born in Windsor, where she met her husband, an American, and followed him to Kalamazoo for work when their children were young.

She became an American citizen in 2015 in order to exercise her right to vote, and still has family in Canada. Her three adult children have made lives for themselves in the U.S.

“Many Americans are heartbroken at what’s happening right now. They apologize to me all the time,” says Russette-Mondoux, who teaches culinary arts at Western Michigan University. “I mean, there’s still people, don’t get me wrong, that are hateful, and they drink everything that is said by the current administration, but the vast majority of people are just mortified at what’s going on right now.”

Russette-Mondoux began throwing Canadiana Fest in Kalamazoo in 2023 as a way of sharing her culture with her adopted home. Attendance grew each year, hitting a high of 2,500 in 2025.

This year, amid the combative rhetoric about Canada pouring from the White House, including the renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” Russette-Mondoux felt the need to tweak the name of the festival to reflect the bonds that the two countries share, especially in this place, home to First Nations; a waterway for French coureurs de bois of the 17 th century, and the adopted home for French-speaking Acadians expelled from what is now Nova Scotia, in the 18 th century.

The event featured Canadian bands and local bands playing Canadian hits, from Rush to Bryan Adams, Alanis Morissette, the Barenaked Ladies, Avril Lavigne, Tom Cochrane and Nickelback.

It also featured a curling demonstration, arts and crafts by local vendors, Canadiana merchandise — and a genealogist to help festival goers trace their Canadian heritage.

Food trucks, which were going to participate in a poutine cook-off, had to cancel, after the event was moved indoors due to weather.

Besides being a punchline for a joke about the middle of nowhere, Kalamazoo is a university town, a blue dot in a sea of red, where proud Democrats feel woefully embarrassed by Trump and his statements about Canadians being clowns, spoiled and difficult.

When asked about Trump and Canada, answers here are often preceded by a pause and a sorrowful shake of the head.

“Relations with other countries will outlast Donald Trump,” says Drew Duncan, the vice-mayor of Kalamazoo, pressed into service as a judge for the best butter-tart contest at the festival.

“And while he is our president and many of us are embarrassed by how he’s conducted himself in office, our relationship with Canada, particularly Canada and Kalamazoo, continues to be strong, and we want to continue to grow that relationship and nurture that relationship regardless of who is in the White House or in office.”

Down the hall, Gloria Baldwin-Wilson, general co-ordinator for Indivisible Greater Kalamazoo, has a message for Canadians.

“We’re sorry. Have patience. We’re trying to get rid of this administration,” says Baldwin-Wilson, whose organization focuses on civic engagement and resisting authoritarianism. The group is working to get people to vote early in the upcoming midterm elections, which could determine how effectively Trump can continue to govern.

In November, voters will decide on all 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and about one-third of the U.S. Senate. A shift to a Democratic majority could result in blocked legislative agendas for Trump, stalled judicial appointments and intense congressional oversight.

“We’re a democracy, and we’re fighting for democracy. The vote is bedrock to that,” says Baldwin-Wilson.

Immigration lawyer Emilia Coto, who staffed a booth at the festival, says applications for Canadian citizenship are up, in the wake of recent changes that make it easier for older residents and for claimants based on ancestry to move to Canada.

“People say: ‘I don’t feel that my values are being represented by the current government, and I want to be in a place that reflects that,” says Coto.

“I’ve also had people that are worried about their children being drafted into potential wars.”

How tariffs hit Michigan’s hidden factories

Kalamazoo is also an industrial Midwestern hub, proud headquarters to S&P heavyweights like Stryker, a titan in the health-care sector, with a market capitalization of $105 billion, and Pfizer’s massive global supply manufacturing facility, which both operate out of nearby Portage, a contiguous suburb.

The local economy is packed with hidden factories that build parts for the transnational auto industry and the office furniture industry, which rely on tightly integrated supply chains that frequently cross borders. Tariffs on steel, aluminum and advanced components hit West Michigan uniquely hard .

Studies have pegged the cost of those tariffs at about $3,200 a year to the average Michigan household in higher prices and business expenses.

The tariffs have created a climate of instability for businesses, says Duncan, speaking generally, and not about a specific business.

“If I went from having something that I could get at a fixed cost one month, and then the next week and the next week and the next week, it’s a different cost, it’s really hard to stabilize my finances as a business,” says Duncan.

Three location changes, zero surrender

Russette-Mondoux is so committed to the festival that she kept it moving despite three location changes this year — the last one driven by weather — pouring rain and threats of thunderstorms. She managed the last venue change in four days, persuading a local businessman, Harvin Sandhu Singh, to loan them his events centre, and persuading as many participants as possible to show up.

The event started at 1 p.m. and at 10 p.m., Mélisande, a Quebec-based group that blends traditional Québecois and Acadian folk music with modern electronic beats and synthesizers, had everyone on their feet — even bone-tired organizers — as the festival drew to a close at 11 p.m.

Music stopped pouring down the stairs to the street.

The lyrics for Rush’s anthem to independent thought, “Tom Sawyer,” faded out too.

stories.title: Branch out with a free tree this National Tree Day
stories.summary: Pick up a free tree this National Tree Day ! The City of London is giving away more than 2,000 trees on Wednesday, September 23 for residents to plant at home.
stories.content:
Pick up a free tree this National Tree Day ! The City of London is giving away more than 2,000 trees on Wednesday, September 23 for residents to plant at home.

This year, the tree giveaway will be held in the south end of London. Meet City staff at Westminster Drive near Colonel Talbot Road between 8 a.m. and 7 p.m. to pick up your free tree.

“We are excited to once again celebrate National Tree Day with a tree giveaway for Londoners,” says Shawna Chambers, Director of Climate Change, Environment & Waste Management. “Each year, we give out more than 5,000 trees to Londoners – and our crews plant about 5,000 across the city. This helps us grow, maintain and protect our thriving urban forest.”

The City’s Urban Forest Strategy sets out a target of 34% tree canopy cover by 2065, and London is on track to meet that goal. Currently, London has over seven million trees, including about 1.8 million that are owned and maintained by the City.

It is important to protect and maintain newly planted trees for the first year after they have been planted. Residents can find helpful tips and resources at London.CA/trees .

List of available trees (while supplies last):

Sugar Maple

Red Maple

Tulip Tree

Bitternut Hickory

Blue Beech

Redbud

Serviceberry

Canada Plum

Pawpaw

White Pine

White Spruce

Tamarack

Black Gum

Honeycrisp Apple

Bartlett Pear

Romeo & Juliet Cherry

Harovin Nova Nectarine

In addition, each car will receive one free bag of Green Bin compost with their tree(s), while supplies last.

Above: Map of tree giveaway site, located on Westminster Drive.

Our tree giveaway will be set up on Westminster Drive near Colonel Talbot Road.

Please also note that you will not be able to turn onto Westminster Drive from Wonderland Road South. This intersection will be closed.

The City is committed to providing accessible accommodations for residents. If you require an accommodation to obtain or plant your tree, please call 519-661-2489, extension 4457.

September 20 to 26 marks National Forest Week. In addition to the tree giveaway, check out the other celebrations taking place across the city:

Learn how to build a mini forest in your backyard on Monday, September 21 at 6 p.m. at Earl Nichols Arena ( registration required )

Guided nature walk at Medway Valley Heritage Forest on Wednesday, September 23 from 6 to 7:30 p.m. ( registration required )

London Forest Fest on Saturday, September 26 from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at Westminster Ponds Environmentally Significant Area (ESA) in partnership with the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority

stories.title: Could these pills help people with anorexia? A new study aims to find out
stories.summary: A new clinical trial is recruiting people diagnosed with anorexia nervosa as researchers hope to discover if fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) capsules could help better manage this eating disorder.
stories.content:
Media Release September 21, 2026

A new clinical trial is recruiting people diagnosed with anorexia nervosa as researchers hope to discover if fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) capsules could help better manage this eating disorder. Led by researchers at London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri), Lawson Research Institute (Lawson) of St. Joseph’s Health Care London, and Western University, the novel study will investigate whether these capsules can restore healthy gut bacteria (the microbiome), improve nutrition, and modify how people make food choices.

Anorexia nervosa is a severe and sometimes life-threatening condition that leads a person to perceive themselves as overweight and that they must restrict food consumption and/or exercise continuously to reduce their weight. Researchers have noticed that patients with anorexia nervosa also have a disturbance in their gut microbiome which could be linked to how they think about food and their body. “There appears to be a direct link between the gut microbiome and how the brain functions,” says study co-lead Dr. Elizabeth Osuch, researcher at Lhscri, Psychiatrist at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and Professor at Western University. “This connection is thought to occur through chemical processes that convey information from the gut to the brain. Since we take the FMT capsules from healthy donors, we think we can enhance the microbiome of people with anorexia nervosa, which in turn could also signal the brain to develop a healthier emotional process, improve nutrition and positively impact self-perception.” The research would not be possible without the pioneering work of the Lawson FMT team, who are collaborators on the study process and who have customized the capsules specifically for this study. The Lawson team – under the leadership of Scientist Dr. Michael Silverman, Medical Director of the Infectious Diseases Program at St. Joseph’s, and Seema Nair Parvathy, Scientific Director of the FMT program at Lawson – screens stool donors, ensuring only healthy stool without harmful bacteria or other issues is used, and processes samples into tasteless, odorless pills. “Eating disorders can be stubbornly difficult to treat, even with a combination of psychological therapy, nutritional counselling and medical monitoring,” says microbiologist Jeremy Burton, Interim Vice-President Research of St Joseph’s and Scientific Director of Lawson and co-leader of the study with Dr. Osuch. “As unconventional as the FMT approach May seem, it could give hope to struggling patients and their families – while also supporting evidence that mental health and physical health are often linked through the gut microbiome.”

Participants will ingest capsules and complete questionnaires as well as provide stool samples before and several times after the intervention. They will be followed carefully to examine the effects of the procedure. Both Lawson and Lhscri are leaders in FMT research and have conducted world-first studies which have also shown promise in the field of cancer. It also is an approved treatment for patients with Clostridioides difficile (C. diff), which is a condition where bacterium produces toxins and infects the colon causing inflammation. The study is being funded by the Academic Medical Organization of Southwestern Ontario (Amoso). “Our hope is that the clinical trial shows positive outcomes for individuals with anorexia nervosa and it becomes a standard treatment option for those whom there are currently very few treatment choices” says Dr. Osuch. The study is seeking to recruit 20 research participants. To be eligible, participants must be:

Ages 16 – 35

Diagnosed with anorexia nervosa, restricting type and not in active cognitive behavioural therapy (and not in hospital)

Able to travel to London Health Sciences Centre at 54 Riverview Avenue and St. Joseph’s Hospital at 268 Grosvenor Street

See full eligibility criteria here

For more information or to express interest, please contact michael.wammes@LHSC.on.CA or 519-646-6000 ext 65196.

Since we take the FMT capsules from healthy donors, we think we can enhance the microbiome of people with anorexia nervosa, which in turn could also signal the brain to develop a healthier emotional process, improve nutrition and positively impact self-perception.” The research would not be possible without the pioneering work of the Lawson FMT team, who are collaborators on the study process and who have customized the capsules specifically for this study. The Lawson team – under the leadership of Scientist Dr. Michael Silverman, Medical Director of the Infectious Diseases Program at St. Joseph’s, and Seema Nair Parvathy, Scientific Director of the FMT program at Lawson – screens stool donors, ensuring only healthy stool without harmful bacteria or other issues is used, and processes samples into tasteless, odorless pills. “Eating disorders can be stubbornly difficult to treat, even with a combination of psychological therapy, nutritional counselling and medical monitoring,” says microbiologist Jeremy Burton, Interim Vice-President Research of St Joseph’s and Scientific Director of Lawson and co-leader of the study with Dr. Osuch. “As unconventional as the FMT approach May seem, it could give hope to struggling patients and their families – while also supporting evidence that mental health and physical health are often linked through the gut microbiome.”

stories.title: Spreading joy through Great Moments
stories.summary: September 21, 2026
stories.content:
Above: Claire Nicholson hugs her Mark and Ollie dollies.

September 21, 2026

In paediatric health care, treating a child's illness is only one part of the equation. Equally important is caring for the whole child: supporting their emotional health, nurturing their sense of identity, and creating moments of comfort and joy amid uncertainty. Across Children's Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), countless staff members contribute to this work every day, often through simple acts of kindness that leave a lasting impression on patients and families.

Two of those team members are Mark Browning, Aide in the Paediatric Medical Day Unit (PMDU), and Ollie, Children's Hospital’s very own therapeutic clown made possible through Children's Health Foundation . Both Mark and Ollie play an integral role in bringing joy to children spending time in hospital, whether it be for a routine appointment or longer inpatient stays.

One patient who has formed a particularly special bond with Mark and Ollie is Claire Nicholson. Claire, now seven, was diagnosed with leukemia just before her first birthday. In those early days, when almost every new face was overwhelming, Mark became one of the first people Claire allowed into her world. At a time when much of her life was filled with medical appointments and unfamiliar environments, Mark offered something different. He was not there to poke, prod, or examine. He was there to play, to laugh, and to connect.

Ollie became part of Claire's journey later on. Over time, both Mark and Ollie became familiar, trusted people in Claire's life. Through long hospital stays, outpatient appointments, and two relapses, Children's Hospital at LHSC became a second home for Claire and her family. Mark and Ollie became part of the family they built there.

"Any time we go to the hospital, Mark and Ollie are the first people Claire looks for," says Claire's Mom, Mandy Nicholson. "It has been incredible to watch their relationship grow as she has grown and to have those moments of joy, not only for Claire, but for me too."

For Nicholson, that joy made an immeasurable difference. During some of their darkest and most frightening moments, Mark and Ollie had a way of shifting the energy in the room.

"I can't imagine going through everything without them," says Nicholson. "They brought so much light to us during such a dark time. Without these interactions, there would have been so much more fear and so many more tears."

Mark and Ollie connected with Claire by remembering the pieces of her personality that make her who she is. They joined in on her humour, her games, and her imagination. To someone outside the room, those moments may have seemed small, but to Claire and her family, they were unforgettable. That understanding helped Mark and Ollie occupy a special place in Claire's care journey. They were part of the hospital, but they were not associated with the parts that scared her. Claire knew they were not coming to do a procedure; they were coming as friends.

Some of the family's most treasured memories reflect that friendship. When Claire had to travel to Toronto for care, Ollie made special 'Mark and Ollie dollies' for her to take along. Years later, she still has them.

"I started making the dolls because children would often ask if I could come with them when they had to receive treatment elsewhere or even one time when a child wanted me to go with them to Florida," says Ollie. "While I can't physically go, I wanted them to be able to take a piece of that connection with them. I made dolls of both myself and Mark for Claire so she could take us with her to Toronto."

For Nicholson, those dolls are a reminder that Mark and Ollie's impact extended beyond the hospital walls. Even when Claire's care journey took her away from the people and places that had become so familiar, Mark and Ollie were always with her.

The connection they have built has endured as Claire has grown. As appointments have become fewer and farther between, the family still looks forward to seeing Mark and Ollie when they visit. Nicholson says there are many people who made a difference during Claire's journey, but some relationships naturally fade over time. Mark and Ollie, however, have remained constant.

One moment in particular stays with Nicholson. When Claire relapsed for the first time and the family returned to the B6 Inpatient Paediatric floor, Mark was there when they arrived.

"He was standing in our doorway, ready to support us through the next phase," says Nicholson.

It is a moment that captures what Mark and Ollie came to represent for Claire and her family. They could not take away the fear or uncertainty of what Claire was facing. But they could stand beside her in it. They could bring laughter to the room and spread the joy Claire's family craved. They could help create moments that felt like childhood, even in the middle of treatment.

Looking back, Nicholson says that joy is what she remembers most about Claire's cancer journey. Not only the difficult days or the medical milestones, but the people who helped make those days easier to bear; people like Mark and Ollie.

[](http://london.ca/newsroom/public-service-announcement/temporary-lane-restrictions-wonderland-road-south-viscount)

Monday, September 21, 2026

The intersection of Wonderland Road South and Viscount Road will have traffic lane restrictions until October 23 while Enbridge Gas completes utility repairs.

The sidewalk at the southeast corner of the intersection will be closed during this work, and people walking will be directed around the closure.

Drivers should follow signage posted around the work, and expect traffic delays and changing traffic conditions. Please give yourself a little extra time if traveling in the area.

Visit the Renew London map for information about this project and other road and infrastructure projects in London.

stories.title: Assault with a weapon investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (September 21, 2026) – A London man was arrested over the weekend in relation to an assault with a weapon that took place in the east end of the city.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (September 21, 2026) – A London man was arrested over the weekend in relation to an assault with a weapon that took place in the east end of the city.

On Saturday, September 19, 2026, at approximately 3:45 a.m., a man was asleep inside a structure in a wooded area near Clarke Road and Oxford Street when a suspect entered and woke him. The suspect struck the man with a sword, causing serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The victim fled the area and called 9-1-1.

Police attended and utilized a Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (Rpas) to assist in locating the suspect.

The suspect was arrested without incident.

The victim and suspect were known to each other.

As a result of the investigation, Heinrich Martens, 36, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

Assault with a weapon; and

Assault causing bodily harm.

The accused was released from custody and is expected to appear in London court on October 28, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .
