stories.title: Tiff 2026: The best (The Debut!), worst (smelly cinemas!) and weirdest (Trudeau?) film festival moments
stories.summary: Plus, the most surprising traffic jam and most confusing cafe experience
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail’s Toronto International Film Festival team presents the highs, lows and all the moments in between from the 51st edition of the festival, which wraps up Sunday.

If you didn’t know who Jordan Firstman was before walking into his feature directorial debut, Club Kid (which he also stars in), then you certainly seared his name into your brain upon leaving the New York-set dramedy, so potent is the filmmaker’s charisma. Audiences felt that same sense of discovery watching Canadian actor Zorga Qaunaq inject a feverish intensity in the satiric thriller In the Heart of the South, during Anthony Ippolito’s pitch-perfect interpretation of a prefame Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky, and taking in Eldar Isgandarov’s hilarious supporting work in both Club Kid and Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut . Barry Hertz

While Prime Minister Mark Carney popped in to the annual Tiff Tribute Awards gala fundraiser to remind all the Hollywood stars that our closest major body of water is called Lake Ontario and not anything else, it was his predecessor Justin Trudeau who was really making the Tiff rounds.

The former prime minister hosted a swanky open-air soiree atop the Tiff Lightbox to launch his new production company , Hope & Hard Work (whatever you do, don’t call it Barack Obama’s Higher Ground 2.0), where he and his former chief of staff, Katie Telford, hobnobbed with well-wishers. He also made the rounds at the annual, and star-packed, Road to the Golden Globes party at the Four Seasons. Will Tiff’s next edition open with Trudeau’s first effort as a big-screen producer? I’m sure that will be controversy-free. B.H.

While several screenings had audiences bursting into applause midway through, only one movie, Eisenberg’s community-theatre comedy, The Debut , brought the house down to the point that on-screen dialogue was drowned out by the sheer enthusiasm of the crowd. Everyone – whether during the film’s premiere at the Princess of Wales or the typically hard-to-please press screenings – could not stop themselves from hooting and/or hollering during one particular sequence, when stars Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti engage in an intense screaming match. It’s just that good, and the response all but confirmed that Moore’s next Oscar nomination is coming down the pike. B.H.

I understand that budgets are tight and no one wants to overspend, but if Tiff could institute a policy that any preshow sponsor must produce at least two versions of their ad, that would go a long way in preventing me from losing my mind every screening. The Rogers ad with Cameron Bailey in the back of the taxi was fun, sure. The first 10 times. But for dedicated festivalgoers who are watching upward of two dozen films over the course of 11 days (which is no small contingent of folks), the sameness of the preroll show can grate. I’m not asking for an entirely new concept, just some alternate dialogue. And for the projection giant Christie, which used the very same (dull) sponsor ad as the year before, maybe it should recalibrate its focus on delivering something new. B.H.

Navigating traffic in Toronto during Tiff is typically nightmarish, what with a portion of King Street West shut down during the festival’s first few days and the nearby Jays games adding to rush-hour woes. This year, add Volodymyr Zelensky to the mix. As I arrived at the Park Hyatt Friday evening for an interview with a filmmaker, I found the Ukrainian President’s motorcade. Dozens of Suvs, with a police escort, were blocking off rush-hour traffic in both directions on University Avenue, waiting for Zelensky to exit the hotel. He was in town meeting with business leaders – not, as far as I know, attending that night’s Tiff premiere of Black Sunflowers , the documentary about Ukrainian youth on the front lines. Radheyan Simonpillai

New to the festival street during opening weekend this year were shimmering DJ booths on either end. During the day, these spots became Instagram shoot locations. (Shoutout to all the festival volunteers who channelled their inner Fellini to take cellphone photos and videos.) As the skies darkened, they became mini dance party venues, with DJs spinning tunes late into the night. Aparita Bhandari

It can get pretty dank in the Scotiabank Cineplex when hundreds of people are going in and out of screenings, leaving seats shuddering in their wake, from 8 a.m. to beyond midnight. But some of the halls were truly stinky, requiring you to breathe shallowly and hope the movie is good enough to distract you from olfactory concerns. A.B.

This goes to the coffee menu at the new press office inside the Sutton Place Hotel. Maybe it was the bleary-eyed exhaustion setting in, but I could not comprehend the options offered by the handsome but mumbling barista in the cramped lounge. You could choose from an espresso, an Americano and a third option that remained a mystery despite the barista repeating the name several times and speaking slowly. Naturally I opted for the incomprehensible option, which tasted great and woke me up for a spell. A.B.

Naturally I opted for the incomprehensible option, which tasted great and woke me up for a spell. A.B.

content_blocks.text: The Globe and Mail’s Toronto International Film Festival team presents the highs, lows and all the moments in between from the 51st edition of the festival, which wraps up Sunday.
Best star-is-born moments

If you didn’t know who Jordan Firstman was before walking into his feature directorial debut, Club Kid (which he also stars in), then you certainly seared his name into your brain upon leaving the New York-set dramedy, so potent is the filmmaker’s charisma. Audiences felt that same sense of discovery watching Canadian actor Zorga Qaunaq inject a feverish intensity in the satiric thriller In the Heart of the South, during Anthony Ippolito’s pitch-perfect interpretation of a prefame Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky, and taking in Eldar Isgandarov’s hilarious supporting work in both Club Kid and Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut . Barry Hertz
Busiest politico

While Prime Minister Mark Carney popped in to the annual Tiff Tribute Awards gala fundraiser to remind all the Hollywood stars that our closest major body of water is called Lake Ontario and not anything else, it was his predecessor Justin Trudeau who was really making the Tiff rounds.

The former prime minister hosted a swanky open-air soiree atop the Tiff Lightbox to launch his new production company , Hope & Hard Work (whatever you do, don’t call it Barack Obama’s Higher Ground 2.0), where he and his former chief of staff, Katie Telford, hobnobbed with well-wishers. He also made the rounds at the annual, and star-packed, Road to the Golden Globes party at the Four Seasons. Will Tiff’s next edition open with Trudeau’s first effort as a big-screen producer? I’m sure that will be controversy-free. B.H.

content_blocks.caption: Former prime minister Justin Trudeau and his former chief of staff, Katie Telford, announce the launch of their new media and entertainment production company at TIFF Lightbox on Sept. 11. Laura Proctor/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Biggest scene

While several screenings had audiences bursting into applause midway through, only one movie, Eisenberg’s community-theatre comedy, The Debut , brought the house down to the point that on-screen dialogue was drowned out by the sheer enthusiasm of the crowd. Everyone – whether during the film’s premiere at the Princess of Wales or the typically hard-to-please press screenings – could not stop themselves from hooting and/or hollering during one particular sequence, when stars Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti engage in an intense screaming match. It’s just that good, and the response all but confirmed that Moore’s next Oscar nomination is coming down the pike. B.H.

content_blocks.caption: Eisenberg waves to fans as he arrives to the red carpet for his film The Debut. Starring Moore and Paul Giamatti, the film brought the house down, Hertz writes. Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Most repetitive preroll

I understand that budgets are tight and no one wants to overspend, but if Tiff could institute a policy that any preshow sponsor must produce at least two versions of their ad, that would go a long way in preventing me from losing my mind every screening. The Rogers ad with Cameron Bailey in the back of the taxi was fun, sure. The first 10 times. But for dedicated festivalgoers who are watching upward of two dozen films over the course of 11 days (which is no small contingent of folks), the sameness of the preroll show can grate. I’m not asking for an entirely new concept, just some alternate dialogue. And for the projection giant Christie, which used the very same (dull) sponsor ad as the year before, maybe it should recalibrate its focus on delivering something new. B.H.
Most surprising traffic jam

Navigating traffic in Toronto during Tiff is typically nightmarish, what with a portion of King Street West shut down during the festival’s first few days and the nearby Jays games adding to rush-hour woes. This year, add Volodymyr Zelensky to the mix. As I arrived at the Park Hyatt Friday evening for an interview with a filmmaker, I found the Ukrainian President’s motorcade. Dozens of Suvs, with a police escort, were blocking off rush-hour traffic in both directions on University Avenue, waiting for Zelensky to exit the hotel. He was in town meeting with business leaders – not, as far as I know, attending that night’s Tiff premiere of Black Sunflowers , the documentary about Ukrainian youth on the front lines. content_blocks.caption: Actress Amanda Seyfried interacts with fans on the red carpet for the film The Life and Deaths of Wilson Shedd on Sept. 13. Keito Newman/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Grooviest pop-up

New to the festival street during opening weekend this year were shimmering DJ booths on either end. During the day, these spots became Instagram shoot locations. (Shoutout to all the festival volunteers who channelled their inner Fellini to take cellphone photos and videos.) As the skies darkened, they became mini dance party venues, with DJs spinning tunes late into the night. Aparita Bhandari

content_blocks.caption: Margaret Qualley greets fans outside the premiere of Love of Your Life at Royal Alexandra Theatre on Sept. 13. Arturo Holmes/Getty Images

content_blocks.text: Funkiest odour

It can get pretty dank in the Scotiabank Cineplex when hundreds of people are going in and out of screenings, leaving seats shuddering in their wake, from 8 a.m. to beyond midnight. But some of the halls were truly stinky, requiring you to breathe shallowly and hope the movie is good enough to distract you from olfactory concerns. A.B.

stories.title: Canada took the trade war to Trump’s backyard. Americans didn’t care
stories.summary: While the Canadian tariffs have undoubtedly inflicted economic hardship on some in the US, can that translate into a change in votes for President Donald Trump's Republican party?
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
Canada looms over Lance Thrailkill’s office as a dead, stuffed bird.

Mounted above the Texas manufacturer’s desk, a Canada goose, flanked by a mallard and four deer heads, fixes a glassy stare on the room. An open bottle of rye whiskey sits on the floor below.

It is a fitting backdrop for a conversation about another Canadian presence hanging over Thrailkill’s business: the escalating trade war between Washington and Ottawa.

At All Metals Fabricating, the third-generation family company he runs near Dallas, the price Thrailkill pays for aluminum has risen 84 per cent since tariffs were first introduced by the US in March 2025, he says. In 2026 alone, it’s up 40 per cent, he says.

But for Thrailkill, the financial pain has not become a political liability – at least not enough to change his vote.

“Certainly, the inability to get a deal done with Canada affects my … approval rating of Trump,” he says. “But it’s not going to change my vote because of all the other things that align with pro-small business, less taxes.”

That distinction is at the heart of Canada’s political gamble.

In August, after Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on $27.6 billion worth of Canadian goods, Ontario Premier Doug Ford urged Prime Minister Mark Carney to impose retaliatory tariffs on products from eight politically pivotal states, including Texas.

“Products from these states should face the full force of Canada’s response,” Ford wrote in a letter dated Aug. 17, days before trade talks between the two countries collapsed . The following day, Carney announced dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs.

But Canada’s retaliation is only one part of a much broader tariff fight. With the midterms approaching, the bigger question is whether tariffs are becoming a political headwind for Trump – and whether Canada’s economic pressure will translate into votes against him at the ballot box on Nov. 3.

With control of Congress being fought over in a narrow field of competitive races, even small shifts in voter sentiment could matter: Cook Political Report currently rates seven Senate contests and 21 House races as toss-ups, including Senate races in Texas.

1:59 Trump’s speech highlights worry over U.S. midterm election turnout

Dallas offered a rare opportunity to test that political calculus.

Last week, Republicans gathered there for the party’s first midterm convention, hoping to rally supporters ahead of November. Yet inside the arena, a trade war that has overwhelmed political debate in Canada barely registered.

Several Texans and Republican voters interviewed by Global inside the American Airlines Center were only vaguely familiar with the dispute with Canada. Those who were aware of it often repeated Trump’s broader argument that other countries had taken advantage of the US, even as they acknowledged frustration with tariffs, prices, or Trump himself. When asked about tariffs, some answered they believed America had been too generous to the rest of the world.

Canada, in other words, was less a major topic of conversation than a bit character in a much larger political grievance.

GOP members, however, were quick to defend the US president.

“It’s not [a hard sell],” former Trump White House press secretary Sean Spicer told Global News, adding that tariffs could be “a tough sell in certain states,” particularly in Senate battlegrounds along the Canadian border or in states with substantial cross-border trade.

Asked whether going into the midterms amid a trade war and a conflict with Iran was wise, he replied: “No, that’s probably not the best recipe.” He nevertheless argued that Republican voters would reward Trump for being willing to fight on their behalf.

Texas might seem like fertile ground for that political risk to play out. Its economy is deeply tied to Canada, yet the relationship barely registers with many voters.

“Canada is the second largest trading partner [for Texas], and Canada buys a lot of stuff that Texas has to offer and vice versa… But it’s under the radar and if you ask the average Texan they kind of shrug their shoulders and say, Canada, I didn’t know that,” says Laura Dawson, the executive director of the Future Borders Coalition and an expert on US-Canada relations, in a Zoom interview.

Texas and Canada exchanged nearly US$69 billion in goods in 2025, while 830 Canadian-owned businesses employ more than 104,000 Texans. Plastics, computers, trucks and aircraft move north; Canadian automobiles, engines, aluminum and vehicle parts move south; and crude petroleum travels in both directions.

Those economic ties create the potential for political pressure. Republicans have dominated statewide politics for three decades, but this year’s US Senate race is unusually competitive, with Democrat James Talarico narrowly leading Republican Ken Paxton in several recent polls.

Trump’s popularity is waning, too.

8:25 Trump suggests Canada-U.S. trade deal could happen ‘fairly soon’

An Ipsos poll conducted after Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed found 57 per cent of Americans opposed additional tariffs on Canada.

Trump’s own approval rating remains low — about 35 per cent, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll, barely above a recent second-term low of 33 per cent. Tracking from public opinion research firm Civiqs found his net approval had also declined in seven of the eight states Ford urged Ottawa to target.

There are signs, then, of political vulnerability for Trump, but Canada is an unlikely culprit.

“The size of the Canadian economy is just not large enough to engage in a full-blown trade war with the United States for very long,” says Dawson. “And it’s small business that gets hit first by that.”

Canada may be able to make Americans pay for the trade war. The harder question is whether Trump will be stuck with the political cheque.

Economic pain, political loyalty

The economic consequences of the confrontation are easier to identify.

After Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed on Aug. 21, Ottawa escalated its response, imposing retaliatory tariffs on roughly $28 billion worth of U.S. goods.

It is unclear whether Ford’s proposed targets influenced Ottawa’s 648-item list. But the measures, which took effect Sept. 8, covered steel and aluminum, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, plastics and electronics – industries with a significant presence in several of the states he named.

That day, when Global News visited Thrailkill at his workshop, he was once again requoting customers as retaliatory tariffs pushed costs higher.

“We’re having to requote every job trying to get in front of it. It’s going up every week,” he said.

2:07 Dairy, liquor, motorcycles among Canadian goods facing U.S. ban

About a third of his orders involve aluminum. They buy through distributors supplied by mills, many of which source from Canada, meaning tariff costs can compound as they move through the supply chain.

While he supports Trump’s “overall vision” on trade, he says his business is being negatively affected. He also criticizes the president, saying the way he talks to people is “wrong.”

But he still plans to vote Republican.

“He actually does what he says he’s going to do. And like it or not, that’s more than you can say about most political people,” says Thrailkill.

That refrain came up repeatedly.

Every Trump voter Global News spoke with applauded his perceived follow-through, and often echoed his argument that the US has carried an unfair burden in global trade.

2:02 U.S. late-night shows take aim at Trump’s trade war with Canada

“He’s saying everybody’s been taking advantage of the US all these years and I’m putting a stop to it – we’re not going to subsidy this country and that,” AirTractor CEO Jim Hirsch told Global News at an Olive Garden outside Dallas.

His company imports engines from Canada, though it is exempt from tariffs.

“If we had to pay 25 per cent on the engines, it would be hurting us really hard,” Hirsch said, acknowledging that direct exposure could change some voters’ minds.

But a clearer example of a company caught in the crosshairs of the trade fight sits in a nearby small town.

American jobs in the crossfire

As Republicans converged on the city, Trump threatened to ban sales of Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier in the U.S. unless it moved production there.

Bombardier responded by pointing out that major components of its aircraft are already produced in the US.

In fact, its facility in Red Oak, a town of about 20,000 people about 30 kilometres south of Dallas, employs 440 full-time Texas workers and a network of specialized contractors to manufacture jet wings.

Red Oak Mayor Mark Stanfill told Global News the factory has a “significant, tangible impact” on the community and local economy.

1:43 Bombardier says it already builds planes in U.S. after Trump threat to block its sales if it doesn’t

“Bombardier is an important part of [Red Oak’s] history, and any federal actions or trade disruptions that jeopardize the stability of their operations could have a significant impact on Texas workers, their families, and our regional economy,” Stanfill said.

Stanfill said he appreciated Trump’s efforts to bring more manufacturing and investment to the US, but said Red Oak’s Bombardier operation is “an example of exactly that.” Similarly, in Wichita, Kansas, where Bombardier has its U.S. headquarters, Mayor Lily Wu has also spoken out to protect local jobs.

But both stopped short of criticizing Trump.

That reluctance illustrates the limits of turning economic exposure into political pressure. Canada also enters the fight from a weaker economic position.

“Canada has more to lose. I mean, it’s the Canadian exports of major commodities that would be hurt first,” Dawson says. “Texas is a large economy. It’s got a lot of absorptive capacity. It’s got a lot of options from other places. So it would be Canada that gets hit first.”

And just a few kilometers away in Dallas, Republicans showed little sign of treating the dispute with Canada as an electoral threat.

Republicans stand by the trade fight

Most Republican officials Global News spoke with cast the trade fight as a test of American resolve rather than a political liability.

US Rep. Randy Weber of Texas acknowledged the stakes for trade-dependent parts of his state. His district has seven ports, he said, and trade and exports are “hugely big.” Tariff policy therefore had to be “reasonable” and “calculated.”

But he expected little political damage for Trump.

“I don’t think it will lose him a lot of popularity,” Weber said, adding that some voters could instead see the confrontation as proof Trump was willing to stand up to other countries.

2:14 Trump staging Republican convention amid slumping poll numbers, midterm pressure

Illinois Rep. Mike Bost similarly argued that Ottawa would “lose more in this tariff fight than we are,” warning that continued Canadian retaliation would be “tougher on you all in Canada.”

Others were more willing to accept the costs.

Patti Lyman, Republican National Committeewoman for Virginia, said the United States had spent too long giving other countries “a free ride.” If the escalation continued, she said, “let’s see in the end who needs whose market the most.”

Higher costs, she suggested, were a price worth paying.

“Everyone will have to take a bit of a haircut.”

Republican congressional candidate Jay Feely was more blunt: “Canada needs us way more than we need Canada.”

Other elected Republicans showed little appetite to discuss the Canada dispute at all. Global News contacted 25 Republican senators and members of Congress about the trade war. Just three offices responded; none answered questions.

0:42 Trump promises $5K payout if Republicans win U.S. midterm elections

And Republicans most exposed to the political risks of tariffs weren’t in attendance – many from trade-reliant northern states distancing themselves from both Trump and his agenda.

For others, such as the party faithful in Dallas, the issue was often filtered through something much broader than the price of aluminum or the details of Canadian retaliation: loyalty to Trump and a belief that the United States had been treated unfairly.

Ronny Dudek, from Fort Worth, wore a shirt marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11, which fell the following day. Dudek acknowledged that “tariffs hurt people,” but argued that unequal trade had already hurt Americans.

“Yes, we should be nice to our neighbours, but trade wars are trade wars,” he said. “We still love the Canadians. The Canadian people still love us.”

He and his group got free convention tickets through the GOP website the week before. “Trump doesn’t want anyone to miss out,” he said.

Others had only a loose grasp of the Canada dispute.

One convention-goer, dressed in Charlie Kirk-themed attire, said her overriding concern was a “Communist Socialist takeover” and acknowledged that she was unfamiliar with the trade war. Her friend then offered an unverified claim that Canada had been importing Chinese goods and reselling them to evade US. tariffs.

Monique Worthy was more blunt. The transgender former Texas congressional candidate said Canada had been taking advantage of the U.S. “for a long time,” blaming previous presidents for allowing the imbalance to persist.

Of Carney, she said: “You’re talking all this hot sh*t, but we’re the ones securing y’all. If there was no America, there’d be no Canada.” She added that Canada would “probably still be speaking German” without the US.

But that blind loyalty to Trump creates another vulnerability.

For much of the convention’s first day, the American Airlines Center was more than half empty. That changed when Trump arrived: plenty of seats remained, but the arena was suddenly far fuller — and louder.

It had been nicknamed “Trump-a-palooza” for a reason.

In his opening-night speech, Trump repeatedly returned to his own role in the midterm campaign.

“Pretend I’m on the ballot,” he told a cheering crowd.

In Trump’s telling, that makes November a referendum on him and his record — tariffs included.

Yet for all the disruption the trade fight was causing beyond the American Airlines Center, the dispute with Canada barely registered inside. Beyond a jibe about Lake Ontario and an insistence that Canada was “dying” to make a deal, Trump said little about the country even as he repeatedly praised tariffs.

One of his more memorable trade discussions had nothing to do with Canada at all.

Standing inside the Mavericks’ home arena, Trump criticized the team for trading NBA superstar Luka Dončić to the Los Angeles Lakers, comparing it to Boston’s infamous sale of Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees more than a century ago.

“Maybe we could redo that trade,” Trump said, drawing cheers from the crowd.

“I redo deals all the time.”

With files from Jackson Proskow and Reggie Cecchini.

Ronny Dudek, from Fort Worth, wore a shirt marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11, which fell the following day. Dudek acknowledged that “tariffs hurt people,” but argued that unequal trade had already hurt Americans.
“Yes, we should be nice to our neighbours, but trade wars are trade wars,” he said. “We still love the Canadians. The Canadian people still love us.”
He and his group got free convention tickets through the GOP website the week before. “Trump doesn’t want anyone to miss out,” he said.
Others had only a loose grasp of the Canada dispute.

One convention-goer, dressed in Charlie Kirk-themed attire, said her overriding concern was a “Communist Socialist takeover” and acknowledged that she was unfamiliar with the trade war. Her friend then offered an unverified claim that Canada had been importing Chinese goods and reselling them to evade US. tariffs.

Monique Worthy was more blunt. The transgender former Texas congressional candidate said Canada had been taking advantage of the U.S. “for a long time,” blaming previous presidents for allowing the imbalance to persist.

Of Carney, she said: “You’re talking all this hot sh*t, but we’re the ones securing y’all. If there was no America, there’d be no Canada.” She added that Canada would “probably still be speaking German” without the US.
But that blind loyalty to Trump creates another vulnerability.

For much of the convention’s first day, the American Airlines Center was more than half empty. That changed when Trump arrived: plenty of seats remained, but the arena was suddenly far fuller — and louder.
It had been nicknamed “Trump-a-palooza” for a reason.
In his opening-night speech, Trump repeatedly returned to his own role in the midterm campaign.
“Pretend I’m on the ballot,” he told a cheering crowd.
In Trump’s telling, that makes November a referendum on him and his record — tariffs included.

Yet for all the disruption the trade fight was causing beyond the American Airlines Center, the dispute with Canada barely registered inside. Beyond a jibe about Lake Ontario and an insistence that Canada was “dying” to make a deal, Trump said little about the country even as he repeatedly praised tariffs.
One of his more memorable trade discussions had nothing to do with Canada at all.

Standing inside the Mavericks’ home arena, Trump criticized the team for trading NBA superstar Luka Dončić to the Los Angeles Lakers, comparing it to Boston’s infamous sale of Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees more than a century ago.
“Maybe we could redo that trade,” Trump said, drawing cheers from the crowd.
“I redo deals all the time.”

stories.title: ‘I’d rather not moonwalk back into the closet’: ‘Neverman’ spotlights transgender people’s dementia fears
stories.summary: Toronto — Cuban-Canadian director Rodrigo Barriuso says he decided years ago he needed to draw attention to the difficulties some Lgbtq+ residents face as they enter long-term care homes, including examples he found "devastating and enraging."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Nicole Ireland, The Canadian Press

Posted September 19, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated September 19, 2026 7:16 am.

Toronto — Cuban-Canadian director Rodrigo Barriuso says he decided years ago he needed to draw attention to the difficulties some Lgbtq+ residents face as they enter long-term care homes, including examples he found “devastating and enraging.”

He was seeing a number of media reports abroad about cases of long-term care homes that weren’t equipped to provide identity-affirming care to residents.

“As a result, they were returning to the proverbial closet because the discrimination that they were facing in these place(s) was so rampant that they would rather live in the closet than subject themselves to it,” said Rodrigo, whose film “Neverman” played at the Toronto International Film Festival.

The generation of the Lgbtq+ community that fought for gay and transgender rights is now aging, with some developing dementia and ending up “sharing a living facility with the bullies who — news flash — also age,” said the Toronto-based director.

In “Neverman,” which is also a finalist for the $25,000 Windsor International Film Festival prize, the fictional long-term care home’s staff try to strip transgender activist Lucia Neverman — played by Justin Vivian Bond — of her identity.

Lucia’s nurse, Eleanor — played by Québécois actor Marie-Josée Croze — makes escalating attempts to dissuade her from wearing makeup and to replace her dresses with masculine clothes.

Lucia faces these repeated aggressions while fearing losing herself to her progressing Alzheimer’s disease.

She expresses that fear early in the film when discussing her prognosis with her neurologist, saying with her characteristic acerbic wit that she’d “rather not moonwalk back into the closet” and mentally regress to her youth.

Although the film is a fictional account, it reflects real-life fears among the aging Lgbtq+ population, experts in dementia and those who work with the community say.

Allison Sekuler, chief scientist at Baycrest Academy for Research and Education who specializes in aging and brain health, said bias and misunderstanding continue to exist in long-term care, often when people haven’t had adequate training on how to provide gender-affirming care.

In Ontario, the office of the minister of long-term care says all homes are expected to meet a strict standard of care.

“This includes treating residents with courtesy and respect in a way that recognizes their dignity, worth, and individuality, regardless of, their race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, marital status, family status or disability,” communications director Mark Hensen wrote in an email on Friday.

The ministry said it has supported the development of resources by various agencies to support Lgbtq+ long-term care residents.

One is a guide called “Welcoming Trans and Gender-Diverse Older Adults to Long-Term Care,” which was just published in August.

Sekuler said although resources are available, the “gap” is whether or not individual care homes use them.

“The law says that trans residents’ gender identity has to be respected, but not everyone will necessarily have been trained in detail on how to do that,” she said.

Trans residents often have very specific needs, Sekuler said.

“If someone is trans and requires hormones, will they be getting the hormones that they need? Right? If they grow facial hair faster than they would like, and they’re identifying as a woman, will someone come to shave them, even though they might normally only do that for someone who identifies as a man?”

Sekuler said it’s also important for caregivers helping transgender residents with bathing and dressing not to make assumptions about “what bits” they have, because some people have surgeries while transitioning and some don’t.

Another upsetting possibility transgender people with dementia face is whether they will mentally regress to a point in their life before they transitioned.

“Sometimes when people have Alzheimer’s and related dementias, their memory shifts, the time that they’re living in can sort of shift,” Sekuler said.

Training staff and family members on how to deal with that regression isn’t widespread, she said, and needs to become part of mainstream training in both long-term care facilities and home care.

“It’s really about meeting the person in the place and time where they are then, and doing what you can to make them as happy and comfortable as you can in that moment.”

Staff turnover in long-term care can also be a difficult issue for Lgbtq+ residents, Sekuler said.

“If you have to keep constantly explaining, ‘this is my (same-sex) wife,’ or ‘I’m a trans woman’ or whatever, it’s too much work on the person to have to keep explaining that.”

Part of the solution should be “more care taken to have personal stories embedded in the care plans so that everybody who’s coming into contact with somebody living in long-term care knows that person’s history from the start,” Sekuler said.

It’s also important for that person’s chosen family to help them get comfortable in the facility and provide insights about who they are, she said.

Bond, who has been in films, TV and plays, but now focuses on live queer performance, returned to film to play Lucia Neverman.

“I thought that it was bringing up a subject that I would be happy to talk about,” she said.

When it comes to the fear of developing dementia and regressing to a place before she transitioned, Bond believes there’s no previous version of herself who would not welcome who she has become.

“I didn’t have the words for it, but I knew I was trans from the very beginning of my life,” she said.

“If I were to regress to childhood and look at the body that I have now, I would think that having prayed every night for the body I have now that my prayers had been answered.”

Bond had a late friend who lobbied for research-based protocols to provide affirmative care to trans people in the health-care system.

“In this particular instance there were no protocols in place for my character,” she said.

Bond said that type of training in long-term care would be “very helpful” — as long as the staff themselves are “caring, thoughtful people.”

“I do think that the people that want to do the right thing would love to be told what the right thing is so that they can do it,” she said.

But both Bond and Barriuso also think it’s important to establish spaces in long-term care specifically for Lgbtq+ residents.

As part of his research for the film, Barriuso volunteered and talked to staff and residents at the Rekai Centres’ Wellesley Central Place in Toronto, which has a designated “Rainbow Wing.”

Staff throughout the facility are trained in Lgbtq+ affirming care, said Barbara Michalik, executive director of community academic partnerships and programming at the Rekai Centres, in an interview.

Many take even more extensive training to become “champions,” wearing the rainbow symbol on their lanyards so Lgbtq+ residents know there is always a safe person to turn to.

Michalik hopes to see more long-term care homes create dedicated spaces where residents feel they can be comfortable as a community.

“They wanna walk inside of a place where they feel that it’s their culture. It’s their home.”

“Neverman” does not yet have a theatrical release date.

stories.title: Nato defence chiefs to decide whether to tap Gen. Carignan for senior Nato post
stories.summary: Ottawa — Nato chiefs of defence are meeting in Copenhagen, Denmark, today to choose the next chair of the alliance's military committee, and Canada's top military commander is in the running.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — NATO chiefs of defence have elected German Gen. Carsten Breuer as the next chair of the alliance’s military committee, over Canada’s top military commander.

Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan ran against Breuer for the top NATO position.

NATO chiefs of defence met in Copenhagen, Denmark, Saturday to choose the next chair. It’s a prestige posting but it doesn’t carry the same level of clout as the alliance’s most senior role of supreme allied commander, a powerful command position that usually goes to an American.

Only three Canadians have ever served as chair of the military committee, and the last time was during the Afghanistan war in the mid-2000s.

In a social media post, Defence Minister David McGuinty congratulated Breuer on his election.

“Canada was proud to nominate Gen. Jennie Carignan, whose strong candidacy reflected her exceptional leadership, experience and deep commitment to Allied collaboration,” he said.

“We remain firmly committed to NATO and our collective defence, and look forward to continuing to work closely with Gen. Breuer and all of our Allies.”

Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill Saturday, McGuinty said Carignan led a good campaign and that the breakdown of the votes was not known.

“The important thing is that Gen. Carignan will continue to serve with her colleagues,” he said.

If she had won, Carignan would have become the first woman to be named to the position, and also would have to step down as leader of Canada’s military, a role she has held since 2024.

Carignan said in a statement posted to social media Saturday that it was an honour to stand as a candidate and to engage with fellow allied chiefs of defence throughout the process.

“I look forward to continuing that collaboration with all of my allied colleagues” she said. “There is important work ahead for our alliance, and I know General Breuer will bring strong leadership to his new role.”

Carignan said that, going forward, her focus remains on serving as chief of the defence staff and leading the transformation of the Canadian Armed Forces.

The current military chair, Italy’s Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, will leave his post next year.

Dragone said on social media that Breuer’s operational judgement, deep familiarity with the alliance and leadership of the German armed forces would “serve NATO well.”

“The Chiefs of Defence have placed their trust in you at a demanding moment for Euro-Atlantic security,” he said. “You will have the full support of the Committee and of the International Military Staff through the transition, and I look forward to working closely with you until the handover.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 19, 2026.

Kyle Duggan and Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Conservatives search for hope amid Mark Carney's tide of good fortune, and find only stoicism
stories.summary: Patience isn't easy in a caucus this restless. The gathering in Penticton this week was an assembly of thoroughly grumpy MPs.
stories.author: Stuart Thomson, Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa AND Penticton, B.C. — As the moon circles Earth, its gravitational pull moves the oceans back and forth, creating the cycle of high and low tides.

A similar law of physics applies to Canadian politics.

As U.S. President Donald Trump spins himself in and out of the news cycle, Liberal party poll numbers move up and down in accordance with the president’s shifting gravitational force. The latest breakdown of trade talks in late August, and the barrage of insults from Washington that followed, predictably delivered another “Trump bump” for Prime Minister Mark Carney who has positioned himself, and is widely perceived as, Canada’s most reliable defender.

That same cycle has been savage for Conservatives, who gathered as a caucus in B.C.’s Okanagan region this week, and are once again relegated to the sidelines while forces outside the party’s control manage its fate.

In a sign that people inside the party May be moving through the stages of grief since losing the 2025 election, Conservative MPs seemed more willing to acknowledge the steep hill they must climb, with their party and their leader trailing Carney and the Liberals by significant spreads.

“The popularity of Mark Carney is what it is,” said Bob Zimmer, who represents the northern B.C. riding of Prince George–Peace River–Northern Rockies, outside the party’s caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C.

Conservatives popularity is now in the low 30 per cents, according to polling aggregators. Having dipped below the psychologically important 30-point mark in a few single polls this year, even the Tory leadership has to admit that things don’t look rosy for the Conservative party these days.

“This is not the position we want to be in at this juncture,” said Conservative deputy leader Melissa Lantsman, to reporters gathered at the caucus meeting.

Most Conservative strategists say that in the current environment, with Carney’s stature and popularity booming and Trump’s belligerence giving the prime minister a new boost every few months, it’s unlikely that the party will be able to close the gap with the Liberals anytime soon.

Trump is scheduled to depart the Oval Office in January 2029, which many Tories will have circled in their calendars. But that means the party is looking down the barrel of a gruelling couple of years. The party’s braintrust either needs to reverse Carney’s advantage on the trade war or grind out the rest of Trump’s term when it, hopefully, goes away.

“Hanging on for two years and hoping things get better, that’s not easy, right?” said Dan Robertson, a former chief strategist for the Conservative party. “You’re basically conceding that your strategy is just hope. And that’s a pretty poor basis for a strategy.”

Even the most optimistic Conservative strategists don’t see a clear path to any big gains for the party soon. Carney is simply too popular right now. And, despite the prayers of Tories across the country, the conflict with Trump hasn’t become any less salient in Canada since the April 2025 election, when Liberals successfully sold their leader as the best man to fight it.

The political backdrop of British Columbia is an ominous one for a Conservative party caucus retreat.

The province has become a cautionary tale. After narrowly losing the 2024 provincial election to the incumbent NDP, the B.C. Conservatives fired their leader. The new one, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, is just over four months into her tenure and has already seen 12 of her MLAs resign from her caucus as a result of a fierce internal battle. There are echoes of skirmishes within the federal party.

Leader Pierre Poilievre even waded into B.C. politics earlier this year, congratulating Findlay for defeating the “Liberal lobbyists from out east” who he said ran her opponent’s campaign. It was widely interpreted as a shot at Kory Teneycke, who previously organized Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s three successful provincial campaigns and had become a fierce critic of Poilievre during the federal election. (Teneycke helped run the campaign of a rival to Findlay, but so had many Poilievre loyalists.) The remarks set off a flurry of unhelpful headlines about party infighting and frustrated Conservatives, who saw them as a distraction and a needless reopening of old wounds.

Other moves by Poilievre in recent months have also landed poorly. The public response was not kind to his October 2025 attack against the RCMP, calling the Mounties’ leadership “despicable” for what he claimed were cover ups of former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s scandals.

And there was his attack on the government in May over early reports that the economy had slipped into a “technical recession” after Statistics Canada reported a slight decline in the first quarter, following a previous decline. Poilievre called for an emergency debate in Parliament over the “full-blown recession,” as headlines focused on economists urging caution about the recession definition and the data’s accuracy. Later revisions by Statistics Canada showed it turned out to not be a recession, by any definition.

I don’t think we should chase shiny objects in Parliament and think that we can land short-term, quick wins on corruption and ‘gotchas’ on the economy

To Ginny Roth, a longtime political strategist who was Poilievre’s director of communications for his successful leadership run in 2022, it looked like the party not seeing the forest for the trees. Rather than a quick “gotcha” attack, the Opposition could have made a substantial case about the economy’s lack of growth over the last decade.

“The reason it’s unclear whether it was a technical recession or not is because we’ve been in this secular stagnation for years and will continue to be, which is obviously a much more compelling and bigger point to make,” she said.

Instead, the Conservatives were forced to wear an unforced error, being technically wrong by declaring a technical recession too hastily.

“I don’t think we should chase shiny objects in Parliament and think that we can land short-term, quick wins on corruption and ‘gotchas’ on the economy,” said Roth. In this unforgiving political environment, she thinks, the smartest approach is to stop reading snapshot polling and focus on the medium- and long-term future. Instead of getting into the weeds of technical recessions, she said, keep reminding Canadians that on cost-of-living, the government is failing Canadians.

But the party would have to get comfortable with the reality that the argument might not land today, or even a year from today. She admits that it will be difficult “from a caucus management perspective because it can feel ungratifying when you don’t score that quick win.”

Poilievre has waged this kind of disciplined campaign before, when he targeted the carbon tax with a dogged effectiveness. Even as conservative-sympathetic voices urged him to move on, he would not relent until a majority of Canadians shared his view — and the Carney government eventually did, too, cancelling the consumer tax last year.

“It requires a great deal of discipline. It will be very challenging. There could be tough moments,” said Roth. “But I think it still would be foolish to try to play Whac-A-Mole on the short-term wins.”

Coming out of the caucus meeting in B.C. this week, there are some indications that Poilievre is thinking the same way.

Even among his supporters in the party, the leader is not known as someone who will easily change course once he’s determined a path. But he has in recent days shown signs that he plans to make tweaks in his approach and messaging.

After frequent criticisms that he’s too quick to take easy political shots at the prime minister and government, Poilievre has lately been projecting something more statesmanlike, including his comment last week in New York that he wouldn’t criticize his government while on foreign soil. The Conservative leader told Cnbc that Canadians were feeling “wounded” by U.S. tariffs and urging cooler heads to prevail. But, he said, “I’m not going to attack my prime minister on foreign soil. It’s just not something I’m going to do.”

He referred to that during a speech Wednesday to his caucus, saying that some U.S. media were “befuddled” that he wouldn’t criticize his opponents.

Poilievre has also emphasized in recent days that he would like the Liberal government to succeed in its trade war with Trump, despite what that would mean for his own aspirations.

“Our duty is country before party,” he told Conservative MPs.

The comments stood out for their willingness to disown a noisy, very online faction of conservative-minded Canadians who have taken Trump’s side against Carney. That has created a more complicated calculus for Poilievre, given a recent poll by the Angus Reid Institute found that 33 per cent of Conservative voters have a favourable view of the U.S. president, while 59 per cent of them have an unfavourable view. (By comparison, 95 per cent of Liberals disapprove of Trump, along with 92 per cent of NDP voters and 94 per cent of Bloc Québécois voters, making a fighting posture far more comfortable for those parties.)

Poilievre was criticized during last year’s federal election campaign for not being clear enough in condemning Trump and his attacks on Canada. But that looks to be changing, too. In his speech on Wednesday, the Conservative leader referred to Trump’s “trolling,” knowing full well that some of his caucus members and party supporters are Trump fans.

Patience and focusing on the long term is an easy strategy to recommend when there doesn’t seem to be any other one on offer.

But it’s not easy imagine it being carried out by a caucus this restless. The gathering in Penticton this week was an assembly of thoroughly grumpy MPs.

Two former high-ranking staffers confirmed that the mood is as bad as they can remember it in the party. People are depressed and, even a year-and-a-half after the election, they are still grieving a loss that they feel was unfairly imposed on them by outside forces.

Since then, Carney has successfully lured four MPs to join his caucus, and won six of seven byelections this year (the exception being Poilievre winning back a seat in Parliament in Battle River–Crowfoot last year, where the Liberals did not run). Conservatives have averaged just 24.6 per cent support across all seven byelections (that includes Poilievre’s 80 per cent victory), a shadow of the 41 per cent support they earned in last year’s election.

When Carney speaks to reporters lately, he almost never mentions Poilievre or the Conservative party by name. It’s a tactic that more than one senior Conservative said (with at least one adding some reluctant admiration) is driving Conservatives mad. Since Carney became Liberal leader, he has tried to convince Canadians his real opposition is the Trump administration, not the other party in the House of Commons, because the Trump contrast is the one that has propelled him to historic highs in the polls.

But that has also blunted Poilievre’s best political skill, which is hand-to-hand combat, and it has only fuelled the party’s feeling of irrelevancy.

The longer-term strategy also doesn’t reckon with the fact that most Conservative MPs fully expect Carney to go to the polls before Trump leaves the scene, although not even Liberals are sure about that. If they’re right, it means the slow-burn approach could still be unhurriedly sputtering along by the time the next election happens.

“Every available piece of public polling shows us that we’re getting absolutely obliterated if there’s an election anytime soon,” said a senior Conservative source.

Conservative members of Parliament, whose jobs are on the line if the party takes a beating in the next election, are as aware of that as anyone else. If projections by the current polls are mapped onto election scenarios, it’s possible that more than four in 10 Conservative MPs could be out of a job as the Liberals romp to a possible 228-seat majority .

The foreboding has fuelled questions in the media about Poilievre’s leadership, although on the ground it’s hard to find anyone who genuinely thinks he is in any imminent trouble.

Even Tories who would prefer to see a new leader in place point to Poilievre’s overwhelming endorsement at the party’s convention in January — from 87 per cent of party members — and the support he stills commands.

“I still don’t think Liberals and non-Conservatives and people who don’t pay attention understand just how dominant a force he has become in the national federal party,” said Ben Woodfinden, who was Poilievre’s director of communications until 2025.

At least half a dozen Conservatives made the point to National Post that if the Reform Act was used to topple the leader (as Conservative MPs had done with Erin O’Toole), Poilievre could simply run in the resulting leadership race to replace himself and win easily.

He is not seen as the kind of guy who would go quietly.

There is also a fear, now being made publicly by some longtime party operatives , that a leadership race in the Trump era would be massively damaging to the party. It would bring internal disputes about the direction of the party into the limelight and it would activate a legion of online influencers that more moderate members of the party believe have been too sympathetic to the U.S. president.

“I don’t see the value in going through a really bloody, nasty leadership race, rip each other apart, open up wounds that don’t need to be reopened up, so that we can throw somebody new in, so that he or she could get f-cking torched,” said Anthony Koch, a longtime Conservative adviser.

And the payoff with a new leader remains extremely questionable. David Coletto, who runs the polling firm Abacus Data, tried to quantify the effect of a hypothetical new leader on the national polls recently, and found that even with an ideal new leader, the Conservatives could gain all of about two percentage points from where they are now.

That would put the Conservatives 11 points behind the Liberals, rather than the current 13-point deficit per the polling average at 338Canada.

Coletto’s hypothetical also has some major caveats. It assumes a new leader with zero negative impressions among voters and it assumes that the new leader will hold all the voters that support the party because of Poilievre.

“What I take from this is that any Conservative leader, this one or the next, faces the same underlying problem: a prime minister who is liked, whose government is approved of, and who is seen as best able to handle the issues Canadians care most about right now: Trump and U.S. file,” wrote Coletto in early September.

The pollster argues that voters aren’t supporting the Liberals because they hate Poilievre, but because they are very impressed with Carney.

Canadians who are open to voting Conservative, but who won’t commit to casting a ballot for the party, actually like Poilievre. The problem for the Conservatives is that they like Carney even more.

Poilievre’s net favourability, which is the percentage of people with positive perceptions minus those with negative impressions, is plus nine. But Carney’s is plus-43.

Although most Tories don’t think Poilievre is under any immediate threat, some are looking ahead to a major test of his leadership that could change that.

On Friday, Conservative MP Larry Brock officially resigned from Parliament, as he promised he would several weeks ago. He won his Brantford—Brant South—Six Nations riding by 11 percentage points in the 2025 federal election. But pollsters are already warning that the Liberals have a chance to wrestle the seat away from the Conservatives in a byelection, which would be a crushing blow for a party that needs to gain and hold seats in the Greater Toronto Area and Southwestern Ontario to have any hope at forming government.

“If there is a movement to get rid of Pierre, it would probably massively intensify following a loss at Brantford. It would be driven by MPs out of just pure self interest,” said one senior Conservative.

One Conservative strategist estimated that losing Brock’s former seat in Brantford would be a sign that the party could be looking at a single-digit seat count in Ontario in a hypothetical federal election, compared to the 52 they hold in the province today.

Conservative MPs who see a threat brewing to their parliamentary salary May not be convinced by Coletto’s data that a new leader would be no saviour. Or they May accept it, yet consider a roll of the leadership dice to be as good an option as any in a desperation situation.

Anyone keeping track of all these possible scenarios for the Conservatives over the next two years will notice there is risk in every path that lies ahead.

Toppling Poilievre could spark an all-out civil war, or it could lead to a vengeful leader returning to regain his place at the top of the party.

Sticking with Poilievre and doing the hard work of holding the government to account could risk the party getting marginalized by the ongoing trade war with Trump. It could also demoralize the caucus and spark one of the most commonly heard fears of Tory insiders: an epidemic of “quiet quitting” among the best and brightest among them, who will begin planning for a future outside of politics rather than grinding out another decade in opposition.

And whatever happens, the Trump effect will loom large over any path the party chooses to take.

But like the ocean’s tides, Trump is a force of nature, impossible to control no matter how much a Canadian party leader might bay at the moon.

Instead, Poilievre May have to channel his experience with the carbon tax, building a case against a popular Liberal agenda and trusting that Canadians will be won over — eventually.

“As our skepticism proves to be correct, that more Crown agencies won’t drive growth, and countless other examples, Canadians will turn to the Conservatives and say, ‘Oh, you guys have kind of been saying this all along, haven’t you? Now it seems to be true’,” said Roth.

It might be a long shot requiring the perseverance and patience that seem hard to find among Conservatives today. But it could be the only shot they have.

Most Conservative strategists say that in the current environment, with Carney’s stature and popularity booming and Trump’s belligerence giving the prime minister a new boost every few months, it’s unlikely that the party will be able to close the gap with the Liberals anytime soon.

Trump is scheduled to depart the Oval Office in January 2029, which many Tories will have circled in their calendars. But that means the party is looking down the barrel of a gruelling couple of years. The party’s braintrust either needs to reverse Carney’s advantage on the trade war or grind out the rest of Trump’s term when it, hopefully, goes away.

“Hanging on for two years and hoping things get better, that’s not easy, right?” said Dan Robertson, a former chief strategist for the Conservative party. “You’re basically conceding that your strategy is just hope. And that’s a pretty poor basis for a strategy.”

Even the most optimistic Conservative strategists don’t see a clear path to any big gains for the party soon. Carney is simply too popular right now. And, despite the prayers of Tories across the country, the conflict with Trump hasn’t become any less salient in Canada since the April 2025 election, when Liberals successfully sold their leader as the best man to fight it.
The political backdrop of British Columbia is an ominous one for a Conservative party caucus retreat.

The province has become a cautionary tale. After narrowly losing the 2024 provincial election to the incumbent NDP, the B.C. Conservatives fired their leader. The new one, Kerry-Lynne Findlay, is just over four months into her tenure and has already seen 12 of her MLAs resign from her caucus as a result of a fierce internal battle. There are echoes of skirmishes within the federal party.

Leader Pierre Poilievre even waded into B.C. politics earlier this year, congratulating Findlay for defeating the “Liberal lobbyists from out east” who he said ran her opponent’s campaign. It was widely interpreted as a shot at Kory Teneycke, who previously organized Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s three successful provincial campaigns and had become a fierce critic of Poilievre during the federal election. (Teneycke helped run the campaign of a rival to Findlay, but so had many Poilievre loyalists.) The remarks set off a flurry of unhelpful headlines about party infighting and frustrated Conservatives, who saw them as a distraction and a needless reopening of old wounds.

Other moves by Poilievre in recent months have also landed poorly. The public response was not kind to his October 2025 attack against the RCMP, calling the Mounties’ leadership “despicable” for what he claimed were cover ups of former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s scandals.

And there was his attack on the government in May over early reports that the economy had slipped into a “technical recession” after Statistics Canada reported a slight decline in the first quarter, following a previous decline. Poilievre called for an emergency debate in Parliament over the “full-blown recession,” as headlines focused on economists urging caution about the recession definition and the data’s accuracy. Later revisions by Statistics Canada showed it turned out to not be a recession, by any definition.
I don’t think we should chase shiny objects in Parliament and think that we can land short-term, quick wins on corruption and ‘gotchas’ on the economy

To Ginny Roth, a longtime political strategist who was Poilievre’s director of communications for his successful leadership run in 2022, it looked like the party not seeing the forest for the trees. Rather than a quick “gotcha” attack, the Opposition could have made a substantial case about the economy’s lack of growth over the last decade.

“The reason it’s unclear whether it was a technical recession or not is because we’ve been in this secular stagnation for years and will continue to be, which is obviously a much more compelling and bigger point to make,” she said.
Instead, the Conservatives were forced to wear an unforced error, being technically wrong by declaring a technical recession too hastily.

“I don’t think we should chase shiny objects in Parliament and think that we can land short-term, quick wins on corruption and ‘gotchas’ on the economy,” said Roth. In this unforgiving political environment, she thinks, the smartest approach is to stop reading snapshot polling and focus on the medium- and long-term future. Instead of getting into the weeds of technical recessions, she said, keep reminding Canadians that on cost-of-living, the government is failing Canadians.

But the party would have to get comfortable with the reality that the argument might not land today, or even a year from today. She admits that it will be difficult “from a caucus management perspective because it can feel ungratifying when you don’t score that quick win.”

Poilievre has waged this kind of disciplined campaign before, when he targeted the carbon tax with a dogged effectiveness. Even as conservative-sympathetic voices urged him to move on, he would not relent until a majority of Canadians shared his view — and the Carney government eventually did, too, cancelling the consumer tax last year.

“It requires a great deal of discipline. It will be very challenging. There could be tough moments,” said Roth. “But I think it still would be foolish to try to play Whac-A-Mole on the short-term wins.”
Coming out of the caucus meeting in B.C. this week, there are some indications that Poilievre is thinking the same way.

Even among his supporters in the party, the leader is not known as someone who will easily change course once he’s determined a path. But he has in recent days shown signs that he plans to make tweaks in his approach and messaging.

After frequent criticisms that he’s too quick to take easy political shots at the prime minister and government, Poilievre has lately been projecting something more statesmanlike, including his comment last week in New York that he wouldn’t criticize his government while on foreign soil. The Conservative leader told Cnbc that Canadians were feeling “wounded” by U.S. tariffs and urging cooler heads to prevail. But, he said, “I’m not going to attack my prime minister on foreign soil. It’s just not something I’m going to do.”
He referred to that during a speech Wednesday to his caucus, saying that some U.S. media were “befuddled” that he wouldn’t criticize his opponents.
Poilievre has also emphasized in recent days that he would like the Liberal government to succeed in its trade war with Trump, despite what that would mean for his own aspirations.
“Our duty is country before party,” he told Conservative MPs.

The comments stood out for their willingness to disown a noisy, very online faction of conservative-minded Canadians who have taken Trump’s side against Carney. That has created a more complicated calculus for Poilievre, given a recent poll by the Angus Reid Institute found that 33 per cent of Conservative voters have a favourable view of the U.S. president, while 59 per cent of them have an unfavourable view. (By comparison, 95 per cent of Liberals disapprove of Trump, along with 92 per cent of NDP voters and 94 per cent of Bloc Québécois voters, making a fighting posture far more comfortable for those parties.)

Poilievre was criticized during last year’s federal election campaign for not being clear enough in condemning Trump and his attacks on Canada. But that looks to be changing, too. In his speech on Wednesday, the Conservative leader referred to Trump’s “trolling,” knowing full well that some of his caucus members and party supporters are Trump fans.
Patience and focusing on the long term is an easy strategy to recommend when there doesn’t seem to be any other one on offer.
But it’s not easy imagine it being carried out by a caucus this restless. The gathering in Penticton this week was an assembly of thoroughly grumpy MPs.

Two former high-ranking staffers confirmed that the mood is as bad as they can remember it in the party. People are depressed and, even a year-and-a-half after the election, they are still grieving a loss that they feel was unfairly imposed on them by outside forces.

Since then, Carney has successfully lured four MPs to join his caucus, and won six of seven byelections this year (the exception being Poilievre winning back a seat in Parliament in Battle River–Crowfoot last year, where the Liberals did not run). Conservatives have averaged just 24.6 per cent support across all seven byelections (that includes Poilievre’s 80 per cent victory), a shadow of the 41 per cent support they earned in last year’s election.

When Carney speaks to reporters lately, he almost never mentions Poilievre or the Conservative party by name. It’s a tactic that more than one senior Conservative said (with at least one adding some reluctant admiration) is driving Conservatives mad. Since Carney became Liberal leader, he has tried to convince Canadians his real opposition is the Trump administration, not the other party in the House of Commons, because the Trump contrast is the one that has propelled him to historic highs in the polls.
But that has also blunted Poilievre’s best political skill, which is hand-to-hand combat, and it has only fuelled the party’s feeling of irrelevancy.

The longer-term strategy also doesn’t reckon with the fact that most Conservative MPs fully expect Carney to go to the polls before Trump leaves the scene, although not even Liberals are sure about that. If they’re right, it means the slow-burn approach could still be unhurriedly sputtering along by the time the next election happens.
“Every available piece of public polling shows us that we’re getting absolutely obliterated if there’s an election anytime soon,” said a senior Conservative source.

Conservative members of Parliament, whose jobs are on the line if the party takes a beating in the next election, are as aware of that as anyone else. If projections by the current polls are mapped onto election scenarios, it’s possible that more than four in 10 Conservative MPs could be out of a job as the Liberals romp to a possible 228-seat majority .
The foreboding has fuelled questions in the media about Poilievre’s leadership, although on the ground it’s hard to find anyone who genuinely thinks he is in any imminent trouble.

Even Tories who would prefer to see a new leader in place point to Poilievre’s overwhelming endorsement at the party’s convention in January — from 87 per cent of party members — and the support he stills commands.

“I still don’t think Liberals and non-Conservatives and people who don’t pay attention understand just how dominant a force he has become in the national federal party,” said Ben Woodfinden, who was Poilievre’s director of communications until 2025.

At least half a dozen Conservatives made the point to National Post that if the Reform Act was used to topple the leader (as Conservative MPs had done with Erin O’Toole), Poilievre could simply run in the resulting leadership race to replace himself and win easily.
He is not seen as the kind of guy who would go quietly.

There is also a fear, now being made publicly by some longtime party operatives , that a leadership race in the Trump era would be massively damaging to the party. It would bring internal disputes about the direction of the party into the limelight and it would activate a legion of online influencers that more moderate members of the party believe have been too sympathetic to the U.S. president.

“I don’t see the value in going through a really bloody, nasty leadership race, rip each other apart, open up wounds that don’t need to be reopened up, so that we can throw somebody new in, so that he or she could get f-cking torched,” said Anthony Koch, a longtime Conservative adviser.

And the payoff with a new leader remains extremely questionable. David Coletto, who runs the polling firm Abacus Data, tried to quantify the effect of a hypothetical new leader on the national polls recently, and found that even with an ideal new leader, the Conservatives could gain all of about two percentage points from where they are now.
That would put the Conservatives 11 points behind the Liberals, rather than the current 13-point deficit per the polling average at 338Canada.

Coletto’s hypothetical also has some major caveats. It assumes a new leader with zero negative impressions among voters and it assumes that the new leader will hold all the voters that support the party because of Poilievre.

“What I take from this is that any Conservative leader, this one or the next, faces the same underlying problem: a prime minister who is liked, whose government is approved of, and who is seen as best able to handle the issues Canadians care most about right now: Trump and U.S. file,” wrote Coletto in early September.
The pollster argues that voters aren’t supporting the Liberals because they hate Poilievre, but because they are very impressed with Carney.
Canadians who are open to voting Conservative, but who won’t commit to casting a ballot for the party, actually like Poilievre. The problem for the Conservatives is that they like Carney even more.
Poilievre’s net favourability, which is the percentage of people with positive perceptions minus those with negative impressions, is plus nine. But Carney’s is plus-43.
Although most Tories don’t think Poilievre is under any immediate threat, some are looking ahead to a major test of his leadership that could change that.

On Friday, Conservative MP Larry Brock officially resigned from Parliament, as he promised he would several weeks ago. He won his Brantford—Brant South—Six Nations riding by 11 percentage points in the 2025 federal election. But pollsters are already warning that the Liberals have a chance to wrestle the seat away from the Conservatives in a byelection, which would be a crushing blow for a party that needs to gain and hold seats in the Greater Toronto Area and Southwestern Ontario to have any hope at forming government.

“If there is a movement to get rid of Pierre, it would probably massively intensify following a loss at Brantford. It would be driven by MPs out of just pure self interest,” said one senior Conservative.

One Conservative strategist estimated that losing Brock’s former seat in Brantford would be a sign that the party could be looking at a single-digit seat count in Ontario in a hypothetical federal election, compared to the 52 they hold in the province today.

Conservative MPs who see a threat brewing to their parliamentary salary May not be convinced by Coletto’s data that a new leader would be no saviour. Or they May accept it, yet consider a roll of the leadership dice to be as good an option as any in a desperation situation.
Anyone keeping track of all these possible scenarios for the Conservatives over the next two years will notice there is risk in every path that lies ahead.
Toppling Poilievre could spark an all-out civil war, or it could lead to a vengeful leader returning to regain his place at the top of the party.

Sticking with Poilievre and doing the hard work of holding the government to account could risk the party getting marginalized by the ongoing trade war with Trump. It could also demoralize the caucus and spark one of the most commonly heard fears of Tory insiders: an epidemic of “quiet quitting” among the best and brightest among them, who will begin planning for a future outside of politics rather than grinding out another decade in opposition.
And whatever happens, the Trump effect will loom large over any path the party chooses to take.
But like the ocean’s tides, Trump is a force of nature, impossible to control no matter how much a Canadian party leader might bay at the moon.
Instead, Poilievre May have to channel his experience with the carbon tax, building a case against a popular Liberal agenda and trusting that Canadians will be won over — eventually.

“As our skepticism proves to be correct, that more Crown agencies won’t drive growth, and countless other examples, Canadians will turn to the Conservatives and say, ‘Oh, you guys have kind of been saying this all along, haven’t you? Now it seems to be true’,” said Roth.
It might be a long shot requiring the perseverance and patience that seem hard to find among Conservatives today. But it could be the only shot they have.

And the payoff with a new leader remains extremely questionable. David Coletto, who runs the polling firm Abacus Data, tried to quantify the effect of a hypothetical new leader on the national polls recently, and found that even with an ideal new leader, the Conservatives could gain all of about two percentage points from where they are now.

Coletto’s hypothetical also has some major caveats. It assumes a new leader with zero negative impressions among voters and it assumes that the new leader will hold all the voters that support the party because of Poilievre.

“What I take from this is that any Conservative leader, this one or the next, faces the same underlying problem: a prime minister who is liked, whose government is approved of, and who is seen as best able to handle the issues Canadians care most about right now: Trump and U.S. file,” wrote Coletto in early September.
The pollster argues that voters aren’t supporting the Liberals because they hate Poilievre, but because they are very impressed with Carney.
Canadians who are open to voting Conservative, but who won’t commit to casting a ballot for the party, actually like Poilievre. The problem for the Conservatives is that they like Carney even more.
Poilievre’s net favourability, which is the percentage of people with positive perceptions minus those with negative impressions, is plus nine. But Carney’s is plus-43.
Although most Tories don’t think Poilievre is under any immediate threat, some are looking ahead to a major test of his leadership that could change that.

On Friday, Conservative MP Larry Brock officially resigned from Parliament, as he promised he would several weeks ago. He won his Brantford—Brant South—Six Nations riding by 11 percentage points in the 2025 federal election. But pollsters are already warning that the Liberals have a chance to wrestle the seat away from the Conservatives in a byelection, which would be a crushing blow for a party that needs to gain and hold seats in the Greater Toronto Area and Southwestern Ontario to have any hope at forming government.

content_blocks.text: “If there is a movement to get rid of Pierre, it would probably massively intensify following a loss at Brantford. It would be driven by MPs out of just pure self interest,” said one senior Conservative.

One Conservative strategist estimated that losing Brock’s former seat in Brantford would be a sign that the party could be looking at a single-digit seat count in Ontario in a hypothetical federal election, compared to the 52 they hold in the province today.

Conservative MPs who see a threat brewing to their parliamentary salary May not be convinced by Coletto’s data that a new leader would be no saviour. Or they May accept it, yet consider a roll of the leadership dice to be as good an option as any in a desperation situation.
Anyone keeping track of all these possible scenarios for the Conservatives over the next two years will notice there is risk in every path that lies ahead.
Toppling Poilievre could spark an all-out civil war, or it could lead to a vengeful leader returning to regain his place at the top of the party.

Sticking with Poilievre and doing the hard work of holding the government to account could risk the party getting marginalized by the ongoing trade war with Trump. It could also demoralize the caucus and spark one of the most commonly heard fears of Tory insiders: an epidemic of “quiet quitting” among the best and brightest among them, who will begin planning for a future outside of politics rather than grinding out another decade in opposition.
And whatever happens, the Trump effect will loom large over any path the party chooses to take.
But like the ocean’s tides, Trump is a force of nature, impossible to control no matter how much a Canadian party leader might bay at the moon.
Instead, Poilievre May have to channel his experience with the carbon tax, building a case against a popular Liberal agenda and trusting that Canadians will be won over — eventually.

“As our skepticism proves to be correct, that more Crown agencies won’t drive growth, and countless other examples, Canadians will turn to the Conservatives and say, ‘Oh, you guys have kind of been saying this all along, haven’t you? Now it seems to be true’,” said Roth.
It might be a long shot requiring the perseverance and patience that seem hard to find among Conservatives today. But it could be the only shot they have.
