stories.title: How a woman’s kidney donation saved her sister – as part of a nationwide transplant chain
stories.summary: Kim Chow donated one of her organs through the Kidney Paired Donation Program
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Kim Chow says it was not a difficult decision to donate her kidney to a stranger knowing it meant her older sister, Stephanie Chow, would receive one in exchange.

In late July, after months of testing and preparation, the sisters went under the knife in Edmonton’s University of Alberta Hospital. Kim’s surgery was first. Her kidney was removed, quickly placed on ice and airlifted to another province, completing one segment of a transplant chain that stretched across the country.

Five days later, another link was completed when Stephanie was wheeled into an operating room and received a kidney from a living donor outside of Alberta. She will never know who or where the organ came from.

The exchange was made possible through the Kidney Paired Donation Program run by Canadian Blood Services. The program matches potential donor-recipient pairs who are incompatible with each other, such as the Chow sisters, with other such pairs across the country. Patients in need get a healthy kidney – just from a stranger instead of a friend or family member.

Stephanie, 42, said the transplant has changed her life.

Before the surgery, she had been on peritoneal dialysis, a treatment for kidney failure that uses the inner lining of the abdomen to filter blood inside the body. She was diagnosed with an autoimmune disorder as a child that attacked her kidneys until they “crapped out” about two years ago.

“My life was very much determined by when I had to plug into the dialysis machine at night and what time I wanted to wake up. I couldn’t really go anywhere or travel anywhere because the machine I would have to carry, the supplies, is in abundance,” Stephanie said.

She continued: “This kidney is now giving me more flexibility. I feel like I have my life back.”

In Montreal, kidney donors and transplant recipients help put hesitant patients at ease

In 2025, nearly 3,200 organs were transplanted in Canada, 59 per cent of which were kidneys, according to data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information. As of Dec. 31 that year, 4,344 Canadians were on transplant wait-lists, a large proportion for a kidney.

The majority of transplants use organs from deceased donors, since a single body can provide multiple organs. Living donors can only safely give specific organs, such as one of their two kidneys, and must pass strict medical and psychological evaluations.

Stephanie is thankful for being part of the exchange program, not only because it cut down her wait time for a transplant, but because a kidney from a living donor lasts longer and generally provides better outcomes.

The sisters want to raise greater awareness about the program, hoping to help others in Stephanie’s position. “A lot of people have no idea this is an option,” she said.

The paired donation program offers three possible chains, explained transplant nephrologist Michel Paquet, who is a medical adviser to Canadian Blood Services. The first is a paired exchange, where two donor-recipient pairs, or four people, swap kidneys.

Then there is a “closed chain,” where the exchange happens between three or more pairs, usually maxing out at seven, and where the final donor gives a kidney to the first recipient, closing a self-contained loop. Finally, there is an “open chain,” where a sequence of transplants is sparked by an altruistic person who donates a kidney but is not connected to a transplant candidate.

Chains are created using a computerized algorithm and there are three match cycles each year, said Dr. Paquet, who is also the medical director of the living kidney donation program at the University of Montreal Hospital Centre. Since the program began in 2009 – first in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario before expanding across Canada – it has led to more than 1,300 transplants, he added.

For the first decade, donors had to travel to the recipient’s city to have the surgery. But COVID-19 pushed the program to transport the organs between cities and provinces, helping to expand its reach. More than 400 organs have since been shipped across the country.

One challenge with the program is that the chains are fragile and can collapse if even one person can no longer donate or receive a kidney. However, Dr. Paquet said it’s “pretty rare” for people to simply back out. When that does happen, it’s more often related to medical issues.

Kim, 38, described the program as an exercise in humanity, where emotions are tangled into every decision of an emotionally and physically taxing process.

She began her journey to become a donor in spring 2024, undergoing countless tests – including blood work, urine samples, physical exams, medical questionnaires, X-rays and CT scans – before the surgery took place this summer.

Kim was told that at any point she could back out. For her, that wasn’t an option.

“As a family member, you want to do everything within your power to help your loved one, right? So, even if for whatever reason things didn’t work out, I wanted to know that I had done everything that I could do to help her in that situation.”

Kim did have some worries, such as the long-term impact of having only one kidney and how difficult recovery would be, but none were big enough to sway her from helping her sister.

Postsurgery, their experiences have differed greatly. While a new kidney has given Stephanie a boost of energy and excitement for the future, Kim has been exhausted as her body adapts to having just one kidney. Over time, her organ will expand to take on the workload of two.

The sisters were close before, but the transplant process has brought them even closer together. And it has given Kim a new perspective on what Stephanie endured.

“I don’t think any of us realized exactly how tired she was and how her failing kidney was impacting her life the way that it was,” Kim said. “If she was even half as tired before her transplant as I was coming out of that surgery and healing, I have a lot more empathy for what she went through.”

Stephanie expects to be able to travel again in about a year, when her medical team is certain the donated kidney is performing as it should. She doesn’t know where she’ll go first – maybe Europe or Asia, potentially a river cruise.

It would be nice, she added, to go somewhere with her sister.

stories.title: Tiff takes over Toronto with the Tribute Awards gala and a Golden Globes-hosted bash
stories.summary: Mark Carney, Seth Rogen and Chris Rock among attendees at awards gala
stories.author: Nolan Bryant
stories.content:
For the past eight years, the Tiff Tribute Awards gala has marked the festival’s opening week. The evening serves as both a fundraiser for the festival and a platform to honour some of the remarkable talent in town.

The hum of activity started during cocktail hour, which was held in one of the ballrooms at the Fairmont Royal York. Prime Minster Mark Carney and his wife, Diana Fox Carney, were early arrivals (the PM was on hosting duties as part of the Canada Investment Summit and stayed for cocktails only). At dinner, the latter was seated a couple of seats over from the Vancouver-born Seth Rogen, who was honoured with the Tiff Tribute Norman Jewison Career Achievement Award presented by the Budman family.

Dame Helen Mirren received the award inspired by Tiff’s women’s empowerment initiative, Share Her Journey, dedicating it to recently departed trailblazers Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem. Penelope Cruz, who is in town for her film La Bola Negra , received the Special Tribute Award for her lasting and extraordinary contributions to film. Presenting her with the award were a trio or directors: Florian Zeller, director of Bunker , and Spanish filmmaking duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the pair behind La Bola Negra , which took home the Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Director.

Chris Rock, director of the film Misty Green , which had its world premiere at Tiff, honoured the film’s star, Rosalind Eleazar, with the Tiff Tribute Performer Award. Director Lee Chang-dong, who received the Tiff Tribute Ebert Director Award presented by the Tory family, took the stage later in the evening to honour his friend, the remarkable French actor Isabelle Huppert, with a Tiff Tribute Performer Award (she’s in town for the North American premiere of Marc Fitoussi’s All About Corinne ).

Among the attendees out to celebrate film were outgoing Tiff board chair Jeffrey Remedios and incoming board chair, former Toronto mayor John Tory; arts supporters Jay Smith, Anne-Marie Canning, Diane Bald and Michael Budman; athlete and activist Rick Hansen, who presented Siân Heder with the Impact Media award; and Tiff’s chief executive, Cameron Bailey. Rolex served as the event’s presenting sponsor.

The previous evening, the Four Seasons Hotel Toronto hosted the Tiff-timed Golden Globes party. Dubbed ‘The Road to the Golden Globes,’ the bash is a countdown of sorts to the 84th edition of the annual awards, which will take place in January in Los Angeles. The party has become an after-after party for the big films premiering on Tiff’s buzziest Saturday night. Most parties during the festival are film-specific, but this one brings them all together.

In one corner, Naomi Watts, in town for The Housewife , caught up with Sarah Paulson, who is at the festival for Closing Night. Jordan Firstman, in Toronto for his anticipated directorial debut, Club Kid (a breakout hit at Cannes) was tête-à-tête with Andrew Scott, at Tiff with director Simon Stone’s latest film, Elsinore . Stars of The Julia Set , including Chloe Bailey, Christopher Briney and Chase Infiniti, popped by a day after their own Hugo Boss-hosted party.

Also in attendance were actors-turned-directors Rebel Wilson, at the festival for Girl Group , and Courteney Cox, premiering her true-crime thriller Evil Genius (her cast Patricia Arquette, David Harbour and Ryan Eggold in tow). Former prime minister Justin Trudeau and his long-time chief of staff, Katie Telford, made the rounds following the announcement of their new media and entertainment production company, Hope and Hard Work. Golden Globes president Helen Hoehne presided over it all.

Dame Helen Mirren received the award inspired by Tiff’s women’s empowerment initiative, Share Her Journey, dedicating it to recently departed trailblazers Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem. Penelope Cruz, who is in town for her film La Bola Negra , received the Special Tribute Award for her lasting and extraordinary contributions to film. Presenting her with the award were a trio or directors: Florian Zeller, director of Bunker , and Spanish filmmaking duo Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, the pair behind La Bola Negra , which took home the Cannes Film Festival Award for Best Director.

Chris Rock, director of the film Misty Green , which had its world premiere at Tiff, honoured the film’s star, Rosalind Eleazar, with the Tiff Tribute Performer Award. Director Lee Chang-dong, who received the Tiff Tribute Ebert Director Award presented by the Tory family, took the stage later in the evening to honour his friend, the remarkable French actor Isabelle Huppert, with a Tiff Tribute Performer Award (she’s in town for the North American premiere of Marc Fitoussi’s All About Corinne ).

content_blocks.text: Among the attendees out to celebrate film were outgoing Tiff board chair Jeffrey Remedios and incoming board chair, former Toronto mayor John Tory; arts supporters Jay Smith, Anne-Marie Canning, Diane Bald and Michael Budman; athlete and activist Rick Hansen, who presented Siân Heder with the Impact Media award; and Tiff’s chief executive, Cameron Bailey. Rolex served as the event’s presenting sponsor.
Road to The Golden Globes Party, Sept. 12, Toronto

content_blocks.caption: (L-R) Chloe Bailey, Rowan Blanchard, Chase Infiniti and a guest at the 'Road to the Golden Globes,' on Sept. 12. Courtesy of The Golden Globes/Supplied

content_blocks.text: The previous evening, the Four Seasons Hotel Toronto hosted the Tiff-timed Golden Globes party. Dubbed ‘The Road to the Golden Globes,’ the bash is a countdown of sorts to the 84th edition of the annual awards, which will take place in January in Los Angeles. The party has become an after-after party for the big films premiering on Tiff’s buzziest Saturday night. Most parties during the festival are film-specific, but this one brings them all together.

Jordan Firstman, in Toronto for his anticipated directorial debut, Club Kid (a breakout hit at Cannes) was tête-à-tête with Andrew Scott, at Tiff with director Simon Stone’s latest film, Elsinore . Stars of The Julia Set , including Chloe Bailey, Christopher Briney and Chase Infiniti, popped by a day after their own Hugo Boss-hosted party.

Also in attendance were actors-turned-directors Rebel Wilson, at the festival for Girl Group , and Courteney Cox, premiering her true-crime thriller Evil Genius (her cast Patricia Arquette, David Harbour and Ryan Eggold in tow). stories.title: ‘The rider just goes flying’: B.C. mayors call for clearer e-scooter rules
stories.summary: They’re convenient and fun, but a surge in injuries involving electric scooters is becoming an issue on the campaign trail ahead of municipal elections in Metro Vancouver, with local leaders calling on the B.C. government to establish province-wide safety rules.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – They’re convenient and fun, but a surge in injuries involving electric scooters is becoming an issue on the campaign trail ahead of municipal elections in Metro Vancouver, with local leaders calling on the B.C. government to establish province-wide safety rules.

“They go from like 0 to 40 in like three seconds,” said Ian Tait of Ambulance Paramedics of B.C. “They go so fast and they can turn on a dime. But if you’re not paying attention they can also wipe out on a dime.”

When riders crash, Tait said, they often have little opportunity to properly break their fall. “When you hit something that’s like a dead weight thing, like a car or a curb, the rider just goes flying off of that scooter,” he said.

E-scooters are illegal in 36 B.C. communities as part of a pilot project that includes age restrictions. Anyone under the age of 16 riding them is breaking the law. But it appears to be happening a lot.

Recent data points to younger riders who have not yet reached the provincial age requirement showing up in emergency rooms after crashes. Figures from the Canadian Hospital Injury Reporting and Prevention Surveillance Program show 13-year-old children made up the highest proportion of emergency room visits for e-scooter crashes at 22 per cent.

There were 81 visits to the B.C. Children’s Hospital emergency department between April 2025 and 2026 related to e-scooter use, more than double those of the previous year.

Illegal riding behavior doesn’t end there. Riders in metro Vancouver are frequently spotted not wearing helmets, doubling —having two riders on at the same time — or appearing to ride while intoxicated. The scooters have even shown up on the highway.

At the same time, municipalities say riders and parents can struggle to understand the rules because regulations vary between communities.

Langley City Mayor Nathan Pachal said he hears from parents who want their children on e-scooters, but they aren’t unsure about what is permitted and what is safe. “People want to do the right thing, but they don’t know how to do it,” Pachal said.

New Westminster Mayor Patrick Johnstone said it’s an issue he keeps hearing about out on the municipal campaign trail. “I’m not exaggerating at all when I say when I go to have a meeting at a seniors’ centre in New Westminster and talk to seniors about their number one issue, it’s not affordable housing right now. It’s not crime on the streets. It is fear of scooters on sidewalks.”

The issue was front and centre at the Union of B.C. Municipalities convention this week, where the cities of Langley, New Westminster and Nanaimo have introduced resolutions asking the province to modernize legislation, create consistent rules for mobility devices, and provide municipalities with the funding and data to eliminate serious injuries and deaths on the roads.

In a statement to CTV News, the Ministry of Transportation and Transit said it will continue to work with local governments and road safety partners to improve road safety and safe access to active transportation infrastructure.

With files from CTV’s Isabella Zavarise and The Canadian Press

stories.title: CTV News in the Arctic: Warship commander says ‘the global order is changing’ as Canada expands presence
stories.summary: Delivered to the Royal Canadian Navy last summer, Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray is the newest Arctic and offshore patrol vessel helping bolster Canada’s presence in the North.
stories.author: Graham Richardson, Stephanie Ha
stories.content:
Near Cambridge BAY, NVT. – Delivered to the Royal Canadian Navy last summer, Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray is the newest Arctic and offshore patrol vessel helping bolster Canada’s presence in the North.

On a brisk September day near Cambridge Bay, Nvt., during Operation Arctic Ghost with the Canadian Coast Guard and the RCMP, Cmdr. Brian Henwood surveys the bridge of the ship like an officer exactly where he wants to be.

“I mean, this is our territory. These are our Arctic waters,” Henwood told CTV News. “Having our ships here, patrolling and making sure people aren’t coming through without our permission is critical.”

“Personally speaking, the global order is changing, and I think the government is responding to that,” he also said.

The navy ship is meeting up with the Canadian Coast Guard this week for joint exercises. CTV News is exclusively embedded on the coast guard’s Des Groseilliers icebreaker.

Construction of the Robert Hampton Gray began in 2022, and the ship was delivered to the navy in 2025.

The current mission, which began in August in Halifax, is the vessel’s first operational deployment as it makes its way to its home port of Esquimalt, B.C. by November. It also marks only the third time a Royal Canadian Navy warship has made a complete transit of the Arctic.

The warship is one of six Arctic and offshore patrol vessels built under a program worth nearly $5 billion, including design, construction and maintenance costs.

“Six is a lot of ships. It’s a lot of money. But this is a vast part of the country many people never even see,” Henwood said.

“It’s presence. It’s security. It’s also backing up what you say about these waters. The purpose of these ships is to conduct sovereignty patrols, make sure we know who and what is operating up here and, if necessary, respond to situations that arise.”

The Canadian Coast Guard, which is now under the Department of National Defence, is also getting two of its own offshore patrol vessels for the Arctic, with one slated for delivery later this year and the other expected in 2027.

Henwood, like most sailors, tends to focus on the mission in front of him. But from the bridge of one of Canada’s newest naval vessels, it is clear the strategic importance of the Arctic has rarely been higher.

The Northwest Passage has been the subject of a sovereignty dispute for decades. Canada maintains the waters are internal and under Canadian control. The United States views the passage as an international waterway through which ships can transit without seeking permission.

For years, the two countries have managed the disagreement through an arrangement under which U.S. vessels seek Canada’s consent before transiting the passage. With tensions in the Canada-U.S. relationship running hot enough to melt ice, some observers are questioning how durable that understanding is.

Henwood said those questions are for governments to answer.

For him, the mission is about contributing to a growing Canadian presence in the Arctic at a time when public awareness of northern security issues appears to be increasing.

“I’ve been in the navy for 26 years, and the public seems more aware of the threats facing Canada right now,” he said. “That includes the Arctic, but also the broader international environment.”

CTV News Ottawa Bureau Chief Graham Richardson is reporting from the Arctic this week while embedded with the Canadian Coast Guard, as Canada looks to assert its presence in the north.

stories.title: Four cruise-ships in one day: what is behind one of Halifax’s biggest cruise seasons yet?
stories.summary: Earlier this week, four cruise ships pulled into Halifax Harbour on one single day, bringing tourists from far and wide into the city. It’s a clear sign of a booming cruise industry which has historically provided a major boost for the tourism industry.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - Earlier this week, four cruise ships pulled into Halifax Harbour on one single day, bringing tourists from far and wide into the city. It’s a clear sign of a booming cruise industry which has historically provided a major boost for the tourism industry.

This month alone more than 60 cruise ships will dock in Halifax. That is not a record for visits, but it is close to it and a clear sign of a booming cruise industry.

“It is our steady, consistent fall season,” said Port of Halifax Manager of Cruise Development, Robyn Stewart.

This year’s boom is due in part to an increased presence of commercial cruise ships docking in Halifax.

MSC Meraviglia from Brooklyn, N.Y, kicked off Halifax’s cruise season with a visit on April 21, prior to its transatlantic voyage to Barcelona. Norwegian Cruise Line increased its Halifax presence in spring and summer with the addition of Bermuda itineraries that included a stop in Halifax, while Carnival Cruise Line made its return to Halifax following its move to new homeport in Norfolk, Virginia.

Based on the latest schedule , 2026 is expected to see 189 cruise ships dock in Halifax, with more than 350,000 visitors.

“It has been the best season we’ve ever had in our company’s history,” said Ambassatours Gray Line’s revenue manager Peter McLaughlin, as he described the number of cruise ship visitors. “It has blown through all of our expectations.”

According to the Cruise Lines International Association , when a tourist arrives on a cruise ship, each one usually disembarks, enjoys the Halifax boardwalk and then spends money, which provides a major boost for the tourism industry.

“Cruise ships bring in about a $200 million economic impact for Nova Scotia and more than 1000 jobs every year,” said Stewart.

Many cruise ship passengers in Halifax said they preferred going on a ship because they don’t like to travel by airplane and they enjoy a slow-paced vacation.

“I don’t have to do my huge research to figure out what to see because it’s kind of packaged for you, and then you get to see it,” said cruise ship passenger Barb Atkin from Chicago.

“I can walk onto a cruise ship and start my vacation,”said Margaret McGovern, visiting from Philadelphia. “The moment I am on board I get to visit all the different places.”

Halifax’s busy cruise ship schedule is not about to wind down anytime soon with close to 100 vessels still expected to visit by time the season ends in November.

According to the Cruise Lines International Association , when a tourist arrives on a cruise ship, each one usually disembarks, enjoys the Halifax boardwalk and then spends money, which provides a major boost for the tourism industry.
“Cruise ships bring in about a $200 million economic impact for Nova Scotia and more than 1000 jobs every year,” said Stewart.
Many cruise ship passengers in Halifax said they preferred going on a ship because they don’t like to travel by airplane and they enjoy a slow-paced vacation.
“I don’t have to do my huge research to figure out what to see because it’s kind of packaged for you, and then you get to see it,” said cruise ship passenger Barb Atkin from Chicago.
“I can walk onto a cruise ship and start my vacation,”said Margaret McGovern, visiting from Philadelphia. “The moment I am on board I get to visit all the different places.”
Halifax’s busy cruise ship schedule is not about to wind down anytime soon with close to 100 vessels still expected to visit by time the season ends in November.

stories.title: Inside some of the hottest Tiff parties: photos
stories.summary: Venues in the city’s Entertainment District were taken over by Hollywood stars who gathered to sip on cocktails after the release of their new films.
stories.author: Denio Lourenco
stories.content:
By Denio Lourenco

Posted September 18, 2026 11:05 pm.

The Toronto International Film Festival is winding down after 11 days of red carpet premieres, special screenings and endless partying along King Street.

Multiple venues in the city’s Entertainment District were taken over by Hollywood stars who gathered to sip on cocktails after the release of their new films.

Actors like Cole Sprouse, Cynthia Erivo, Orlando Bloom, Penelope Cruz, Rami Malek and more were spotted out on the town.

Below are photos from some of the hottest parties.

CINEDINE hosted multiple cocktail receptions and dinners at Punch Restaurant inside Le Germain Hotel on Mercer Street. The guests included actors Antonio Banderas, Forest Whitaker, Diego Luna and Cole Sprouse.

All photos by Photagonist.

Greek restaurant Petros82 on Adelaide Street was transformed into RBC House where it hosted industry parties for some of the festival’s most anticipated premieres. It hosted big names like Michelle Yeoh, Cynthia Erivo, Orlando Bloom and Lily-Rose Depp.

Photos by Ryan Emberley and Matt Tibbo/Getty Images for RBC.

The afterparty for “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been” was hosted at a new venue in the St. Lawrence Market area called “Darling Girl.” The guest list included American singer and actress, Darlene Love; the documentary’s director, Barry Avrich; and producers Taraji P. Henson and Mark Selby.

All photos by Ryan Emeberley.

Cassius Cucina Contemporanea on King Street hosted premiere celebrations, cocktail receptions and private events tied to some of TIFF’s most anticipated films. The venue held multiple events throughout every night of the festival and hosted celebrities such as Cole Sprouse, James McAvoy and Annie Murphy.

All photos by Photogandist.

Rogers Communications, the presenting partner of the Toronto International Film Festival, held a gala at Blue Bovine steakhouse inside Union Station on Sept. 12. The guest list included former prime minister Justin Trudeau, Toronto Blue Jays manager John Schneider and Breakfast Television’s Dina Pugliese.

All photos by George Pimentel.

stories.title: RCMP made internal inquiries over possible FBI intelligence sharing halt after Patel’s CBC criticism, sources say
stories.summary: Inquiries followed Kash Patel’s criticism of a CBC memo on coverage of the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11
stories.author: Mercedes Stephenson
stories.content:
The RCMP began making internal inquiries to determine whether the FBI halted intelligence sharing with the Mounties after an Aug. 27 tweet by agency director Kash Patel, sources say.

Mr. Patel was critical of an internal CBC/Radio-Canada guideline about removing the word terrorism from coverage of the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11.

The post from the Federal Bureau of Investigation director said that “any agency in Canada that doesn’t publicly reject” the CBC’s internal guidance “will no longer have a friend in this FBI.”

The public broadcaster subsequently reversed the policy .

The Globe and Mail spoke to three national-security sources with direct knowledge of the probe who stated that the RCMP has not found any indication that intelligence sharing between the two police forces has been interrupted.

Two of the sources said the RCMP did not receive any official notifications from the FBI about co-operation being suspended.

The Globe is not naming the sources, who were not authorized to speak publicly about the matter.

The New York Times reported on Friday that Mr. Patel “temporarily halted” co-operation in response to the CBC policy. The newspaper said that involved cancelled meetings, though it did not provide specifics.

The FBI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis issued a statement that attacked the CBC policy but did not answer questions about the New York Times story.

The RCMP and the FBI frequently co-operate on cross-border investigations related to national security, terrorism, drug trafficking and other crimes, including several high-profile investigations in just the past year. For example, RCMP Commissioner Mike Duheme appeared alongside Mr. Patel at a news conference earlier this year to announce the arrest of alleged Canadian drug trafficker Ryan Wedding.

The RCMP released a statement that declined to comment on whether there was any impact on its work with the FBI but noted that the force and the RCMP have a long-standing history of working together.

“Given the shared border between Canada and the United States, the RCMP works with U.S. law enforcement partners to address cross-border criminal threats and protect public safety,” the statement said.

The controversy around the CBC policy on terrorism unfolded at a time of increasing animosity between the two countries amid President Donald Trump’s trade war. Mr. Patel’s post on X came a week after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that his government was walking away from trade negotiations with the United States.

The CBC has faced criticism over a leaked copy of a memo that outlined what the broadcaster said was its long-standing policy to attribute the term terrorism to officials or experts.

The broadcaster announced the same day as Mr. Patel’s X post that it was changing its guidance to no longer require attribution when describing the Sept. 11 attacks as an act of terrorism.

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Viral post raises discussions about open-air drug use in London
stories.summary: "Police pretty much Dgaf". That is the caption on a recently viral post of a man doing drugs outside the Londo...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
“Police pretty much Dgaf”. That is the caption on a recently viral post of a man doing drugs outside the London Police Station. The reddit post, which at the time of publication has achieved over 53 000 upvotes, provoked many different discussions about the open drug use in London. “lol it’s London Ontario, seems pretty normal” said one commenter. “Gotta smoke it all before he goes in.” Another joked.

Sightings of open-air drug use such as this have grown all the more common in London, despite the fact that London Police have issued a specialized project to combat this type of drug use, called “Project Pathways”.

Project Pathways consists of police officers, being assisted by mental health and addiction professionals, confronting people using drugs in public, while taking on a more compassionate, helpful approach, rather than a punitive one. Some experts however, feel that this program isn’t doing enough to fight against the core of this issue.

“ There’s going to be occasions when that seems like a good fit, but it’s still the same as anything else.” Said Dean Anderson, an addiction and clinical counselor, and founder of “Epic Recovery”. “T he vast majority of individuals are probably just going to get up and move on.

“What we want in society is we want instant satisfaction.” Anderson continued. “We want it that you walk up to somebody doing open drug use, you say the magic words and they get up and they’ll even go, okay, I’ll never do that again, a nd that’s not how it works. It works through interactions.”

Anderson also thinks that society focusing more on instant satisfaction leads to posts like the man outside the police station to become popular, and

stories.title: Ottawa will not interfere with workers’ right to strike, Hajdu says
stories.summary: A government review found employers and unions sharply divided on whether Ottawa should intervene in labour disputes
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the federal government will not interfere with workers’ right to strike as Ottawa considers legal changes to improve labour relations.

Ms. Hajdu’s department held months of consultations with unions, employers and other stakeholders over the spring and summer about the state of the Canada Labour Code. Feedback from those sessions is meant to inform future legislation.

A report summarizing what the government heard during that review found that unions and employers were split over the degree of power Ottawa should have to intervene in disputes.

Most employers argued the government should have the ability to step in to quash a labour action when Canada’s national interests are at risk. Unions were staunchly opposed to any measure that could threaten their right to strike.

Fifteen months into his tenure as Prime Minister, Carney is drawing the ire of union heads

Ms. Hajdu was asked Friday in Ottawa whether she would respect unions’ concerns.

She said the government heard in the review that Canada needs a stronger labour regime to foster better relationships between workers and employers. The focus of the review was to find new supports for both parties, with an eye to leveraging the federal mediation service to maintain industrial peace.

“I can stand here and say that we will never interfere with a worker’s right to bargain or to strike, but we do all agree that there are circumstances where better tools are needed,” Ms. Hajdu said.

The minister would not say whether legislation to change the Canada Labour Code will come in the fall session of Parliament, which is set to begin Monday.

Canadian Labour Congress president Bea Bruske said in a media statement that the government’s labour review report did reflect what unions told Ottawa about its priorities.

“Canada needs stronger labour laws that protect the right to strike, support free collective bargaining and hold employers accountable when they break the rules,” Ms. Bruske said.

A Senate committee report published in June argued that labour disruptions in critical industries like transportation can harm Canada’s reputation as a reliable trading partner at a time when Ottawa is trying to diversify its trade beyond the United States.

Ms. Bruske said in her statement that worker protections, decent wages and collective bargaining are critical to making Canada’s economy more resilient in the face of U.S. trade aggression.

Carney promises sweeping economic legislation, fast pace this fall during caucus meeting

Ms. Hajdu was at Algonquin College on Friday to explain the federal government’s plan to get young workers paid, ON-the-job experience in the skilled trades.

Starting early next year, young Canadians will be able to access paid job placements for up to four months, giving them hands-on experience before beginning an apprenticeship.

The $880-million in funding for that program comes from a bigger pot of $8-billion the Liberals have set aside since the spring economic update to promote the skilled trades across Canada.

The federal government has stressed the importance of recruiting and training a new generation of skilled tradespeople, such as carpenters, electricians and welders.

Later this fall, any tradesperson who has completed an apprenticeship and earned a certification in a Red Seal trade since April, 2025, will also receive a $5,000 bonus.

The federal government will roll out a program over the fall to help small- and medium-sized businesses offer more apprenticeships and Ottawa also plans to top up employment insurance payments for apprentices during training starting next spring.

stories.title: Politics Insider: Carney promises sweeping new economic legislation
stories.summary: And, Ontario Premier Doug Ford says his comments about Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow were not an endorsement
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Prime Minister Mark Carney promised sweeping new economic legislation and a punishing pace this fall as his caucus met in Ottawa today ahead of Parliament’s return on Monday.

Stephanie Levitz reports that Carney said the economic bill is a follow-through on the momentum of the past seven days: a meeting with Ukraine’s President , a landmark investment summit and a whirlwind trip to Europe to forge a new relationship with that continent.

“It’s a lot, but that was just the warm-up,” he told his MPs in a speech at the start of their caucus meeting today. His benches now have three new members after the Liberals won several by-elections in August.

Carney said the legislation – which he called the Building Canada Strong Act – is the next phase of his government’s promise to speed up infrastructure and other projects.

In other news today, Laura Stone reports that Ontario Premier Doug Ford took to the airwaves today to try to clarify that he definitely did not endorse Olivia Chow for Toronto mayor when he spoke publicly about supporting her earlier this week.

In a friendly radio interview with former Toronto mayor John Tory on Newstalk 1010, Ford said he gets along well with Chow, but insisted he didn’t issue a full-throated endorsement of her candidacy when he praised her and told reporters to “read between the lines.”

“Let’s be very, very clear. When I endorse someone, which I’m not, you come out and fully endorse them. You don’t say read between the lines,” Ford told Tory.

The confusion started earlier this week when Ford, asked by a reporter whether he’s endorsing anyone for mayor, talked up his working relationship with Chow. The two were side-by-side, along with federal ministers, this week at the opening of a new biomanufacturing facility in Toronto.

“I just want to say the Mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship. Phenomenal. And we’ve given the City of Toronto more money than they’ve ever seen in their lives, over $9-billion,” he said.

“We’re going to continue supporting the Mayor. She’s doing an incredible job. So, read between the lines.”

Ford said today that the “read between the lines” reference meant he’s going to continue to work things out with the mayor, whom he once predicted would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city before she was first elected in 2023.

After Chow’s main opponent in the race, councillor Brad Bradford, declared that Ford had endorsed Chow because she has “never stopped Doug Ford from doing exactly what he wanted to do,” the Premier’s Office released a late-night clarification Thursday trying to walk back Ford’s comments.

Several ex-Ford staffers are supporting Bradford’s campaign, including the Premier’s former executive director of communications, Laryssa Waler, and his longtime campaign manager Kory Teneycke.

Eby vows to scrap plan to buy ferries from afar: B.C. Premier David Eby made a series of election-style promises during a press conference after a speech to the Union of B.C. Municipalities Conference in downtown Vancouver, including committing to pause a controversial expansion of the provincial sales tax, and to build future generations of ferries at home instead of sourcing them from elsewhere.

B.C. Conservatives lose 10th MLA since August: Claire Rattée issued a scathing exit statement that says she was among at least 10 Conservatives who signed a letter calling on party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay to quit.

‘Father of Nunavut’ challenges territory’s refusal to pay for his housing, home care in Iqaluit: John Amagoalik, a former politician in his late 70s, is credited for his involvement in the creation of the territory in April, 1999.

Ottawa mayoral candidate charged over alleged death threats against Mark Sutcliffe, Doug Ford: Ottawa mayoral candidate Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas was arrested on Sept. 15 in Ottawa and has been charged with two counts each of criminal harassment and uttering death threats, along with several weapons-related offences.

MPs return to Ottawa: The House of Commons sits again on Monday after its summer break. The Senate sits again on Sept. 28.

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney today addressed a national caucus retreat on Parliament Hill. The retreat is being held today and Saturday. On Sunday, Carney is visiting Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron.

Party Leaders: Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet will be at a caucus meeting in the Quebec municipality of Cantley on Sunday. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May attended a community meeting on Salt Spring Island in British Columbia. No schedules released for other party leaders.

McPherson to focus on unity: NDP Leader Avi Lewis says Alberta MP Heather McPherson is leaving her role as NDP caucus house leader to campaign for unity ahead of the Alberta referendum. Don Davies will assume McPherson’s role in addition to his parliamentary leader duties, while Jenny Kwan will take over from Davies as whip.

Newly appointed diplomat: Joël Dupuis is Canada’s new ambassador to Belgium, succeeding Nicholas Brousseau.

Ahead of the return of the House of Commons on Monday, Liberal MP Marilyn Gladu talks about what she has read this past summer.

“I read so much non-fiction (mostly articles, papers and reports) at work that I usually read for entertainment, and it is typically an Agatha Christie-type “ who done it”. This summer , I decided to try three authors I have never read that write this similar type of novel," Gladu wrote.

Dead in the Morning by Margaret Yorke (First published by Geoffrey Bles, 1970) – A delightful British mystery set in a small village with a dysfunctional family. Excellent! (I then went on to read the rest of the things she has written.)

Death at the Fireside Inn by Kitty Kildare (K.E. O’Connor Books, 2024) – Veronica Vale, the eccentric but brilliant crime solver accompanied by her little dog Benji gets to the bottom of a murder that happened in one of the inns the family owns. Turns out they own a lot of inns and so I read the rest of her series as well.

Her Silent Bones by Pamela Fagan Hutchins (StoryFire LTD, 2024) – Terrific first book in a series about Detective Delaney Pace, ex-trucker, and the solving of gruesome murders.

Political Books this Fall:

As the fall political scene gets under way, here’s a look at some of the political books coming soon:

The Dawn of Competitive Party Politics in Alberta, An End to Solitude by Anthony M. Sayers, Royce Koop and David K. Stewart, Sept. 15 (UBC Press)

A look at Alberta’s political history and party politics from the birth of the province through to its political evolution in the last two decades.

Justin Trudeau: Power, Promise, and the Fight for Canada by David Olive - ECW Press, Sept. 29, 2026 (ECW Press)

Journalist Olive ponders the legacy of Canada’s 23rd prime minister, contrasting Trudeau with those who most influenced him.

Into the Breach, A Soldier’s Journey by General Wayne Eyre, Oct. 6. (Simon & Schuster)

The former chief of defence staff chronicles a 40-year career in the Canadian armed forces.

Unreliable Boyfriend, An Insider’s View of Dealing with a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats and Other Complicated People by Chrystia Freeland. (Simon and Schuster) Oct. 13

A mixture of polemic and memoir from the former deputy prime minister.

24 Sussex Drive, The Past and Future of Canada’s Official Residence by Dean Beeby and Ian Bailey, (Sutherland House Publishing), Oct. 20

Ahead of the move to renovate the prime ministerial residence, a look at the history and challenges of sustaining one of Canada’s most famous addresses.

Here for Canada: Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister by Stephen J. Harper. Nov. 3. (Penguin Random House Canada)

The first prime-ministerial memoir since Paul Martin’s 2009 title Hell or High Water: My Life in and out of Politics, Harper’s 656-page title covers his time in office as Canada’s 22nd prime minister.

Joe Clark: Progressive, Conservative, Canadian by Matthew Hayday. March 16. (McGill-Queen’s University Press)

The professor of Canadian history at the University of Guelph looks at the life of Canada’s 16th prime minister as well as the issues that animated his life in politics.

“I don’t think it’s ever a bad idea to ask British Columbians, especially at a moment like this, about which direction we should be going. I don’t have an announcement about an election today, but there are absolutely crucial issues in our province.” - Premier David Eby, speaking to reporters following a speech today to the Union of British Columbia Municipalities, addresses the issue of a possible snap election in B.C. amidst turmoil rocking the opposition B.C. Conservatives.

Former prime minister Stephen Harper has written his memoirs. Here for Canada, Memoirs of the 22nd Prime Minister will be released in November. But who was the first Canadian prime minister to write their memoirs?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

We May look back on this as the week Canada began to take its fate into its own hands

There are, as Lenin apparently did not say, decades when nothing happens, and weeks when decades happen. This was one of those weeks: a remarkable series of policy and diplomatic moves that give unmistakable form to what until lately had been mostly rhetorical flourish. The Carney doctrine remains only partly visible, and May only be partly developed, but there’s no denying any more that there is a doctrine. — Andrew Coyne, Columnist

Mark Carney has become the heir to C.D. Howe

Mark Carney succeeded Justin Trudeau as Prime Minister. But it feels more spiritually accurate to say that he succeeded C.D. Howe, who transformed Canada’s industry and infrastructure before, during and after the Second World War, much of it with foreign money. — John Ibbitson is a writer, journalist and the author of The Duel: Diefenbaker, Pearson and the Making of Modern Canada.

The Quebec election could result in a ripple, not a wave

With two televised debates down, and one to go, Quebec’s party leaders are running out of chances to move the needle in an election campaign that has lacked any sparkle. — Konrad Yakabuski, Columnist

Follow along for our stories on Canada-U.S. relations as news develops

Got a news tip that you’d like us to look into? E-mail us at tips@globeandmail.com . Need to share documents securely? Reach out via SecureDrop .

The answer to today’s question: Sir Charles Tupper, Conservative prime minister for 68 days from May to July of 1896, wrote Political Reminiscences of the Right Honourable Sir Charles Tupper. It was published in 1914. Canada’s sixth prime minister died in 1915 in England.

content_blocks.text: Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.
Prime Minister Mark Carney promised sweeping new economic legislation and a punishing pace this fall as his caucus met in Ottawa today ahead of Parliament’s return on Monday.

Stephanie Levitz reports that Carney said the economic bill is a follow-through on the momentum of the past seven days: a meeting with Ukraine’s President , a landmark investment summit and a whirlwind trip to Europe to forge a new relationship with that continent.

“It’s a lot, but that was just the warm-up,” he told his MPs in a speech at the start of their caucus meeting today. His benches now have three new members after the Liberals won several by-elections in August.
Carney said the legislation – which he called the Building Canada Strong Act – is the next phase of his government’s promise to speed up infrastructure and other projects.

In other news today, Laura Stone reports that Ontario Premier Doug Ford took to the airwaves today to try to clarify that he definitely did not endorse Olivia Chow for Toronto mayor when he spoke publicly about supporting her earlier this week.

In a friendly radio interview with former Toronto mayor John Tory on Newstalk 1010, Ford said he gets along well with Chow, but insisted he didn’t issue a full-throated endorsement of her candidacy when he praised her and told reporters to “read between the lines.”
“Let’s be very, very clear. When I endorse someone, which I’m not, you come out and fully endorse them. You don’t say read between the lines,” Ford told Tory.

The confusion started earlier this week when Ford, asked by a reporter whether he’s endorsing anyone for mayor, talked up his working relationship with Chow. The two were side-by-side, along with federal ministers, this week at the opening of a new biomanufacturing facility in Toronto.
“I just want to say the Mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship. Phenomenal. And we’ve given the City of Toronto more money than they’ve ever seen in their lives, over $9-billion,” he said.
“We’re going to continue supporting the Mayor. She’s doing an incredible job. So, read between the lines.”

Ford said today that the “read between the lines” reference meant he’s going to continue to work things out with the mayor, whom he once predicted would be an “unmitigated disaster” for the city before she was first elected in 2023.

After Chow’s main opponent in the race, councillor Brad Bradford, declared that Ford had endorsed Chow because she has “never stopped Doug Ford from doing exactly what he wanted to do,” the Premier’s Office released a late-night clarification Thursday trying to walk back Ford’s comments.
Several ex-Ford staffers are supporting Bradford’s campaign, including the Premier’s former executive director of communications, Laryssa Waler, and his longtime campaign manager Kory Teneycke.

Eby vows to scrap plan to buy ferries from afar: B.C. Premier David Eby made a series of election-style promises during a press conference after a speech to the Union of B.C. Municipalities Conference in downtown Vancouver, including committing to pause a controversial expansion of the provincial sales tax, and to build future generations of ferries at home instead of sourcing them from elsewhere.

B.C. Conservatives lose 10th MLA since August: Claire Rattée issued a scathing exit statement that says she was among at least 10 Conservatives who signed a letter calling on party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay to quit.

‘Father of Nunavut’ challenges territory’s refusal to pay for his housing, home care in Iqaluit: John Amagoalik, a former politician in his late 70s, is credited for his involvement in the creation of the territory in April, 1999.

Ottawa mayoral candidate charged over alleged death threats against Mark Sutcliffe, Doug Ford: Ottawa mayoral candidate Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas was arrested on Sept. 15 in Ottawa and has been charged with two counts each of criminal harassment and uttering death threats, along with several weapons-related offences.
MPs return to Ottawa: The House of Commons sits again on Monday after its summer break. The Senate sits again on Sept. 28.

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney today addressed a national caucus retreat on Parliament Hill. The retreat is being held today and Saturday. On Sunday, Carney is visiting Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron.

Party Leaders: Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet will be at a caucus meeting in the Quebec municipality of Cantley on Sunday. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May attended a community meeting on Salt Spring Island in British Columbia. No schedules released for other party leaders.

McPherson to focus on unity: NDP Leader Avi Lewis says Alberta MP Heather McPherson is leaving her role as NDP caucus house leader to campaign for unity ahead of the Alberta referendum. Don Davies will assume McPherson’s role in addition to his parliamentary leader duties, while Jenny Kwan will take over from Davies as whip.
Newly appointed diplomat: Joël Dupuis is Canada’s new ambassador to Belgium, succeeding Nicholas Brousseau.
Ahead of the return of the House of Commons on Monday, Liberal MP Marilyn Gladu talks about what she has read this past summer.

“I read so much non-fiction (mostly articles, papers and reports) at work that I usually read for entertainment, and it is typically an Agatha Christie-type “ who done it”. This summer , I decided to try three authors I have never read that write this similar type of novel," Gladu wrote.

Dead in the Morning by Margaret Yorke (First published by Geoffrey Bles, 1970) – A delightful British mystery set in a small village with a dysfunctional family. Excellent! (I then went on to read the rest of the things she has written.)

Death at the Fireside Inn by Kitty Kildare (K.E. O’Connor Books, 2024) – Veronica Vale, the eccentric but brilliant crime solver accompanied by her little dog Benji gets to the bottom of a murder that happened in one of the inns the family owns. Turns out they own a lot of inns and so I read the rest of her series as well.
Her Silent Bones by Pamela Fagan Hutchins (StoryFire LTD, 2024) – Terrific first book in a series about Detective Delaney Pace, ex-trucker, and the solving of gruesome murders.

stories.title: Canada's building a war-fighting army with tip of spear at CFB Edmonton
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s June announcement of an $82-billion package for Canada’s defence sparked noticeable changes.
stories.author: Jackie Carmichael
stories.content:
A new shoulder patch will come with new war-fighting preparedness levels not seen since the Second World War at Edmonton’s army base, set to grow by another 1,000 personnel over the next five years.

The newly reorganized 1st Canadian Division headquarters has coast-to-coast responsibility for regular-force units with an operational and expeditionary focus.

Previously, the 3rd Canadian Division headquartered in Edmonton, it was responsible for all of the army elements from Thunder Bay to the Pacific — reserve, regular force, training, institutional support all fell under one boss, said Col. Robert Tesselaar, commander of the Canadian Support Group West.

That division was officially stood down in a ceremony last week.

“Most simply, what the Army’s reorganization has done is it moved us from a geographical model, where across the country we had four separate divisions that were responsible for the province or provinces that they had troops in a functional model,” Tesselaar told Postmedia in a phone interview.

“Under the new 1st Canadian Division headquarters here in Edmonton, the commander is going to have coast-to-coast responsibilities, but it will only be the regular force units with an operational expeditionary focus,” Tesselaar said.

“It’s a functional alignment within the Army. The new 1st Canadian Division will be a warfighting division, and Canada has not actually operated in combat at a division level since the Second World War.”

In Afghanistan, Canada provided leadership and staff to what would be considered a divisional level headquarters, but it wasn’t truly a Canadian division, more of a contribution to an allied mission, a coalition formation, Tesselaar said.

“As we look at how the world has changed since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and the threat that has posed to our Nato allies, how it has destabilized some of our security assumptions around the world, we’re also learning from our Ukrainian partners and recognizing that if Canada is going to operate at that level of of warfighting, there are capabilities that we don’t currently have, such as long-range precision strike, which is going to be addressed through buying some systems from the Americans.”

Those systems are bound for the Shilo, Man., base.

Equipment-wise, new capabilities will include long-range precision strike, drones, air defence, electronic warfare, new logistics vehicles, updated uniforms and protective equipment, and a new Canadian-made Colt rifle that will have a distinctly different, modern look.

With drone capabilities thrown in, the reinvigorated warfighting division in Edmonton will be able to reach a battlefield 100 km away. These combine with air defence capabilities and electronic warfare capabilities not seen since the peak of the Cold War, Tesselaar said.

Such measures weren’t deemed necessary in the more relaxed strategic environment of the 1990s and early 2000s.

“Understanding how the world was perceived at the end of the Cold War and the fall of the Berlin Wall, there was a bit of a search for a peace dividend,” he said.

Between the fiscal state of government and the realization that the military isn’t cheap, it was perhaps considered a discretionary spend.

“The leaders probably had to make some tough decisions, just as we’re making tough decisions now about where we continue to invest taxpayer dollars to be able to give the Government of Canada the military options that they May need in the current environment,” Tesselaar said.

“Now the threat picture has changed and we’ve got to redevelop some of those capabilities.”

The new heightened preparedness comes with a price tag. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s June announcement of an $82-billion package for Canada’s defence was an infusion that sparked noticeable changes.

“The investment that we are seeing into the military right now is certainly something I haven’t seen before in my 30-plus years of service, including when we were fighting in Afghanistan,” Tesselaar said.

For starters, a recruiting push that will swell local ranks by 150 new positions next year, rising to 1,000 over the next decade.

“There’s some new units that are being established to help us develop the capabilities that we’re going to need to enable a division headquarters as a war-fighting headquarters. There’s some that are going to be based here in Edmonton,” Tesselaar said.

More could be based in Shilo, Wainwright or Suffield as well, he said.

While 150 people on a base of about 4,000 to 5,000 soldiers doesn’t seem like much, over the next decade that’s probably going to be 1,000 to 1,500 people, he said.

That aligns with earlier announcements on housing investment in the base, he said.

Under the reorganization, Tesselaar’s own responsibilities will shift a bit.

“I’ve just got a bit more opportunity to engage with provincial authorities to talk about things that affect all three of my bases regionally, or to continue to co-ordinate with other army or CAF elements in the West to ensure that the support they require is still being delivered, rather than having my higher headquarters do it on my behalf,” he said.

All army bases coast-to-coast will now report to a new commander in Kingston, whose focus will be entirely the institutional support of the army.

stories.title: Appeal hearing continues over fired Regina police chief
stories.summary: 'Flirtatious' texts between former Regina police chief, Farooq Sheikh, and a member of the Regina Board of Police Commissioners were discussed at the appeal hearing.
stories.author: Hannah Sangster
stories.content:
Text messages described as “flirtatious” between former Regina police chief Farooq Sheikh and a member of the Regina Board of Police Commissioners have been a key focus during four days of appeal proceedings.

Sheikh was fired in October 2025 after a months-long investigation by the province’s Public Complaints Commission into allegations of inappropriate conduct. The allegations were made by a member of the police board, who is being referred to as the complainant due to a publication ban.

Regina Mayor Chad Bachynski, who also sits on the police board, testified about how commissioners came to the conclusion that Sheikh’s conduct with the complainant was inappropriate.

Bachynski said he was shown the text messages in an investigation report in September 2025 and described his reaction as one of betrayal.

“This is not how the public would expect a chief of police to act,” Bachynski testified.

The mayor also described receiving what he called a “very frantic” phone call from Sheikh in mid-March, before the complaint was filed.

He said Sheikh described his relationship with the complainant during the call as being “like a sister to me.”

Bachynski testified that the call confused him at the time, but that he later viewed it different after the complaint was filed.

“I feel like I was being pre-manipulated to understand what May happen, which ultimately was a complaint being brought forward,” he said.

Additional texts reveal Sheikh sent text messages to two board members in December 2024, during a private in-camera meeting where board members were discussing his contract. Sheikh had been excluded from the meeting and testified he became impatient. The complainant responded to his messages while the meeting was underway. He admitted to this being an error and agreed it could erode trust of the board. He also acknowledged he did not disclose the messages to the board before they were later uncovered through the legal process.

When asked whether he agreed his actions were unethical or lacked transparency, he said, “I agree.”

“I made a couple of errors through frustration in my contract. I do accept that,” he testified.

Another issue examined during the proceedings stems from a February 2025 drug investigation in which the complainant was found to have a connection to one of the people charged.

The complainant subsequently resigned and was later removed from the board.

A recording of a Feb. 26, 2025 phone call between Sheikh and the complainant was also played during the hearing.

In the recording, Sheikh can be heard asking whether the call was being recorded and telling the complainant to delete text messages between them because he was concerned they could be misconstrued if someone else saw them.

When asked about Sheikh’s actions, Bachynski testified that it “speaks to the lack of trust and accountability to follow direction.”

“Ultimately we are the chief’s employer, when we lay direction, there is an expectation for that to be respected,” he said.

Sheikh testified to initially developing a relationship with the complainant to support them in their role as a new board member, and said it evolved from there.

Sheikh said he has since deleted their text messages. When asked whether he did so because of the complainant’s potential connection to the drug investigation, Sheikh said he did so because he was embarrassed by the messages, but maintains it had nothing to do with the investigation.

He also acknowledged some of the messages had sexual innuendo, and the pair communicated through third-party apps, including WhatsApp.

Sheikh testified that he should not have allowed the exchanges to develop as they did, but said his intent was limited to “flirtatious humour and banter” that was “all fun and cheeky.”

The appeal is expected to continue next week.

Hannah Sangster has more in the video above.

stories.title: Air India families shocked after RCMP tells them its investigation is at a dead end after 41 years
stories.summary: Some relatives of the 1985 Air India bombing victims are devastated after the RCMP told them the investigation has hit a dead end.
stories.author: Kim Bolan
stories.content:
Some relatives of the 1985 Air India bombing victims are devastated after the RCMP told them the investigation into Canada’s deadliest terrorist attack has hit a dead end.

At a meeting near Toronto’s Pearson Airport on Sept. 12, about 40 relatives learned police have no new investigative leads to pursue.

Sanjay Lazar, who lost his whole family in the June 23, 1985 bombing, said he was furious at the message conveyed by the RCMP.

“What police agency gives up after 41 years?” Lazar said in an interview Friday.

He said the investigators who flew from B.C. to Toronto confirmed that the investigation was “inactive.”

Air India Flight 182, travelling from Canada to India via London, was downed off the coast of Ireland when a B.C.-made suitcase bomb exploded, killing all 329 on board. A second B.C.-made bomb, destined for another Air India flight, blew up at Tokyo’s Narita Airport the same day, killing two baggage handlers.

Two B.C. men linked to the Babbar Khalsa terrorist group were acquitted on all counts in 2005. A third, Inderjit Singh Reyat, was convicted of manslaughter in both bombings, but is now out of prison.

A subsequent judicial inquiry exposed investigative and intelligence failures by the RCMP and Csis both before and after the bombings.

Lazar, who lives in Pune, India, said the most “shocking” point in the meeting was when the RCMP asked families to provide them with tips police could pursue.

Lazar has now written to Prime Minister Mark Carney about his disappointment at the status of the terrorism investigation.

“As the son of my late parents, and the last surviving member of that family, I feel duty bound to express my disgust, hurt and anger at the expressed intention of the RCMP to wind down the Air India Bombing investigations,” Lazar’s letter said.

He also suggested that if the RCMP has no leads, the case should be handed to “others who May be more capable.”

Bob Rae, Canada’s former UN ambassador who did a preliminary Air India inquiry in 2005, said the message to the families at the meeting was “deeply regrettable.”

“It’s a terrible signal,” Rae said Friday. “The fact that 331 people (in total) were killed, and that it was clearly a terrorist attack means that this is a file that never closes, and it can’t possibly close because they still haven’t found enough about who else could have been responsible for what took place.”

Toronto’s Lata Pada, who lost husband Vishnu and daughters, Arti and Brinda, said Friday that she too was upset after the meeting, especially when she attended thinking the RCMP would tell families about breakthroughs they’d made.

“It was very disappointing and extremely upsetting because we, from the families, don’t believe that the investigation is over. There are still quite a few people who need to be pulled out of the woodwork and spoken to,” she said.

Pada and others at the meeting suggested that a reward, which had been as high as $1 million, be renewed to encourage people to come forward.

Shipra Rana also expected to hear about progress in identifying more suspects in the bombing that killed her sister Shyla, a member of the Air India flight crew.

“The moment they said that they had no more evidence to go through, and if we had any evidence then to come to them with it, that’s the time I got up, I thanked them for coming, and I said I am leaving, and I left,” Rana said, adding that she relives the day of the bombing with every disappointment in the case.

A spokesperson with the RCMP’s federal policing Pacific region, said in an email Friday that “there are still officers working on the investigation.” But she confirmed what the families were told.

“At this time, we have exhausted all investigative avenues but stand ready to advance any new information,” she said.

Sudha Berry, whose 16-year-old brother Sharad was aboard the ill-fated flight, also sent a letter Friday to Carney and the RCMP’s leadership over her disappointment about what transpired.

“This is tantamount to the RCMP laying down its arms and passively waiting for new information to be brought to their attention,” the letter said.

“In 1985, one could understand your ignorance and lack of expertise in addressing the divisive forces that led to the bombing of (Air India Flight 182), however, now we have no choice but to conclude that your failure to pursue the investigation is evidence of the RCMP’s systemic bias.”

She laid out a number of steps the RCMP could take to further the investigation and keep the families better informed.

“An active approach is urgent and vital to procuring evidence before the individuals who have relevant information pass on,” the letter said.

stories.title: Holocaust educator Judy Weissenberg Cohen believed history could show the warning signs of hatred
stories.summary: She gave talks across Canada, helped fellow survivors tell their own stories and created a website offering Holocaust education through a gender lens
stories.author: Hannah Alper
stories.content:
In 1993, Judy Weissenberg Cohen was nearing her 65th birthday and mandatory retirement when, during a lunch-break stroll through downtown Toronto, she saw a group of young people clad in black leather marching in a circle and shouting, “White power! White power!”

A certain fear was automatic, she later wrote in her memoir, like the feeling of her stomach clenching when she witnessed people being selected for death at Auschwitz-Birkenau.

“For a terrifying few seconds, the lines were blurred between past and present. I wondered, was I looking back at history or ahead?”

As she approached the curious audience, she realized she had come face-to-face with members of the Heritage Front, a white supremacist, neo-Nazi organization.

Instead of turning away, Ms. Cohen marched toward the group’s leader, Wolfgang Droege. When he claimed there had been no Black slavery in the U.S., she assumed the Holocaust would be the next thing he denied.

Before he got the chance, Ms. Cohen stepped between him and the crowd and implored those watching not to listen. She later humbly joked she was not especially heroic, since four police officers were nearby.

“Lady, don’t aggravate yourself. They only have a permit for 20 minutes.”

“My luck!” Ms. Cohen later wrote. “I caught the 20 minutes that would soon spur me to action.”

For the next three decades, she dedicated herself to Holocaust education and public speaking, urging people — particularly students — to recognize the warning signs of hatred and become witnesses to history. She also became a leading advocate for raising awareness about women’s experiences during the Holocaust, eventually creating a website devoted to preserving those stories.

Ms. Cohen died on Sept. 6 at 97 years old.

“The memory of the death camps and being victims of the Nazi Holocaust never fades, but I no longer consider myself a victim,” she wrote. “Instead, through the decades, I became a politically and socially aware activist. I must work relentlessly to ensure that memories like mine will not become the memories of future generations.”

In 1938, when Judy was 10, news of the war reached her family in Hungary. She wrote that the children absorbed the adults’ grave concerns by osmosis.

By 1944, Hungarian Jews were forced to wear yellow Stars of David in public. Judy attached one to her jacket but covered it with the books and notes she held as she travelled to and from local tutoring gigs. She called it her “little act of resistance.”

A few months later, Judy and her family were forced into the overcrowded Debrecen ghetto. It was only a month before they, along with hundreds of others, were packed into cattle cars. They were only given two pails: one filled with clean water, and one to be used as a toilet.

Three days later, they arrived at Auschwitz-Birkenau, where an estimated 1.1 million people were murdered. Men and women were immediately separated. It was the last time she saw her father, her mother and her sister-in-law, who was holding her infant son.

Then the processing began. The women’s body hair was shaved, they took a brief shower and were given clothing previously worn by other prisoners. Judy found herself looking at hundreds of now-identical prisoners. After shouting through the crowd to find her sisters, they could barely recognize one another.

“We started to painfully laugh, how drastically we changed within a few hours.”

One night, around 700 women crowded into a barracks to observe Yom Kippur. Jewish religious practices were forbidden in the camps, but the kapos – prisoners appointed to supervise other prisoners in exchange for special privileges – allowed 10 minutes while guarding the doors for SS officers.

Someone lit a candle and a hush fell over the barracks. One woman began to recite Kol Nidre, the prayer that opens Yom Kippur.

The prayer turned into “the sound of this incredible cry of hundreds of women.” The moment eventually inspired the title of Ms. Cohen’s memoir, A Cry in Unison .

Her older sister Böske helped keep her alive, carving spoons from wood and sneaking her extra pieces of bread, until they were eventually separated. In her sisters’ absence, Judy found solace and strength in two young women who became her “camp sisters.”

As the war neared its end, Judy and the women she was with were forced on a death March, and what she called a never-ending road with no food and no water, wrapped in dirty rags and seeing corpses that looked like them dotting the path. One morning, after they slept in an abandoned barn, the mayor of the town woke them shouting, “Fräulein, sie sind frei!” This translates to: “Women, you are free.”

When Judy returned to Debrecen in August, 1945, she reunited with her brother Laci in her hometown and her sister Evi in the Bergen-Belsen Displaced Persons Camp in Germany.

Judy was later accepted to move to Montreal when a garment commission came to Bergen-Belsen looking for people to work in Canada’s clothing industry.

Entering a country filled with new people who spoke a completely new language, Judy learned to put her trauma on the back burner, as when she tried to talk about it, she was often met with apathy.

She met her future husband, Sidney Cohen, whom she would move to Toronto to be with and eventually raise their kids, Michelle and Jonathan. She took a business course and found jobs in bookkeeping and real estate.

“Mom set an example for us. She was active in the community. She was very proud to vote regularly, to do things to help other people. Not to show that she was any better than anybody else, but because it was the right thing to do,” Jonathan said.

While she tried to put the past behind her, she wanted to understand what had happened to her and the millions who perished. After her encounter with the neo-Nazis, she visited what is now the Toronto Holocaust Museum, asking how she could combat “this emerging assault on the Holocaust and the historical truth.” While this was no small feat, Ms. Cohen read intently about the events that lay beneath the decisions and actions of the Holocaust perpetrators as well as the experiences of its victims.

“She was always thinking, always theorizing, always researching. She and my father encouraged the value of education, books, learning, culture, art and definitely of treating other people well,” Jonathan said.

Over the final three decades of her life, Ms. Cohen emerged as a public speaker in high schools and universities across North America. As she found her voice, she became co-chair of the Holocaust Centre Speakers Bureau to help fellow survivors tell their own stories. She participated in four March of the Living trips, travelling to Poland and Israel with students as a survivor-faciliator. Her goal was not to make young people sad to hear her story, but “to be historically knowledgeable, and be able to recognize the signs if and when something similar re-emerges and combat it.”

As Ms. Cohen dove deeper, she noticed that most of what she was reading was written by male authors, seen through the eyes of men. Recognizing that the collective voices of survivors help bring attention to what happened, she felt like half of survivors’ experiences were excluded: those of women.

She learned about women’s roles in the ghettos and in the resistance, and “the immense suffering of women and their struggles to survive in the places I knew so intimately myself.” She made it clear that learning about gender differences doesn’t mean competing in a hierarchy of suffering. “The aim of researching gender-specific suffering in the Holocaust is to hear the voices of all the victims … so as to enhance our understanding of history.”

Armed with determination, a friend’s technical help and her husband’s patience, her website Women and the Holocaust — a Cyberspace of Their Own , was born. It offered essays, book reviews, poems, stories and educational material about women’s experiences to reach all audiences. She also contacted other survivors, transcribing and publishing their stories under the heading “Women of Valour.” Little by little, the research grew and the site became a home for Holocaust education, specifically through a gender lens.

Ms. Cohen’s voice will continue to be shared long into the future. Her testimony is available through the Toronto Holocaust Museum, and she was also one of the first survivors to record an audiobook version of her memoir with the Azrieli Foundation.

Last month, Ms. Cohen offered a reflection with the Temple Emanuel congregation.

“I turn 98 on Sept. 17. I never imagined I was going to live this long, honestly. I wish I were wise enough to have a message for the next generation, but I am a pessimist, that’s where I start.”

While she was a pessimist, she married it with real action. Audiences left every room she spoke in feeling inspired to act, and to be precise in how that action happens.

“For even a good ideology can go astray in the hands of people who are using it, not toward the original goal. That’s politics. People say politics is a dirty word but we have to understand that and handle it. This is my message for any generation,” Ms. Cohen said.

stories.title: Owner of one of London’s first Italian pizzerias dies
stories.summary: Vito’s Cave on Hamilton Road East was known to be a London hotspot in the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Vito’s Cave on Hamilton Road East was known to be a London hotspot in the 1950s, ’60s and ’70s.

Vito Moretti who immigrated to Canada from Bari, Italy started operating Vito’s Pizza in 1956.

When it first opened there was a large front window where people would gather to be entertained as they watched pizza dough getting thrown in the air.

A few years later Moretti transformed the shop into Vito’s Cave, serving up Italian cuisine.

The restaurant closed in 1985 after about 30 years of business.

Earlier this week, Moretti passed away following a brief illness.

His daughter Teresa Moran says he was in good spirits until the end, “He still had a wonderful sense of humour,” she added. “We had one last family gathering and he was the one who planned the whole meal.”

Moretti was 94. Funeral arrangements are set for Sept. 25 at St. Mary’s Catholic Church on Lyle Street.
