stories.title: How this Toronto park became an international model for ecological restoration
stories.summary: Tommy Thompson Park, once a construction waste dump, is now a haven for birds, beavers and Torontonians alike
stories.author: Tavia Grant, Photography by Melissa Tait
stories.content:
Andrea Chreston is standing at a lookout point at the edge of a wetland, pointing to a pair of trumpeter swans with three cygnets cruising through a blanket of lily pads.

It’s hard to believe that in years past, this green oasis on Toronto’s waterfront was a barren wasteland.

“This was a moonscape twenty years ago,” says Ms. Chreston, senior project manager at the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority. “The vegetation has really come a very long way, and it’s providing all this essential habitat for wildlife communities.”

Tommy Thompson Park, a former construction waste dump, is an urban wilderness park that has become a model of ecological restoration.

It is also a biodiversity hotspot, with river otters, white-tailed deer, monarch butterflies and red-breasted mergansers, as well as wildflower meadows and wetlands that teem with life. It is known as one of the best spots for birdwatching in the city, with more than 300 recorded species.

Named for the city’s first commissioner of parks, the wildlife magnet sits on the Leslie Street Spit, a peninsula just minutes away from the city’s downtown core. The five-kilometre park attracts an estimated 300,000 visitors each year, most of them cyclists, walkers and birders. Many locals refer to the park as “the Spit.”

It is unique in Canada, and possibly North America, in that the land is entirely man-made; it wasn’t initially intended to be a park and it is surrounded by water. The Trca says it isn’t aware of any other examples like this, of a rubble landform in a lake that has transformed into wilderness park.

Construction of Leslie Spit began in 1959, to create a breakwater for Toronto’s harbour. Initially, it was also planned as part of an expansion of Toronto’s port capabilities, but the anticipated shipping boom never happened; for years, the spot was simply a dumping ground. Over decades, Toronto deposited sediment dredged from the lake bottom and waste from demolished buildings and subway construction, slowly creating the five-kilometre peninsula.

In 1973, the province gave the Trca responsibility for developing a plan for a public park, and the conservation authority has been working on habitat restoration projects since 1995. Today’s park is the result of both targeted restoration efforts and natural succession. Wildlife has come on its own, says Ms. Chreston.

“Everything that’s happened at Tommy Thompson is wild and natural, but we’ve created these habitats that they’re thriving in.”

The park was bustling with wildlife during a recent two-hour visit. A meadow vole darted across the pathway; monarchs danced amongst the milkweed, and a garter snake slithered over the path. Ms. Chreston points out nests of barn swallows and cliff swallows, bat boxes and a floating raft for common terns.

Its location, jutting out into Lake Ontario, has made it a crucial stopover point for birds and butterflies. It has received official designation as important for birds, environmentally significant and a key biodiversity area. Indeed, the park is home to animals not always expected in large cities, including painted turtles, milk snakes and largemouth bass, and mammals such as beavers, foxes, mink and coyotes.

Its success has attracted global attention: This spring, a delegation of officials from Korea visited the park to learn how to establish plants in a site like this. “There’s definitely a lot of international interest,” as well as from places across North America, says Ms. Chreston. And in November, 2025, the Trca won an award for the park as a model of ecological restoration and protection, presented at the Global Forum on Human Settlements in Geneva.

The Trca is also sharing what it has learned more locally. In May, a new conservation area opened in nearby Mississauga that incorporated lessons learned from Tommy Thompson. Jim Tovey Lakeview Conservation Area is a waterfront park with restored habitat for birds, butterflies and other wildlife.

Toronto resident John Carley has been visiting the Spit since the 1980s. “Just walking out there, and being out there with water and waves and away from the city is what I love,” said Mr. Carley, who is co-chair of Friends of the Spit, a group founded in 1977 that advocates to keep the Spit as a car-free public urban wilderness.

His group has checklists of all the sightings of flora and fauna on its website – around 400 plant species, 336 species of birds, 22 kinds of mammals, more than 50 butterfly species, and more than 40 dragonfly and damselfly species.

Nature is, as the federal government said this year, foundational to Canadian identity. Ottawa announced a new strategy to protect the natural environment in March; among its goals is to restore degraded ecosystems.

And it’s working. The habitat is thriving and the animals have come. In the past few years, white-tail deer have begun breeding in the park. River otters too. “They’re super secretive, so it’s very difficult to find them, but that’s a species that was absent from the Toronto waterfront for a century,” said Ms. Chreston. Those trumpeter swans, native to the area and once rare, are growing in population: This is the 13th year they have nested in the park and this year a total of 16 cygnets hatched from three nests.

It’s weird, in a wonderful way. A nature park built atop rusted rebar and broken ceramic tiles, slabs of concrete and weathered bricks, gravel, stones and sand. People make spontaneous art out of the random, textured found objects along the shoreline.

Mr. Carley hopes it will remain a place that is not manicured, a little rough and largely left to its own devices. His philosophy for the park is, “as much as possible, letting nature rule.”

River otters too. “They’re super secretive, so it’s very difficult to find them, but that’s a species that was absent from the Toronto waterfront for a century,” said Ms. Chreston. Those trumpeter swans, native to the area and once rare, are growing in population: This is the 13th year they have nested in the park and this year a total of 16 cygnets hatched from three nests.

It’s weird, in a wonderful way. A nature park built atop rusted rebar and broken ceramic tiles, slabs of concrete and weathered bricks, gravel, stones and sand. People make spontaneous art out of the random, textured found objects along the shoreline.
Mr. Carley hopes it will remain a place that is not manicured, a little rough and largely left to its own devices. His philosophy for the park is, “as much as possible, letting nature rule.”
Everyone loves a puffin. Scientists are stumped about their beaks
How did this teen with Adhd find her focus? In a word, birds
New Zealand sees results in fight to save its strange birds

Far across town from Tommy Thompson Park, birds of prey have a big job to do at Pearson airport. The Globe paid the animals a visit to see their struggle against geese, ducks and gulls that could threaten planes.
The Globe and Mail

article_images.caption: Trumpeter swans are native to this area of Toronto, but the landscape beneath them at Tommy Thompson Park is not exactly natural. The city spent decades creating it from dredged earth and waste.
While it was under construction in the 20th century, the Leslie Street Spit was a more forlorn-looking place. The restoration of nature would come later.
For humans, the Spit is a spot to relax away from home. For birds, like these cliff swallows, it is home.
There have been beavers at Tommy Thompson for more than 20 years.
As the light fades, visitors take their last looks and leave. The park closes to the public at 9 p.m. every day; opening hours vary through the week.
The yellow black-eyed Susans in this meadow are native to Ontario, but many species around it are not.

stories.title: U of T called out for 'despicable' research group dedicated to anti-Zionism theories
stories.summary: The university said the group's existence "does not imply institutional endorsement of the views expressed by its individual participants."
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Canada

Israel & Middle East

'It is anti-Jewish activism masquerading as legitimate academic work,' wrote vice-president of Canadian advocacy group Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs

Last updated 2 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/u-of-t-called-out-for-despicable-research-group-dedicated-to-anti-zionism-theories#comments-area)

A demonstrator waves a Palestinian flag inside an anti-Israel encampment at the University of Toronto campus on May 2, 2024. Photo by Cole Burston /AFP via Getty Images

The University of Toronto has been called out by prominent leaders on social media for its “despicable” research group dedicated to anti-Zionism theories, as explained in its description.

The working group, titled Bridging Theories of Anti-Zionism, is comprised of grad students and faculty at the university’s Jackman Humanities Institute who conduct research and engage in scholarly exchanges.

In the group’s description online, it asks the question: “What does it mean to critique Zionism as a political ideology, and how have the last three years of genocide in Palestine changed the scholarly engagement with this question?”

Columnist Jesse Kline keeps you up to date with what’s happening in Israel and the effects of antisemitism on life here in Canada. Friday mornings.

It explains: “This working group seeks to map these varied streams of anti-Zionist thought and construct a critical genealogy that can inform contemporary scholarship across multiple fields.”

The webpage is no longer available online.

Dr. David Jacobs, part of U of T’s governing council and president of the Ontario Association of Radiologists, said in a social media post on Wednesday that he would be “remiss” in his duties if he “stayed silent on this latest working group.”

He pointed out that he would expect the university not to “indulge in this type of activity,” given the 2026 Canadian Heritage federal report that found 95.7 per cent of Jewish post-secondary students in Canada experienced or witnessed antisemitism on campus over the prior year.

I would be remiss in my duties as a University of Toronto Governor if I stayed silent on this latest working group. After the 2026 Canadian Heritage federal report revealed that 95.7% of Jewish post-secondary students in Canada experienced or witnessed antisemitism on campus… pic.twitter.com/zOG3oPWrkc — David Jacobs (@DrJacobsRad) September 17, 2026

Richard Marceau, author and vice-president at Canadian advocacy group Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, also posted on X.

“This is despicable, (U of T),” he wrote.

“Zionism is simply the modern expression of the connection between a people — the Jewish people — and a land — the Land of Israel. That connection has been central to Jewish identity and Judaism since antiquity,” he continued.

“This is not scholarship. It is anti-Jewish activism masquerading as legitimate academic work.”

This is despicable, @UofT. Zionism is simply the modern expression of the connection between a people—the Jewish people—and a land—the Land of Israel. That connection has been central to Jewish identity and Judaism since antiquity. This is not scholarship. It is anti-Jewish… pic.twitter.com/7unt5phXfQ — Richard Marceau (@richardmarceau) September 16, 2026

Casey Babb, a senior fellow with the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said on X that he was “disgusted.”

“Less than 24 hours after I spoke at (U of T) about the civilizational dangers of antizionism, I’ve come to learn that the university has created a new working group to defend and actually legitimize this hate movement. Note the genocide reference on the page,” he wrote.

A spokesperson for the University of Toronto told National Post in an emailed statement that “the existence of a research group examining theories of anti-Zionism does not imply institutional endorsement of the views expressed by its individual participants.”

“The university takes persistent action to address discrimination and harassment against Jewish and Israeli members of our community, including conduct directed at individuals because they identify as Zionist,” said the statement.

The spokesperson did not provide comment on if the webpage had been intentionally taken down.

Director of the Jackman Humanities Institute, professor Randy Boyagoda, said in a statement that the institute “affirms the academic freedom of the individual faculty members involved with all of its working groups and does not endorse particular perspectives associated with any of them.”

“The JHI receives proposals from faculty members seeking to convene working groups on various subjects,” he said. “These proposals are assessed by fellow faculty members. As the new director, I have focused on the re-conceptualization and renewal of the Jhi’s programming since taking up my appointment in July. This includes working groups, among other activities.”

stories.title: Tiff 2026: Canadian director Richie Mehta revisits an infamous chapter of history with Phoolan
stories.summary: The film tells the story of a marginalized teenager who dared to resist patriarchy – becoming the most famous outlaw in Indian history
stories.author: Aparita Bhandari
stories.content:
For most kids growing up in North India, the word dacoit, or bandit, usually evoked two infamous figures. The first was the fictional character of Gabbar Singh, from the 1975 curry-Western Sholay . And the second was Phoolan Devi, a fearsome real-life outlaw who joined a group of bandits in the Chambal ravines to seek revenge for her brutal gang-rape.

As a young Punjabi kid growing up in Mississauga, Richie Mehta knew of Gabbar Singh. His first encounter with Phoolan Devi’s story was through Bandit Queen , he says. Directed by Shekhar Kapur ( Elizabeth , The Four Feathers ), the movie played at Cannes and the Toronto International Film Festival in 1994. It starred Seema Biswas, who was later seen in Canadian filmmaker Deepa Mehta’s films Water, Cooking With Stella and Midnight’s Children .

Can Tiff navigate a global film industry facing a ‘turning point’?

“I saw [ Bandit Queen ] in the early 2000s, when I was getting well-versed in alternative Indian cinema. And then Seema Biswas was at Tiff in 2005 [with Water ],” says Mehta. Biswas would go on to play a lead role in Mehta’s debut feature Amal , which screened at Tiff in 2007.

Now, Mehta is back at Tiff with his own version of that story with Phoolan , his fourth feature to have a world premiere at Tiff.

Set in the heartland of India, Mehta’s film tells the story of a marginalized teenager who dared to resist patriarchy – becoming the most famous outlaw in Indian history and the target of 2,000 policemen sent to kill her.

Phoolan came about after Mehta was approached by Mumbai-based film production house Namah Pictures, which has acquired the rights to Phoolan Devi’s autobiography. Mehta had already established himself as the filmmaker behind popular crime procedurals – the first season of the Netflix series Delhi Crime (2019) and the Amazon Prime series Poacher (2023).

Delhi Crime is based on the infamous 2012 New Delhi gang rape and murder case that shook India and the Delhi Police investigation that followed. Poacher is inspired by the extensive police probe aided by forest officials that led to the dismantling of an ivory poaching ring in Kerala in 2015.

At first Mehta resisted making Phoolan . But he couldn’t let go of the idea.

“After finishing Delhi Crime, and sitting in the space of a similar subject matter for a while – I didn’t want to do it, but it was still fresh in my mind,” he says. He kept thinking about the young woman who had been gang-raped in New Delhi, and her struggle to stay alive for two weeks.

“She left this earth almost as if saying that ‘I’ve done what I can. Can you sort this out?’ And then things just got worse and worse and worse in this world. As I asked myself, what kind of justice is that for that kind of courage?” says Mehta. “Would she pick up a weapon if she was still around? Is it the angry version we need now?”

Reading Phoolan Devi’s autobiography, ON which the film is heavily based, was harrowing for him.

Born to a low-caste family in 1963, Phoolan Devi was 10 when she started to raise her voice against a family dispute over land ownership. At 11, she was married off to a man three decades her senior and returned home when she was 12, deemed a ruined woman. Despite being ostracized, she continued to rail against the injustices. Eventually, her uncle orchestrated Phoolan Devi’s kidnapping at the hand of a band of dacoits.

Phoolan Devi’s legend is grounded in the account of her gang-rape and public humiliation when she was 17. The following year she joined another group of bandits and convinced them to help her seek revenge. Twenty-two men died as a result, and she became notorious for being wanted for murder. She eventually surrendered to the police, and served 11 years in prison.

A tuxedo, a projector and a rejected film: Atom Egoyan’s unlikely road to Tiff

It would have been impossible to tell Phoolan Devi’s entire life story in a film, says Mehta. It couldn’t have helped that previous accounts such as Bandit Queen had drawn criticism from the likes of Arundhati Roy and Phoolan Devi herself, who disputed Kapur’s fictionalized version of her life. Bandit Queen was seen as a simplistic and sanitized version of Phoolan Devi’s complexities.

Instead, Mehta chose to focus on a 48-hour period that is also central to her mythology. A two-day window where she’s on the run, chased by armed personnel deployed to a single village to apprehend a young girl. By focusing on that event, he could represent broader themes such as power, systemic inequality and resistance. He could also tell her story with dignity, versus exploiting it for narrative gain.

Yet, he was unsure of this approach until he happened to find the village where the siege happened – a location that doesn’t come up on internet searches – and speak with villagers about the incident that they remembered vividly.

“Nothing had changed in this village. There is one road, one electrical line,” says Mehta. The villagers told him about their account, which filled in some blanks for him – including a cop who questions the official narrative behind the orders to kill Phoolan Devi and addresses the injustices she faced.

“That’s the yang I couldn’t find in the book,” he says. “As the world progresses in a certain direction that I certainly find incomprehensible – I keep trying to say if the world is this messy, and there is so much malice in the world, can I latch on to something that is hopeful?”

“I have to be able to tell my kids in some capacity, there are more good people than bad.”

Bringing Phoolan to Tiff is also a full-circle moment for Mehta.

“This film is made by Amazon MGM Studio, with a full Indian cast, and I am a Canadian doing it. We can do this,” he says. “And it’s always wonderful being back at Tiff. I started as a volunteer here in 1997, had my feature debut in 2007 here. This is like coming home.”

Special to The Globe and Mail

Phoolan screens at Tiff on Sept. 19, 2:30 p.m. (tiff.net).

Yet, he was unsure of this approach until he happened to find the village where the siege happened – a location that doesn’t come up on internet searches – and speak with villagers about the incident that they remembered vividly.

“Nothing had changed in this village. There is one road, one electrical line,” says Mehta. content_blocks.text: For most kids growing up in North India, the word dacoit, or bandit, usually evoked two infamous figures. The first was the fictional character of Gabbar Singh, from the 1975 curry-Western Sholay . And the second was Phoolan Devi, a fearsome real-life outlaw who joined a group of bandits in the Chambal ravines to seek revenge for her brutal gang-rape.

As a young Punjabi kid growing up in Mississauga, Richie Mehta knew of Gabbar Singh. His first encounter with Phoolan Devi’s story was through Bandit Queen , he says. Directed by Shekhar Kapur ( Elizabeth , The Four Feathers ), the movie played at Cannes and the Toronto International Film Festival in 1994. It starred Seema Biswas, who was later seen in Canadian filmmaker Deepa Mehta’s films Water, Cooking With Stella and Midnight’s Children .
Can Tiff navigate a global film industry facing a ‘turning point’?

“I saw [ Bandit Queen ] in the early 2000s, when I was getting well-versed in alternative Indian cinema. And then Seema Biswas was at Tiff in 2005 [with Water ],” says Mehta. Biswas would go on to play a lead role in Mehta’s debut feature Amal , which screened at Tiff in 2007.
Now, Mehta is back at Tiff with his own version of that story with Phoolan , his fourth feature to have a world premiere at Tiff.

Set in the heartland of India, Mehta’s film tells the story of a marginalized teenager who dared to resist patriarchy – becoming the most famous outlaw in Indian history and the target of 2,000 policemen sent to kill her.

content_blocks.text: Phoolan came about after Mehta was approached by Mumbai-based film production house Namah Pictures, which has acquired the rights to Phoolan Devi’s autobiography. Mehta had already established himself as the filmmaker behind popular crime procedurals – the first season of the Netflix series Delhi Crime (2019) and the Amazon Prime series Poacher (2023).

Delhi Crime is based on the infamous 2012 New Delhi gang rape and murder case that shook India and the Delhi Police investigation that followed. Poacher is inspired by the extensive police probe aided by forest officials that led to the dismantling of an ivory poaching ring in Kerala in 2015.
At first Mehta resisted making Phoolan . But he couldn’t let go of the idea.

“After finishing Delhi Crime, and sitting in the space of a similar subject matter for a while – I didn’t want to do it, but it was still fresh in my mind,” he says. He kept thinking about the young woman who had been gang-raped in New Delhi, and her struggle to stay alive for two weeks.

“She left this earth almost as if saying that ‘I’ve done what I can. Can you sort this out?’ And then things just got worse and worse and worse in this world. As I asked myself, what kind of justice is that for that kind of courage?” says Mehta. “Would she pick up a weapon if she was still around? Is it the angry version we need now?”
Reading Phoolan Devi’s autobiography, ON which the film is heavily based, was harrowing for him.

content_blocks.text: Born to a low-caste family in 1963, Phoolan Devi was 10 when she started to raise her voice against a family dispute over land ownership. At 11, she was married off to a man three decades her senior and returned home when she was 12, deemed a ruined woman. Despite being ostracized, she continued to rail against the injustices. Eventually, her uncle orchestrated Phoolan Devi’s kidnapping at the hand of a band of dacoits.

The following year she joined another group of bandits and convinced them to help her seek revenge. Twenty-two men died as a result, and she became notorious for being wanted for murder. She eventually surrendered to the police, and served 11 years in prison.
A tuxedo, a projector and a rejected film: Atom Egoyan’s unlikely road to Tiff

stories.title: Sophie Roland named dean of Don Wright Faculty of Music
stories.summary: Faculty of Music dean Sophie Roland brings decades of leadership, teaching and performance experience to her new role at Western University.
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
Music education at Western University is entering a new chapter under a respected scholar, performer and administrator. Sophie Roland has been appointed dean of the Don Wright Faculty of Music for a five-year term that takes effect immediately. She has led the faculty as acting dean since July 1.

“I feel very much at home in this university and am proud to serve in this role,” Roland said.

She first came to Western as a graduate student, earning master’s degrees in musicology and performance voice before returning several years later to join the faculty as a professor. Over her 21 years at Western, she has earned the Faculty Scholar Award, the Western University Teaching Fellowship and multiple national and international honours for her artistic work.

Western provost and vice-president (academic) Florentine Strzelczyk said Roland has made exceptional contributions to Western as well as the broader academic and artistic communities.

“Professor Roland has demonstrated exemplary leadership, service and commitment to excellence in music education and the performing arts. Through her work, artists, educators and institutions in Canada and abroad have built lasting relationships,” she said.

Now, as dean, Roland will build on the momentum in the Don Wright Faculty of Music, one of Canada’s largest music schools. The faculty offers a wide range of programs, enrolling about 650 students and hosting over 350 concerts, recitals and public performance events each year. It’s one of only a few Canadian music faculties offering multi-stream undergraduate and graduate programs that train scholars, music educators and performers in the same institution.

Roland’s vision for the faculty is to equip students to find new ways of strengthening the relationship between musicians, their audiences and the art they create.

“I have this immense opportunity to build more human connection through music. I’m looking forward to writing that future playbook with students.”

Roland’s teaching and leadership helped drive innovation in music education. For the last fifteen years, she was chair of Music Performance Studies, leading curriculum renewal in one of the most comprehensive programs in Canada, well known for its exceptional performance opportunities.

### “The breadth of music within our faculty is one of our greatest strengths. Our students encounter everything from classical and jazz to popular and global music traditions. That encourages curiosity, collaboration and artistic growth, ultimately helping each student develop a stronger, more distinctive voice of their own.” – Sophie Roland, dean of Don Wright Faculty of Music

As dean, Roland aims to keep growing that approach to ensure students graduate with a scope of knowledge “beyond what they imagine” when they first come to Western. Whether as a professor, researcher, mentor or administrator, Roland has worked to create environments where students’ passion for music can blossom, believing it’s not merely the reward of mastering musicianship, but the force that makes mastery possible.

“Our role is not only to recognize that passion, but to nurture it – create an environment in which it can deepen, grow and flourish,” she said.

Don Wright Faculty of Music dean Sophie Roland, newly appointed to the role at Western University, brings decades of leadership, teaching and performance experience. (Claus Andersen/Don Wright Faculty of Music)

An acclaimed mezzo-soprano, Roland has continued to pursue her own musical passion alongside her growing administrative responsibilities. Most recently, she performed a number of recitals in Europe. Opera has long captivated her, particularly its ability to create an intimate emotional experience within a grand spectacle.

“Amid large casts and stages, vocalists convey human emotion through unamplified voices that fill a hall. There is something extraordinary about the immediacy of the human voice carrying feeling from performer to audience. That power to move us is what I have always loved about opera.”

One of Roland’s proudest accomplishments is nurturing that passion in students beyond the classroom through two summer programs: the Canadian Operatic Arts Academy in London, Ont., and a corresponding program in Italy and the Netherlands. They ran for nearly a decade before the pandemic, drawing about 600 students from Western and around the world.

Several of those students now perform in opera houses internationally. Their success is one of the most rewarding parts of Roland’s career so far.

“It’s really heartwarming that we were part of a chain of education that kept the fire alive for them, and that they, in turn, will carry it forward for generations of musicians to come.”

For Roland, taking the helm in the Faculty of Music just as artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to remake nearly every field is an opportunity, not a hurdle to overcome. She believes AI is only sharpening the case for live music.

“There’s a shared energy between audience and performers that comes from being together in a room and experiencing something as it happens. People are hungry for that kind of human connection and shared sense of purpose, perhaps more than ever,” she said.

Roland’s commitment to creating opportunities for students to thrive extends to university governance. She continues to contribute to Western and higher education more broadly, chairing Western Senate committees and contributing to provincial academic policy, serving on the Council of Ontario Universities.

Through all her roles at Western and beyond, students have remained the primary focus and they will continue to anchor her priorities, Roland said.

“Music has reinvented itself many times throughout its history, and I believe we are at another one of those extraordinary moments. As technology changes the world around us, the need to create, connect and make meaning through live music remains profoundly human. Our responsibility is to prepare our students not simply to respond to what comes next, but to help shape it.”

Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.

stories.title: There’s one place where I can forget about my phone, and I love it
stories.summary: Amid the beauty of the lake, the calls of loons and the crisp, clean air, there’s one other thing I love about Killarney, Ont.: zero cell coverage
stories.author: Hasan Meral
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

It’s hard to find a place to completely get away. A place without emails, calls or a constant stream of news. But Canada is unique and we are lucky that these places still exist, you just have to keep driving north.

I grew up in Sudbury in northern Ontario, where a 20-minute drive could lead to complete isolation by a lake or in a forest. Because of my specialized work, I now live in southern Ontario, in the city of Oakville, and that drive to find solitude is much longer. But I miss the quiet.

Fortunately, my oldest friend still has his family cottage in Killarney, Ont., and I have visited every year for nearly 30 years. Killarney is located on the Canadian Shield at Georgian Bay and almost an hour’s drive off the Trans Canada highway - it’s a special place that feels almost completely isolated from the rest of the world. It takes me 3.5 hours to drive, and then another half-hour boat ride to reach the camp. I drive up each year with another friend who lives near me. Amid the beauty of the lake, the calls of loons and the crisp, clean air, there is one other thing I love: zero cell coverage.

Here we can all truly connect with nature. It brings me back to my childhood - a time where there were no cell phones. We go exploring. We relax. We have fun.

The wedding dress that’s been worn by our family for generations

And with our phones turned into cameras only, we get to connect with each other, too. The three of us prepare meals together and spend our time helping out with cabin tasks such as painting. An old battery powered radio with real knobs plays our favourite Sudbury radio stations.

There is no running water, or electricity. This means hauling up lake water for dishes and using an outhouse that has a resident spider. We used to use candles for light but now a solar-powered battery feeds a few lightbulbs at night. What a luxury!

There are activities here that I do only once a year, which makes them that much more enjoyable: chopping wood, reading newspapers, starting fires.

Evenings are spent in a wonderfully old-fashioned way. We play card games. It always takes a few minutes to remember the rules to euchre and cribbage, after all it’s usually been a year since we last played, but eventually we get the hang of it. After that, the highlight of our time at camp is the sauna, an old wood-burning sweat room that we carefully take turns feeding throughout the day, or “logging-in,” as we like to call it. By evening it’s ready, and there’s nothing like sitting inside with the smell of cedar, then jumping into the cold lake when it gets too hot.

When I emerge from that cold plunge I am met with the most beautiful sight in the sky – thousands of stars, completely clear without any city light blocking them out. I spot the few constellations I remember learning about from my father. It’s magnificent.

After repeating the sauna-lake-sauna routine a few more times we head to bed. And I can honestly say it’s the best sleep I get all year.

I’ve learned to love admitting I’m from Biggar, Sask.

Part of the joy of being at camp is the guest book. The old yellow binder houses decades of memory jotted down onto sheets now protected by sleeves. One of the first entries is from the early 1990s, written by my father, whom I accompanied as a young child when the camp was first purchased. Then, starting when we were high school age in the early 2000s there are regular entries from the three of us.

The pages of this guestbook tell a story of our adulthood. The kinds of things we found humorous, world events and life milestones and goals. There are notes from other people in our lives that we no longer hear from, old friends, ex-partners and some who are no longer with us at all.

While the three of us have changed in so many ways, the camp has remained constant. We keep coming back, year after year. As our lives speed up, the camp slows everything down and reminds us of the importance of unplugging and connection.

Hasan Merali lives in Oakville, Ont.

It’s hard to find a place to completely get away. A place without emails, calls or a constant stream of news. But Canada is unique and we are lucky that these places still exist, you just have to keep driving north.

I grew up in Sudbury in northern Ontario, where a 20-minute drive could lead to complete isolation by a lake or in a forest. Because of my specialized work, I now live in southern Ontario, in the city of Oakville, and that drive to find solitude is much longer. But I miss the quiet.

Fortunately, my oldest friend still has his family cottage in Killarney, Ont., and I have visited every year for nearly 30 years. Killarney is located on the Canadian Shield at Georgian Bay and almost an hour’s drive off the Trans Canada highway - it’s a special place that feels almost completely isolated from the rest of the world. It takes me 3.5 hours to drive, and then another half-hour boat ride to reach the camp. I drive up each year with another friend who lives near me. Amid the beauty of the lake, the calls of loons and the crisp, clean air, there is one other thing I love: zero cell coverage.
Here we can all truly connect with nature. It brings me back to my childhood - a time where there were no cell phones. We go exploring. We relax. We have fun.
The wedding dress that’s been worn by our family for generations

And with our phones turned into cameras only, we get to connect with each other, too. The three of us prepare meals together and spend our time helping out with cabin tasks such as painting. An old battery powered radio with real knobs plays our favourite Sudbury radio stations.

There is no running water, or electricity. This means hauling up lake water for dishes and using an outhouse that has a resident spider. We used to use candles for light but now a solar-powered battery feeds a few lightbulbs at night. What a luxury!
There are activities here that I do only once a year, which makes them that much more enjoyable: chopping wood, reading newspapers, starting fires.

Evenings are spent in a wonderfully old-fashioned way. We play card games. It always takes a few minutes to remember the rules to euchre and cribbage, after all it’s usually been a year since we last played, but eventually we get the hang of it. After that, the highlight of our time at camp is the sauna, an old wood-burning sweat room that we carefully take turns feeding throughout the day, or “logging-in,” as we like to call it. By evening it’s ready, and there’s nothing like sitting inside with the smell of cedar, then jumping into the cold lake when it gets too hot.

When I emerge from that cold plunge I am met with the most beautiful sight in the sky – thousands of stars, completely clear without any city light blocking them out. I spot the few constellations I remember learning about from my father. It’s magnificent.
After repeating the sauna-lake-sauna routine a few more times we head to bed. And I can honestly say it’s the best sleep I get all year.
I’ve learned to love admitting I’m from Biggar, Sask.

Part of the joy of being at camp is the guest book. The old yellow binder houses decades of memory jotted down onto sheets now protected by sleeves. One of the first entries is from the early 1990s, written by my father, whom I accompanied as a young child when the camp was first purchased. Then, starting when we were high school age in the early 2000s there are regular entries from the three of us.

The pages of this guestbook tell a story of our adulthood. The kinds of things we found humorous, world events and life milestones and goals. There are notes from other people in our lives that we no longer hear from, old friends, ex-partners and some who are no longer with us at all.

While the three of us have changed in so many ways, the camp has remained constant. We keep coming back, year after year. As our lives speed up, the camp slows everything down and reminds us of the importance of unplugging and connection.
Hasan Merali lives in Oakville, Ont.

stories.title: What the U.S. Fed hiking rates means for the loonie and for borrowers
stories.summary: The U.S. Federal Reserve hiked interest rates for the first time in three years on Wednesday, and several economists say this could add pressure on the Bank of Canada.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The U.S. Federal Reserve hiked interest rates for the first time in three years on Wednesday , and several economists say this could add pressure on the Bank of Canada to raise borrowing costs for Canadians sooner than later.

Canadian borrowing rates aren’t directly tied to changes made by the U.S. Fed, but there are some ripple effects, including changes to the loonie, which could influence future changes.

Derek Holt, economist and vice president at the Bank of Nova Scotia, said in a statement on Wednesday that he would be surprised if the U.S. rate hike doesn’t “add one more ingredient to pave the way” for Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem to begin hiking soon.

Central banks, like the Fed and the Bank of Canada, aim to maintain the balance of their economies by ensuring inflation stays within a sustainable range (usually between one and three per cent), while also keeping borrowing rates low enough to allow the economy to grow.

The main way they strike that balance is by adjusting benchmark interest rates, and Canadians and businesses alike could wind up paying more to borrow money and take out mortgages and other loans if the Bank of Canada hikes its key rate.

Canada’s consumer inflation has been hovering around three per cent through July and August, while U.S. inflation was last reported at 3.4 per cent.

One of the main reasons the Bank of Canada could move to raise interest rates is if inflation gets too high, and a weaker Canadian dollar in the face of a stronger U.S. dollar can risk inflation rising in Canada. That’s because the currency diversion makes imported goods more expensive in Canada.

When the Fed’s rate announcement happened on Wednesday afternoon, the U.S. dollar increased in value, which sent the Canadian dollar’s equivalent value down by more than a quarter of a cent almost instantly.

Doug Porter, chief economist at the Bank of Montreal, says although that’s a relatively small drop, if the trend continues, then the Bank of Canada may lean more towards raising rates, like the Fed did.

“I don’t think the Bank of Canada will be overly concerned about a mild decline in the Canadian dollar, [but] they would take it into account for sure,” says Porter.

“Were the Canadian dollar to soften a little bit more, it would put a bit of pressure on the Bank of Canada to possibly follow the Fed. But I don’t think we’re close to being there yet.”

The Fed’s new benchmark sits at minimum 3.75 per cent, while the Bank of Canada’s is 2.25 per cent. That divergence in key lending rates could also add pressure to the Canadian dollar because of the difference in borrowing costs, especially for businesses.

“They’re more than a percentage point and a half higher, so we’re starting off at much, much lower rates,” says Porter.

“Perhaps those really low interest rates in Canada are not sustainable for long if inflation stays at three per cent.”

4:01 Global bond yields surge

But the Fed’s rate hike could affect Canadian borrowing costs even without a Bank of Canada rate hike, and that’s because of recent bond market jitters.

Bonds yields, or the interest they pay out to owners of those bonds, increases or decreases depending mostly on supply and demand. If there is less confidence in the U.S. government to rein in inflation, then U.S. government bond owners may sell those bonds because of the perceived risk.

U.S. bond yields have been spiking recently, especially since the start of September, and higher interest rates and inflation typically leads to higher bond yields.

“The ripple effect [from the Fed’s rate hike] is basically transmitted through the bond market, through longer-term interest rates,” says Porter.

“We are seeing slow but steady upward pressure in longer-term interest rates, like say a five-year mortgage rate. They have been rising because of the pressure that we’re seeing on these bond yields.”

stories.title: Season starts with just 4 NHL first-round picks in the OHL. 3 are on the London Knights
stories.summary: New Ncaa and NHL rules are reshaping the OHL – and concentrating elite talent in London.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The Ontario Hockey League has changed in a hurry.

In the 2025 championship series, there were nine players involved who were NHL first-round picks or soon to reach that status in following drafts. That London-Oshawa series – which featured the likes of Easton Cowan (Maple Leafs), Sam Dickinson (Sharks), Beckett Sennecke (Ducks) and Calum Ritchie (Avalanche choice, now with the Islanders) – appears to be a thing of the past.

The new OHL season is starting this week with likely four – possibly five – NHL first-rounders across the entire 20-team league, let alone the final. The kicker is three of them belong to one team, the London Knights, and not a single one was born in Canada.

Senators prospect Jaxon Cover learned his ice hockey while attending prep school in the Greater Toronto Area, but the slick forward was born in Miami, Fla., and raised in Cayman Islands. Giant Russian defenceman Maksim Sokolovskii (Flyers) hails from Kazakhstan and incoming 2026 Ducks first-rounder Marcus Nordmark is a Swedish world junior hopeful.

Peterborough’s Adam Novotny, a Czech winger, went 24th overall to the Canucks in June. Saginaw’s Nikita Klepov, the OHL’s reigning scoring champ and Anaheim’s 15th overall pick, could still return to the Spirit but his immediate future is still in the air.

The 18-year-old was born in Florida but grew up in Russia.

Even if the talented point-getter is back with Saginaw, that’s still not a ton of NHL first-round talent represented in OHL rinks.

NEW Path: There are three factors at play.

The first is the Ncaa’s ruling allowing Canadian Hockey League players to be eligible for the U.S. college ranks. The Windsor Spitfires, who the Knights open against Friday (7 p.m. at Canada Life Place) are without 2024 OHL No. 1 overall pick Ethan Belchetz (Mammoth) and Jack Nesbitt (Flyers) because of it.

Belchetz is committed to play at Michigan State this fall while the 19-year-old Nesbitt joined the University of Michigan and will team up with Landon DuPont, who played in the Memorial Cup final with Everett last spring and is the favourite to be the top choice in the 2027 NHL draft.

The draw to the Ncaa is the chance to make serious money right away, face some older players, but also practice and work out more with fewer scheduled games.

That reality has been available for a couple of years now.

The second wrinkle is the new clause in the CHL/NHL agreement allowing big-league clubs to develop their 19-year-old first-rounders in the pros instead of the traditional route of sending them back to junior again.

Some GMs felt that was redundant, especially when players of the same age were picked out of Europe and leagues like the Ushl and permitted to make the jump.

Before this rule change, Soo Greyhounds captain Brady Martin, for example, would have to either make Nashville out of training camp or head back to the Hounds. Now if there is a logjam on the Predators roster, he can start in the American league and the same goes for London defenceman Henry Brzustewicz with Los Angeles.

If the blue-liner can’t crack the Kings as a teenager, he can play for the Ontario Reign farm team.

The third, of course, is the influx of well-prepared talent flowing into the NHL. For a few years, teams were willing to keep younger players as cheap labour when up against the salary cap.

Now that the cap has increased, it will be interesting to see if they are more patient. But there will always be junior superstars ready to make the jump like reigning Calder trophy winner Matthew Schaefer, who is still eligible to play for the Erie Otters, and exceptional 19-year-old Michael Misa, who played a half-season with the Sharks at age 18 last year.

The OHL brass has discussed this trend and, across the CHL, it is being monitored closely with no firm counter-moves yet. So far, the party line is that many more U.S. college-committed players are opting to try junior hockey than there are players exiting the three leagues for the Ncaa’s Name, Image and Likeness greenbacks.

The issue is the outflow of some of the biggest stars – like Porter Martone (Flyers) leaving Brampton last year for Michigan State and the Soo’s Chase Reid (Kraken) following suit to Spartan-land this time.

In London, the general concern is how good the team is going to be and what players will show up.

“All you’re trying to do,” Knights GM Mark Hunter said, “is run a good program where players want to come.”

Knights View: London was ranked fourth to start the CHL season. Division rival Guelph is first, Saginaw is fifth and Ottawa is ninth. Interestingly, the Knights played two exhibition games in Victoria a couple of weeks ago and the Royals check in at No. 3 – right in front of them.

“We’re excited about our team,” Mark Hunter said. “We’re anticipating if we get everybody here, we can put this team together (and win). We have some good pieces but those pieces are only good if we play as a team.”

More Goals: The Knights didn’t score enough last season and it resulted in a fourth-place finish and first-round exit against Sault Ste. Marie. They don’t anticipate the same struggles this time and Nordmark’s inclusion after Ducks camp should wash away those concerns.

“He’s highly skilled and can make plays and score,” Mark Hunter said. “He’s a first-round (NHL) pick and those kinds of players seem to do well most of the time here in London.”

There’s a strong history of development under head coach Dale Hunter, for sure. It’s unmatched in junior hockey.

It’s not just Nordmark, either. There are a half-dozen other threats, including Cover, speedy Evan Van Gorp, Dallas prospect Ryan Brown, two-way centre Carson Harmer, pesky Cohen Bidgood and American over-ager Thomas Zocco, who racked up points in his final Ushl season.

“I think Zocco will score,” Mark Hunter said. “We need scoring across our lineup. I don’t think we had enough of that last year from the fourth to the third and second line.

“They all need to contribute.”

Young Guns: The Knights will have another player picked in the first round of the NHL draft next June.

It’s just a matter of who and how many.

Forward Luca Santala has size, plays with his head up and is hungry to be the latest in the list of productive Finns to wear the Knights jersey. The 17-year-old knows the exploits of 2025 OHL playoff MVP Kasper Halttunen (Senators) and the excellence of defenceman Olli Maatta (Wild) in these parts.

Fellow rookie Kane Barch is wearing his father Krys’s old Knights No. 10 and wants to experience a run to the OHL final like Dad did in 1999 at the old Ice House. Cooper McAslan, a standout with the Nationals last season, is a major part of a London defensive corps that is long on talent but short on major junior experience.

In that vein, the Knights on Wednesday acquired 19-year-old rearguard Jonathan Kapageridis from North Bay for a fourth-round pick in 2029. The 6-foot, 182-pounder from Vaughan has 60 OHL games under his belt.

“They’ve got work to do,” Mark Hunter said of the group. “I use an example like (Kings prospect Jared) Woolley. The second half of his 17-year-old season, we brought him up and he was ready to go. Sometimes at that age, they need a little more time, that’s all.”

They need to listen and be quick learners. The potential is there to be a great back end, especially if the goaltending stands tall.

Good Shape: The Knights have the ability to get better.

Front-running Guelph has already made a ton of moves and doesn’t have a ton of assets to deal at the deadline for more help. London has recouped all its draft picks and can pursue the best available players if need be in January.

It matters. Kitchener’s acquisition of Knights captain Sam O’Reilly made all the difference in its OHL and Memorial Cup title runs.

London has the first half to prove to the Hunters the roster will live up to its contender status. It could be a bit rocky early on, with bigger names still at NHL camps, but the Knights have overcome that problem many times in the past.

Still, five of their first six games out of the gate are at home. You don’t want to dig too big a hole, so a good start would be a major step in the right direction.

Now if there is a logjam on the Predators roster, he can start in the American league and the same goes for London defenceman Henry Brzustewicz with Los Angeles.
If the blue-liner can’t crack the Kings as a teenager, he can play for the Ontario Reign farm team.
The third, of course, is the influx of well-prepared talent flowing into the NHL. For a few years, teams were willing to keep younger players as cheap labour when up against the salary cap.

Now that the cap has increased, it will be interesting to see if they are more patient. But there will always be junior superstars ready to make the jump like reigning Calder trophy winner Matthew Schaefer, who is still eligible to play for the Erie Otters, and exceptional 19-year-old Michael Misa, who played a half-season with the Sharks at age 18 last year.

The OHL brass has discussed this trend and, across the CHL, it is being monitored closely with no firm counter-moves yet. So far, the party line is that many more U.S. college-committed players are opting to try junior hockey than there are players exiting the three leagues for the Ncaa’s Name, Image and Likeness greenbacks.

The issue is the outflow of some of the biggest stars – like Porter Martone (Flyers) leaving Brampton last year for Michigan State and the Soo’s Chase Reid (Kraken) following suit to Spartan-land this time.
In London, the general concern is how good the team is going to be and what players will show up.
“All you’re trying to do,” Knights GM Mark Hunter said, “is run a good program where players want to come.”

Knights View: London was ranked fourth to start the CHL season. Division rival Guelph is first, Saginaw is fifth and Ottawa is ninth. Interestingly, the Knights played two exhibition games in Victoria a couple of weeks ago and the Royals check in at No. 3 – right in front of them.

“We’re excited about our team,” Mark Hunter said. “We’re anticipating if we get everybody here, we can put this team together (and win). We have some good pieces but those pieces are only good if we play as a team.”

More Goals: The Knights didn’t score enough last season and it resulted in a fourth-place finish and first-round exit against Sault Ste. Marie. They don’t anticipate the same struggles this time and Nordmark’s inclusion after Ducks camp should wash away those concerns.
“He’s highly skilled and can make plays and score,” Mark Hunter said. “He’s a first-round (NHL) pick and those kinds of players seem to do well most of the time here in London.”
There’s a strong history of development under head coach Dale Hunter, for sure. It’s unmatched in junior hockey.

It’s not just Nordmark, either. There are a half-dozen other threats, including Cover, speedy Evan Van Gorp, Dallas prospect Ryan Brown, two-way centre Carson Harmer, pesky Cohen Bidgood and American over-ager Thomas Zocco, who racked up points in his final Ushl season.
“I think Zocco will score,” Mark Hunter said. “We need scoring across our lineup. I don’t think we had enough of that last year from the fourth to the third and second line.
“They all need to contribute.”
Young Guns: The Knights will have another player picked in the first round of the NHL draft next June.
It’s just a matter of who and how many.

Forward Luca Santala has size, plays with his head up and is hungry to be the latest in the list of productive Finns to wear the Knights jersey. The 17-year-old knows the exploits of 2025 OHL playoff MVP Kasper Halttunen (Senators) and the excellence of defenceman Olli Maatta (Wild) in these parts.

Fellow rookie Kane Barch is wearing his father Krys’s old Knights No. 10 and wants to experience a run to the OHL final like Dad did in 1999 at the old Ice House. Cooper McAslan, a standout with the Nationals last season, is a major part of a London defensive corps that is long on talent but short on major junior experience.

In that vein, the Knights on Wednesday acquired 19-year-old rearguard Jonathan Kapageridis from North Bay for a fourth-round pick in 2029. The 6-foot, 182-pounder from Vaughan has 60 OHL games under his belt.

“They’ve got work to do,” Mark Hunter said of the group. “I use an example like (Kings prospect Jared) Woolley. The second half of his 17-year-old season, we brought him up and he was ready to go. Sometimes at that age, they need a little more time, that’s all.”
They need to listen and be quick learners. The potential is there to be a great back end, especially if the goaltending stands tall.
Good Shape: The Knights have the ability to get better.

Front-running Guelph has already made a ton of moves and doesn’t have a ton of assets to deal at the deadline for more help. London has recouped all its draft picks and can pursue the best available players if need be in January.
It matters. Kitchener’s acquisition of Knights captain Sam O’Reilly made all the difference in its OHL and Memorial Cup title runs.

London has the first half to prove to the Hunters the roster will live up to its contender status. It could be a bit rocky early on, with bigger names still at NHL camps, but the Knights have overcome that problem many times in the past.
Still, five of their first six games out of the gate are at home. You don’t want to dig too big a hole, so a good start would be a major step in the right direction.

stories.title: Former MP Raj Grewal, two Sikh temples sued by lenders of $15M loan
stories.summary: Case adds to long list of legal actions that accuse Grewal, his former firm and associated lawyers of missteps in real-estate deals
stories.author: Tom Blackwell
stories.content:
The growing saga of financial allegations around former MP and lawyer Raj Grewal has taken another surprising turn, as not only the former politician but two Sikh temples are named as defendants in a new lawsuit.

The case filed last week by a pair of non-bank lenders alleges that RSG Law, the firm Grewal founded, represented the temples in Toronto and nearby Brampton as they jointly obtained a $15-million loan last year from Ssmt Management Inc. and Oculus Mortgage GP Inc.

The loan was guaranteed by Grewal, as well as by a man who is president of both “gurdwaras” and the treasurer of one of them, according to the lawsuit.

Despite repeated promises, the law firm never registered the debt against one of the two temples, a standard requirement that would provide security for the lenders in the event of a default, the lawsuit charges.

And, in fact, the seven-month mortgage had not been paid off by the end of the term in January, and the last monthly interest payment of $187,000 was made in April, the statement of claim filed by the lenders alleges.

No statement of defence has been filed and none of the allegations has been proven in court.

Simon Bieber, one of Grewal’s lawyers, told the National Post Wednesday that he understands “the issue is resolved.”

Maria Naimark, one of the plaintiffs’ lawyers, declined to comment when asked if the case had already been settled, just days after being launched.

The other defendants in the case did not respond to requests for comment.

Balpreet Singh, a spokesman for the World Sikh Organization — the faith’s main Canadian association — said he didn’t know enough about the case to comment on it or its impact on the community, noting that statements of claim tend to be very one-sided.

The case adds to a long list of legal actions that accuse Grewal, the firm he founded but no longer owns and associated lawyers of fraud, misappropriation of client funds and other wrongdoing in a series of real-estate transactions.

In some cases, defendants have been accused of borrowing money against clients’ property without the property owners’ authorization, providing fake title insurance that fails to protect lenders and misusing client money in trust funds. Recently filed lawsuits estimate that about $200 million is in dispute.

The Law Society of Ontario has also accused Grewal of financial transgressions, saying that to leave him practising law as its investigation proceeds would pose a “significant risk of harm to the public.” He has voluntarily given up his law licence pending a decision on the regulator’s request to suspend those credentials. The society has already suspended the licence of Davinder Khattra, the current head of RSG Law.

But the involvement of non-profit religious organizations — which are subject to strict federal tax rules and in this case are close to the hearts of the area’s large Sikh community — would seem to add a new complexion to the situation.

None of the allegations against Grewal and others has been proven in court. Lawyers for Grewal have said that the 41-year-old former politician had limited involvement in the RSG firm’s day-to-day operations after handing it over to lawyer Khattra, 29, in 2024 and that the various lawsuits are a result of the “falling out” that can happen in business transactions.

According to the new lawsuit, the Sikh Spiritual Centre Toronto and Nanaksar Thath Ishar Darbar — which runs a gurdwara in Brampton — jointly obtained a mortgage of $11 million, later increased to $15 million. About $12 million was forwarded and over $13 million, including outstanding interest, is still owed to the two lenders, the statement of claim says.

The loan was supposed to be secured against both temples. But despite promises from lawyer Khattra of RSG Law, the charge was never registered against the Brampton property, the lawsuit alleges.

stories.title: Calgary fire officials say landfill blaze could last months
stories.summary: A stubborn blaze that has been burning for the last 10 days at a Calgary landfill could take months to fizzle out, the fire service said Wednesday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary – A stubborn blaze that has been burning for the last 10 days at a Calgary landfill can cover multiple Canadian football fields and take months to fizzle out, the fire service said Wednesday.

Calgary fire Chief Steve Dongworth said the fire at the Ecco Recycling facility in the southeast part of the city has an estimated volume of one million cubic metres.

He said it can cover up to eight Canadian Football League fields.

The fire has also been difficult to tackle as it’s located in deep pockets, he said, and under a mountain of garbage.

“Although we should be able to control smoke from the fire in the next few days, this incident could last weeks or even months until on-site fire risk is fully mitigated,” Dongworth said in a statement.

Firefighters responded to the blaze at Ecco, a private landfill and recycling business, ON Sept. 6.

The smoke billowing from the fire has become a nuisance for locals and has prompted a health advisory from the fire service.

One resident has said the smoke has triggered his daughter’s asthma and he is considering temporarily leaving the community.

Dongworth said the smoke is set to flare up as crews fight the blaze.

“Our immediate efforts remain focused on actions that reduce smoke impact on communities,” said Dongorth.

“This includes identifying hot spots, applying water where required and using soil to cap and smother remaining areas of fire.”

He said he appreciates the community for being patient.

stories.title: Three Nova Scotia communities to launch crime prevention projects
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia government has announced it will use federal money to establish public safety projects aimed at preventing crime in three municipalities.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The mayor of a central Nova Scotia town says she’s hopeful a new community safety initiative announced Thursday will help address serious safety concerns that have been escalating in the community.

New Glasgow Mayor Nancy Dicks said challenges related to a local 20-bed emergency shelter were behind the town’s decision to take part in a pilot project organized by the province.

“This is certainly no secret, that the town of New Glasgow is facing very serious safety issues right now,” Dicks told reporters after a news conference in Halifax announcing the province’s plans to use federal money to establish safety projects aimed at preventing crime in three communities.

“We’re not going to hide behind that and we’re not going to ignore it,” she added.

The Town of New Glasgow passed a unanimous motion last month asking the province to shut down the emergency shelter, saying the facility was not addressing the needs of people experiencing homelessness and addiction.

Multiple media reports say local residents have complained about public drug use, vandalism, assaults, property damage and thefts near the downtown facility, known as Northstar Shelter.

The council’s motion said a health-focused approach was needed to provide people with a chance to “stabilize” and receive treatment. The council also said it wanted the province to develop a residential rehabilitation centre.

Meanwhile, the non-profit organization behind the Northstar Shelter said last month it supports the call for more support for homeless people, but the group said it doesn’t make sense to shut down the facility before those services are in place.

Dicks said conversations with the provincial government about the council’s call for the shelter’s closure have just begun.

On Thursday, provincial Justice Minister Scott Armstrong said New Glasgow, East Hants and the Queens Municipality will share $550,000 from Public Safety Canada to develop individual plans tailored to local needs.

The mayor said people from across Pictou County go to New Glasgow for health care, housing and other support, which “gives us a close view” of how challenges involving mental health, addictions, housing and poverty affect residents.

“The nature of these challenges has changed significantly in recent years,” she said. “They are becoming more complex. And the solutions often extend beyond what police or municipal government can provide on their own.”

Dicks said she expects her community’s plan will be aimed at tackling those complex issues.

Armstrong said the initiative is a response to recommendations from the inquiry into the 2020 Nova Scotia mass shooting that claimed 23 lives. The Mass Casualty Commission called for stronger community safety planning and greater investment in crime prevention.

“Public safety is about more than responding when something goes wrong,” Armstrong said. “It’s also about preventing harm, reducing risk and helping communities address problems before they have crises.”

The final report from the inquiry was released in March 2023. It included 130 non-binding recommendations, about half of which were focused on improvements to policing.

One recommendation called for provincial and territorial governments to enact laws to create a statutory framework for community safety and well-being initiatives by April 2024.

stories.title: Younger Canadians most divided on academic freedom protecting political views: poll
stories.summary: New polling reveals a generational divide over academic freedom and the protection it offers professors who get unnecessarily political.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Political advocacy in a post-secondary classroom where it does not relate to the subject matter could become a “threat to academic freedom” if left unchecked, warns Association for Canadian Studies president Jack Jedwab.

While new polling for the organization indicates the majority (60 per cent) of Canadians firmly feel academic freedom shouldn’t protect a professor who uses class time to push personal political views unrelated to the curriculum, the 18-24-year-old cohort was the most conflicted, with only 38 per cent sharing that opinion, 32 per cent in support of protection and 30 per cent unsure.

Generation Xers between 55-64 (70 per cent) and boomers 65 and over (73 per cent ) were most likely to disagree.

Jedwab isn’t surprised most respondents feel “there’s a line” for academic freedom protection and reasoned the youngest cohort, predominantly students, are divided due to their exposure.

“It’s hard to contend when your professor advocates a particular cause,” he told National Post in an interview. “It can be very challenging to reflect on whether this is crossing a line or not.”

He highlighted the recent Campus Anti-Semitism Student Experiences report commissioned by Heritage Canada, which he co-authored, which found that 34 per cent said a professor brought up Jews, Judaism, Israel, or Zionism when unrelated to the course subject.

“In a course that had nothing to do with Israel, my professor spent three weeks talking about Gaza and the creation of the State of Israel,” one Jewish student told researchers. “He never mentioned the Holocaust as a precursor to its founding, repeatedly calling the state a ‘Zionist political project.’”

Jedwab, a Ph.D. himself, stopped here to stress the critical importance of academic freedom, but said it’s also critical to have a frank conversation about the checks and balances “when it comes to the roles and responsibilities of academics around controversial issues that are not within the purview of what they’re being asked to teach.”

“The risk is that academic freedom is being abused by some parties in pursuit of a particular cause,” he added.

Polling also identified that among those who support academic freedom protection in those instances, “are also considerably more likely to regard the justification of terrorism, the denial of documented atrocities and the minimization of their victims as acceptable.”

Almost four in 10 (39.6 per cent) think it’s very or somewhat acceptable to say that a well-documented historical atrocity might not have occurred. More than a third (36.5 per cent) felt it was acceptable, to some degree, to exaggerate or minimize the number of victims of historical atrocities and more still (37.4 per cent) think it’s to some degree acceptable to say that members of a religious group are collectively responsible for the actions of a foreign government.

Jedwab said that adds to the need “to reflect on the extent to which these types of freedoms are indeed detrimental to the well-being of individual Canadians.”

Perhaps more alarming, nearly one in four (24 per cent) believe acts of terrorism can sometimes be justified. (67.3 per cent said it cannot and 8.7 per cent were unsure.)

“It’s showing you that there’s a risk when we don’t have this conversation,” Jedwab said, “that ideas that we consider very worrisome to public safety can manifest themselves in certain situations, and the academy is not outside that altogether, as we can see.”

Part of the challenge with the youngest demographic group is addressing their distrust of historical atrocities, which is partially fuelled, Jedwab said, by mass exposure to misinformation via social media continually blurring the line between what’s real and isn’t.

“We do need to give a lot more reflection about the way in which information is being conveyed to people,” he said.

The poll of 1,538 respondents, conducted by Leger on behalf of the Association for Canadian Studies, was conducted Sept. 4-6. A margin of error cannot be associated with a non-probability sample in a panel survey for comparison purposes. However, a probability sample of this size would have a margin of error of 2.5 per cent, 19 times out of 20.​
