stories.title: Read a transcript of Carney’s speech to the European Parliament
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney made a pitch for cooperation with the EU in industries like artificial intelligence, critical minerals and defence.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament on Thursday, calling for deeper cooperation and trade between Canada and the European Union and making a pitch for cooperation with the EU in industries like artificial intelligence, critical minerals and defence.

Here is a transcript of Carney’s speech, edited for clarity.

President Metzola, dear Roberta, President von der Leyen, dear Ursula. Honourable members of the European Parliament, distinguished colleagues. Thank you for granting me the honor of addressing you t the beginning of this decisive session.

I shall speak to you today about the way in which our response to the current geopolitical rupture must include a new dimension. But first of all, I should like to refer to something older, something which considerably pre-dates EU-Canada relations because the depth of our bonds, those which unite us, cannot be measured by trade or what is written in treaties alone.

Our bonds are deeply rooted in our lands.

In the heart of Germany, above Weimar, there is a wooded ridge called Ettersberg. And for decades Goethe walked, thought, and wrote there. An oak on that ridge came to bear his name, a living monument to the highest ideals of European culture.

As the 20th century turned dark, that same oak became trapped behind the barbed wire of Buchenwald, a silent witness to humanity’s deepest moral failure.

Goethe understood that ideals must be fought for, that values do not defend themselves. Indeed, at the end of Faust, the old man’s last vision is of a free people on free ground.

Freedom and life must be earned every single day. Every day. Every day, not once in 1945 or 1956 or 1989, every day, including this one.

Freedom was gained thanks to the heroism of the European wartime resistance. It was nurtured by the founders of the European coal and steel community in the aftermath of war. It was fostered by the creation of the European community. It was preserved by the establishment of the European Union, and it was developed thanks to the European Union’s enlargement after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

The values embodied by that Goethe oak have also endured in part because the ideals that flourished beneath its branches also crossed the Atlantic.

In 1917, amidst the devastation of the Battle of Vimy Ridge, a young Canadian lieutenant named Leslie Miller gathered a handful of acorns from the shattered European landscape. He carried them home and planted them in Canadian soil near Milken, Ont., where they grew into a majestic forest.

A century later, a profound circle of renewal was completed. Because graphs from Leslie Miller’s Canadian Oaks were repatriated to France and replanted on the same Vimy Ridge where they had been born.

This is the essence of the Canada-European Union partnership. Seeds, values, ideas, trade, people, and progress carried back and forth across the Atlantic for centuries.

We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication.

We hold common values, for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant. We believe that a strong economy is not an end in itself, but a means to a just society. We are committed. We are committed stewards of our natural heritage.

We believe that our prosperity grows when it’s shared. These values – this is a sharing of choice, not coincidence. In his writings, Goethe borrowed a word from the chemists of his day: Wahlverwandtschaften, or the elective affinity of different elements that combine because of their inherent attraction.

Canada and Europe are not bound by geography, even though our Danish friends know that we share a 3,000 kilometer border in the Arctic. We are bound by an affinity — elective, chosen, renewed — and stronger for being so.

Today our societies are being battered by new storms. The disruption caused by climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, the weaponization of trade. The multilateral organizations we used to count on have been weakened.

Today, it is hard to reconcile sovereignty and openness. Economic integration is now being weaponized. Tariffs being used to exert pressure. Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited.

Technology is transforming the nature of warfare, the structure of our economies and state’s ability to govern. Tech platforms aspire to sovereignty. They want to set access rules. They want to dictate the rules for regulation and even circumvent them. They want to control our data, spread disinformation and steal our children’s childhoods.

This combination is a ferocious storm.

A single tree will come down in it.

A forest will not.

And that’s because beneath the forest floor, the roots of an oak intertwine with those of its neighbors, exchanging nutrients, adding strength to strength, creating a resilient, self-sustaining ecosystem.

Together, Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive. This is about sovereignty. Our ability to live as we wish. It’s about the freedoms we must fight for every day. Because sovereignty requires resilience, the ability to withstand shocks.

Sovereignty today goes beyond being able to feed, fuel, and defend ourselves. It now requires secure access to AI, semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems, clean energy technologies, vaccines, space-based communications. And we all have important gaps in these strategic capabilities, and we each must rely on individual nations or individual companies to fill them.

And that creates vulnerabilities, particularly when supposedly global companies prove national in the breach. Closing these gaps is not possible alone, but it’s very achievable collectively.

Canada and Europe are each strong. Europe and Canada are stronger together.

The institutions we’ve inherited are organized by geography. The strategic capabilities that we need are organized by function. We can ally by function if we are bold and deliberate. And we shouldn’t be cowed by the perceived scale of the task.

Just as dominance is the arrogance of the hegemon, perfection is the enemy of the good. The economics of this are clear. The leverage of the powerful and an exploitive relationship collapses well before complete independence is achieved, because diversity confers advantage. The objective is not self-sufficiency, it’s collective resilience.

And it’s this mutual advantage that’s at the core of the case for a deeper partnership between Canada and Europe. Europe brings so many things: market power, research depth, advanced manufacturing, the ability and the will to set standards that the world frequently adopts, a defence industrial base that’s being rebuilt at speed.

Canada brings energy at huge scale and in every form that the transition requires. We have one of the world’s largest endowments of critical minerals, deep capabilities in space, AI and quantum, amongst the strongest banking systems and the most expert pension capital.

We have unique Arctic geography and privileged access to both Atlantic and Pacific networks. And where our strengths differ, they complement. Where they overlap, they create scale. We should build on each other’s strengths deliberately, systematically, and rapidly.

We’ve already begun, and I thank this Parliament. We’ve already begun with Ceta, one of the world’s most successful trade agreements. And I thank President von der Leyen and President Costa for our strategic partnership agreement struck last June. We’re developing that and deepening it.

We’ve also begun to take advantage of Canada’s role as the first non-European member of Safe. But we should recognize that the ecosystem we’ve built is not yet equal to the ferocity of the changing climate. And nor is it moving fast enough to match the speed of the upheaval.

Yesterday, President von der Leyen spoke of moving beyond Ceta to an alliance for the future, opening the door to Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member.

Canada welcomes this ambition and I will tell you polling shows that an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties with Europe.

An alliance for the future is a unique, positive approach that we will define together, building on our common strengths and based on our shared values. But let me take this opportunity to say plainly what Canada proposes.

Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments.

We should move towards seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services. We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to work, study, and live where they want on either side of the Atlantic.

Canadian membership of Erasmus Plus would give your students and ours more opportunity to learn at some of the world’s top universities, to broaden their horizon, and to build those lasting ties that will sustain our alliance for the future. Canadian membership of the next generation of Horizon would allow us to pool resources, cooperate on frontier technologies, leverage our world-class research institutes and universities.

Yesterday, President von der Leyen announced, and I quote, ‘a new European corporation on critical raw materials to obtain and stockpile the material needed for electric cars, for chips and batteries, clean tech and defence.’ I’ll observe that Canada has deposits of over 34 critical minerals, and we are among the top producers of the 10 most essential for the energy transition.

Our alliance can help fill Europe’s need for reliable supply, Canada’s desire for advanced processing capabilities, and our common objective to complete value chains in the transition and our defence.

Canada can contribute LNG and hydrogen at large scale to support Europe’s energy security, including by developing and leveraging new port infrastructure in our high north and on our east coast. And Canada in turn can benefit from your leadership in so many clean energy technologies.

We can pool new sovereign compute capacity and build more secure broadband connections between Europe and Asia via our common geography. Canada and Europe can join forces to develop AI safety protocols, coordinate common standards, and strengthen transparency, all while developing applications so that our governments and our companies can serve our citizens better.

Canada and Europe should consider exploring an integrated market for financial services to broaden choice and reduce costs for our citizens, to improve access to capital for our companies while maintaining our world-leading financial resilience.

These are some of the opportunities.

But the fundamental point is that the opportunities that can be created by an alliance for the future are the product of our common values, our compatible systems, our complementary strengths. And deepening and widening our relationship will strengthen our sovereignty, improve affordability and opportunity and security for our citizens, while safeguarding our abilities to live our lives as we choose.

Now I also want to be precise about what I am not proposing.

I’m not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival only with better manners. We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.

It’s these motivations, these fundamental motivations combined with our latent hard power, mean that we can help to create the next just, stable, and prosperous world order. A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies, an alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for – freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability.

An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens and our citizens to do, for themselves. An alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices, an alliance open enough that others can join, an alliance principled enough that our strength reinforces international law rather than seeks to replace it.

And to conclude, in my country it’s often said that Canada became a nation during that battle of Vimy Ridge. And certainly, the thousands of Canadians who didn’t return from that battle sacrificed their lives for something much bigger than themselves.

One who did come home stopped first to pick up some acorns. And today, the same Vimy Oaks grow in Canada as in France. Living proof that what we cultivate together can survive the darkest winter to thrive again.

So let us now deepen those roots, widen this canopy, and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground every single day. Thank you very much.

content_blocks.text: Today, it is hard to reconcile sovereignty and openness. Economic integration is now being weaponized. Tariffs being used to exert pressure. Financial mechanisms have been used for coercion. Supply chains constitute weak points to be exploited.

stories.title: Michigan CEO apologizes for 'Lake America' post shared before travelling to Halifax
stories.summary: "I made a mistake. I own that mistake, and I am committed to learning from it," said Jane Smith in a statement.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
A Michigan credit union CEO has apologized following pushback online for a social media post showing her and her family wearing “Lake America” sweatshirts and stating that she is “not sure” Canada would like them. The family was preparing to embark on a trip to Halifax.

Jane Smith, head of the Family First Credit Union in Saginaw, Michigan has since explained that the photo in the post, which was shared on several social media platforms, was generated using ChatGPT.

And she has apologized for it. In a statement to ABC12 , an ABC news affiliate in Michigan, Smith said the image was in poor taste, an attempt at humour using AI gone wrong.

“Last week, when traveling with my family we decided to take a photo in the Detroit airport and used ChatGPT to generate an image to show what we would look like if we were all wearing ‘Lake America’ sweatshirts,” she said in the statement.

She admitted to sharing the AI-generated image on her personal Facebook page and stated “it was insensitive, distasteful, and in poor judgment. It should never should have been created or shared. Though the image did not depict a real event, I understand that the image was hurtful and offensive.”

Taking further accountability for the stunt, she confessed, “I made a mistake. I own that mistake, and I am committed to learning from it.”

The credit union board issued its own statement to ABC12, indicating its support for Canada and saying that despite the post being a personal one, it is reviewing appropriate steps for Smith.

“Although the post involved Ms. Smith in her personal capacity in connection with a family vacation, the post is unacceptable. … We support and respect our Canadian neighbors, and we completely disavow Ms. Smith’s actions, which were undertaken without the authorization or knowledge of the Credit Union.”

Smith’s Facebook post was reposted by news website, Breaking News Canada . That Facebook post stated that the group of Americans “apparently travelled to Halifax” wearing the matching Lake America sweatshirts. It went on to state that the post “has sparked backlash online from Canadians calling the stunt disrespectful.”

BNC also reposted Smith’s post on Instagram with the same commentary.

And indeed, the backlash has been evident.

Instagram user, Chelsea Przygodzka wrote in response: “Imagine coming to another country to visit and shop and dine at our businesses while actively disrespecting them and expecting great service and kindness 😂 i wonder how many spit burgers and drinks they consumed.”

As previously reported by National Post, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the name of the lake on Aug. 27, which directed the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases to reflect the new name.

Politicians on both sides of the border have condemned the name change, with Ontario Premier Doug Ford erecting a new Lake Ontario sign at a cost of $25,000 , soon after Trump signed the executive order. In the U.S., politicians including former U.S. secretary of state Hillary Clinton and Vermont senator Bernie Sanders have criticized Trump’s actions on social media .

Polling has shown that most Americans are against the name change , with Economist/YouGov research finding 68 per cent of Americans strongly or somewhat disapproved of the move. A poll conducted by Ipsos published a similar result, with 63 per cent opposing Trump’s executive order.

Another Instagram user, Cathy Wolters, took a direct shot at Smith’s post, stating that “American arrogance is a reason why American tourists are disliked. Just another example.” As National Post has reported , polling shows that Canadians are increasingly unhappy with Americans since the trade war began, even seeing them as the “enemy.”

Rachael Marsland pointed out that “Doing this over 9/11 in a city that a welcomed tons of planes on 9/11 is f***ing wild.” The comment is in reference to the terrorist attack in New York City, and how a total of 239 flights were diverted to 17 Canadian airports , with an estimated 33,000 displaced passengers.

A Reddit account, r/AmericansInCanada , posted commentary about Smith’s post from Culture Alberta , an Alberta news website.

The photo spread quickly, wrote Culture Alberta, pointing out the tone of online reaction: “Canadians are tired of the joke … It landed in the middle of a much bigger fight over Trump, tariffs, maps, and how far the United States can push a joke before Canadians stop laughing.”

Trump has consistently made derogatory comments at Canada’s expense , including a vague threat described humorously by Prime Minister Mark Carney that he might get shot at the White House, despite receiving an honorary key from the President.

stories.title: Man sentenced to 12 years for Alberta sex attacks
stories.summary: A judge has sentenced a man to 12 years in prison for a series of sexual assaults on vulnerable women at a rural home near Calgary.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Calgary – A judge has sentenced a man to 12 years in prison for a series of sexual assaults on vulnerable women at a rural home near Calgary.

Richard Robert Mantha, 62, was convicted of six offences, including drugging one of his victims, that happened between 2019 and 2023.

He was also found guilty of uttering threats against a fourth woman.

Court heard most of the victims worked in the sex trade.

Justice Judith Shriar says Manta showed “callous disrespect” by laughing as one terrified victim fled his rural property, fearing for her life.

The judge gave Mantha credit of five years and three months for time he has already served in custody, meaning he has a little less than seven years left to serve.

The Crown had asked for 10 to 13 years in prison, while the defence recommended between five and seven years.

The trial, which started in January 2024, faced several lengthy delays because Mantha fired previous lawyers and had a stroke.

One woman told court she’ll never forget what Mantha did to her.

Aimee Ert, who successfully requested the court lift a publication ban on her name, testified she was drugged, choked and sexually assaulted after she agreed to go with Mantha to his acreage. She was able to escape, and ran from the property partially clothed.

She told the sentencing hearing last month that she forgives Mantha and hopes he gets the help he needs.

“I also am forgiving myself for allowing him to hurt me. However, I will never forget what he did to me. I have struggled on a daily basis to get through everything that I have experienced in the past,” she said.

Western University is recognizing one of Canada’s most distinguished community leaders by conferring an honorary degree duringfall convocation.

Mitch Frazer, LLB’99, a respected lawyer, educator and philanthropist, will be celebrated Oct. 21 during the ceremony at Canada Life Placein downtown London, Ont.Frazer, who graduated from Western’s Faculty of Law, will address graduates before they receive their degrees.

Mitch Frazer

Frazer has made significant contributions to law and higher education. He is the current chancellor of Ontario Tech University and a managing partner of Mintz LLP. In 2019, he was named one of the 25 most influential lawyers in Canada by Canadian Lawyer magazine. His two published books draw on his expertise in Canadian pension law.

Frazer co-founded theNational Institute on Ageingat Toronto Metropolitan University and is a past chair of that university’s board of governors.He is a former adjunct professor at theUniversity of Toronto Faculty of Law, and a former chair of the Toronto French School Board of Directors, where he remains a member.

His longstanding philanthropy has supported a range of educational and health-related organizations and causes.He currently serves as chair of the North York General HospitalBoard of Governors.

An avid runner, Frazer has completed all sevenAbbott World Marathon Majors, a prestigious series of the world’s leading marathons: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York City, Sydney and Cape Town, which will be added in 2027.

Frazer has received numerous awards and honours including the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal, the King Charles III Coronation Medal, the Ontario Bar Association Award of Excellence in Pension and Benefits Law and the CCAE Friend of Education Award. He has also been appointed to the Order of Ontario.

Frazer will receive an honorary doctor of laws at Western’s convocation ceremony on Oct. 21.

stories.title: Fanshawe students navigate crowded study spaces
stories.summary: With a new school year starting, Fanshawe College students are settling into classes and looking for places to...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
With a new school year starting, Fanshawe College students are settling into classes and looking for places to study. With the hallways, common areas and the library always being packed, it can be hard for students to focus, especially during busy times.

We spoke with students Miguel Mendoza, Noralhudn Abdulrahman, Anna Jimenez from student services, and Front Desk Administrator Fanshawe Student Union (FSU), Moria Jasquez about whether they think Fanshawe has enough spaces, and if there’s any plans on building more.

“..If I’m not focussed, I’m not putting in my 100 per cent effort..” said Miguel Mendoza.

Photo by: Torey Joseph Legarrie, Miguel Mendoza, Electrical Engineering Technology, year 1

The biggest issue with the study spaces that students are talking about is not knowing how to book-out a study space .

The main request students have for Fanshawe College is to post more on how to book-out the spaces. “Maybe posting more about the study rooms, how to book them or doing a little tutorial for students. I think that will help.” said Anna Jimenez, student services.

Moria Jasquez, front desk administrator for FSU, said “… I do know however, that the school has been working to refresh spaces and make it more welcoming for students… Expansion wise, not too sure.. but it is in mind.”

Photo by: Torey Joseph Legarrie, Moria Jasquez, front desk administrator FSU

Students need a space to be able to relax and study. It is a crucial part in school so that students are able to have good mental-health, and finish work on time.

Fanshawe students can walk around for several minutes to only find a seating area that has crowds of loud students.

Noralhudn Abdulrahman said, “[It is] so hard. There’s always people in it, so it’s so hard to find a space here.”

Photo by: Torey Joseph Legarrie, Noralhudn Abdulrahman, practical nursing, year 1

For students who are having trouble finding a suitable place to study, checking different areas of campus and asking staff about avaliable spaces can provide additional options. “Specifically within the student centre.. we do have a lot of lounges.” said Moria Jasquez.

With classes now in session, access to study space remains part of the everyday student experience at Fanshawe College.

Here is my interview with Miguel Mendoza, Noralhudn Abdulrahman, Anna Jimenez, and Moria Jasquez:

stories.title: Gun-toting U.S. man flees Canadian border agents, leads RCMP on high-speed chase
stories.summary: An armed U.S. man was arrested and charged by Manitoba RCMP after a high speed chase that started at the Canadian border.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Manitoba Mounties were forced to use their vehicles to end a high-speed chase with a pickup truck driven by an armed U.S. man who allegedly fled from border agents on his way into Canada on Saturday evening.

The 44-year-old from North Dakota is in custody, police said Wednesday , and faces a raft of charges from an incident that prompted a response from multiple RCMP detachments.

Around 6:30 p.m., Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) notified police that a man who’d arrived at the Emerson port of entry in southern Manitoba via North Dakota “fled at a high rate of speed” after agents directed him to secondary screening.

Two RCMP detachments and its Integrated Border Enforcement Team (Ibet) were dispatched to intercept the vehicles on Highway 75, the most direct route to Winnipeg about 110 kilometres north.

Officers from nearby Morris, about 44 kilometres north of the crossing, were unable to stop him, and Mounties from St-Pierre-Jolys also watched as the truck’s driver allegedly “manoeuvred around” a roadblock they’d set up at the intersection with a provincial road, drove through a ditch and nearly hit an officer as he kept speeding north toward Winnipeg.

The pursuit continued until officers, based on photos, appeared to box him in using two to three RCMP cruisers, one of which suffered damage to its front end. No officers were injured.

About 40 minutes after the chase began, the man “was safely removed from the vehicle and arrested.”

Inside the truck, police found and seized a loaded handgun on the front passenger seat and different types of ammunition

“This was a dangerous situation involving an armed male fleeing the port of entry and travelling at high speeds toward Winnipeg,” Manitoba East District Commander Supt. Chris Hastie said in a press release, thanking the officers’ coordinated effort to bring it to an end.

“We are now working closely with Cbsa, law enforcement in the United States and our colleagues within RCMP Federal Policing to determine why the male fled the border.”

The man’s driving-related charges include dangerous operation of a conveyance, flight from a peace officer, and assault on a peace officer with a weapon. stories.title: B.C. Conservative leader vows to stay as allegations emerge party funds were used to spy on critics
stories.summary: The party is prepared to fight if B.C. Premier Eby calls snap election, Kerry-Lynne Findlay says
stories.author: Andrea Woo, Mike Hager
stories.content:
BC Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay is vowing to lead her fractured party into a potential snap election amid mounting speculation that Premier David Eby could soon send British Columbians to the polls.

Addressing the Union of BC Municipalities convention in Vancouver on Thursday, Ms. Findlay made clear she has no intention of stepping aside, even as fresh allegations surfaced that party funds were used to hire a private investigator to spy on potential critics both inside and outside of her caucus.

“I’m not going anywhere,” Ms. Findlay told the gathering of local government and First Nations leaders.

Her address followed a remarkable month of upheaval for an opposition that came within three seats of forming government in 2024. Leaked recordings have fuelled allegations of misconduct, nine MLAs have quit the Conservative caucus in the past month and police have interviewed some of them over claims of illegal inducements .

Meanwhile, Ms. Findlay is campaigning to secure a seat in the legislature through a Sept. 26 by-election in the riding of Abbotsford-Mission, while preparing for the possibility that Mr. Eby could take advantage of the Conservatives’ weakened state by calling an election two years early.

On Wednesday, Conservative Party of BC president Mauro Francis informed members by e-mail that former executive director Elaine Allan had allegedly hired a private investigator to “look into your activities” as part of a push to unmask the owner of the “Findlay Files” account on the social-media platform X, three of the recipients confirmed to The Globe and Mail on Thursday.

Sitting Conservative MLA Claire Rattée also confirmed news of the notification publicly, saying she was “deeply troubled” by the allegation.

Ms. Allan was hired as executive director in early August and dismissed by the board the same month. Neither Ms. Allan nor Bruce Hallsor, a lawyer hired by the party to investigate what happened, responded to The Globe’s requests for comment on Thursday.

The Globe is not naming the three e-mail recipients because they said they could not discuss the matter publicly.

Ms. Findlay denied any knowledge of claims that a private investigator had been hired to surveil her critics, including former and sitting Conservative MLAs, an NDP staffer and a journalist. She said her party is looking into the matter.

“This allegation just came forward yesterday,” Ms. Findlay told reporters on Thursday. “I have no details.”

In her prepared remarks to the municipal leaders convention, Ms. Findlay sought to steer attention away from party turmoil and back toward what she called the basics of government, attacking the NDP’s record on the economy, public safety and forestry.

“We all know the routine: big announcement, big promises, rap songs, plaid shirts and then crickets,” Ms. Findlay said, taking a jab at Mr. Eby’s choice of attire at a recent news conference.

She said her party, if elected, would scrap the province’s planned PST expansion, provide municipalities with more stable infrastructure funding and give local governments more say in provincial decisions.

But questions about the party’s internal problems continued in a media scrum that followed her address. After questions about the private investigator allegations, Ms. Findlay was asked for comment on reports that some current Conservative members had asked her to resign as recently as the day before.

“No, I can’t,” Ms. Findlay responded. “That’s up to them to tell you.”

Another reporter asked whether her leadership style was to blame for the recent exodus of MLAs.

“I don’t think it’s my leadership style per se, but of course I take responsibility,” said Ms. Findlay, who was flanked by caucus members.

“There have been adjustments. There have been changes. And what is really important is: Do we have a working team that’s cohesive? And here we are. I’m proud of them all, and we are moving forward together.”

The media availability, scheduled for 20 minutes, was cut off after eight minutes.

Speculation about an early election reached new heights during the week-long convention. On Wednesday, Mr. Eby confirmed that he had lined up interim chief of staff Cheryl Oates as the NDP’s provincial campaign director and that he has told both Elections BC and his caucus to be election-ready.

Elections BC confirmed that it is preparing for an early vote by inquiring about electoral office and voting place availability, restocking supplies and recruiting officials.

“Based on the current landscape in B.C., timelines for procuring election materials in the face of global supply chain challenges and recent public commentary and speculation, we have determined we need to assume an increased readiness state,” the agency said in a statement provided by communications director Colleen Hildebrandt.

Aileen Machell, a communications and strategy consultant and former deputy chief of staff to Mr. Eby, told The Globe that the NDP government is likely weighing the need for stability amid the trade war against more partisan considerations, including its own election readiness and the divisions within the opposition.

Ms. Rattée said in a Substack post published Wednesday that Ms. Findlay had chosen not to attend caucus meetings she herself had called and was not responding to multiple requests for a phone call.

A shifting political landscape could also benefit Mr. Eby, whose approval rating had fallen in recent months, in part over concerns about the province’s finances.

An Angus Reid Institute poll released Wednesday put the Premier’s approval at 41 per cent, up from 31 per cent in June, with the organization pointing to his response to U.S. President Donald Trump as a possible factor in the rebound.

Union of BC Municipalities president Cori Ramsay expressed concern over the potential impact that a snap provincial election could have on the province’s municipal elections, scheduled for Oct. 17.

“Local elections should provide space for discussions for local priorities without being overshadowed by a concurrent provincial campaign,” Ms. Ramsay said Thursday. “UBCM’s concern is fundamentally about protecting the integrity and effectiveness of local democracy.”

stories.title: Explainer: How the European Union works and how it’s changing
stories.summary: Ottawa — The European Union is a complex assembly of countries that is taking on an increasingly important role for the world and for Canadian interests.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 1:30 pm.

Last Updated September 17, 2026 1:43 pm.

Ottawa — The European Union is a complex assembly of countries that is taking on an increasingly important role for the world and for Canadian interests.

Here’s a look at what the EU is and how it works.

Where did it come from?

In the wake of two devastating world wars, some of the continent’s leaders banded together with the idea that trade could not only boost economic growth but make future wars less likely.

France and Germany have always been at the heart of the EU project. They exercise huge influence over its operations, though their governments don’t always agree with EU policies.

In 1952, France and West Germany joined Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands in launching a project to pool coal and steel resources.

That resource pool was the seed from which the European Union grew over the decades, bringing in more member countries and expanding its influence. The EU has become a global leader in regulation and has been praised for enabling the flow of trade — while its critics accuse it of over-regulation.

The bloc has created deeper integration across the continent’s vast regions, with a single border encompassing almost all of Europe outside Ireland and Cyprus. Some EU countries abstain from the euro and use their own currency.

The United Kingdom left the EU in 2020. Other countries, including Ukraine, Serbia and Turkey, have been in talks for years on joining the bloc. Norway and Switzerland have never been EU members but co-ordinate with the EU on certain policies. Iceland voted against EU membership last month.

How is the EU structured?

The EU operates through a complex system based on three institutions. The European Commission, which proposes policy, is led by its president, Ursula von der Leyen. It meets in the Berlaymont Building in Brussels — sometimes referred to as the “Berlaymonster.”

The Parliament consults elected representative from member states. It holds plenaries in Strasbourg, France, in a parliamentary building nicknamed after the popular cheese Caprice des Dieux.

The European Council manages political issues, such as negotiation with and between EU members. Its building in Brussels is often dubbed the “space egg.”

University of Guelph political scientist Edward Koning said many European voters are confused by the system that governs them.

“One of the main struggles that the European Union has had since its inception is to communicate with its citizens,” he said. “The institutional structure of the EU is quite complex.”

What strengths and drawbacks does the EU have?

To its supporters, the EU is the defender of peace and prosperity on a continent that suffered centuries of war and lost global supremacy as its colonies regained their sovereignty.

EU enthusiasts argue the bloc has brought up living standards through a common labour market, harmonized regulations, equalization payments and shared fiscal policy. They argue the EU has made poorer countries more prosperous and stable, while driving down the costs richer countries cover for defence and state institutions.

They say the EU’s market of 450 million consumers has helped it protect itself from American and Chinese coercion, and that working together is the only way to address climate change and Russian threats.

Critics say the bloc has stripped countries of autonomy and made it easier for refugee claimants to reach countries that sit far from the Mediterranean or Middle East.

The 2009 eurozone crisis caused huge tensions within the bloc. Countries like Greece and Ireland saw themselves hit hard by policies imposed by Brussels, while countries like Germany and the Netherlands felt they were being forced to pay for other nations’ wasteful spending.

While the EU is good at setting regulations, critics say it makes business slow and costly. The commission has non-elected officials who, like cabinet ministers, are appointed to portfolios touching on things like social media regulation and fisheries.

How has U.S. President Donald Trump changed the EU’s role?

The EU, which has had a foreign service for decades, has to balance the bloc’s interests with those of member states. The EU signed a trade deal with Canada and deals with trade irritants, but it leaves it to individual countries to promote their own trade.

Koning said foreign policy is “one of the more sensitive areas” for the EU, as it typically seeks unanimity across its 27 member countries.

Trump has targeted Europe by threatening sanctions and calling for the annexation of Denmark’s partly autonomous territory of Greenland. He has threatened to leave the Nato alliance just as Russia ramps up hybrid attacks on the bloc over its support for Ukraine.

This has led the EU to play a larger role in negotiating trade access by threatening retaliatory tariffs, and to co-ordinate autonomous production of weapons and defence systems.

The EU has an Anti-Coercion Instrument — often dubbed “the bazooka” — which has never been used but which some have threatened to deploy against Washington. If fully enacted, it would drastically restrict trade access, instantly suspend intellectual property rights and bar access to government contracts.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has spent the past year trying to build some form of bridge between the EU and a Pacific Rim trade bloc called Cptpp, so that middle powers can better resist economic coercion from the U.S. and China.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 17, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: London airport unveils biggest-ever winter sun schedule
stories.summary: Expanded seasonal service gives London travellers more ways to get away this winter.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Expanded seasonal service gives London travellers more ways to get away this winter.

WestJet Flight 557 to Winnipeg rolls down the runway past the terminal at London International Airport on Friday, July 17, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

The London International Airport has released its winter flight schedule, calling it the most extensive lineup of warm-weather destinations in its history.

On Wednesday, the airport announced its winter schedule in partnership with Porter Airlines, Air Transat, WestJet and Sunwing Vacations. Airport officials said the expanded schedule gives Southwestern Ontario travellers more choice and flexibility than ever before to fly direct from London to destinations in Mexico, the Caribbean and the United States.

Nine flights weekly to Cancun, Mexico

Three flights weekly to Orlando, Fla.

Four flights weekly to Fort Lauderdale, Fla.

Three flights weekly to Montego Bay, Jamaica

Two flights weekly to Punta Cana, Dominican Republic

Weekly service to Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic

Airport officials said the addition of more “sun service” strengthens its role as a key transportation gateway for Southwestern Ontario.

“We know travellers value convenience and choice,” airport chief executive officer Scott McFadzean wrote in a press release. “By continuing to expand our sun flight offerings, we’re helping more people start their vacations closer to home while supporting the continued growth of air service in our community.”

Last month, the airport announced Porter Airlines would launch service in London for the first time.

Starting in November, Porter will begin four nonstop seasonal routes to destinations in the United States, Jamaica and Mexico. The airline has also committed to building a domestic network out of London by summer 2027.

stories.title: Crews rescue ‘completely exhausted’ horse from mud pit in Saskatchewan
stories.summary: An 'exhausted' horse was saved after it spent several hours trapped in a mud pit in Melfort, Sask., the city's fire department said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A horse was rescued in Saskatchewan after being stuck in a pit for several hours, the Melfort Fire Department (MFD) said.

The animal was stuck in a mud pit in Melfort, Sask., according to a social media post from the local fire department. Crews responded to reports of the stuck horse around 7:34 a.m. Wednesday.

“It is believed that the horse had been there for several hours throughout the night, and was completely exhausted,” the fire department’s post said.

An attempt to lift the animal using a sling and loader failed after the horse panicked and slipped out of it, MFD continued.

Crews then dug a gradual slope to help guide and pull the horse out of the pit. This attempt worked, and the horse was freed from the mud, the fire department said.

stories.title: Police find one-year-old in Montreal homeless encampment
stories.summary: Montreal police say an investigation is underway after officers located a woman and a one-year-old child in a homeless encampment in the city’s east end.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal police say an investigation is underway after officers located a woman and a one-year-old child in a homeless encampment in the city’s east end.

Police say they received a call about the woman and a child on Sept. 11 in the eastern Montreal borough of Mercier—Hochelaga-Maisonneuve.

Police spokesperson Jean-Pierre Brabant says officers located the woman and child after conducting a search and noticed what they described as concerning elements.

Brabant says police are collaborating with Quebec’s youth protection agency on the investigation.

He also says the infant’s health and safety were not at risk.

Brabant could not say if the woman was under investigation.

In a social media post published last night, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada called the situation “heartbreaking” and a “wake-up call.”

Martinez Ferrada said the city could no longer wait for the Quebec government to address what she called a provincewide issue and said the city would take action on the Notre-Dame site.

She also thanked residents who intervened to help the child, as well as first responders and police.

stories.title: 10/3 podcast: Byelection fallout and Alberta’s looming referendum
stories.summary: Alberta politics are ramping up, with a surprising byelection result in Calgary, and 10-question referendum about a month away.
stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
Alberta politics are ramping up as we head into the fall, with a surprising byelection result in Calgary, and 10-question referendum about a month away.

The NDP seized a riding that had been held by the UCP, with many political watchers tying the vote to discontent over a referendum seen as a sop to a separatist faction in the governing party.

Calgary Herald columnist Don Braid joins host Dave Breakenridge to discuss the recent byelection, the looming referendum and what the fallout could be for the premier.

stories.title: Top pick Gavin McKenna lines up with John Tavares and William Nylander at Leafs’ camp
stories.summary: McKenna, the 18-year-old from Whitehorse had a few flashy moments, including the setup of a Tavares goal in the slot.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Jim Hiller elected to keep fans and media guessing.

The Toronto Maple Leafs head coach declined to publicly divulge where No. 1 overall pick Gavin McKenna would slot in at his first training camp practice.

The curtain was lifted about thirty minutes into Thursday’s session.

McKenna skated on a line with John Tavares and William Nylander with the team’s NHL group.

Other lines included Matthew Knies with Auston Matthews and Jack Roslovic, Easton Cowan with Nick Paul and Colton Sissons, and a line of Dakota Joshua, Teddy Blueger and Brandon Duhaime. Steven Lorentz was the odd man out early on.

The 18-year-old from Whitehorse had a few flashy moments, including the setup of a Tavares goal in the slot and a battle drill against the big-bodied forward Knies where the youngster ended up with just one glove — and the puck behind goaltender Anthony Stolarz.

McKenna is slated to live with Tavares at his family home for his first professional season as he gets acclimated to the NHL as a rookie.

Toronto finished last in the Atlantic Division in 2025-26 before beating May’s lottery odds for the right to pick McKenna, who’s living with Tavares and his family this season, with the top selection in June.

stories.title: Snowbird replacements ‘extremely manoeuverable, powerful,’ Rcaf commander says
stories.summary: The Royal Canadian Air Force is welcoming the first two of its new Siskin II trainer aircraft, the same aircraft that will replace the old Tutor jets flown by the Snowbirds aerial demonstration team.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The turboprop planes will soon be headed to 15 Wing Moose Jaw, where the air force eventually will station 19 of them to serve as its main training fleet.

Acquiring the Siskin II, also known as the Pilatus PC-21, is part of the Rcaf’s plan to modernize its fleets and overhaul its training.

Rcaf Commander Lt.-Gen. Jamie Speiser-Blanchet said the modern aircraft are well suited both to aerial acrobatics and to preparing pilots for the more advanced aircraft the air force is bringing online.

“It has an advanced cockpit and capabilities and the design is just a very contemporary one that is used by other allies as well. We’re very excited that we’re able to bring this on board,” she said.

The commander made the comments just after one of the new planes buzzed overhead in a ceremonial first flypast at the airport in Gatineau, Que.

Speiser-Blanchet said these are “excellent” stunt planes that shouldn’t be underestimated — even though some have questioned whether a propeller aircraft is a suitable replacement for jets.

“It is extremely manoeuverable and capable, and powerful, actually. More so than perhaps people’s understanding of other propeller aircraft from the past,” she said.

While the Siskin II has a slower top speed than the CT-114 Tutor and is not as loud as a jet, Speiser-Blanchet said “it’s not a quiet aircraft” and it will “really wow Canadians” once the shows are up and running.

The federal government announced this spring it would replace the roughly 60-year-old Tutor jets, which have encountered various problems with upgrades meant to extend their lifespans out to 2030. Costs, timelines and the growing scarcity of replacement parts threw a wrench into plans to keep them in the air longer.

Speiser-Blanchet said that because so many Canadian pilots will be training on this aircraft, the air force will have a much larger pool of potential candidates for the Snowbirds. Having the multi-purpose aircraft based out of Moose Jaw will also make servicing and support easier to manage, she said.

The Rcaf has never before used a Pilatus-built aircraft, although the previous trainers were effectively modified versions of the Pilatus PC-9.

Ioannis Papachristofilou, deputy CEO of Pilatus in Switzerland, said the aircraft are advanced, high-performance machines that use Pratt and Whitney’s powerful PT6A-68B turboprop engine, which is made in Canada.

“This aircraft has an embedded mission-simulation suite, which allows you to simulate, for example, sensors like radar,” he said, adding the technology allows pilots to train faster on fighter jets in later phases of training.

The fleet of Siskins will work alongside other types of trainers under the new Future Aircrew Training program, which covers 71 training aircraft split up across five fleets.

SkyAlyne, a partnership between CAE and KF Aerospace, won a contract in 2024 for the 25-year, $11-billion training program, referred to within the air force as FAcT. It will replace the commercial pilot training aspects of the Rcaf program.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 17, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Hockey jersey, selfies and applause: Carney mobbed by fans at EU speech as one member chanted 'USA'
stories.summary: European politicians have thrown their support behind Mark Carney after he gave an address in the European Parliament on Thursday morning.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
The PM's address was delayed by around ten minutes after dozens of European lawmakers huddled around to shake his hand

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s highly anticipated address to the European Parliament on Thursday was frequently interrupted by applause from the lawmakers in the room, and ended to a hearty standing ovation followed by expressions of support on social media from politicians across Europe.

Carney, who has welcomed the European Union’s invitation to become its first-ever “associate member,” pitched Canada as a natural ally for the bloc of 27 European countries in the face of increasing trade volatility by U.S. President Donald Trump .

And the Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) appear to have thrown their support behind him following the speech in the European Parliament’s hemicycle in Strasbourg, France, ON Thursday morning.

Carney’s popularity with European lawmakers became evident before his speech even began, with the MEPs already present in the hemicycle breaking into applause as the PM walked in.

In fact, Carney’s address to the European Parliament was delayed by roughly ten minutes as dozens of European lawmakers huddled around to shake his hand, exchange some words and, occasionally, take a selfie.

Video footage from the minutes before his address showed Carney surrounded by photographers as he made his way around the room and interacted with the other politicians.

Canada's Carney arrives in European Parliament Earlier, Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU's 'associate member' pic.twitter.com/6qHumXhYoG — RT (@RT_com) September 17, 2026

Among the MEPs showing their support for Carney was Terry Reintke, a German politician and co-president of the Greens–European Free Alliance Group.

She wore a Sidney Crosby Team Canada jersey and was all smiles as she posed for a picture with Carney before he spoke, while MEPs cheered in the background.

Sharing a picture of them on social media shortly after, Reintke wrote: “Welcome bienvenue Canada,” accompanied by emojis depicting the Canada flag, the European flag and a red heart.

View this post on Instagram

As Carney took the stand, Siegbert Droese — one of the few MEPs from the populist right-wing Europe of Sovereign Nations Group attending the speech — chanted “USA! USA!” earning himself groans from other lawmakers and a laugh from the prime minister.

Someone in the European Parliament yells “USA! USA!” as Canada’s PM Mark Carney is about to begin his speech. Carney laughs. pic.twitter.com/noOpL597ed — Clash Report (@clashreport) September 17, 2026

Though members of the most right-wing political groups in the room appeared to remain silent for the rest of Carney’s speech, the PM was frequently interrupted by applause from other MEPs in the room.

In a press conference after his speech, Carney argued that the U.S. would benefit from Canada deepening its ties to Europe, saying: “It will make Europe stronger. It will make Canada stronger. It will make… Canada a better partner with the United States.”

Concluding his speech with a symbolic reference to the Vimy oaks that grow in both Canada and France, Carney said: “Let us now deepen these roots, widen this canopy, and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground. Every single day.”

His address ended to a hearty standing ovation, hoots and hollers from nearly all MEPs present. The applause lasted over a minute, only dying down when Carney left the hemicycle.

Carney’s speech ends with a long round of applause https://t.co/gdWv0USNOr pic.twitter.com/aWMEVKSPEd — RT Intl (@RT_on_X) September 17, 2026

Reintke is not the only European politician who welcomed Carney to the hemicycle with a social media post.

The Prime Minister of Spain, Pedro Sánchez, showed his support for Canada becoming an associate member of the EU shortly after the PM’s speech in Strasbourg wrapped up.

And the Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) appear to have thrown their support behind him following the speech in the European Parliament’s hemicycle in Strasbourg, France, ON Thursday morning.
Carney’s popularity with European lawmakers became evident before his speech even began, with the MEPs already present in the hemicycle breaking into applause as the PM walked in.

In fact, Carney’s address to the European Parliament was delayed by roughly ten minutes as dozens of European lawmakers huddled around to shake his hand, exchange some words and, occasionally, take a selfie.
Video footage from the minutes before his address showed Carney surrounded by photographers as he made his way around the room and interacted with the other politicians.

Among the MEPs showing their support for Carney was Terry Reintke, a German politician and co-president of the Greens–European Free Alliance Group.
She wore a Sidney Crosby Team Canada jersey and was all smiles as she posed for a picture with Carney before he spoke, while MEPs cheered in the background.
Sharing a picture of them on social media shortly after, Reintke wrote: “Welcome bienvenue Canada,” accompanied by emojis depicting the Canada flag, the European flag and a red heart.

As Carney took the stand, Siegbert Droese — one of the few MEPs from the populist right-wing Europe of Sovereign Nations Group attending the speech — chanted “USA! USA!” earning himself groans from other lawmakers and a laugh from the prime minister.

Someone in the European Parliament yells “USA! USA!” as Canada’s PM Mark Carney is about to begin his speech. Carney laughs. pic.twitter.com/noOpL597ed — Clash Report (@clashreport) September 17, 2026

stories.title: Cash stolen from wedding guests at North Middlesex event
stories.summary: Investigators allege two unknown males entered the private event on Sept. 12 and stole several items, including cash contained in purses and bags.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Middlesex County OPP are asking for the public’s help as they investigate a theft that happened during a wedding in North Middlesex.

Police say officers were called to a property on Argyle Street on Sept. 14 after receiving a report that items had been stolen from a wedding held two days earlier.

Investigators allege two unknown males entered the private event on Sept. 12 and stole several items, including cash contained in purses and bags.

The first suspect is described as a white male between 15 and 20 years old, with a slim build and standing between five-foot-nine and six feet tall. Police said he has short light brown hair and was wearing a white tank top and possibly grey jogging pants.

The second suspect is also described as a white male between 15 and 20 years old, with a slim build and standing between five-foot-nine and six feet tall. According to police, he has dark hair and was wearing a black T-shirt and a backward ball cap.

Police have not announced any arrests and say the investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact Middlesex County OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can also be submitted through Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (Tips), where callers May be eligible for a cash reward of up to $2,000.

stories.title: Alberta man gets 12-year sentence for sexual assaults on vulnerable women
stories.summary: Richard Robert Mantha was convicted of six offences, including drugging one of his victims, that happened between 2019 and 2023
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
A judge sentenced a man to 12 years in prison Thursday for sexually assaulting three vulnerable women at a rural home near Calgary.

Richard Robert Mantha, 62, was convicted of six offences, including drugging one of his victims, that happened between 2019 and 2023. He was also found guilty of uttering threats against a fourth woman.

Court heard most of the victims worked in the sex trade.

Provincial court Justice Judith Shriar said Mantha showed disrespect by laughing as one of the women fled the property partially clothed, fearing for her life.

“She used all her strength to push him off and ran out yelling and crying, pants partly down with no shoes on. She recalled him laughing. She did not know where she was or where she was heading,” the judge said in her sentencing decision.

Shriar said the victim impact statement from that woman, Aimee Ert, was one of the most moving she has heard. The court earlier granted a request from Ert to lift a publication ban on her name.

“Mr. Mantha’s laughing at the terrified, half-dressed Miss Ert as she ran away is aggravating, demonstrating a callous indifference to her condition and a high degree of moral culpability,” said the judge.

Shriar gave Mantha credit of five years and three months for time he has already served in custody, meaning he has a little less than seven years left to serve.

The Crown had asked for 10 to 13 years in prison, while the defence recommended between five and seven years.

The trial, which started in January 2024, faced several lengthy delays because Mantha fired previous lawyers and had a stroke.

Ert told reporters outside of court that she’s feeling some closure with the sentence.

“Anybody that can actively harm someone in the ways that he did will get what they deserve. He’s a very little man, and I can’t even say a man,” she said.

“I couldn’t help but look at him and just pity that ... terrible person that will suffer and is suffering because of his own actions.”

Prosecutor Dominique Mathurin said it’s a relief the case is over.

“The road to today has been long. We are so grateful to each of the victims for coming forward and giving their testimony, which takes immense bravery and without whom a conviction would not have been possible.”

stories.title: Report: Raptors, Leonard nearing agreement on contract extension
stories.summary: Leonard is eligible to sign a two-year deal for a maximum of $126.1 million that would take him through the 2028-29 season.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
Kawhi Leonard might be in Toronto for longer than one season this time.

The Raptors and Leonard are nearing agreement on a contract extension, NBA insider Jake Fischer reported on Thursday .

Leonard is eligible to sign a two-year deal for a maximum of $126.1 million that would take him through the 2028-29 season.

He is under contract this season for $50.3 million, the last of a three-year deal signed with the Los Angeles Clippers.

The 35-year-old wing is coming off a season where he averaged a career-high 27.9 points and posted a 62.9 per cent true shooting mark for the Clippers to finish seventh in MVP voting.

Leonard arrived back in Toronto after a long-agreed-upon trade with the Clippers was made official on Monday. The Raptors sent Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two unprotected first-round picks, one first-round pick swap and two second-round picks back to the Clippers in the deal.

Toronto put the proposed trade on hold in July pending the outcome of the NBA’s salary-cap circumvention investigation into the Clippers.

Sportsnet’s Blake Murphy reported that Leonard is waiving his entire 15 per cent trade kicker. The Raptors will still be hard-capped at the first apron.

stories.title: Convoy leader Tamara Lich denied permission to travel internationally
stories.summary: Lich was found guilty of mischief last October for her role in the mass protest and was sentenced to 12 months of house arrest
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
An Ontario judge says Tamara Lich, one of the key organizers of the 2022 “Freedom Convoy” protest in Ottawa, will not be allowed to travel abroad.

Last October, Lich was found guilty of mischief for her role in the mass protest which blockaded downtown Ottawa around Parliament Hill for nearly a month.

She was sentenced to 12 months of house arrest.

In July, Lich applied to the court for permission to travel internationally, including to participate in a cruise for her job at Rebel News.

Ontario Court Justice Heather Perkins-McVey said Lich has abided by the conditions of her sentence but the material circumstances of her situation haven’t changed.

Perkins-McVey says allowing international travel would diminish the punitive and deterrent effects of her sentence.

stories.title: Cost of Canada Child Benefit program jumped sharply during post-COVID inflation, PBO says
stories.summary: Cost of administering program rose 16% to $29.2-billion between the 2022-23 and 2024-25 benefit years
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Ottawa’s fiscal watchdog says a surge in inflation a few years back drove a substantial jump in the cost of delivering the Canada Child Benefit after the pandemic.

The Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer says the cost of delivering the federal payment to families increased $4.2-billion between the 2022-23 and 2024-25 benefit years.

That 16-per-cent increase brought the total cost up to $29.2-billion in 2024-25.

The budget office says the increase over those two years outpaced the higher costs during the COVID-19 pandemic, when the benefit was given temporary boosts to help families cope with economic uncertainty.

The Canada Child Benefit is indexed annually to inflation, which hit 8.1 per cent in 2022 and accounted for the bulk of the cost increase over the ensuing years.

The report says the rapid pace of immigration also increased the cost of the program because there were more families eligible for the support.

stories.title: Martin McDonagh on being scared of John Malkovich, the CIA and ‘Wild Horse Nine’
stories.summary: Toronto (AP) — Stop me if you've heard this before. Martin McDonagh has unveiled a dark comedy of mischievous wit and melancholy soulfulness, and it's immediately been hailed as one of the best movies of the year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Jake Coyle, The Associated Press,

Posted September 17, 2026 11:23 am.

Last Updated September 17, 2026 11:48 am.

Toronto (AP) — Stop me if you’ve heard this before. Martin McDonagh has unveiled a dark comedy of mischievous wit and melancholy soulfulness, and it’s immediately been hailed as one of the best movies of the year.

Yes, the British-Irish writer-director of “The Banshees of Inisherin,” “In Bruges” and “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” has been here before. But McDonagh’s latest, “Wild Horse Nine,” is also something different and more provocative.

The film, which has played to standing ovations across the Venice , Telluride and Toronto film festivals, stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA officers who have recently laid the groundwork for the 1973 coup in Chile. But they’re now taking a trip to Easter Island, as one says, “to see the heads” — the Moai stone sculptures. Chris (Malkovich) is dying of cancer and increasingly loose-lipped about his colorful CIA past, including a presidential assassination.

Their conversation, as is typical in McDonagh’s brilliant, barbed dialogue, is laced with deeper ruminations on regret and death, with more absurd digressions mixed in. In one memorable scene, Chris traces a connection between democracy, homosexuality and good cheese.

“I wanted those guys to feel like an old married couple in a way,” McDonagh says.

He recently met a reporter for coffee in Toronto to talk about “Wild Horse Nine” and why he’s so eager for the conversation it might generate. Searchlight Pictures releases the film Nov. 6.

AP: You wrote “In Bruges” after a trip to the Belgian city. This came out of a trip to Easter Island. How important is travel to your writing?

McDonagh: Very much. I love to travel. I like traveling alone. It always prompts some kind of thinking. Bruges was just a weekend trip for fun and the town became a character literally while I was there. Fifteen years ago I went to Easter Island with the hope that something similar would happen to the Bruges scenario. It looked like a beautiful backdrop to some kind of story to tell but it took a bunch of iterations of it before it became what you saw.

AP: Do you feel like being removed from regular life frees you?

McDonagh: Maybe things seem much more cinematic. I never had any desire to write something set in London, for instance, and I never have. I don’t see it with fresh eyes. I do like traveling around America. I used to get trains around America a lot. It feels like a CinemaScope window across the West. I feel like finding the place is going to be key to my next project, which I don’t have right now. Part of that is: Where do you want to spend six months of your life? South of France sounds good! And where is cinematic that hasn’t been captured before?

AP: Do you tend to start with two characters talking? Some of your films are centered on odd couples.

McDonagh: The odd couple talking thing, I did three or four versions of that. They were talking fine but there was no purpose or reason for them to be there. But I had always been fascinated with what the CIA did in Chile in the 1970s. When I thought about that, everything fell into place. It wasn’t just two cranky old guys talking.

AP: I’ve never seen a CIA agent character like Malkovich’s character — a guy who just wants to spill all the beans.

McDonagh: I don’t think they’re as classy as John. I think we’re painting way too good a picture of the CIA. He’s erudite. He’s got a sense of humor. He regrets stuff. And I don’t think they do.

AP: He’s ready to be up front about some of the U.S.’s underhanded dealings. Do you feel like it’s a time for frankness about America’s darker side?

McDonagh: Even while we were still editing it, it felt more and more like it was a commentary on the modern day, especially with a lot of the recent stuff that Trump’s been doing. It wasn’t the direct purpose of it, but I kind of liked that it felt that way. The tragic thing is: history keeps repeating itself, and more and more stupidly and less and less secretively. They kept their horrible stuff secret back then. It’s like they don’t care what people think about it anymore. I think that’s a darker place we’re in now. Shame doesn’t come into it.

AP: There’s a moment in the film when Malkovich’s character suggests peaceful protest marches have no effect. What do you think?

McDonagh: Whether or not I agree with it or not is for a later chat. I’m not saying the pacifist version is wrong or doesn’t work at times. But I do think the CIA and KGB and most vicious governments around the world are more happy with polite protest marches.

AP: You had twice before, for “Seven Psychopaths” and your play “A Behanding in Spokane,” tried to work with Malkovich. What drew you to him?

McDonagh: He can be ultra dangerous and you feel scared of him more than most. Maybe Joe Pesci. I was scared the first time I had a Zoom with him. But also his dexterity with comedy. But mostly knowing that in the silent moments you’d see acres of sorrow and regret when he’s seemingly not doing anything — when he’s just looking out of a window or listening to a Dictaphone or smoking a cigarette.

AP: Was it at all purposeful to have Malkovich playing a memoir-writing CIA officer like he did in the Coen brothers’ “Burn After Reading”?

McDonagh: Not at all. In fact, I had kind of forgotten that whole section of that film until I rewatched it a few months ago. I hope that they don’t think I stole the whole memoir-of-a-CIA-guy bit from him. (Laughs) But John’s so good at everything that history is going to repeat itself.

AP: As much acclaim as Malkovich is rightly getting, Rockwell is also great even if his performance is less eye-catching.

McDonagh: It’s not but it’s completely generous. I think it’s still one of his best-ever performances. It’s not as showy as some of the previous things I’ve done with Sam or some of Sam’s other brilliant work. But there aren’t many who could convey the love that’s there without bawling his eyes out. You feel like it’s an equal two-hander at the same time as John’s character will always be the lead.

AP: Do you identify more with either of their characters?

McDonagh: John’s got a lot of me. I like the outrageousness and the danger of where he goes sometimes. In my more sarcastic, anarchistic moments, I find that sort of stuff funny. He’s an awful guy, he’s done awful things. But on top of that, I do feel like he says a lot of funny stuff that I agree with — even if it’s just cheeses. (Laughs) A scene like that, you know you’re being naughty but I think the principle of it is actually sort of loving and weirdly pro-democratic, pro-gay and pro-cheese.

AP: Coming out of the pandemic, you talked about committing to writing a movie every year.

McDonagh: That’s gone away! (Laughs) I realize after a year or two I’m fundamentally lazy. But this feels like a quite short time between.

AP: Well, choosing to make a movie on Easter Island probably doesn’t speed things up.

McDonagh: But it does combine vacation time on an island with making a movie. (Laughs) That’s what I’m going to do next. Tahiti, 1900, two blokes.

Jake Coyle, The Associated Press

content_blocks.html: TORONTO (AP) — Stop me if you’ve heard this before. Martin McDonagh has unveiled a dark comedy of mischievous wit and melancholy soulfulness, and it’s immediately been hailed as one of the best movies of the year.

content_blocks.text: Yes, the British-Irish writer-director of “The Banshees of Inisherin,” “In Bruges” and “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” has been here before. But McDonagh’s latest, “Wild Horse Nine,” is also something different and more provocative.
content_blocks.html: Yes, the British-Irish writer-director of “The Banshees of Inisherin,” “In Bruges” and “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri” has been here before. But McDonagh’s latest, “Wild Horse Nine,” is also something different and more provocative.

content_blocks.text: The film, which has played to standing ovations across the Venice , Telluride and Toronto film festivals, stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as CIA officers who have recently laid the groundwork for the 1973 coup in Chile. But they’re now taking a trip to Easter Island, as one says, “to see the heads” — the Moai stone sculptures. Chris (Malkovich) is dying of cancer and increasingly loose-lipped about his colorful CIA past, including a presidential assassination.

content_blocks.text: AP: You wrote “In Bruges” after a trip to the Belgian city. This came out of a trip to Easter Island. How important is travel to your writing?
content_blocks.html: AP: You wrote “In Bruges” after a trip to the Belgian city. This came out of a trip to Easter Island. How important is travel to your writing?

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: Very much. I love to travel. I like traveling alone. It always prompts some kind of thinking. Bruges was just a weekend trip for fun and the town became a character literally while I was there. Fifteen years ago I went to Easter Island with the hope that something similar would happen to the Bruges scenario. It looked like a beautiful backdrop to some kind of story to tell but it took a bunch of iterations of it before it became what you saw.

content_blocks.text: AP: Do you feel like being removed from regular life frees you?
content_blocks.html: AP: Do you feel like being removed from regular life frees you?

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: Maybe things seem much more cinematic. I never had any desire to write something set in London, for instance, and I never have. I don’t see it with fresh eyes. I do like traveling around America. I used to get trains around America a lot. It feels like a CinemaScope window across the West. I feel like finding the place is going to be key to my next project, which I don’t have right now. Part of that is: Where do you want to spend six months of your life? South of France sounds good! And where is cinematic that hasn’t been captured before?

content_blocks.text: AP: Do you tend to start with two characters talking? Some of your films are centered on odd couples.

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: The odd couple talking thing, I did three or four versions of that. They were talking fine but there was no purpose or reason for them to be there. But I had always been fascinated with what the CIA did in Chile in the 1970s. When I thought about that, everything fell into place. It wasn’t just two cranky old guys talking.

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: I don’t think they’re as classy as John. I think we’re painting way too good a picture of the CIA. He’s erudite. He’s got a sense of humor. He regrets stuff. And I don’t think they do.

content_blocks.text: AP: He’s ready to be up front about some of the U.S.’s underhanded dealings. Do you feel like it’s a time for frankness about America’s darker side?

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: Even while we were still editing it, it felt more and more like it was a commentary on the modern day, especially with a lot of the recent stuff that Trump’s been doing. It wasn’t the direct purpose of it, but I kind of liked that it felt that way. The tragic thing is: history keeps repeating itself, and more and more stupidly and less and less secretively. They kept their horrible stuff secret back then. It’s like they don’t care what people think about it anymore. I think that’s a darker place we’re in now. Shame doesn’t come into it.

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: Whether or not I agree with it or not is for a later chat. I’m not saying the pacifist version is wrong or doesn’t work at times. But I do think the CIA and KGB and most vicious governments around the world are more happy with polite protest marches.

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: He can be ultra dangerous and you feel scared of him more than most. Maybe Joe Pesci. I was scared the first time I had a Zoom with him. But also his dexterity with comedy. But mostly knowing that in the silent moments you’d see acres of sorrow and regret when he’s seemingly not doing anything — when he’s just looking out of a window or listening to a Dictaphone or smoking a cigarette.

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: Not at all. In fact, I had kind of forgotten that whole section of that film until I rewatched it a few months ago. I hope that they don’t think I stole the whole memoir-of-a-CIA-guy bit from him. (Laughs) But John’s so good at everything that history is going to repeat itself.

You feel like it’s an equal two-hander at the same time as John’s character will always be the lead.

content_blocks.text: AP: Do you identify more with either of their characters?

content_blocks.text: McDonagh: John’s got a lot of me. I like the outrageousness and the danger of where he goes sometimes. In my more sarcastic, anarchistic moments, I find that sort of stuff funny. He’s an awful guy, he’s done awful things. But on top of that, I do feel like he says a lot of funny stuff that I agree with — even if it’s just cheeses. (Laughs) A scene like that, you know you’re being naughty but I think the principle of it is actually sort of loving and weirdly pro-democratic, pro-gay and pro-cheese.
