stories.title: Frank Stronach to be sentenced today for 1977 indecent assault
stories.summary: The conviction is the only guilty finding out of 12 offences initially alleged involving seven women in a trial that went badly sideways.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Canada

The conviction is the only guilty finding out of 12 offences initially alleged involving seven women in a trial that went badly sideways over the course of the spring

Last updated 48 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/frank-stronach-to-be-sentenced-today-for-1977-indecent-assault#comments-area)

Canadian businessman Frank Stronach leaves the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Toronto, ON June 19, 2026.Photo by Nick Kozak for Postmedia News

Autoparts billionaire Frank Stronach, 94, is due in a Toronto courtroom Thursday morning for a sentencing hearing for the crime of indecently assaulting a woman in a Toronto apartment in 1977.

Justice Anne Molloy, who found Stronach guilty in June, is to hear Crown and defence arguments before sentencing him for a crime that technically no longer exists, as it was rewritten in 1983 into the broader Criminal Code offence of sexual assault.

An offender can only be charged with a crime that was in force at the time of the alleged offence. Today’s legal arguments will be based on the law of indecent assault as it then was for the substance of the offence, guided by more recent precedent and comparable sentences.

All were historic complaints, some older than the modern law of sexual assault itself, most in the 1980s. The charges were laid in 2024.

The trial started provocatively, as the Crown sought to use each case to bolster the credibility of the others. But by trial’s end, only three complainants remained. One woman had an emotional breakdown on the witness stand and gave evidence so garbled and disjointed the judge decided no conviction could flow from it. Another gave such self-contradictory evidence, especially over the year the alleged crime occurred, that Molloy decided she could not convict. One woman tried to apologize after lying on the witness stand about whether she had read another complainant’s account in the media. Another was revealed in cross-examination to have an extensive history of controversial business litigation involving what a judge described as her deceit and dishonesty, and a more recent instance of allegedly falsely reporting to police that a man she had a dispute with threatened to kill her. All those charges failed.

Two guilty findings were recorded in June involving two women. Then a few days later with the trial still in the hands of Molloy, a civil lawyer for one of them made an attempt to extract money through Stronach’s lawyer, but ended up sharing information that contradicted the woman’s testimony under oath. That led Molloy to declare a surprise mistrial over the woman’s charge, leaving only the indecent assault conviction involving the other woman. Chronologically, it was the first of the 12 crimes initially alleged.

This woman was also the alleged victim in another charge of attempted rape, which is likewise a historic charge that no longer exists in criminal law, but Molloy found Stronach not guilty on that count.

Now 74, the woman was a 25-year-old legal secretary at the time of the offence in 1977. When she testified, she said she knew Stronach from Rooney’s, the Toronto bar he owned.

“After dinner there, she agreed to go to a nearby apartment with him. He came up from behind her, flipped her forwards over the upholstered arm of a chair, lifted her skirt, and ground his groin into her pelvic area over her panties. There is no evidence that he took his penis out of his pants. At law, this cannot be attempted rape, as alleged in Count 5, but it indecent assault under Count 6,” Molloy wrote.

“It happened so quickly. I was just pushed forward, face first, from behind, fairly forceful. It wasn’t violent but it was firm… Frankly, it was kind of bizarre,” the victim testified. “It was kind of pathetic… I have to say I felt betrayed… I freed myself from this bizarre event and I gathered up my things and I left.”

Stronach faces a separate trial with similar charges and six complainants in York Region that is not yet scheduled.

Another gave such self-contradictory evidence, especially over the year the alleged crime occurred, that Molloy decided she could not convict. One woman tried to apologize after lying on the witness stand about whether she had read another complainant’s account in the media. Another was revealed in cross-examination to have an extensive history of controversial business litigation involving what a judge described as her deceit and dishonesty, and a more recent instance of allegedly falsely reporting to police that a man she had a dispute with threatened to kill her. All those charges failed.

Two guilty findings were recorded in June involving two women. Then a few days later with the trial still in the hands of Molloy, a civil lawyer for one of them made an attempt to extract money through Stronach’s lawyer, but ended up sharing information that contradicted the woman’s testimony under oath. That led Molloy to declare a surprise mistrial over the woman’s charge, leaving only the indecent assault conviction involving the other woman. Chronologically, it was the first of the 12 crimes initially alleged.

This woman was also the alleged victim in another charge of attempted rape, which is likewise a historic charge that no longer exists in criminal law, but Molloy found Stronach not guilty on that count.
Now 74, the woman was a 25-year-old legal secretary at the time of the offence in 1977. When she testified, she said she knew Stronach from Rooney’s, the Toronto bar he owned.

“After dinner there, she agreed to go to a nearby apartment with him. He came up from behind her, flipped her forwards over the upholstered arm of a chair, lifted her skirt, and ground his groin into her pelvic area over her panties. There is no evidence that he took his penis out of his pants. At law, this cannot be attempted rape, as alleged in Count 5, but it indecent assault under Count 6,” Molloy wrote.

“It happened so quickly. I was just pushed forward, face first, from behind, fairly forceful. It wasn’t violent but it was firm… Frankly, it was kind of bizarre,” the victim testified. “It was kind of pathetic… I have to say I felt betrayed… I freed myself from this bizarre event and I gathered up my things and I left.”
Stronach faces a separate trial with similar charges and six complainants in York Region that is not yet scheduled.

stories.title: Blue Jays staying loose with 9 games left in season and a playoff spot on the line
stories.summary: The 42-year-old Scherzer (3-8) pitched five innings of one-run ball, allowing three hits and three walks but striking out three.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By John Chidley-Hill, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 6:27 am.

If the Toronto Blue Jays are nervous about reaching the post-season, it doesn’t show.

Myles Straw wore small, silver 1990s-style sunglasses as he answered questions from reporters following a 2 for 4 performance in Wednesday’s 5-1 win over the Detroit Tigers. As he spoke, Blue Jays teammates like Louis Varland and Shane Bieber stopped to take photos or videos, while Andres Gimenez stood near the media scrum shaking his head ruefully.

“I think they look good. I’m not sure. I got these guys over here laughing at me,” said Straw who drove in a run in the fourth inning. “I don’t know why they’re all looking.

“I mean, (infielder) Josh Smith. He gave them to me, so he’s got the same pair. I’m not the only one.”

The Cleveland Guardians beat Chicago 6-3 earlier in the day to take the lead in the American League Central. The White Sox now hold the AL’s third and final wild-card berth and the Blue Jays are 1 1/2 games behind them.

The Texas Rangers defeated the Boston Red Sox 7-3 later in the day to sit one game back of Chicago.

“Today was huge. Obviously, that was like a must-win,” said Straw. “Obviously, we’ve got, what, nine more (games), so anything can happen.

“That’s plenty of baseball, but I think today was a good one to get, for sure.”

Toronto’s rookie class like centre-fielder Brett Bateman and relief pitchers Spencer Miles and Brendan Cellucci were all duded up in short jean shorts, sleeveless plaid shirts and cowboy hats for the Blue Jays trip down to Texas for a critical three-game series against the Rangers.

“That was (veteran pitcher) Max Scherzer. He was excited to show me that a couple days ago,” said Straw. “I saw it, and I thought it’d be great.

“Hopefully, there’s some pictures. I’m sure there will be pictures posted, and you guys will definitely like it.”

The 42-year-old Scherzer (3-8) pitched five innings of one-run ball, allowing three hits and three walks but striking out three. Mason Fluharty, Miles and Varland combined for four scoreless innings to preserve the win.

It was Scherzer’s best start in three outings, keeping Toronto in the game long enough for shortstop Ernie Clement and Straw to drive in some runs. Scherzer had given up six runs over five innings in a 7-4 loss to the Baltimore Orioles on Sept. 11 and three runs over 5 2/3 innings in a 4-3 win over the Kansas City Royals on Sept. 5.

“It’s great when you have to come to the field, and it’s must-win baseball. That’s how we’ve felt for a while now,” said Scherzer. “We know this position that we’re in. We’re aware of the standings, but at the end of the day, you’ve got to come here and win ball games.

“You can’t worry about everything else. You’ve got to worry about yourself. Today we had a good game, and everybody did their job.”

Blue Jays manager John Schneider said that he was going to try and relax on Thursday, the team’s off day, by golfing with his wife. He said he encouraged all of his players to also spend time with their families or think about anything other than baseball.

“I’ve been scoreboard watching for a while,” said Schneider. “I May take a break and just try to focus on going 1-0 every day with the Blue Jays.

“Whatever’s going to happen is going to happen. There’s a lot of moving pieces, and there’s going to continue to be a lot of moving pieces. I think if we can kind of worry about us, that’s the best thing to do.”

Before Wednesday’s win over Detroit, Schneider said that pitcher Trey Yesavage felt good after a conditioning start with the triple-A Buffalo Bisons and could pitch for the Blue Jays as soon as Sunday.

Schneider said that the rookie’s physical readiness was more important than his stat line for the Bisons after he threw 2/3 of an inning, giving up two hits and two runs, one earned, against the Rochester Red Wings.

Yesavage has a 5-5 record for Toronto this season with a 3.65 earned-run average over 18 starts. He’s struck out 91 batters over 93 2/3 innings pitched. He had been out after having surgery on his left knee to repair a meniscus injury suffered Aug. 4 against the Houston Astros.

Bieber, a former Cy Young Award winner, had a setback, however, and will have to delay his next side session. Bieber (5-2) has a 4.37 ERA, striking out 44 over 55 2/3 innings this year.

With nine games left in the regular season, Bieber’s runway to return from inflammation of the right teres major muscle is getting very short.

stories.title: MP Leslyn Lewis sues her alma mater, and professor for 'traumatizing' job interview
stories.summary: Leslyn Lewis is seeking $3 million after failing to get a scholar position reserved for a Black person of African descent
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Canada

Lewis claims York University prof Sean Rehaag derailed her candidacy for a scholar position by allegedly alerting decision makers to defamatory claims she was racist, anti-gay and anti-refugee

Last updated 25 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/MP-leslyn-lewis-sues-her-alma-mater-and-professor-for-traumatizing-job-interview#comments-area)

Conservative MP Leslyn Lewis speaks during question period in the House of Commons in Ottawa, April 20, 2026.Photo by Blair Gable/Postmedia

Seeking damages of more than $3 million, Leslyn Lewis, the MP for Haldimand-Norfolk in rural southern Ontario and a former leadership candidate for the Conservative Party of Canada, has brought a defamation claim against her alma mater law school at York University and a professor of refugee law over Lewis’s failed application to a scholar position reserved for a Black person of African descent.

Lewis claims Sean Rehaag derailed her short-listed candidacy from the start, by allegedly scheming behind the scenes to alert academic decision makers to his defamatory allegations that Lewis was racist, anti-gay, anti-refugee and opposed women’s reproductive freedom.

In her statement of claim filed in Ontario Superior Court, Lewis also alleges the school was negligent in exposing her to a “traumatizing” job interview process by allowing a “toxic culture” of “wokeism” and “groupthink” to develop at Osgoode Hall law school.

She claims Rehaag “blindsided” her with these defamatory allegations about her politics as she gave a presentation about her candidacy, “ganged up” on her with other academic decision makers to verbally abuse her, and that he did this to “embarrass and humiliate” her in public and in front of academic colleagues.

She claims she has been “de facto vetted-out of any future prospect in academia.”

She claims Rehaag told her that people like her had no place at Osgoode and she was not welcome.

In a statement of defence, Rehaag specifically denies this. York denies the environment was “dangerous, hostile, or abusive.” Both deny there was ever any campaign of “vetting out” or “lobbying” against Lewis.

The conflict dates to March of 2021, when Lewis was simultaneously running as a high-profile candidate for the federal Conservatives and applying for this newly created job at York’s Osgoode Hall, where she once took a doctorate.

The job in the Osgoode’s Centre for Refugee Studies “supported York’s Affirmative Action program, in recognition of the underrepresentation of Black faculty,” according to York’s statement of defence. Lewis’s claim says the job “was created in response to the racial awareness that emerged from the George Floyd murder, and the law school sought a faculty member that also shared the lived-experience as a person of Black-African Descent who could continue to advance causes of racial equality.”

Lewis had been involved with the centre as a student in the 1990s, and later worked in refugee law. She says in her statement of claim that she “advocated for members of the Lgbtq+2 community, with a specific focus on Jamaica (the country of her birth). Another area of focus was women fleeing domestic assault.”

stories.title: Skies clearing overnight in London
stories.summary: A few showers will linger Thursday morning, but some sunshine will break out heading into the afternoon.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
Skies will become partly cloudy Thursday night as high pressure from northern Ontario moves into the region. London will drop to 12 C overnight, while temperatures along the Lake Huron shoreline will remain around 15 C and reach 14 to 16 C near Lake Erie.

As we head into the weekend however, the chance for showers increases. “We have some rain in the forecast for Saturday and Sunday, it looks like it won’t arrive until Saturday late afternoon, early evening,” said Atchison.

“Then we’ll be into the official start to fall with fall officially arriving on Monday.” Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Thursday: Cloudy. 40 percent chance of showers near noon. High 23. Humidex 28. UV index 5 or moderate.

Thursday night: Cloudy. Clearing after midnight. Low 12. Friday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 22. Humidex 25. UV index 7 or high. Saturday: Cloudy with 60 percent chance of showers. High 19. Sunday: Cloudy with 70 percent chance of showers.

High 20. Monday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 17.

stories.title: Harry Potter drone show will bring a magical open-air spectacle to Canadian cities starting this week
stories.summary: Drones will perform to the soundtrack of the film series, which is celebrating its 25th anniversary
stories.author: Amber Dowling
stories.content:
If the skies around major Canadian cities look a little brighter this month, it’s not a magic trick. It’s the debut of DroneArt Show: Harry Potter , an open-air spectacle that will use drones instead of fireworks to celebrate 25 years of the boy wizard and his famous friends.

The inaugural experience is a collaboration between live-entertainment tech platform Fever, Warner Bros. and Nova Sky Stories, with stops in both Edmonton and Montreal on Sept. 18 and 19, and in Toronto on Sept. 25 and 26. The show debuted at Dodgers Stadium in Los Angeles this past June, with subsequent stops across the United States and Europe. Tickets are available online.

On each night of the show, a swarm of 1,200 synchronized drones take flight with choreography set to the soundtrack and dialogue from the eight Harry Potter films. A live violinist, selected from each city by Fever’s global music curation team, performs as the drones ebb and flow, and guests will sport synchronized LED wristbands that add to the overall magic.

“Harry Potter is one of the most ambitious projects we’ve been able to bring to Canada,” said Annie-Lou St-Amant, the regional manager for Fever Originals Canada. “It’s one of the largest drone shows that exist in the market.”

The hour-long show is pre-programmed with specialized software and GPS systems that allow the drones to stick to precise flightpaths that create the three-dimensional choreography and aerial formations. It launches with a single command as a team of trained operators supervise positioning, battery levels and overall quality.

“That is what allows hundreds of drones to move in harmony together,” Ms. St-Amant added.

Finding the venues to host a spectacle of this level posed a challenge. In Edmonton, the show takes place at the Exhibition Lands racetrack. Montreal hosts it at Quai Jacques-Cartier, and Toronto has set aside space at YZD, the former Downsview Airport.

As with any outdoor show, the Harry Potter drone experience is subject to weather conditions. Rain and winds not only have an impact on the audience, but on the main performers.

“The drones can only fly above a certain temperature, otherwise the batteries drain too fast,” said Ms. St-Amant. “That’s why in Canada we prioritize summer times. It also has to be dark outside, so the timing of the show is really important.”

This November marks the 25 th anniversary of the release of Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone , the first film based on J.K. Rowling’s books. The movie has grossed more than US$1.02-billion worldwide over its lifetime at the box office and has made a household name out of its star, Daniel Radcliffe.

Recently, Cineplex re-released all eight films in the series in select theatres across Canada to commemorate the anniversary. There have also been several special events at Universal theme parks, studio tours in London and Tokyo, and a slew of special merchandise and collectibles popping up at various retailers.

Potterheads, as fans call themselves, are especially interested in the upcoming TV series that is set to launch on HBO (and Crave in Canada) on Christmas Day. Dominic McLaughlin stars as the title character alongside Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

Other cast members include John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Minerva McGonagall, Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy and Kit Harington as Gilderoy Lockhart.

stories.title: Music listening parties offer opportunities for organic connection
stories.summary: Event organizers hope to bring back communal music listening, while encouraging attendees to make new friendships
stories.author: Mira Miller
stories.content:
Within 15 minutes of arriving at a music listening party at a café in Montreal’s Saint-Henri neighbourhood in late August, I was approached by a stranger who struck up a conversation. Her name was Hanna Eik, and she’d come to the event alone with the intention of making new friends.

“I was looking for organic ways to meet people in person,” said the 24-year-old, who is originally from Norway. “ I saw this event and thought, ‘This is such a cool idea for people to bond over music.’ ”

The music is both the main draw and social lubricant at the “5 à Set” events – a series of Montreal-based listening parties where people mix and mingle with like-minded music fans. (The name is a play on the Quebec term for a postwork social gathering.)

Want a unique nightlife experience? Try going somewhere without your phone

The ticketed events, which vary in price but typically remain between $10 and $20, are held at a variety of local businesses including bars, restaurants and cafés. They range from small, low-key gatherings where attendees sit and listen to a full album on vinyl, to larger, upbeat events that May cover a genre more broadly and often turn into lively dance parties. As another solo attendee, Julian Camacho, told me: “ Socializing is a bit awkward but if there’s good music, that’s something to look forward to.”

The main idea, co-organizer Juliane Larin said, is to use music as a means of connecting with others. The concept of music as a social activity has all but disappeared in the digital age thanks to headphone culture, streaming platforms and algorithms, which create ultrapersonalized, curated music feeds that keep us listening in isolation. With their listening parties, Larin and her co-host Maïté Gray aim to revive the vintage act of intentionally digesting an entire album, artist catalogue or specific genre in a community of fellow music lovers. And they hope attendees make new friends in the process.

Larin and Gray aren’t the only ones hosting communal music listening parties. In Toronto, an event series hosted by Davie Studios called The Listening Room gathers small groups to jam, listen to and discuss landmark albums at various local music venues, while Doze Hifi in Vancouver is a travelling vinyl pop-up series that sets up vintage sound systems throughout the city for people to gather, listen and socialize.

The 5 à Set party last month marked Gray and Larin’s 24th event. Roughly 90 reggaeton lovers gathered at Savsav café one evening to listen to a curated playlist titled Best of Puerto Rico. Best friends Gray, 25, and Larin, 24, started the event series last November as a way to combat seasonal depression, flex their creative muscles, indulge their love of music and offer a place to gather. It’s been so successful that they’ve since made it their full-time jobs.

“You might come home from 5 à Set on a Friday night at 3 a.m. and you’ll have danced all night, and then on Tuesday you can come and have a nice little coffee and sit back and listen to some jazz,” Larin said. They choose the artists and genres based on music they like (R&B, soul, funk, jazz, Latin music), but they also take requests from their more than 5,000 Instagram followers .

Regardless of the type of event, one thing remains the same: People show up with a willingness to mingle. Many arrive alone, and return to later events with the friends they made the first time around.

”It was always important for us to help people make connections and then we started noticing that it was just happening on its own,” Larin said. “ I think people were really craving that third space.”

Eik and Camacho were not the only ones who’d come to the party looking to make friends. In every corner of the room, there were people hugging, shaking hands and sharing Instagram handles.

Camacho, 23, is originally from Ecuador and completed his bachelor’s degree in Fredericton last year before moving to Montreal in March. He had been following 5 à Set on Instagram for a while, eager to put himself out there and attend one of their events. He was waiting for a theme that spoke to him when he saw their post for a reggaeton listening party and knew it was the right time, given his love for Bad Bunny.

“It’s a bit complicated to have a social life once you graduate, but you have to make the effort so that’s why I’m here,” Camacho said. “We can dedicate ourselves to our professional life and that’s very good, but it’s also important to have community.”

Creating an environment where people feel comfortable to attend on their own is no small feat. Gray and Larin greet every person at the entrance and regularly circulate the room, checking in on those who are alone and introducing fellow solo attendees to one another.

“We really try our best to make everyone feel welcome and not left out,” Larin said.

What makes a great bash? Partygoers and throwers share their favourite memories

Many of the partygoers make this a priority, too. Omer Othman, 28, was at his fourth 5 á Set party with his partner and a close friend, but they had intentionally split up to “avoid being cliquey” and meet new people.

“We’re human and we’re social animals,” he said. “I’m here tonight to see people be people, to really connect with others and make sure we’re escaping our everyday 9-to-5 life.”

While the reggaeton event attracted a relatively young crowd, Gray and Larin said that was likely because of the genre’s younger fan base. Typically, their events are intergenerational; past listening parties for artists such as Sade, Al Green and Stevie Wonder have brought in listeners of all ages.

“It can feel as though there is an age limit to the clubbing scene or the dancing scene and that can be limiting,” Gray said.

On top of their Montreal events, Gray and Larin have been hosting monthly listening parties at the 1 Hotel in Toronto since April, and they’re currently working on hosting an event in New York some time this fall.

They’re excited about the success they’ve found with this passion-project-turned-business, but even more so about the community they’ve created in the process.

“I think one of our favourite sentences that we hear now is, ‘We met at 5 à Set,’ ” Gray said.

stories.title: Ontario launches medical school tuition grants worth $220-million for family doctors
stories.summary: Recipients must commit to spending five years practising family medicine in the province
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
Ontario family doctor residents can begin applying Thursday for a new grant that will pay their medical school tuition retroactively in exchange for practising comprehensive primary care anywhere in the province for at least five years.

Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, will mark the opening of applications by announcing plans to spend a total of $220-million for about four years on tuition grants for more than 2,000 future family doctors – more than the government promised when the program was announced in principle two years ago.

The main goal of the program is to incentivize more of the physicians who train in family medicine to actually provide the type of office-based, cradle-to-grave primary care that is in short supply.

A study published in the Annals of Family Medicine in May, 2025 found that nearly 40 per cent of the 6,310 family doctors who entered the physician workforce in Ontario between 1993 and 2022 worked in other settings, including emergency rooms and clinics specializing in sports medicine, addiction treatment and cosmetic medicine.

“This is to ensure that the students, after finishing their studies, are going to be, [for] five years, practising as a comprehensive primary-care family medicine physician anywhere in Ontario, and that’s the ultimate goal of this program,” Mr. Quinn told The Globe and Mail in an interview ahead of a news conference in London Thursday.

A message to Canada’s new medical students: These are hard times, but not hopeless times

Ontario’s expansion of its learn-and-stay grant program – which is already available to nurses, paramedics and medical lab technicians who agree to work in high-needs areas – to family doctors is the latest example of a provincial government using carrots and sticks to convince young physicians to practice in ways that fill gaps in the public-health system.

What’s different in this case is the tuition grant doesn’t force doctors to work in small towns or rural areas, as other student loan forgiveness programs, including the federal one , do.

Ontario’s grant, which also covers books and supplies, is available to Ontario medical school graduates enrolled in a family medicine residency training program, who agree to practice comprehensive primary-care with a full roster of patients, even in a big city.

They have to have lived in Ontario for 12 consecutive months without being in full-time postsecondary studies – a rule that should reserve the grants for people from Ontario.

The province hasn’t said how many patients count as a full roster. Doctors who fail to fulfill the five-year commitment will see their grants converted to repayable loans.

The provincial government said in January that the number of Ontarians without a primary-care provider had dropped to 1.98-million, down from an earlier estimate of 2.5 million as of 2023.

Ontario and most other provinces have other ways of pushing doctors toward practising in regions desperate for physicians, although one such program was deemed illegal by a British Columbia court in a decision released last Friday.

B.C. Supreme Court Judge Matthew Kirchner ruled the province couldn’t force international medical graduates (IMGs) to work for two or three years in an underserved area in exchange for a residency training spot without mandating the provision, known as return of service, through a law or regulation. Terms are currently imposed through contracts with individual IMGs.

Family doctor study finds disparities in primary care across Canada

The case was brought by a group representing Canadians who graduated from medical schools abroad.

“I find that the imposition of the return of service obligation on those IMGs who match to an IMG residency position engages their liberty interest to decide where to live free from government interference,” Judge Kirchner wrote. “A person’s choice of where to live is a fundamentally personal decision which engages what it means to enjoy individual dignity and independence.”

The judge suspended his decision for 60 days to give the province time to respond.

B.C. Health Minister Ravi Kahlon told reporters Wednesday that his government will take whatever legal steps are necessary to preserve the return-of-service rule for IMGs.

“The bottom line is this: This program is too important,” he said. “We’re going to do whatever is required to make sure this program continues to function.”

As for Ontario’s newly expanded grant program, Tara Kiran, a family physician and researcher at St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto, said it was “reasonable” for the province to cover tuition for all eligible family doctors, regardless of whether they practise in a big city or small town.

She was an author of the study that found many of Ontario’s family doctors work somewhere other than a primary-care office.

“Frankly, we’re short of family doctors pretty much everywhere in the province right now,” she said.

stories.title: PM Carney: ‘Europe and Canada are even stronger together’
stories.summary: Carney's speech comes a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to open discussions to becoming the EU's first "associate member."
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says deeper cooperation and trade between Canada and the European Union can bolster sovereignty on both sides of the Atlantic and help create the “next just, stable, and prosperous world order.”

Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France Thursday morning, Carney made a pitch for stronger economic ties with the EU in industries like artificial intelligence, critical minerals and defence.

“I want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners,” Carney said.

“We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) trickled in to Carney’s speech Thursday morning, with the prime minister’s speech receiving applause and a standing ovation from the 791-member legislature. One legislator received jeers from his peers for chanting “USA! USA!” as Carney took the podium. The prime minister appeared to hear the chant, but did not acknowledge it.

But the U.S. under Trump was very present in Carney’s remarks to the European politicians — albeit only in indirect references.

“Just as dominance is the arrogance of the hegemon, perfection is the enemy of the good. The economics are clear: the leverage of the powerful in an exploitive relationship collapses well before complete independence is achieved. Diversity confers advantage,” Carney said.

“The objective is not self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience.”

Carney’s speech came as Canada and the EU explore deepening political, security and economic ties. That process started in June 2025, but has accelerated with both Canadian and EU officials hinting at a significant new formal partnership over and above the Canada-EU Trade Agreement (Ceta).

On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was inviting Carney to “open the door” to becoming the EU’s first “associate member” — a designation that does not currently have a basis in the economic and political bloc’s treaty.

Later that day, Trump said if Canada becomes the first associate member of the European Union it could be a “hostile act.”

Speaking to reporters in North Carolina, the president said if it’s done with “bad intentions” he will “put very heavy tariffs on Europe.”

Trump also called Canada a “terrible trade partner” after earlier Wednesday signing a memorandum directing federal agencies overseeing government procurement in the United States to remove all products of Canadian origin.

At a press conference with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola, Carney said the push for an “alliance for the future” with Europe is not a reaction to Trump’s hostile actions on trade, but a “positive” project aimed strengthening both sides of the Atlantic.

“This is about building,” Carney told reporters.

Addressing the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France Thursday morning, Carney made a pitch for stronger economic ties with the EU in industries like artificial intelligence, critical minerals and defence.
“I want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival – only with better manners,” Carney said.

“We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) trickled in to Carney’s speech Thursday morning, with the prime minister’s speech receiving applause and a standing ovation from the 791-member legislature. One legislator received jeers from his peers for chanting “USA! USA!” as Carney took the podium. The prime minister appeared to hear the chant, but did not acknowledge it.
But the U.S. under Trump was very present in Carney’s remarks to the European politicians — albeit only in indirect references.

“Just as dominance is the arrogance of the hegemon, perfection is the enemy of the good. The economics are clear: the leverage of the powerful in an exploitive relationship collapses well before complete independence is achieved. Diversity confers advantage,” Carney said.
“The objective is not self-sufficiency. It is collective resilience.”

Carney’s speech came as Canada and the EU explore deepening political, security and economic ties. That process started in June 2025, but has accelerated with both Canadian and EU officials hinting at a significant new formal partnership over and above the Canada-EU Trade Agreement (Ceta).

stories.title: Exclusive: Canada’s claim to the Arctic faces growing threats. The coast guard is trying to remind the world, ‘We’re here.’
stories.summary: Embedded with the Canadian Coast Guard in the Arctic, CTV News is getting an exclusive look at how Canada is protecting northern sovereignty and security.
stories.author: Graham Richardson, Stephanie Ha
stories.content:
Above THE Arctic Circle -- After nearly 40 years in the Arctic and countless voyages through the Northwest Passage, Michel Dufresne, captain of the Canadian Coast Guard icebreaker Des Groseilliers, says no two trips north are ever the same. Especially now.

“Thirty-nine years ago, the Arctic was totally different,” Dufresne said. “We can see that the Northwest Passage is open a lot more than it was in the past. It’s not always the same.”

As global warming accelerates and Arctic waters become increasingly navigable, Canada’s claim to the region is facing growing scrutiny from countries like Russia and China. Recent tensions with the United States and its threat to annex Greenland earlier this year, have also underscored the importance of asserting Canadian sovereignty and security from coast to coast to coast.

Embedded with the Canadian Coast Guard in the Arctic, CTV News is getting an exclusive look at how Canada is protecting northern sovereignty and security.

Even the Northwest Passage has become a strategic flashpoint between Canada and the U.S. While Canada insists the passage is internal waters under Canadian sovereignty, the U.S. argues it’s an international strait.

Since coming into office, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has pledged more than $40 billion over the next decade for Arctic defence, infrastructure and security. Carney has described the investment as a significant departure from what he called the “piecemeal” approach of previous governments.

Many experts say the shift is long overdue. But, as with nearly everything in the Arctic, it will come at a high cost and take years, if not decades, to achieve.

“If you are not there, and if you’re not sovereign, your lack of presence is ceding your sovereignty to someone else,” said Maj.-Gen. (Ret’d) Scott Clancy, former director of operations for Norad.

“I think we are seeing a generational transformation in the Canadian Armed Forces, not just in terms of its spending, but in its focus, especially in the Arctic.”

The Canadian Coast Guard, meanwhile, officially moved from Fisheries and Oceans Canada to the Department of National Defence last year, in part to improve co-ordination at sea, especially in the Arctic.

Exercise Arctic Ghost

CTV News is embedded aboard the Des Groseilliers for the next several days. The icebreaker is scheduled to rendezvous with the Royal Canadian Navy’s newest Arctic and offshore patrol vessel, Hmcs Robert Hampton Gray, for a series of joint exercises that will also involve the RCMP as part of Exercise Arctic Ghost.

The drills are designed to demonstrate how federal agencies can work together to patrol vast stretches of the Arctic and strengthen security in the region.

“If we are going to talk about a presence, you need a whole-of-government approach to presence,” Clancy said.

This Arctic season, which spans from June to November, the Canadian Coast Guard will be deploying eight icebreakers and three vessels -- two deployed in the Mackenzie River and one in Rankin Inlet, Nunavut. Their combined Arctic presence will add up to 852 cumulative days in the Arctic, along with 26 crew changes.

Amid a renewed focus on Arctic sovereignty, Dufresne says he hopes Canadians will begin to understand what the Coast Guard does up north.

“With what’s happening in the world, our presence here makes a little bit more sense and just making sure that yes, we’re here. It’s not an uncovered territory,” Dufresne said.

New icebreakers on the way

In the next few years, the federal government will be replacing its aging fleet of icebreakers, including Des Groseilliers , which first entered service in 1982.

Two polar icebreakers and six other program icebreakers have been ordered, totaling billions of dollars, as part of Canada’s National Shipbuilding Strategy.

While Dufresne says it’s a milestone he welcomes, he admits it will be difficult to say goodbye to the ship that has defined so much of his career.

“It’s like getting a new car,” Dufresne said. “But for me, it will be a little pinch in the heart to let this one go. Every seaman, every mariner, has a ship that holds a special place in his heart. For me, this one is very important.”

CTV News Ottawa Bureau Chief Graham Richardson will be reporting from the Arctic this week while embedded with the Canadian Coast Guard, as Canada looks to assert its presence in the north.

stories.title: Key transcripts that led to Project South probe will remain under publication ban, Ontario Superior Court rules
stories.summary: Transcripts contain comments that would ‘deeply offend’ the public and sway potential jurors, Justice Laura Bird says
stories.author: Molly Hayes, Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Transcripts of key recordings that led to the Project South takedown will remain under a publication ban, after an Ontario Superior Court judge ruled Wednesday that inflammatory comments attributed to a Toronto police officer charged in the corruption case would “deeply offend” the public and create an indelible impression on potential jurors.

The ruling is in response to an application by The Globe and Mail and other media outlets to make public more than 500 pages of court documents and warrant applications that were unsealed earlier this year. Those files included what are known as information to obtain documents, which investigators use to get judicial authorization to conduct searches and make arrests.

While much of the content of those documents was released in July , portions were placed under a publication ban as the Crown and media outlets argued over whether their release should be shielded to protect fair trial rights.

In a ruling on Wednesday, Justice Laura Bird maintained a publication ban on some of that material, including a verbatim transcript of conversations alleged to have taken place between Toronto Police Constable Timothy Barnhardt and an alleged organized-crime figure, Brian Da Costa.

The pair were unaware at the time that they were central targets in a large-scale police corruption probe by York Regional Police, and that investigators were listening in on their calls.

“During their conversation, Mr. Barnhardt said things that would rightly deeply offend members of the public,” Justice Bird wrote of the alleged back-and-forth. “The comments attributable to him are made worse because he was sworn to uphold the safety of the public but demonstrated a complete indifference to extreme violence.”

While she stressed in her ruling that “the importance of public scrutiny in this case cannot be overstated,” she agreed with the Crown that these particular statements by the constable should not be made public. Constable Barnhardt, 56, is the only officer in custody, having twice been denied bail. His charges include accepting bribes, unauthorized use of police computers, trafficking police uniforms, conspiring to obstruct justice, and cocaine trafficking.

In addition to Constable Barnhardt, six other TPS officers – Sergeant Robert Black, Sgt. Carl Grellette, Constable Saurabjit Bedi, Constable Elias Mouawad, Constable Derek McCormick and Constable John Madeley Jr. – were charged on an array of allegations that include bribery and drug trafficking. One retired constable, John Madeley Sr., was also charged.

In late July, Mr. McCormick, who retired from the police service this summer after his arrest, pleaded guilty to breach of trust and one count of theft under $5,000. The 57-year-old received a 10-month conditional sentence after admitting to stealing cellphones that had been turned in by members of the public while he was working a front desk at downtown’s 52 Division. Court heard that he was struggling with an addiction to painkillers at the time.

The allegations against the other officers have not been tested in court.

Estimated to take a year and a half, the review will look at police-officer screening, supervision and substance abuse. It will also look at evidence management and how to safeguard law-enforcement databases.

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Carney says Canada welcomes ambition to deepen alliance with Europe
stories.summary: Strasbourg — Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada welcomes the ambition to become the European Union’s first associate member, though what exactly that would entail still needs to be defined.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says an enhanced partnership with the European Union will be put up for debate and a final vote in Parliament.

Carney says Canada welcomes the ambition to become the European Union’s first associate member, though what exactly that would entail still needs to be defined.

Addressing the European Parliament, Carney referred to EU President Ursula von der Leyen’s speech the day before , in which she pitched moving the relationship beyond a trade partnership to making Canada the European Union’s first associate member.

“We welcome this ambition — polling shows an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties,” he said in his address Thursday.

His remarks come after Canadian officials previously downplayed the characterization of a deeper relationship with the European Union as being an “associate member.” Canadian officials continue to stress that a specific name for that enhanced partnership with Europe still needs to be determined.

Carney said Canada and Europe should have deeper ties on critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence and energy security.

He said the two should move forward in allowing youth to live, work and study on either side of the Atlantic, and create an integrated market for financial services.

Carney did not mention U.S. President Donald Trump by name, though his speech alluded to strained relations between both Canada and Europe with the American administration.

“We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals. Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication,” Carney said.

“We hold common values, for which we have always fought, and in whose defence we must always remain vigilant.”

Trump said Wednesday in North Carolina that he views Canada potentially becoming an associate member of the European Union as a hostile act and threatened “serious” tariffs against the EU if they moved forward.

Carney said the goal of this partnership is not to create a “third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners.”

“We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one — no one — can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law,” he said.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s incoming ambassador to the European Union, said Wednesday that the name of the partnership was still being finalized, as well as specific details. He said that is expected to be formally announced in October during the EU-Canada Summit in Montreal.

He added any new labour mobility programs would be limited and would require consultation with the provinces.

The prime minister will take questions from reporters before heading back to Ottawa.

Conservative MPs have suggested associate membership in the EU might compromise Canadian sovereignty. They have warned of chaos from open borders, heaps of tax revenue going to Brussels and newcomers taking Canadian jobs — though it’s not clear that any of those changes would come from associate membership.

Ten of 27 EU countries still haven’t ratified a trade deal with Canada that has been in place provisionally for nine years. Canadian businesses have not taken up market access provided to them in Europe to the same extent that European industries have in Canada.

stories.title: As the debate over AI’s safety rages on around the world, where does Canada stand?
stories.summary: Ottawa — Warnings about the risks AI poses to humans have triggered a heated global debate over the past week. The heads of some of the biggest AI companies in the world are calling for action — something U.S. President Donald Trump opposes vehemently.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 17, 2026 5:15 am.

Ottawa — Warnings about the risks AI poses to humans have triggered a heated global debate over the past week. The heads of some of the biggest AI companies in the world are calling for action — something U.S. President Donald Trump opposes vehemently.

Here’s a quick look at what happened and where Canada fits into the picture.

Why are we talking about an existential threat from AI?

When generative AI models hit the mainstream a few years ago, Yoshua Bengio, one of the so-called “godfathers” of AI, was a prominent voice warning the technology could pose a threat to humanity.

Such warnings largely faded from the headlines as the anti-regulation Trump administration took office and multiple countries, including Canada, began focusing more on the economic benefits of AI technologies.

Last week, researcher Jacob Coxon, who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, said in a post on X that neither company was acting responsibly. He accused both firms of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives” and claimed those building the technology “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

Where does Canada stand?

On Wednesday, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said the growing appetite for AI regulation is a “good thing.”

But when Solomon was asked during an appearance at a conference in Montreal whether he believes AI poses an existential risk, he didn’t answer directly.

“We take all the risks seriously,” he said.

Solomon added that such warnings aren’t new. “The reason I say that is not to discount the seriousness of it, but to say that we’ve already taken a lot of action as these models move towards the frontier,” he said.

He pointed to Canada’s AI Safety Institute, which received $50 million in the recent national AI strategy.

On Wednesday, Solomon also announced an investment of up to $300 million by Canada and Germany in the development of safe AI by Bengio and his LawZero non-profit.

“LawZero’s flagship approach, called Scientist AI, treats reliability as a core capability, centring on developing a fundamentally new form of AI designed to be trustworthy and safe from inception,” the organization said in a press release.

What are AI companies asking for?

Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the pace of AI development should be slowed down, which would require industry co-ordination. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he agreed with Amodei that “we need to pace the frontier,” while xAI CEO Elon Musk posted, “Dario is right.”

But Aidan Gomez, CEO of Canadian AI company Cohere, has taken issue with Amodei’s request for the U.S. government to loosen antitrust restrictions to allow companies to work on AI safety. He called it a red flag.

“It shouldn’t be a few companies in Silicon Valley setting the bar and trying to pull up the ladder behind them and implement regulatory capture,” Gomez said Wednesday while speaking on the same panel as Solomon.

He called for a “multi-stakeholder approach that is much more grounded in the reality of the technology as it exists today and what we can foresee in the near future.”

Gomez also took issue with those who quantify the risk of extinction.

“They throw out numbers, like 10 per cent chance that there’s going to be extinction of our species due to this technology. That’s not a mathematical result, and it’s extremely misleading to the public to throw out these numbers that are just, like, your gut vibe check on what might be coming, as though it’s a concrete quantitative measurement,” he said.

Are we going to see action on regulation in Canada?

In an interview with Bloomberg earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney called for a global “technology stability” body. He said there is a need for international co-ordination and that “ultimately, a technology stability board, in our view, along the lines of the Financial Stability Board would make sense.”

Carney was in France on Wednesday, where he attended a speech by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.

Von der Leyen said Europe is “in the position to shape global efforts on how to tackle” AI.

“We will step up together with our like-minded partners like Canada, the United Kingdom and others. We want to team up on model evaluation, verification, early warning, AI security and much more,” she said.

She said she would invite “the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier.”

Solomon was asked Wednesday whether Canada was going to lead the charge on a global technology stability body. He said that’s something Carney has talked to other leaders about.

“These are not conversations that are coming out of thin air, nor are there conversations that one country is trying to take credit for,” he said.

Trump, meanwhile, is claiming the mounting calls for regulation are the product of a conspiracy.

“I am the Hoax Buster, and I’m right now breaking another Hoax — That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!” he wrote in one recent online post.

He’s not the only skeptic. The French finance minister said Wednesday that calls to slow down AI development serve the interests of U.S. AI companies.

Roland Lescure said they “are now coming from those at the top of the class … Making everyone behind them slow down so they can stay in first place,” Reuters reported.

Karsten Wildberger, Germany’s digital transformation minister, appeared on Wednesday’s panel in Montreal alongside Solomon and Gomez.

Wildberger told the audience the alliance between Germany and Canada — they signed an agreement on AI in Montreal a year ago — was “very much” about avoiding dependence on the U.S. and China.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 17, 2026.

stories.title: Sentencing hearing today for billionaire businessman Frank Stronach
stories.summary: Toronto — A sentencing hearing is scheduled today for Canadian auto parts mogul Frank Stronach on the historical offence of indecent assault.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canadian auto parts mogul Frank Stronach will be sentenced on December 11, but won’t face jail time, Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy said on Thursday.

Prosecutors were seeking a sentence of six months behind bars for Stronach on the historical offence of indecent assault.

In a sentencing hearing this morning, Crown attorney Jelena Vlacic said there are several aggravating factors in the case, including that the indecent assault was “sudden and disorienting” and had an enduring impact on the complainant.

She also pointed to the 20-year age gap between Stronach and the complainant, who was 25 at the time of the incident in 1977.

Vlacic also noted several mitigating factors, such as Stronach’s lack of criminal record before the offence and his role as a high-profile business leader who for decades represented one of Canada’s biggest success stories.

She argued, however, that the court should give limited weight to more than a dozen character reference letters from former employees and other supporters who state they never saw Stronach behave inappropriately toward women.

Stronach’s defence lawyer, Leora Shemesh, argued the Crown’s position is “excessive” as she began making her own submissions on sentence.

The hearing takes place even as prosecutors are challenging the judge’s decision to declare a rare post-verdict mistrial on Stronach’s sexual assault conviction.

Stronach, who is 94, was found guilty in June of both charges, which relate to separate allegations brought by two of the women in his Toronto criminal trial.

Weeks later, Justice Molloy granted the mistrial on the sexual assault conviction after emails from the complainant’s lawyer in a separate civil case were presented in court.

Stronach’s lawyer argued those emails told a story that was inconsistent with the woman’s testimony in the criminal trial. At the time, Shemesh told The Canadian Press that the court did not hear from the complainant before the judge made her decision.

The Crown’s appeal argues the guilty verdict on the sexual assault charge should be restored and the case sent back to Superior Court for sentencing.

The billionaire businessman initially faced 12 charges related to allegations brought by seven complainants and dating as far back as the late 1970s. The Crown later withdrew one charge and agreed Stronach should be found not guilty on four more.

Soon after, Molloy said she couldn’t convict Stronach on two charges related to one complainant whose evidence she deemed unreliable.

Five charges related to three complainants remained, and Stronach was found guilty of two, until the mistrial was granted.

He is set to stand trial before a jury in Newmarket, Ont., next year in a sexual assault case involving six complainants.

stories.title: First Nations youth continue fight over Carney’s major projects agenda, summit
stories.summary: Ottawa — As Canadian politicians were pitching their major projects plans to foreign investors at a first-of-its-kind summit in Toronto, First Nations youth in Ottawa were making a pitch to Canadians on why they should join the fight to stop them.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 17, 2026 5:15 am.

Ottawa — As Canadian politicians were pitching their major projects plans to foreign investors at a first-of-its-kind summit in Toronto, First Nations youth in Ottawa were making a pitch to Canadians on why they should join the fight to stop them.

Jeronimo Kataquapit and his cousin Ramon had just returned from a weeks-long journey on the coast of James Bay, a body of water that straddles Quebec and Ontario at the southern tip of the Hudson Bay.

Jeronimo called it “hardcore camping,” where he, Ramon and his parents roughed it on the shorelines, spotting polar bears, flocks of geese and caribou along the way.

The trip wasn’t for rest and relaxation for the family from Attawapiskat First Nation. It was part of their ongoing efforts to leave physical traces of First Nations occupancy on the land and waters as the provincial and federal government work to develop the mineral-rich Ring of Fire — a so-called “major project” the Kataquapit family vehemently opposes.

“I didn’t want to wait around for our elected leaders to take action,” Jeronimo told attendees at an event held in St. Andrew’s Presbyterian Church on Tuesday evening, steps away from Parliament Hill.

“We needed to make our presence known on the river.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s tenure has, so far, been defined by his desire to build major projects in an effort to strengthen the Canadian economy in the face of increasing trade hostility from U.S. President Donald Trump.

The two-day summit in Toronto on Tuesday — a gathering of hundreds of domestic and global executives with trillions of dollars collectively in assets under management — sought to address both historic and fresh concerns about Canada’s investment climate.

Canadian officials and business leaders were trying to buck the country’s reputation as a tough place to earn a return and replace it with a message to the world that Canada is “open for business.”

The Kataquapits say it isn’t — or, at least, not in the way Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are making it out to be.

“They talk about the region as if it’s a statistic, as if it’s a number, as if it’s money to be made,” Jeronimo said, sitting in a wooden pew in the oldest Presbyterian Church in Ottawa, as the mostly non-Indigenous attendees funnelled out of the Together for Nature tour.

“But it’s people’s homes … We know what’s at stake. It’s our future that will be affected.”

The Together for Nature Tour, organized by Ontario Nature and Legal Advocates for Nature’s Defence, is seeking to build solidarity between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians to protect the environment and push back on Carney’s major projects agenda.

Carney’s government faced some loud opposition from Indigenous leaders last year when it pushed through legislation to speed up major projects. First Nations leaders warned his fast-track approach to development could infringe upon their rights, and accused Carney of sidelining their concerns in favour of investors.

The tone has changed since then from elected community leaders, but not for the youth who warn developments could irrevocably harm the landscapes and waterways they’ve known their entire lives, and that have sustained their ancestors for time immemorial.

It’s the message the Kataquapits are taking across the province this week, with stops in Ottawa, Toronto, Kitchener and London. And it’s the message they want attendees to share with their networks long after the events wrap.

“It’s all about the dollar (for Carney and investors). It’s about money and what they can gain in the short term,” Ramon said. “But when the long term comes to bite them and their children when they’re in the spirit world, they’ll wish that they would have done what was right.”

The summit was protested by Indigenous leaders, environmental groups and union leaders who said they rejected the idea of leaving Canada’s economic future in the hands of CEOs.

“Canada is getting very good at blackmailing the public,” Wet’suwet’en Hereditary Chief Na’Moks said at one such demonstration in Toronto, citing the prime minister’s argument that Canada needs to build more major projects to protect itself from predatory U.S. trade policy.

“That’s their story. Their story is false, the same way that they think that these projects will go on without your support, without our support.”

Youth on the other side of the country are making similar efforts to note their displeasure with the actions of their provincial and federal government.

Katisha Paul, founder and principal consultant of Nepenek and women’s representative for the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs, called the investment summit an “extraction pitch” and questioned whose “national interest” is being served by politicians and the business leaders they’re trying to court.

“Right now it’s not Canadian citizens. It’s a banker (Carney) sitting in front of a trillion dollars, deciding that their own national interest exists above any taxpayer. And he’s going to do anything that he can to further that.”

Paul worries about the salmon in her territories, the whales and the land.

More importantly, she’s worried about consent, saying the federal government is failing to adequately consult with First Nations title- and rights-holders who are often on the front line opposing developments.

“Everybody around the world loves the idea to stand up against somebody like Trump,” Paul said.

“But at the same time, what are we giving up? Who’s going to be hurting in the end?”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

— With files from Craig Lord

stories.title: Tim Hortons ‘flight roast’ coming to WestJet flights, companies link loyalty programs
stories.summary: Toronto — Tim Hortons' coffee is cleared for takeoff.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 17, 2026 5:15 am.

Toronto — Tim Hortons’ coffee is cleared for takeoff.

As Canadian brands increasingly search for ways to differentiate themselves in a crowded retail marketplace, the café giant is teaming up with WestJet.

Starting Nov. 30, a special in-flight brew from the café giant will be available on board the airline’s flights as part of a partnership between the two brands that will later include a loyalty program collaboration.

Dubbed the “flight roast,” Tim Hortons says the coffee features a unique blend specifically designed for passengers’ tastebuds at high altitudes. Hope Bagozzi, Tims’ chief marketing officer, called it distinct from the original and dark roast blends that customers are used to drinking at its restaurants.

“Our coffee teams sort of set to work saying, ‘OK, the first fundamental is we’re going to leverage the same 100 per cent premium arabica beans,’ so that’s a given. But the actual roast itself, we needed it to be a bit different because things taste different at high altitudes,” she said in an interview.

“Taste perceptions do change at altitudes, so we wanted to make sure that our roast suited that. So things like higher pressure, shorter brew times, a different temperature, all those matter.”

The second leg of the partnership is set to begin in 2027, when WestJet Rewards and Tims Rewards members will be able to link their accounts to earn points from both programs when they make eligible purchases at Tim Hortons.

The companies said account linking will also unlock exclusive offers and promotions. Additional details regarding the loyalty partnership and member benefits will be announced closer to the rollout, which is likely around a year away.

“It’s pretty simple in the sense that it’s pretty low friction, you link your account once, you go and every Timbit gets you closer to your next vacation,” said Steve McClelland, the airline’s vice-president of loyalty and strategic partnerships.

He called it a “natural partnership,” especially at a time when the buy Canadian trend is seeing a resurgence amid trade tensions with the United States. While the team-up with Tims is not a “response” to the geopolitical situation, McClelland said the “broader context of the world at large today certainly reinforces that fit.”

“There are only a few brands that are as Canadiana, as like deeply entrenched in the Canadian culture, as Tims,” he said.

“There’s only maybe a handful, if that, and we’re partnered with already quite a few of them.”

Tims has also been joining forces with other Canadian companies recently. Earlier this month, it announced a separate loyalty program collaboration with Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd.

Under that deal, customers who link their Triangle Rewards and Tims Rewards accounts can earn between two and five per cent in Canadian Tire money in addition to Tims points on select Tims purchases.

Canadian Tire money can be redeemed for savings on purchases at the retailer as well as its other banners, including SportChek, Mark’s and Party City. Tims points can be used to purchase food and beverages at the chain.

Canadian Tire has about 12 million Triangle Rewards members and 1,600 locations across its banners. Tims counts eight million loyalty program users and 4,000 restaurants in Canada.

Bagozzi said the moves are about being “realistic” that customers May prefer to save up for larger purchases such as flights or home goods rather than just coffee and doughnuts.

“We would have been having conversations even before any political changes, but having said that, even some of the celebrities that we partner with, hockey stars, we tend to gravitate to Canadian partners because we’re such a quintessential Canadian brand,” she said.

“It just kind of makes sense for us to do that.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 17, 2026.

Under that deal, customers who link their Triangle Rewards and Tims Rewards accounts can earn between two and five per cent in Canadian Tire money in addition to Tims points on select Tims purchases.

Canadian Tire money can be redeemed for savings on purchases at the retailer as well as its other banners, including SportChek, Mark’s and Party City. Tims points can be used to purchase food and beverages at the chain.
Canadian Tire has about 12 million Triangle Rewards members and 1,600 locations across its banners. Tims counts eight million loyalty program users and 4,000 restaurants in Canada.
Bagozzi said the moves are about being “realistic” that customers May prefer to save up for larger purchases such as flights or home goods rather than just coffee and doughnuts.

“We would have been having conversations even before any political changes, but having said that, even some of the celebrities that we partner with, hockey stars, we tend to gravitate to Canadian partners because we’re such a quintessential Canadian brand,” she said.

stories.summary: Travelling around London, I see a lot of rarely used bike lanes and poorly arranged bus rapid transit (BRT) lanes.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Cyclists use the bike lanes on Dundas Street, west of Adelaide Street, in London on Monday, May 19, 2025. (Dale Carruthers/The London Free Press)

Travelling around London, I see a lot of rarely used bike lanes and poorly arranged bus rapid transit (BRT) lanes.

Why are BRT lanes on Wellington Road south and downtown in the middle of the road?

The bike path at Ridout Street and Commissioners Road is rarely used.

Go back to the old way: Sidewalks used by humans, their kids and bikes.

Roy Hanson, London

Last week, council’s planning and environment committee endorsed a proposed eight-storey apartment building on Sarnia Road, not far from the university. This replaces two once-posh homes in a beautiful family neighbourhood. Nimby, yes, but sometimes offensive non-descript structures don’t fit.

But a few months ago, council rejected a proposed retirement home community development at 945 Bluegrass Dr. It was well planned and documented for a retirement home community. But neighbours killed the four-storey build in a clear case of Nimby.

These two decisions show this city needs some consistent planning principles.

stories.title: Defying the odds: Renal patient celebrates 37 years on dialysis
stories.summary: September 17, 2026
stories.content:
September 17, 2026

Thirty-seven years ago, in 1989, music artists like Chicago, Paula Abdul, and Bette Midler were topping the charts (and future chart topper Taylor Swift was born). Movies such as Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, Back to the Future Part II, and The Little Mermaid were bringing in huge audiences to theatres and only about 1.5 per cent of the Canadian population had a cell phone.

Technology looked a lot different. You had an actual camera to take photos, a paper map for directions, and a Walkman to play music on-the-go.

What else happened thirty-seven years ago? Maria Medeiros started dialysis.

Maria was diagnosed with polycystic kidney disease (PKD) in the 1980s. PKD is an inherited disorder that causes fluid-filled cysts to grow in the kidneys.

"I was diagnosed with PKD a number of years before I started dialysis through blood work," Maria explains. "But it reached a point where my kidneys were not functioning properly anymore and I needed to start dialysis. I started my dialysis at the old Victoria Hospital in 1989 and went there for one year before going to Base Line Road when they had the dialysis centre. Now I go to Westmount as they transferred the program there."

Over the 37 years, Maria has also been the recipient of three kidney transplants, but unfortunately, they did not take. She became quite sick after her transplants and even ended up in intensive care.

"I am the only person in my family with polycystic kidney disease - none of my siblings have this. And when I started dialysis, I already had three children," shares Maria. "When my family was being tested as possible kidney donors, my siblings were not a match, but my daughter, who was 17 years old at the time, was. However, she was too young to donate, so I had to move forward with unrelated donors."

Maria notes the difficulties she experienced balancing raising three small children (the oldest was 10 years old when she started dialysis) and going to dialysis treatment in- centre three times a week. She shares that her social worker at that time helped her with balance when she was starting dialysis.

All of Maria's original care team members have left or retired, but she remains grateful for everyone's excellent care over the decades.

Maria says that "Dialysis has felt like a family where the team made it feel less medical. The staff have been great and always accommodate whatever I need. I like to make food, especially around Christmas, and bring it in for staff because I know they always do their best."

While having to go into the clinic three times a week for dialysis has been taxing in some ways, Maria is grateful for her care and hopes for many more years to spend with family.

"My children and I are close, and I have a granddaughter now. It's been a pleasure to see my children grow up and to meet my grandchild," Maria says.

"I've been a nurse practitioner for almost three decades," says JulieAnn Lawrence, Nurse Practitioner, Westmount Hemodialysis Unit, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC). "And while it's not frequent that I continue to care for patients from when I began, I've had about five of my patients approach the 30-year mark in their dialysis treatment."

Lawrence emphasizes the patient's strict adherence to the many lifestyle restrictions that come with kidney disease.

"Restrictions in diet, managing medications, keeping to dialysis schedules, attention to small deviations in their health status require an intense amount of energy, dedication, and resilience to incorporate in their everyday life," Lawrence explains. "That helps provide longevity, but people living with kidney disease have their own journey. Over the past decades there have been improvements to primary care support for the management of kidney disease, advancement in transplantation and immunosuppressive medication, as well as innovations and improvements in various dialysis modalities that not only extend life but enhance the quality of life."

Thanks to advancements and improvements in funding and the model of care, more recently, patients are treated holistically in the early stages of kidney disease to slow or reverse progression. Lawrence shares that this means that when patients end up needing dialysis, they will have support along the way as they participate in decisions around the treatment that suits their experience and care pathways that enhance patient outcomes.

Lawrence says, "There are still many kidney diseases that are related to autoimmune disorders and genetic conditions, such as Maria's polycystic kidney disease, and as more inheritable conditions are identified, there will hopefully be early surveillance and intervention opportunities in the future so those future generations May not need dialysis or transplantation."

A lot has changed in 37 years in dialysis, and Lawrence notes that improvements in access and the therapies themselves have helped give people more years to their life, and life to their years.

"Thankfully, now with regional hemodialysis programs, optimization of home therapies such as home hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, as well as the introduction and improvements made to virtual care – more patients are able to access dialysis and enjoy a reasonable quality of life," Lawrence shares.

content_blocks.text: A lot has changed in 37 years in dialysis, and Lawrence notes that improvements in access and the therapies themselves have helped give people more years to their life, and life to their years.

"Thankfully, now with regional hemodialysis programs, optimization of home therapies such as home hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, as well as the introduction and improvements made to virtual care – more patients are able to access dialysis and enjoy a reasonable quality of life," Lawrence shares.

stories.title: Serious motor vehicle collision
stories.summary: London, ON (September 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section are investigating a serious motor vehicle collision involving a cyclist that took place in the downtown core yesterday afternoon.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (September 17, 2026) –Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section are investigating a serious motor vehicle collision involving a cyclist that took place in the downtown core yesterday afternoon.

On Wednesday, September 16, 2026, at approximately 4 p.m., emergency services responded to the intersection of Dundas and Maitland streets after a collision involving a motor vehicle and a cyclist.

An adult male cyclist was transported to hospital by paramedic services with life-threatening injuries. He remains in critical condition.

The driver of the involved vehicle remained at the scene.

The investigation has been reassigned to the LPS Road Safety Section and remains ongoing.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 3:45 p.m. and 4 p.m. on September 16, 2026, who May have dash-cam footage, or residential or business video surveillance, to contact police.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously toLondon Middlesex Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Base Line Road East will close for underground servicing work
stories.summary: Starting Monday, September 21, Base Line Road East will be closed between High Street and Ridout Street South until approximately September 2
stories.content:
Starting Monday, September 21, Base Line Road East will be closed between High Street and Ridout Street South until approximately September 24 while private underground servicing work connects water, storm sewers, and sanitary sewers to a property in the area.

A detour will be posted via High Street, Emery Street East, and Ridout Street South.

The south sidewalk will also be closed. Access to homes in the area will be maintained.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules.

This work is taking place near Wellington Gateway Phase 2A and 2B construction. Drivers should expect delays and changing traffic conditions in the area and follow posted signs and detours.
