stories.title: Canada Investment Summit live: Ottawa to raise billions by privatizing airport operations, Carney says
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto has entered its second day. Read the latest news here.
stories.author: Financial Post Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto has entered its second day, as the government looks to drum up billions in commitments to jumpstart the economy.

Fund managers controlling upwards of $120 trillion in assets have travelled from as far abroad as Australia and Singapore, as well as from the United States. They are here to evaluate infrastructure projects such as pipelines, ports and transportation networks and explore opportunities in Canada’s resource sector, from energy to critical minerals.

For more in-depth coverage from the Canada Investment Summit, click here.

Here’s the latest news from the Canada Investment Summit:

Prime Minister Mark Carney kicked off the main day of the Canada Investment Summit Tuesday by announcing that Canada will seek private investment to operate the country’s four biggest airports and use the capital raised — expected to be in the “tens of billions of dollars” — to reinvest in other priorities.

“Following best practice in other countries, the Government of Canada will retain ownership of the underlying land and assets, but we will unlock their true value, by bringing in new capital and expertise into their operations and growth,” Carney said in his opening remarks.

The four largest airports are Toronto Pearson , Vancouver International, Montreal Pierre Elliott Trudeau International and Calgary International.

“Canadian pension funds already invest successfully in many airports around the world. It is time to bring that same expertise home to more directly benefit all Canadians,” Carney said.

The prime minister also said during the address that the government is on track to balance its “operating budget” ahead of schedule next year, “while maintaining the lowest overall deficit in the G7.”

Carney’s government split the budget into operating and capital segments.

–Financial Post Staff

“Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponized. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said. “Financial plumbing as coercion. Supply chains as vulnerabilities to be exploited.”

He said in such a situation, “First, we must take care of ourselves,” and that means building strength at home and diversifying trade partnerships abroad.

He also reiterated the federal government’s goal of catalyzing $1 trillion of investment in Canada over the next five years in sectors such as energy, transportation, data and defence.

“We are unleashing our full potential as an energy superpower,” he said.

Canadian businesses now enjoy tariff-free access to 1.5 billion consumers, Carney said, and Ottawa intends to double that through new trade deals from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to India over the next six months.

He also had a message for the United States.

“We will always be neighbours and Canada will continue to be the U.S.’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. “After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties.”

But these arrangements will only work when “we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”

He said Canada will be an even better partner, one that’s stronger, more resilient and more independent, when those opportunities return.

Radical Ventures announced the first close of its Radical Breakouts Fund, touted as the largest-ever venture capital fund in Canadian history, with over US$1 billion in commitments raised so far to support AI scale-ups.

The announcement came Tuesday at the investing summit in Toronto which featured a panel on Financing Canada’s Frontier Technology Champions.

“Canada has never had a shortage of world-class AI companies. What we have lacked is capital at the scale required to keep them here as they grow,” said Jordan Jacobs, Radical Ventures co-founder in a news release.

“For decades that meant our best companies looked to the U.S. to fund their most important years, and much of the value they created went with them. The Radical Breakouts Fund closes that gap.”

The fund is backed by some of Canada’s biggest pension funds including PSP Investments, CPP Investments and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan (Hoopp), as well as Toronto-Dominion Bank Group, Bank of Montreal Financial Group, CI Global Asset Management and other leading global investors.

Its portfolio includes Cohere Inc. and Xanadu Quantum Technologies, and several other firms, such as Discovery Loop, co-founded by former Google chief scientist Jeff Dean, and self-driving technology company Waabi Innovation Inc.

Canada has a reputation of being slow, Deborah Orida, who heads PSP investments, one of Canada’s largest pension funds, told Mark Carney on stage at the summit.

He responded by saying Ottawa has recognized the issue and the federal government is going to work towards being more predictable for investors.

“If we’re going to say ‘no,’ a quick no is necessary,” he said.

He also said Ottawa will look to make legislative changes to speed up reviews of potential projects, like it has done for the roughly two dozen projects under the Major Projects Office , which is a government body advancing key Canadian projects.

Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said none of the pledges to invest more in Canada will amount to much if they aren’t followed by action.

“This is a start, not an end,” he said. “We’re doing things like putting in place more favourable tax treatments; we’re improving our regulatory timelines; we’re creating new tools to create new partnerships with indigenous peoples. We’re doing all the things that are going to make this a long-term sustainable trend.”

He said the success of the summit should not be measured by how many of the 167 projects that the federal government included in a prospectus handed to investors at the conference receive new capital commitments, but by how many are actually built in the coming years.

Still, Hodgson said Canada is seeing “record inward foreign investment” and likened the summit to a victory lap of sorts, in which his government can reap the rewards from the work it has already done and continues to do to make the country more investable.

“Canada has taken action to make it a more predictable place for investment, a more welcoming place for investment,” he said. “We started that with a new tone in government.”

— Gabriel Friedman

The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. have announced a new $50-billion Maple Fund for large-scale investments in Canada, including funding for critical infrastructure and “strategic industries.”

The fund, which will be a joint cooperation framework, will structure the investments on a 50-50 basis, with up to $25 billion in equity capital from each organization over an initial five-year period.

According to a news release, the Maple Fund will focus on opportunities with total project values greater than $5 billion in equity capital. Other investors are also welcome to partner with the two companies to expand the capital and capabilities on individual investments.

Each project will be independently assessed and approved by CPP Investments and Brookfield.

“Canada is entering a period of new ambition to advance major projects and build for the future, creating compelling investment opportunities across the country,” said John Graham, chief executive of the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, in the release Tuesday morning.

“The Maple Fund positions us well to meet this moment and move with speed on opportunities of unusual scale and complexity when they offer compelling value for the CPP Fund.”

Connor Teskey, chief executive of Brookfield Asset Management Ltd., said the Maple Fund can help drive a generational investment program that will invest in critical infrastructure, industries and businesses that will, in turn, support the growth of globally competitive Canadian businesses.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s goal to attract $1 trillion in investments at his Toronto summit “won’t be enough” to turn around decades of underspending, one economist says.

“While $1 trillion in investment over the next five years sounds impressive, it will not be enough,” Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said in a note, adding that decades of underinvestment have left Canada badly trailing other countries when it comes to capital per worker.

“The gap continues to grow every year,” he said.

He estimated that the “bare minimum” just to stop Canada falling further behind other Oecd countries will require $180 billion to $200 billion in investment per year or $0.9 trillion to $1.1 trillion over the next five years.

Narrowing the gap would require $400 billion to $450 billion per year over the next decade, he said.

Most of those funds will have to come from foreign investors with Canada’s domestic sectors including households, government and corporations in no position to be lenders.

But foreign lenders won’t invest in Canada just because it’s seen as more secure. Canada still has to compete with the rest of the world to attract funds, he said.

“Attracting foreign capital will require returns, but also greater certainty about project completion and reduced risks,” St-Arnaud said.

The economist said there are some risks associated with foreign investment including that profits leave the country and that foreign investors have more influence over government policy.

“Despite these risks, foreign investment is undoubtedly beneficial to the Canadian economy; without it, only a fraction of the investment needed to improve Canada’s economy would move forward, and Canada’s challenges would only get bigger,” St-Arnaud said.

Tuesday’s docket at the Canada investment summit is packed with big name CEOs and investment powerbrokers from around the world. Here is a look at some of the highlights.

8:50 AM: Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers keynote address and fireside chat.

9:20 AM: Panel session on critical minerals featuring Tim Gitzel, chief executive of Cameco Corporation and Jonathan Price, chief executive of Teck Resources Ltd.

9:55 AM: Panel session on technology featuring Aidan Gomez, chief executive of Cohere Inc. and Christian Weedbrook, chief executive of Xanadu Quantum Technologies.

1:10 PM: Panel session on global capital featuring Larry Fink, chief executive BlackRock Inc. and Jon Gray, chief operating officer of Blackstone Inc.

1:50 PM: Panel session on defense and advanced manufacturing featuring Daniel Goldberg, chief executive of Telesat Corporation and Éric Martel, chief executive of Bombardier Inc.

2:25 PM: Panel session on growth equity in Canada featuring Dave McKay, chief executive of Royal Bank of Canada.

4:00 PM: Panel session on financing Canada’s future from a global perspective featuring Christian Sewing, chief executive at Deutsche Bank AG and C.S. Venkatakrishnan, group chief executive at Barclays.

4:20 PM: Panel session on Canada’s energy sector featuring Rich Kruger, chief executive at Suncor Energy Inc. and François Poirier, chief executive at TC Energy Corporation.

5:55 PM: Closing remarks delivered by former prime minister Stephen Harper

Toronto-Dominion Bank and the Bank of Scotia have joined the other big Canadian banks in committing to deploy billions of dollars in the next five years into sectors critical for the Canadian economy.

TD has committed $150 billion with a focus on energy, critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence and infrastructure.

“Canada is entering a defining period of investment and industrial growth that will shape the country’s economy for decades to come,” chief executive Raymond Chun said in a statement on Monday. “TD will connect investors with opportunity, help businesses scale and strengthen the sectors critical to Canada’s next era of growth.”

Scotiabank is committing $100 billion to similar sectors and is launching an institute to help policymakers, business leaders and markets decide what’s best for Canada’s competitiveness.

In an interview with Bloomberg News at the Canada Investment Summit, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he is not going to slow down expanding trade with other nations, but that a deal with the United States is still possible.

Negotiations fell apart last month, with both sides pointing the finger when it comes to who’s to blame.

The U.S. has since upped tariffs on Canada to as much as 50 per cent and Canada has responded in kind with dollar-for-dollar tariffs of their own.

“We’ll sit down when it makes sense,” Carney said. “Canada and the U.S. have a very long relationship. We sometimes go through periods where there are tensions in that relationship. Provided we continue this approach, we’ll come to some agreement at some point.”

With files from Barbara Shecter, Naimul Karim and Bloomberg News

content_blocks.text: He also had a message for the United States.

“We will always be neighbours and Canada will continue to be the U.S.’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. “After all, even at times of disagreement during our long history, we have always maintained deep ties.”
But these arrangements will only work when “we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”
He said Canada will be an even better partner, one that’s stronger, more resilient and more independent, when those opportunities return.
Radical Ventures raises over US$1 billion to support AI scale-ups

Radical Ventures announced the first close of its Radical Breakouts Fund, touted as the largest-ever venture capital fund in Canadian history, with over US$1 billion in commitments raised so far to support AI scale-ups.
The announcement came Tuesday at the investing summit in Toronto which featured a panel on Financing Canada’s Frontier Technology Champions.

“Canada has never had a shortage of world-class AI companies. What we have lacked is capital at the scale required to keep them here as they grow,” said Jordan Jacobs, Radical Ventures co-founder in a news release.
“For decades that meant our best companies looked to the U.S. to fund their most important years, and much of the value they created went with them. The Radical Breakouts Fund closes that gap.”

The fund is backed by some of Canada’s biggest pension funds including PSP Investments, CPP Investments and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan (Hoopp), as well as Toronto-Dominion Bank Group, Bank of Montreal Financial Group, CI Global Asset Management and other leading global investors.
content_blocks.html: The fund is backed by some of Canada’s biggest pension funds including PSP Investments, CPP Investments and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan (HOOPP), as well as Toronto-Dominion Bank Group, Bank of Montreal Financial Group, CI Global Asset Management and other leading global investors.

content_blocks.text: Its portfolio includes Cohere Inc. and Xanadu Quantum Technologies, and several other firms, such as Discovery Loop, co-founded by former Google chief scientist Jeff Dean, and self-driving technology company Waabi Innovation Inc.
Canada has a ‘slow’ reputation: PSP Investments
Canada has a reputation of being slow, Deborah Orida, who heads PSP investments, one of Canada’s largest pension funds, told Mark Carney on stage at the summit.
He responded by saying Ottawa has recognized the issue and the federal government is going to work towards being more predictable for investors.
“If we’re going to say ‘no,’ a quick no is necessary,” he said.

He also said Ottawa will look to make legislative changes to speed up reviews of potential projects, like it has done for the roughly two dozen projects under the Major Projects Office , which is a government body advancing key Canadian projects.

content_blocks.text: In for the long haul, Hodgson says

content_blocks.alt: Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson attends the 2026 Annual General Assembly of Assembly of First Nations (AFN) in Ottawa on July 16, 2026.
content_blocks.caption: Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Tim Hodgson attends the 2026 Annual General Assembly of Assembly of First Nations (AFN) in Ottawa on July 16, 2026. Photo by HYUNGCHEOL PARK/Postmedia

content_blocks.text: Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said none of the pledges to invest more in Canada will amount to much if they aren’t followed by action.

“This is a start, not an end,” he said. “We’re doing things like putting in place more favourable tax treatments; we’re improving our regulatory timelines; we’re creating new tools to create new partnerships with indigenous peoples. We’re doing all the things that are going to make this a long-term sustainable trend.”

He said the success of the summit should not be measured by how many of the 167 projects that the federal government included in a prospectus handed to investors at the conference receive new capital commitments, but by how many are actually built in the coming years.

Still, Hodgson said Canada is seeing “record inward foreign investment” and likened the summit to a victory lap of sorts, in which his government can reap the rewards from the work it has already done and continues to do to make the country more investable.
“Canada has taken action to make it a more predictable place for investment, a more welcoming place for investment,” he said. “We started that with a new tone in government.”
— Gabriel Friedman

content_blocks.text: CPP, Brookfield launch $50-billion Maple Fund

The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. have announced a new $50-billion Maple Fund for large-scale investments in Canada, including funding for critical infrastructure and “strategic industries.”
content_blocks.html: The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. have announced a new $50-billion Maple Fund for large-scale investments in Canada, including funding for critical infrastructure and “strategic industries.”

content_blocks.text: The fund, which will be a joint cooperation framework, will structure the investments on a 50-50 basis, with up to $25 billion in equity capital from each organization over an initial five-year period.

According to a news release, the Maple Fund will focus on opportunities with total project values greater than $5 billion in equity capital. Other investors are also welcome to partner with the two companies to expand the capital and capabilities on individual investments.
Each project will be independently assessed and approved by CPP Investments and Brookfield.

“Canada is entering a period of new ambition to advance major projects and build for the future, creating compelling investment opportunities across the country,” said John Graham, chief executive of the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, in the release Tuesday morning.
“The Maple Fund positions us well to meet this moment and move with speed on opportunities of unusual scale and complexity when they offer compelling value for the CPP Fund.”

Connor Teskey, chief executive of Brookfield Asset Management Ltd., said the Maple Fund can help drive a generational investment program that will invest in critical infrastructure, industries and businesses that will, in turn, support the growth of globally competitive Canadian businesses.
Carney’s $1 trillion investment goal ‘not enough,’ warns economist
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s goal to attract $1 trillion in investments at his Toronto summit “won’t be enough” to turn around decades of underspending, one economist says.

“While $1 trillion in investment over the next five years sounds impressive, it will not be enough,” Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said in a note, adding that decades of underinvestment have left Canada badly trailing other countries when it comes to capital per worker.
“The gap continues to grow every year,” he said.

He estimated that the “bare minimum” just to stop Canada falling further behind other Oecd countries will require $180 billion to $200 billion in investment per year or $0.9 trillion to $1.1 trillion over the next five years.
Narrowing the gap would require $400 billion to $450 billion per year over the next decade, he said.
Most of those funds will have to come from foreign investors with Canada’s domestic sectors including households, government and corporations in no position to be lenders.
But foreign lenders won’t invest in Canada just because it’s seen as more secure. Canada still has to compete with the rest of the world to attract funds, he said.
“Attracting foreign capital will require returns, but also greater certainty about project completion and reduced risks,” St-Arnaud said.
The economist said there are some risks associated with foreign investment including that profits leave the country and that foreign investors have more influence over government policy.

“Despite these risks, foreign investment is undoubtedly beneficial to the Canadian economy; without it, only a fraction of the investment needed to improve Canada’s economy would move forward, and Canada’s challenges would only get bigger,” St-Arnaud said.
What’s on the docket today?
Tuesday’s docket at the Canada investment summit is packed with big name CEOs and investment powerbrokers from around the world. Here is a look at some of the highlights.

content_blocks.text: TD, Scotiabank commit billions

Toronto-Dominion Bank and the Bank of Scotia have joined the other big Canadian banks in committing to deploy billions of dollars in the next five years into sectors critical for the Canadian economy.
TD has committed $150 billion with a focus on energy, critical minerals, defence, artificial intelligence and infrastructure.

“Canada is entering a defining period of investment and industrial growth that will shape the country’s economy for decades to come,” chief executive Raymond Chun said in a statement on Monday. “TD will connect investors with opportunity, help businesses scale and strengthen the sectors critical to Canada’s next era of growth.”
Scotiabank is committing $100 billion to similar sectors and is launching an institute to help policymakers, business leaders and markets decide what’s best for Canada’s competitiveness.

In an interview with Bloomberg News at the Canada Investment Summit, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he is not going to slow down expanding trade with other nations, but that a deal with the United States is still possible.
Negotiations fell apart last month, with both sides pointing the finger when it comes to who’s to blame.
The U.S. has since upped tariffs on Canada to as much as 50 per cent and Canada has responded in kind with dollar-for-dollar tariffs of their own.

“We’ll sit down when it makes sense,” Carney said. “Canada and the U.S. have a very long relationship. We sometimes go through periods where there are tensions in that relationship. Provided we continue this approach, we’ll come to some agreement at some point.”

stories.title: B.C. journalist, harassed by ‘cult-like’ China protest group, wins defamation payout
stories.summary: The group of up to 60 people distributed pamphlets describing their baseless claims that the journalist and commentator was a traitor and an agent of China.
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
The crowds of protesters gathered outside Gao Bing Chen’s home on a cul-de-sac in Surrey, B.C., for 11 weeks, rain or shine.

The group of up to 60 people distributed pamphlets describing their baseless claims that the journalist and commentator was a traitor and an agent of China.

They played funeral music outside Gao’s house, upsetting his wife, young daughter and mother-in-law, and livestreamed the protests around the world, where they were watched by up to 100,000 people.

They harassed his wife and told her to get a divorce.

Two of them beat up a friend of Gao’s outside the home, resulting in assault convictions.

Now, six years after his ordeal began, Gao has been awarded $275,000 in defamation damages from one of his tormentors, Yun Fei Zhu.

“Justice might be delayed, but it will never come too late,” said Gao in an interview in Mandarin on Monday.

“This is likely the first case in Canada where protesters managed to move cyberbullying directly from the internet to my doorstep, livestreaming for five hours a day for 77 consecutive days. If I were not tough enough, I might have lost my mind already.”

Last week’s ruling says Gao suffered “severe distress” from the defamatory comments, forcing him to consider moving his family out of Canada entirely.

The harassment stemmed from Gao’s criticism of exiled Chinese businessman and convicted fraudster Guo Wengui, who had set up a project called the New Federal State of China with Steve Bannon, the former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump.

It was presented as a political movement to overthrow the Chinese Communist Party, and had a presence in Vancouver and Toronto, but the B.C. Supreme Court defamation ruling says critics regarded Guo and the New Federal State of China as “unreliable, conspiratorial and cult‑like.”

Gao was himself a critic of China’s government, testifying that he was well known in the Chinese Canadian community “as a pro‑democracy activist and commentator.” But the trouble began when he took issue with Guo’s movement.

Zhu, who lives in White Rock, B.C., livestreamed the protests that ensued outside Gao’s home for weeks, five hours a day. They began on Sept. 15, 2020.

“In the course of those livestreams, Gao was called many things, including a spy whose hands were covered in the blood of democracy activists. There is no evidence to suggest any of that is true,” says the ruling by Justice Richard Hewson.

While Gao said the ruling brought him tears and relief, it could not undo the harm to him, his family and their neighbours.

Zhu is described in the ruling as a freelance handyman and goldsmith who operates a YouTube channel about events of interest in the Chinese-Canadian community.

He “does not appear to be a man of means,” the ruling notes, adding that paying the defamation award will be a considerable hardship.

But the impact on Gao was extreme.

“His standing in the Chinese-Canadian community was destroyed,” the ruling says. “He is no longer able to participate in the community in the ways and to nearly the extent that he had in the past. He deserves to have his reputation vindicated.”

Hewson awarded $250,000 in general damages, plus $25,000 in aggravated damages.

Gao said the accusations against him outlined in the pamphlets, which were also distributed to neighbours, were all nonsense.

“These protesters tried to cancel me from my neighbourhood, my family, my community,” said Gao.

“Every time my wife tried to leave home, they would approach her, asking her to ‘hurry up and file a divorce,’ saying she shouldn’t have married a spy from the Chinese Communist Party and if she didn’t do it, our marriage would fail.”

When the protests started up again in 2023, Gao briefly left Canada, hoping his family would be left in peace.

“There were clear allegations of criminal conduct, including treason, all of which were made without any investigation of the truth,” Hewson’s ruling says.

“(Gao) knew they were being extensively circulated. He considered moving his family out of the area and perhaps leaving his home in Canada entirely.”

The ruling says Zhu admitted that in 2024 and 2025 he continued to make similar statements about Gao.

Zhu could not immediately be reached for comment.

As for Guo, he was sentenced to 30 years in a U.S. jail for fraud in July.

Judge Analisa Torres in the Southern District of New York said Guo “preyed on those seeking to bring democracy to China,” taking their money so he could live lavishly, saying he had called upon supporters “to harass and intimidate those who dare to speak out against him.”

Although he is relieved, Gao said he’s still haunted by the months-long protest.

“I am hoping to move on, but it’s hard. The fear and trauma lingers,” he said.

stories.title: Price reduction on Summerhill townhouse uncorks three offers
stories.summary: Three-bedroom home sells for almost $2-million
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
60 Alcorn Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $1,999,995 (June, 2026)

Previous asking price: $2.15-million (June, 2026)

Selling price: $1,975,000 (June, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $1,005,000 (June, 2011); $667,000 (February, 2004); $717,900 (August, 2003); $419,000 (November, 1996)

Taxes: $9,901 (2025)

Days on the market: Three

Property days on market: 24

Listing agents: Debbie Penzo and Graeme McIntosh, Chestnut Park Real Estate Ltd.

This three-bedroom townhouse in Summerhill west of Yonge Street is only 250 metres from Cottingham Junior Public School. Listed for sale in June, it became a popular stop for house hunters.

“We had lots of open houses and lots of people through,” said agent Graeme McIntosh.

“[For homes] east of Yonge, kids have to cross Yonge Street to get to the school and parks, whereas if they were here, west of Yonge, you’re already on the other side of the busy street.”

After three weeks with no offers, the asking price on the freehold property was reduced by $150,005. Within days, the owners received three bids.

“My team, with the seller, discussed this price improvement strategy and it generated immediate momentum with 13 showings in three days, which resulted in three competitive offers,” Mr. McIntosh said.

“One buyer’s agent told me they were looking up to $2-million, and when we were priced at $2.15-million, it wasn’t in their range.”

This three-storey townhouse was built in 1980 on the site of a former bakery. It has a street-level entrance with heated steps and a built-in garage facing a lane behind the 14- by 76-foot lot.

There is an eat-in kitchen and a dining area, as well as a living room with a gas fireplace, 17-foot ceilings and access to a terrace.

A smaller deck is on the third floor. Bathrooms are on each level, including the basement.

“These are called The Bakery Townhomes, and there are about three or four models,” Mr. McIntosh said.

“This one was move-in ready, and it also has 17-foot ceilings on the main floor in the living room.”

stories.title: Seller accepts market decline, condo sold below purchase price
stories.summary: Corner unit has an east-facing balcony off the den and a south-facing balcony off the kitchen by the living room
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
1480 Bayly St., No. 1212, Pickering, Ont.

Asking price: $548,800 (July, 2026)

Selling price: $545,500 (August, 2026)

Previous selling price: $561,504 (January, 2023)

Taxes: $5,501 (2025)

Days on the market: 11

Listing agent: Trevor C. Nicolle, Royal LePage Signature Realty

The owners of this two-bedroom plus den unit bought it preconstruction for $561,504 and intended to move in after completion in 2022. In the interim, they found a larger unit, essentially leaving this one empty within a multitower development near Pickering GO station and Highway 401. They decided to sell it this summer and, despite a similar unit going up for sale in the building, their agent staged it and priced it under $550,000.

“In today’s market, you have to be sharp with your pricing and understand there’s been a pullback in values in condominiums in the GTA as a whole,” said agent Trevor C. Nicolle.

“I also did a very aggressive marketing campaign with photography and videography on Instagram, Facebook and LinkedIn, and that’s the best way to get exposure on a listing.”

The 950-square-foot unit only had four visitors before one buyer purchased it for $545,500.

“The sellers knew values have pulled back,” Mr. Nicolle said. “At the same time, they’ll free up equity.

“It was an opportunity for someone to get into a brand-new unit, only lived in for three or four days.”

This corner unit has an east-facing balcony off the den and a south-facing balcony off the kitchen by the living room.

There are two bedrooms, two full bathrooms and a laundry closet.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $889 include heating.

“It’s a unique unit with two balconies,” said Mr. Nicolle.

“The appeal of this development is it’s right beside the Pickering GO station … and it’s south of the 401.”

stories.title: More than half of parents helping adult children financially, RBC report says
stories.summary: Parents gave more than $6,100 on average for groceries, rent and other expenses
stories.content:
A new report by RBC says just over half of Canadian parents with adult children say they are still helping them out financially with expenses including groceries and rent.

The report says 51 per cent of parents with adult children aged 18 to 40 surveyed say they provided financial support in the past year.

Of those helping out, 56 per cent say the money was to help pay for groceries, while 43 per cent have helped with an unexpected or emergency expense.

Twenty-four per cent say the money was to help pay for rent.

On average, the report finds parents who provided financial support gave $6,151, while 24 per cent gave more than $10,000.

The report was based on an online survey of 1,000 Canadian parents with children aged 18 to 40 done for RBC between July 2 and July 8.

The polling industry’s professional body, the Canadian Research Insights Council, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

stories.title: CPP Investments and Brookfield launch $50B fund to invest in big Canadian projects
stories.summary: Toronto — Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. have announced a new $50-billion fund for large-scale investments in Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. have announced a new $50-billion fund aimed at backing critical infrastructure and strategic industry projects across Canada.

The so-called Maple Fund will see the two organizations invest on a 50-50 basis, with each committing up to $25 billion in equity over an initial five-year period.

The fund is one of the marquee announcements to emerge at a new investment summit in Toronto hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney in partnership with CPP Investments and PSP Investments, two of Canada’s largest pension investors.

CPP Investments chief executive John Graham said Canada is entering a period of new ambition to advance major projects and build for the future, creating compelling investment opportunities across the country.

“CPP Investments has the capital, long-term investment horizon and expertise to pursue these opportunities,” he said in a statement. “The Maple Fund brings together our strengths with Brookfield’s strong origination and development capabilities to help move ambitious projects from opportunity to investment.”

Graham added: “The Maple Fund positions us well to meet this moment and move with speed on opportunities of unusual scale and complexity when they offer compelling value for the CPP Fund.”

Connor Teskey, CEO of Brookfield Asset Management, said the fund brings together two companies with a shared commitment to investing in the country’s future.

The Maple Fund “can help drive a generational investment program to invest in critical infrastructure, industries and businesses that will support the growth of globally competitive Canadian businesses,” he said.

The inaugural Canada Investment Summit is a two-day gathering of global investors, Canadian business leaders and governments that seeks to help attract $1 trillion in new investment to Canada over the next five years.

The country’s big banks have also announced plans for billions in financing to support Canadian companies and projects in recent days.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 15, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:BAM, TSX:BN)

stories.title: Alberta's separatists have a Mark Carney problem
stories.summary: Whereas federal liberal policy normally helps Alberta's separatists, Prime Minister Mark Carney's popularity is having the opposite effect.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
In late 2024, Alberta’s separatists were riding high on a wave of anti-Trudeau sentiment. Public support for the Liberal government had hit fresh lows, and a decade of activist policymaking under the former prime minister had reinforced the province’s longtime skepticism that Ottawa could properly represent its interests.

Two years on, some Alberta separatists say that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s growing popularity among Canadians — as well as a new oil pipeline deal between Ottawa and Alberta — has likely changed the calculus for many voters ahead of the province’s October referendum.

“If Justin Trudeau had stayed in power, I’m quite sure we would have been able to (separate),” said Michael Wagner, a committed separatist and author of ‘No Other Option: Self-Determination for Alberta.’ “Because Mark Carney is trying to extend an olive branch, that’s kind of hurting our cause.”

Wagner, who was partaking in a pro-separatism event in Calgary on the weekend called “Capitalism & Morality,” was reflecting the views of many staunch separatists in attendance. While Carney’s efforts to appease Alberta haven’t convinced the separatist movement’s core supporters, people said, the swing in popularity could be enough to nudge more neutral voters away from outright separation.

“It’s reverse psychology, but our biggest salespeople have always been the Liberals,” Wagner said.

A new Leger poll puts Carney’s support at 49 per cent in September, up three points from a month earlier. That widens the gap over Pierre Poilievre’s Conservatives, which Leger put one point lower, at 33 per cent. It’s a sharp reversal of Liberal fortunes from late 2024 and early 2025, when Trudeau’s support had slumped to just over 20 per cent, according to various polls at the time.

Much of Carney’s growing support is a result of U.S. President Donald Trump’s taunts against Canada, both in matters of trade and sovereignty, which have galvanized federalist sentiments among Canadian voters.

Colby Cosh: Is Alberta's separatist movement already waning?

The fight for Alberta's 'soft separatists' — the conservatives who want to send Carney a message

In November, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Carney that includes a promise to build a new one-million-barrel-per-day pipeline to the B.C. coast, among other energy-related policies and targets.

The roughly $40-billion project, led by federal Crown agency Trans Mountain Corp., still needs to overcome a long list of political and legal hurdles before it is completed. The pipeline still has no private-sector company to lead the development, and doesn’t yet have the right-of-way to build a proposed terminal on the B.C. coast, south of Vancouver.

Drew Barnes, a former United Conservative Party member who was ousted from Jason Kenney’s caucus in 2021, said there are various headwinds facing the separatist movement. Smith’s increasingly vocal support for Alberta remaining in Canada is one, he said, as well as a “fragmented” media landscape that has stifled pro-independence voices.

“It’s a hard road now to get a message out,” he said.

Barnes, for his part, said he didn’t think that separatist support has lessened in recent months, but nonetheless acknowledged that the pace of growth has slowed since the closure of the pro-independence petition.

“I don’t think it’s waned, but it hasn’t grown with the momentum it started with,” he said.

If Justin Trudeau had stayed in power, I’m quite sure we would have been able to (separate)

Barnes, who was voted out of the UCP after he challenged Kenney over COVID-19 restrictions, said he is deeply skeptical of the proposed Alberta-Ottawa oil pipeline, which he noted will be funded almost entirely by taxpayers.

“Ottawa already gets too involved in our oil and gas business by playing with the environmental rules, and here we are allowing them to have direct ownership,” he said. “It’s just a step towards more inefficient government, more monopoly protection, the things that most Albertans disagree with.”

Wagner also said that the pipeline MOU was likely putting a damper on the separatist message.

“I do think it’s reducing our support, the MOU. Danielle Smith is saying: ‘look, it’s working for us.’”

By nature, Wagner said, Alberta’s separation movement is built on a sort of “reluctant support” in the sense that many Albertans would rather stay in Canada, if only they felt that the Canadian government would properly represent their interests. Yet, many Albertans see that as a mathematical impossibility given the province’s inherent underrepresentation in both the House of Commons and Senate.

Alberta is holding its referendum on Oct. 19, which will include 10 questions on a range of issues from separation to immigration to Senate reform.

stories.title: Developers look toward hotels for adaptive reuse
stories.summary: Plans pivot from condo, office projects amid softening of markets
stories.author: Wallace Immen
stories.content:
A Toronto skyscraper that was once the tallest building in the British Empire is set to take on a new life, transforming from downtown offices into a new luxury hotel.

The Beaux-Arts-style Canadian Pacific Building, a historic 15-storey 1913 landmark at the southeast corner of Yonge and King streets, will soon be converted into a 162-room hotel operated under Marriott International’s Tribute Portfolio, a mid-to-upscale collection of boutique accommodations.

The property was acquired by Montreal-based developer Artifact Group this past spring. It was previously owned by H&R Reit, which initially began planning to convert the office building into condominiums in 2022.

In Canada, developers are increasingly looking toward hotel conversions as the office and condo markets have softened in recent years, says Nicole Nguyen, senior vice-president of Cbre Canada’s Hotels Valuation and Advisory Services group.

Between 2022 and the first quarter of 2025, condo sales dropped by 75 per cent in Toronto and 37 per cent in Vancouver census metropolitan areas, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation . Inventories of unsold units have also more than doubled, with prices down by 7.5 per cent this year compared to last, says a report from the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board.

Ms. Nguyen says there’s ample room for growth in hotel development, which was stalled during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Since 2020, Canada has seen hotel development growth of just 0.5 per cent annually. Prior to that, annual hotel room growth averaged 1.5 per cent or more, according to a Cbre market report .

For 2026, average daily room rates were also forecast to grow by about five per cent, the report says.

“Since we haven’t been pumping a ton of new supply into the system, occupancy rates have stayed at record-high levels,” Ms. Nguyen says. “That makes developers want to get new supply into the pipeline.”

As a result, she expects the sector to see some of the strongest hotel supply growth it has seen in years.

“Overall, the Canadian accommodation sector continues to demonstrate resilience despite ongoing economic and geopolitical uncertainty,” Ms. Nguyen adds.

As of the second quarter of this year, a record 345 hotel projects with a total of 47,874 rooms are in the construction pipeline, according to a new report from hotel market data company Lodging Econometrics. This represents a four-per-cent increase in projects and a seven-per-cent increase in rooms compared to 2025.

Ontario is leading the charge on hotel constructions with 190 projects, representing 55 per cent of the total pipeline. British Columbia also has a record high of 77 projects, representing 22 per cent of the total, up by 13 per cent from 2025.

The cities in Canada developing the most hotels include Toronto with 71, Vancouver with 24 and Niagara Falls, Ont. with 41.

The Canadian Pacific Building at 69 Yonge St. in downtown Toronto housed the offices of the Canadian Pacific Railway, now part of Cpkc, until 1988.

Since then, H&R Reit acquired the building before Artifact Group bought it in April 2026, with the intention to turn it into a luxury Marriott hotel.

“The property will be repositioned through an adaptive reuse strategy into a 162-key lifestyle luxury hotel under Marriott International’s Tribute Portfolio brand, with a focus on design, wellness and elevated guest experience,” says Gaurav Gupta, Artifact Group’s president.

Details of the redevelopment, which is being planned by Giannone Petricone Associates Inc. Architects with interior design by Montreal-based Ivy Studio, have not yet been announced. However, Artifact Group expects renovations to begin in early 2027, with an anticipated opening in 2028.

The project is Artifact Group’s first in Ontario, complementing the company’s recent expansion of its Quebec hospitality portfolio with the acquisition of the 595-room, four-star DoubleTree by Hilton Montreal Downtown Hotel – a major part of the Complexe Desjardins shopping complex in the city’s Entertainment District.

Ms. Nguyen cautions that the speed of the hotel development pipeline will be dependent on the recovery of both the residential and commercial real estate markets.

While Vancouver and Toronto land values have dropped from their peaks a few years ago, they haven’t declined enough to make building an urban hotel profitable enough to support construction costs without some kind of additional residential component, she says, making it even more attractive to convert existing buildings into hotels.

Downtown Toronto hotels sometimes include residences for sale or rent.

Among recent examples, one includes Nobu Hotel Toronto , which opened last year atop the west tower of a 700-unit condominium building, designed by Teeple Architects and Turner Fleischer Architects. The new luxury hotel incorporates the façade of the former Pilkington Glass factory on Toronto’s Mercer Street.

The 224-room Le Méridien Toronto Pinnacle Hotel by Marriott is also scheduled to open later this year, occupying the bottom 12 floors of the 106-storey SkyTower condominium complex at Pinnacle One Yonge .

Amid the condo market slump, some developers have cancelled or delayed project construction starts since they were not able to sell at least 70 per cent of units beforehand – the threshold required to obtain construction financing from lenders.

But even if the real estate market recovers suddenly, the flow of new projects through the pipeline won’t immediately surge, Ms. Nguyen says.

“To get any new development approved and completed in Toronto takes a minimum of five years, so even if things were to magically rebound tomorrow, substantial openings are still several years out from today,” she adds.

stories.title: A tuxedo, a projector and a rejected film: Atom Egoyan’s unlikely road to Tiff
stories.summary: Egoyan says the biggest inspiration from his early years at Tiff was learning what it meant to be a filmmaker beyond the craft
stories.author: Aparita Bhandari
stories.content:
As the 51st Toronto International Film Festival takes over the city Sept. 10-20, this series of articles examines some of the Canadian directors whose lives and careers have been shaped by Tiff.

Atom Egoyan remembers his excitement when his first feature film, Next of Kin , was invited to screen at the Toronto International Film Festival in 1984 (then called the Festival of Festivals).

“The theatre was packed. There was a short [film] playing in front of it, and I thought, ‘Wow. This is great!’ Then once the short finished, 90 per cent of the people left. They had come to see the short. So that was sobering,” he says.

Egoyan’s debut might have been anticlimactic, but it was the inception of an illustrious film career spanning 16 feature films, two Oscar nominations, awards at Tiff, Cannes and other film festivals, eight Genie Awards and multiple honours including the Order of Canada. In addition to being one of the country’s most celebrated filmmakers, Egoyan’s body of work includes theatre, music, opera, television and art installations.

Born in Cairo to Armenian parents who immigrated to Canada in 1962, Egoyan fell into filmmaking through his early love for theatre. As a student at Glenlyon Preparatory School in Victoria, he wrote plays and presented them at a local drama festival.

“That’s important because the idea of festivals was really ingrained from there,” he says. “They were adjudicated; there were prizes.”

When Egoyan moved to Toronto to study international relations and classical guitar at the University of Toronto, he submitted a play to the school’s drama society. He remembers feeling confused when the play was rejected.

“I was obviously now a very small fish in a very large pond,” he says. “In Victoria, I was kind of a school star – writing these plays. And I was just so distressed that I thought, out of spite, I’ll make it a movie, because there was a film club at [U of T’s] Hart House,” he says, laughing at the memory.

Although it was trendy to make independent films, hardly any other students were doing it, he adds. “I think I was using the same camera that David Cronenberg used when he made his student film at U of T.”

Egoyan began writing movie reviews for The Newspaper , U of T’s community paper, eventually becoming film editor in the early days of Tiff.

“I had access to all these incredible, independent filmmakers who were coming into this city as I was making my short films. I got to meet Charles Burnett and John Sayles. And I realized that’s what I wanted to do,” he says. “And so, I had a dream of maybe one day making a film that would get into Tiff.”

Egoyan’s first attempt to get a short film shown at Tiff is part of the festival’s lore . When the film was rejected, Egoyan and fellow filmmaker Bruce McDonald, whose short didn’t make the cut either, rented a generator, got a 16mm projector, put on tuxedos and screened their films on the sidewalk outside the old University Theatre on Bloor – until the police shut them down.

“But we did an interview with Jeanne Beker at MuchMusic, so that was a big thing,” says Egoyan.

With Next of Kin , Family Viewing and Speaking Parts , Egoyan became a key member of the “Toronto New Wave” of English-Canadian filmmakers in the ’80s, says Jason Anderson, lead programmer at Tiff. Early successes at Cannes, Berlin and other festivals helped build Egoyan’s prominence at the same time as Tiff was developing its own international reputation.

“Atom had perfect timing in that respect,” says Anderson. “Films like The Adjuster and Exotica put forward this idea of cool, arty, auteurist Canadian cinema.” Mainstream success would follow in 1997 with Egoyan’s The Sweet Hereafter , which earned him two Oscar nominations and commercial success.

Egoyan says the biggest inspiration from his early years at Tiff was learning what it meant to be a filmmaker beyond the craft as he watched other directors present their films to audiences.

“Just to see how they introduced their work – the types of questions they were fielding, the whole persona of what it meant to be a director,” he says.

In recent years, he has served as a jurist at Tiff, which he says helps him stay in touch with the full spectrum of what is being made in Canada and elsewhere. For example, he had a chance to interact with American filmmaker Jane Schoenbrun as Jury Head for the 2024 Platform program.

“They asked me to write the introduction to the [screenplay] book of their film I Saw the TV Glow ,” he says. “We just became really close during the jury session, and it’s wonderful when you can connect with the next generation of filmmakers.”

Egoyan was a pioneer when it comes to themes around trauma and repression, says Anderson, specifically how those emotional responses and defence mechanisms May be expressed in behaviours we don’t understand. He points to a set piece in Exotica that occurs throughout the film, where Francis (Bruce Greenwood) visits a strip club to see exotic dancer Christina (Mia Kirshner) perform.

The two characters are “trapped in grief and repression,” says Anderson, “but it comes out in this sexualized ritual inside the strip club.”

Even though that establishment is “the least realistic strip club of all time,” he notes, “it doesn’t matter. It works for the movie. It’s very poignant; there’s even a Leonard Cohen song.”

Anderson adds that some young directors today are taking a similar approach by making films with that sexual charge.

“Jane Schoenbrun [is] one of them. You can see [Egoyan’s] influence on We’re All Going to the World’s Fair and I Saw the TV Glow . Or Censor by Prano Bailey-Bond. Or Babygirl by Halina Reijn,” says Anderson. “The arthouse erotic thriller idea was key to a lot of his films. And there’s a bit of a comeback for that now.”

stories.title: Developer billed $553K from building department after accelerating high-rise project at city hall’s urging
stories.summary: To ensure London achieved its provincial housing target before the end of 2025, city hall urged Westdell Development Corp. to accelerate its timeline for breaking ground on a residential high-rise.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
To ensure London achieved its provincial housing target before the end of 2025, city hall urged Westdell Development Corp. to accelerate its timeline for breaking ground on a residential high-rise, but breaking ground early resulted in a half-million-dollar bill from the city’s building department.

On Monday, the local development firm appealed the interest applied to the project’s development charges (DCs) in front of a tribunal made up of Council members who sit on the Infrastructure and Corporate Services Committee (Icsc).

“What we’re asking the committee to consider is the fairness of the circumstances surrounding this particular project,” Paul Kitson of Westdell Development Corp. explained to the tribunal.

City staff had calculated a $553,547 bill for interest on DCs for constructing the 26 storey, 225 unit building at 15 Capulet Walk in west London.

Westdell received its building permit on Oct. 30, 2025, just four days before the province changed the Development Charges Act to prevent municipalities from requiring statutory interest payments on DCs.

“The timing May be unfortunate, but it does not make the original determination incorrect or establish an error in applying the bylaw,” Deputy Chief Building Official Kyle Wilding told the tribunal.

However, Mayor Josh Morgan acknowledged that Westdell was asked to apply for a building permit earlier than initially planned, so that it could get the concrete foundation could be poured before Dec. 31, a requirement so that the new residential units would be counted towards London’s provincial housing target in 2025.

“The city was helped out by projects being moved forward, at our request, to meet our Building Faster Fund targets, which ultimately led to [the City of London] receiving almost $12 million from the province,” Morgan explained to colleagues on the tribunal.

CTV News had attended a groundbreaking ceremony on the construction site in early Nov. 2025 led by Mayor Morgan and Ontario Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing Rob Flack.

Rules limited the reasons that the tribunal could cite for supporting the appeal by Westdell.

So instead, the tribunal denied the appeal, then the council members reconvened the committee (Icsc) meeting to recommend referring the matter back to staff with direction to renegotiate an Alternate Payment Agreement that removes the interest charge.

“That does not cost taxpayers money,” Morgan explained.

“We’re simply not collecting the interest charges on the DCs, which is commonplace today given the current provincial law.”

After the meeting, the mayor emphasized that he felt it was a matter of fairness, “There was no benefit to the applicant in moving it forward, aside from helping the city try to achieve its housing targets, particularly the ones tied to funding programs.”

Council will make a final decision Sept. 22.

stories.title: Latest U.S. tariffs take effect on a small number of Canadian goods, some removed
stories.summary: Washington — The latest U.S. tariffs on a small number of Canadian goods went into effect Tuesday as Washington presses on in its trade war with Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
WASHINGTON — The latest U.S. tariffs on a small number of Canadian goods took effect Tuesday as Washington continued to pursue its trade war with Canada.

The White House said last week it would impose 50 per cent tariffs on goods representing about 0.6 per cent of U.S. imports from Canada, including outboard motorboats and metal and paper products.

American officials also said 50 per cent tariffs on goods representing about 0.5 per cent of U.S. imports from Canada, including cement, sugar, toilet paper and fishing rods, would be removed.

It’s the latest stage of an evolving trade war that erupted after Canada walked away from formal trade negotiations last month.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the Americans made last-minute demands that would have undermined Canada’s sovereignty.

While the trade war has escalated in recent weeks, Carney said at an investment summit in Toronto on Tuesday that if a “mutually beneficial deal” on trade with the White House emerges, Canada stands “ready to develop that and pursue it.”

“It has to be one that there’s clear alignment of interests, and a sequencing that is consistent with implementation,” Carney told a Tuesday news conference.

U.S. President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods in August. Ottawa replied with retaliatory tariffs on American products.

Trump also has ordered bans on imports of Canadian-made liquor and a handful of dairy products that will take effect Sept. 29.

After trade talks between Canada and the United States collapsed last month, Trump claimed that Canada delayed certifying Gulfstream’s latest jet models because it wanted to maintain full market access for its own aircraft sector.

In a post from Trump’s Truth Social account on Sept. 7, he specifically called out Bombardier.

“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough! Over 50% of their revenue comes from the United States — They live off American Buyers, American Companies, American Airports, and American Service — All while Canada blocks our GREAT American Banks, and Companies, throughout the U.S.A. They even blocked Gulfstream Aerospace from doing business in Canada — Completely unjust and unfair!” he wrote.

Speaking to reporters at the investment summit, CEO of Bombardier Eric Martel said the trade dispute with the U.S. isn’t getting in the way of the company’s expansion plans.

“We, Bombardier, are creating tens of thousands of jobs in the United States,” he said. “We have a strong presence and we have plans also to invest.”

Linda Hasenfratz, CEO of manufacturing company Linamar, also said the trade war isn’t having an impact on business.

“We’ve actually been taking advantage of the fact that our customers are on-shoring product from Asia and Europe into North America,” she said at the summit.

“They are happily awarding business to all of Canada, the U.S. and Mexico. And in fact, if I look at the last 12 months, we’ve won record levels of new business for our Canadian plant.”

Matthew Bromberg, president and CEO of the Montreal-based flight simulator company CAE, told reporters the U.S. remains its largest market.

“We’re not seeing any slowdown in interest on either side,” he said. “The demand is strong. The partnerships run decades and there’s continued interest in what we have to provide.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 15, 2026.

— With files from Craig Lord in Toronto, Aaron Sousa in Edmonton and Kyle Duggan in Ottawa

stories.title: Timeline: Kawhi Leonard’s road to, from and back to Toronto
stories.summary: Kawhi Leonard is officially a returning member of the Toronto Raptors after the team acquired him from the Clippers on Monday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Kawhi Leonard is returning to Toronto seven years after leading the Raptors to the franchise’s only NBA championship. Here’s a look at key dates from Leonard’s first stint with the Raptors to his return to Toronto:

July 18, 2018 — The Toronto Raptors acquire Kawhi Leonard and Danny Green from the San Antonio Spurs in exchange for DeMar DeRozan, Jakob Poeltl and a protected first-round draft pick.

Sept. 24, 2018 — Leonard is introduced at Raptors media day, where his awkward “I’m a fun guy” comment becomes a viral moment.

Oct. 17, 2018 — Leonard scores 24 points in his Raptors debut, a 116-104 victory over the Cleveland Cavaliers.

Nov. 29, 2018 — Leonard returns to San Antonio for the first time since requesting a trade. The Spurs defeat the Raptors 125-107.

May 12, 2019 — Leonard hits a buzzer-beating shot over Philadelphia’s Joel Embiid to lift Toronto to a 92-90 Game 7 victory and its first Eastern Conference final appearance.

June 13, 2019 — Leonard scores 22 points as the Raptors defeat the Golden State Warriors 114-110 in Game 6, winning the franchise’s first NBA title. He is named NBA Finals MVP.

June 17, 2019 — More than two million people attend the Raptors’ championship parade in downtown Toronto. Leonard’s “What it do, baby?” greeting to the crowd becomes another memorable moment from his lone season with the franchise.

July 6, 2019 — Leonard leaves Toronto after one season, signing as a free agent with the Los Angeles Clippers.

July 10, 2019 — The Clippers formally introduce Leonard after his return to his home state of California.

July 2021 — Leonard undergoes surgery to repair a torn ACL suffered during the Clippers’ playoff run, causing him to miss the entire 2021-22 season.

September 2025 — The NBA opens an investigation following allegations first reported by journalist Pablo Torre that Leonard signed a US$28-million “no-show” endorsement deal with Aspiration, an environmental financial technology company, that required no work beyond remaining with the Clippers.

2019-26 — Leonard battles injuries throughout his seven years with the Los Angeles Clippers but averages a career-high 27.9 points in 65 games in the 2025-26 season.

stories.title: Warm, windy Tuesday ahead for London
stories.summary: London can expect a warm but unsettled Tuesday, with spotty showers and gusty southwest winds throughout the day, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London can expect a warm but unsettled Tuesday, with spotty showers and gusty southwest winds throughout the day, according to CTV London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

The temperature will climb to 25 C but feel closer to 30 with the humidity.

“The rain will be spotty through the day today. Not everyone will see showers,” Atchison said.

The risk of showers will continue into Wednesday, with a chance of thunderstorms along a frontal boundary moving through the region.

Daytime highs are expected to remain well above normal this week, reaching 25 to 26 C. Showers will remain possible through the week, with clearing expected by Friday.

stories.title: Disturbing Cat in the Hat trend explained after B.C. girl chased home and arrests made in U.S.
stories.summary: A disturbing social media trend that involves threatening depictions of the Cat in the Hat has led to police warnings and arrests in the U.S.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
RCMP in West Kelowna, B.C., are investigating after a teenage girl was chased by a suspect dressed in a Cat in the Hat costume last month.

The incident occurred at around 9 p.m. on Aug. 24 and, although the girl was able to reach her residence safely, police are seeking to identify the person in the costume.

It comes as a disturbing trend emerges on social media, involving sinister depictions of the children’s book character making threats to individuals and communities in Canada, the U.S. and elsewhere in the world.

The posts have prompted police departments and schools to issue warnings about engaging in the trend, which has also resulted in a number of arrests.

The trend involves online videos depicting a sinister version of the Dr. Seuss character, the Cat in the Hat, outside schools, homes, or on streets at night. Much of the footage is made with AI, but some videos include real people dressed up as the character, and they often include threatening messages.

On TikTok, a quick search for “Cat in the Hat” returns hundreds of videos, some of which have garnered millions of views, of people dressed as the character wandering streets at night.

Other videos from anonymous accounts show the Cat in the Hat dancing next to a list of names of people it is “coming for,” while some users have posted content or comments sharing unverified claims that the Cat in the Hat has been involved in violent assaults and even murder.

The trend bears resemblance to similarly frightening online conspiracies from recent years, including the “Momo” hoax, which claimed children were being encouraged to harm themselves through viral videos, and widespread claims of knife-wielding clowns terrorizing small towns in 2016.

The broadcaster suggests the trend May have been accelerated by an X post shared by DiscussingFilm on Aug. 8, which revealed that the original Cat in the Hat costume worn by Mike Myers in the 2003 film was being auctioned off by Prop Store Auction .

The post has since received 11 million views, with many comments referencing the internet trend and calling the costume “nightmarish” and “truly terrifying.”

“Regardless of whether the individual intended the behaviour as a joke, following a young person and causing them to fear for their safety is extremely concerning,” Cpl. Gerrits of the West Kelowna RCMP said in a statement concerning the recent incident in B.C. “People should understand that behaviour intended as a prank can have serious consequences when it causes another person to reasonably fear for their safety.”

Police are reminding parents and youth that if they believe they are being followed or pursued, they should move toward a safe, populated location, contact a trusted adult and call 911 if they are in immediate danger.

Meanwhile, the Nechako Lakes School District in B.C.’s central Interior said it was aware of the social media trend and asked community members to report the posts to police.

In the U.S., several police departments have issued warnings or comments on the growing social media trend.

This includes the Baldwin Park PD in California, which said in a social media post that it is aware of “concerning” content regarding the trend. “We are actively reviewing these posts and will investigate any potential threats or criminal activity,” it said.

Florida’s St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office said it was investigating content involving county schools but had not identified a credible threat, adding, “Out of an abundance of caution, there will be an increased law enforcement presence on school campuses across the county.”

Citrus County Sheriff’s Office , also in Florida, said it had received multiple reports of AI posts featuring the Cat in the Hat with threatening messages, but that after “thoroughly reviewing” each report, none were found to be credible.

In Ireland, where the trend is thought to have originated, An Garda Síochána, the country’s national police force, shared a post on Instagram dismissing the Cat in the Hat sightings.

“Fortunately, we can rule out the issue, which is essentially an AI prompt that places the character into images/videos of familiar places,” it said.

Though the Cat in the Hat trend has broadly been dismissed as a hoax, several arrests have been made in the U.S. in connection with threatening social media content.

In Tennessee, the Warren County Sheriff’s Department said on Sept. 2 that a student had been charged “following an extensive investigation into a reported online threat involving an AI-generated image of the ‘Cat in the Hat.'”

In Colorado, Grand Juntion Police Department arrested a 14-year-old student in connection with a social media post related to the trend, and charged the juvenile with interference with staff, faculty, or students of educational institutions and harassment. Police also increased presence at a local high school “out of an abundance of caution.”

Elsewhere, in Kansas, a 15-year-old was arrested after allegedly posting a video on social media that made “ominous threats toward students” as part of the Cat in the Hat trend. The juvenile was charged with two counts of criminal threat, according to a statement shared by Hutchinson Police Department on Sept. 1.

West Kelowna RCMP said in a statement that while wearing a costume is not in itself a criminal offence, “following or pursuing another person in a manner that causes them to reasonably fear for their safety May constitute criminal harassment.”

It added: “Other potential offences, including assault, uttering threats or intimidation, May also be considered where the evidence supports them.”
