stories.title: Canada’s best dressed: Embracing a style evolution
stories.summary: These sartorial standouts know how to embrace the perpetual change of style
stories.author: Haley Steinberg, Nadia Pizzimenti, Santanae Luzige, Nolan Bryant, Randi Bergman
stories.content:
Decade after decade, a sense of fashion shifts with time, trends and life’s big changes. The Canadians in our 2026 portfolio of sartorial standouts are learning a lot while forever discovering their personal style.

These lessons – fit comes first, style inspiration crosses generations, and good wardrobes work no matter where they travel – illustrate how to embrace this perpetual evolution.

Model-turned-writer Dominique Bertrand finds her closet sparks creativity beyond what she chooses to wear

When she’s out and about in Montreal, Dominique Bertrand’s clothes always enter a room second. They’re wonderful – often spectacular – of course, but Bertrand’s fashion magic trick is the innate ease with which she wears them.

The former model-cum-editor-turned-author was born in Laval, Quebec, and whisked into the fashion world in her early 20s. Working with designers like Oscar de la Renta, Valentino and Hubert de Givenchy, she would go on to spend time in front of the lenses of Richard Avedon and Robert Mapplethorpe. “You had to be so strong and still,” she says of Horst P. Horst’s famously lengthy and gruelling sittings.

Now 68, she still holds on to the principles of suitability and fit that she picked up preparing for countless shoots and shows.

“When you model, they make you wear so many styles – every neckline, waist, and length – I know what’s not for me,” she says. She’s learned that if the colour and fabric work, a local seamstress can often tweak the fit. “A few adjustments and it will look like it’s been made for you,” she says.

Bertrand doesn’t think much of style edicts, especially ones related to age.

“If we listen to all the rules that they’re trying to impose on us, we’re going to go out in pyjamas,” she says. “Nothing will be allowed anymore.” Her latest signature is her natural grey hair. “I don’t think it makes women look older; I think it softens the visage,” she says.

Bertrand is currently writing a new novel (her 2024 book, La Caravane des Anges, is being adapted into a film) and admits she’s been to fewer events as a result. But her collection of custom dresses still comes in handy.

“When I’m stuck with what I’m writing and need to put myself in the creative mood, I dress like a princess,” she says. “I put on the most beautiful things I have and it pushes the button of creativity.”

– Nolan Bryant

Editor Allyson Shiffman lets insider tips inform where her personal style goes next

“I find style is best experienced in person,” says freelance fashion and culture journalist Allyson Shiffman on a call from Stockholm, Sweden, where the 36-year-old, Toronto-born writer is currently based.

Shiffman’s preferred way of finding style inspiration has always been to soak up her surroundings, beginning in New York City as a freelance fashion journalist writing for titles including W, Interview and Nylon.

“I think developing my taste there was pretty formative because it’s a city that really values eclecticism and personal expression,” she says. “It was in the early days of Instagram, so it felt like I was free to develop my own sense of style without feeling a lot of outside pressure.”

It wasn’t until Shiffman moved to Sweden in her early 30s that her style took on a more polished edge, a result, she claims, of the Scandi penchant for minimalism and effortless dressing.

“I find a lot of inspiration in my friends and colleagues. If I see someone looking really cool, at a party, or even at the office, I’ll want to interpret it in my own way.”

She singles out Swedish painter and film director Marie-Louise Ekman as one of the most vibrant and sartorially inspiring women in her network.

Shiffman served as the fashion news director at Vogue Scandinavia for the last five years, a role that allowed her to spotlight the emerging designers who became the cornerstones of her personal style today. Dilara Findikoglu made her wedding dress, and she is often spotted wearing young Scandinavian brands such as Nicklas Skovgaard, Anne Sofphie Madsen, and Danish label Taus.

More recently, Shiffman has ventured out on her own, covering fashion and culture while working on a range of freelance projects. Among them was interviewing Giovanna Engelbert, another former Vogue editor and the global creative director of Swarovski, for a series looking back at the seven extraordinary couture gowns she wore on her wedding day. It was a project Shiffman describes as a kind of fashion fantasy.

– Nadia Pizzimenti

Men’s-wear pro Somsack Sikhounmuong has built a career around embracing the familiar

Creative directors bowing at the end of runway shows in all black has become a bit of a fashion trope, synonymous with the tyranny of so-called good taste (read: safe, restrained, maybe a bit boring). But looking at Alex Mill creative director Somsack Sikhounmuong’s wardrobe of breezy classics, you’ll find colour, fun and an aesthetic so closely matched to the label he designs for that he’s practically a walking poster boy for its sense of laid-back Americana.

“Everything I wear stems from the familiar, whether it’s something your grandparents might have worn or something you’d find in a vintage store,” says Sikhounmuong, who was also a design director at J.Crew in the 2010s.

When we meet for coffee in New York’s SoHo, the 50-year-old creative director is wearing olive green cargo pants and a perfectly rumpled periwinkle button-down, both from Alex Mill, and a baseball cap from the cult-popular Japanese workwear brand A.Presse.

“I just love old, familiar clothes over trendy ones,” he says.

Born in Thailand, raised in Oshawa, Ont., and New York City-based since relocating for fashion school in the mid-1990s, Sikhounmuong has a wardrobe full of colourful staples that feel like a patchwork of these influences: army jackets, sneakers, beaded jewellery and great jeans, all paired with the unseriousness of someone who’s been in the game for a while.

“The older you get, you just know what you feel great in and what you look great in,” he says. “I just don’t care enough to try to be something that I’m not anymore.”

Sikhounmuong attributes much of this confidence to his time at J.Crew during its heyday. “The people around me dressed similarly, and we fed off each other,” he says. “‘I thought, ‘Okay, I think I found my place.’”

When I ask who Sikhounmuong’s ultimate inspirations are, he references Belgian designer Dries Van Noten and a 2001 photo of actor Matthew McConaughey wearing a black T-shirt with a sarong and flip-flops.

“If I could walk around in a sarong all day long, I would,” he says.

– Randi Bergman

No matter how hard algorithms and comments try to nudge Emmanuel Uddenberg in a different direction, the Toronto content creator’s look stays the course

Emmanuel Uddenberg was on track to become a Bay Street banker when an outfit transition video he posted on social media went supernova.

Since then, the 26-year-old Toronto creator has made a career out of sharing his minimalist style and home decor online, attracting partnerships with brands such as Dyson, Givenchy and DeLonghi. (Being self-managed, he also gets to flex his business school chops).

“I went from having a private Instagram, private everything, to having so many eyes on me,” he says of his 220K-plus followers.

It isn’t hard to see why: Uddenberg has mastered the art of aspirational everyday dressing, with the consistency of what could be considered a uniform. He largely adheres to well-tailored basics in neutral tones such as brown, black, grey, denim and white.

“There’s still a lot of intention behind it, even though it may just be an all-black outfit,” he says. “I try to elevate it through silhouettes or interesting pieces.” That might come in the form of a big slouchy bag, pointed toe brogues or a sleek metal bracelet watch.

Does he ever feel pressured to switch up his understated, logo-free style, particularly in such an oversaturated influencer landscape? Not really.

“I do try to spice things up here and there, but I feel like it all exists in the same realm of being minimal and true to me,” he says. Occasionally, Uddenberg receives comments asking him to wear more colour, “but 90 per cent of my audience understands that’s just not me.”

He’s a fan of New York men’s-wear label Daniel Simmons and favours the easy, clean silhouettes of brands such as Our Legacy, Lemaire and Jil Sander. But Uddenberg’s earliest and most enduring style influence is his mother, Sonia Martin, with whom he shares his restrained sensibility, partiality to darker colours and love of a good bag.

“I steal her bags, she steals my bags,” he says.

– Haley Steinberg

Maturing has helped writer and model Lydia Okello understand where feminine and masculine style intersect

Lydia Okello was the kind of kid who obsessed over what to wear on the first day of school and relished dressing up.

“I fantasized all August getting ready for how epic my first day outfit was going to be and trying to convince my mom to buy me platform Spice Girl shoes,” says the 36-year-old writer, model and digital creator. (Growing up, the Vancouverite’s nickname was “Imelda Marcos,” the former First Lady of the Philippines who was known for her extensive shoe collection).

Okello’s parents, immigrants from Uganda, fed this interest in fashion – particularly their father, who has since passed away.

“My dad, I think because he was raised in the British era of Uganda, was very preppy,” they say. “He loved knits, loved collared shirts, loved polos [and] always wore trousers over jeans, or slacks.”

Okello’s style is a mash-up of English prep and bold colours and textures, such as lemon-hued knits and mixed-plaid skirts from brands such as Simone Rocha and Cawley. It’s evolved as they’ve moved into their 30s and become more confident in their style sensibility.

“When I first started posting outfits, I dressed very femme and vintagey,” Okello says. “I was really obsessed with Lula Magazine and Zooey Deschanel, and I wanted to be that kind of 1950s, 1960s archetype.”

Realizing they were non-binary shifted how they think about fashion.

“It gave me way more freedom, because I didn’t feel as narrow about what I could wear.” They feel more comfortable expressing their masculine side as well as the contradictions of their style.

“I think there’s a part of my style that would be perceived as extremely feminine. I love tulle, I love ruffles, I really love the colour pink,” Okello says. “But I love those things paired with hardness and a bit of an edge.”

A move to Paris shows stylist Irene Kim the value of wardrobe evolution over reinvention

When personal stylist Irene Kim decided to split her time between Toronto and Paris, she rejected a total wardrobe overhaul.

At 45, confident in her style and unbothered by transient trends, she relied on an internal compass to help her sense of style adapt. “It’s never about moulding into some caricature of a city,” she says.

For Kim, ease doesn’t equal casual; it is a function of cut and proportion. This philosophy was tested when her beloved Tibi Calder sweatpants, the centrepiece of her Toronto wardrobe, had no place on the streets of Paris, where athleisure is virtually non-existent.

Instead of parting with them, they were relegated to travel days across the Atlantic. Replacing them with sculptural denim allowed Kim to stay grounded. It’s a choice that respects the Parisian dress code while incorporating the architectural silhouettes that help define her style DNA.

The city’s year-round transitional weather also caught her by surprise. While Canada demands dressing for extreme seasons, Paris requires trading heavy knits for breathable cotton layers. This shift meant updating her retail preferences. Her usual Toronto stops at COS have been replaced by visits to the Parisian label Soeur, where she sources foundational pieces.

Kim’s excitement for Ashlyn, the New York label helmed by 2025 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund winner Ashlynn Park, has made it an anchor for a closet caught between two time zones.

Ultimately for Kim, style reinvention is less important than staying true to yourself. Confidence comes from clothes that fit well, feel good and remain functional. When those principles align, your wardrobe will feel grounded wherever you land.

– Santanae Luzige

Rather than downloading style tips to a new generation, fashion entrepreneur and musician Julian Finkel looks to them for inspiration

As the founder of Model Citizen, an iconic Dundas West boutique that defined local retail for over 15 years, Julian Finkel is a true pillar of the Toronto fashion scene.

Today, his focus is Panther City Coffee, the 9-to-5 persona of west end music venue the Piston. He jokes that his daytime schedule is “bonkers” for a musician used to nightlife, but it connects him directly to a shifting style landscape.

These days, that means watching the cool kids come in for afternoon matcha – including his kid Luca and their crew – sporting giant fur hats, bright pink hair, and rainbow-dyed bangs.

Observing the younger generation experiment reminds Finkel of his own style evolution. At 62, his approach to getting dressed is anchored in a Shambhala Buddhist philosophy: clothes are your armour, and dressing cleanly is an expression of respect for yourself and others.

For Finkel, that mindset is best expressed in a well-cut suit. When performing under his musical moniker, Julian Fuego, he brings that same philosophy onto the stage, injecting sharp tailoring while adding a rebellious edge with an Italian neckerchief or a pearl earring gifted by his son, John Wolf, who sourced it from Kensington Market’s Courage My Love.

When asked for style advice, Finkel refuses to hand down rigid rules, insisting kids wouldn’t listen anyway. Instead, he is inspired by their curiosity and love of vintage, championing the independent Toronto spots feeding that creative spirit. He praises Kensington vintage staples like Exile, the custom tailoring at Sydney’s, and Absolutely Fabrics, where he is excited to explore its new men’s-wear offering this fall.

For Finkel, keeping style alive is a genuine act of joie de vivre. Ultimately, aging well simply means you haven’t given up.

HOW WE DID IT

To compile this list, a group of Globe and Mail editors and contributors reached out to their networks of wardrobe watchers, dug deep into their social-media feeds and surveyed past nominees to create a roster of candidates. After narrowing the contenders down to the final list, photographers in Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, New York and Paris were commissioned to capture the subjects’ signature styles.

Have a best-dressed suggestion of your own? Post a photo of your fashionable contender to Instagram and tag the picture @globestyle and #GlobeStyleBestDressed .

content_blocks.text: Creative directors bowing at the end of runway shows in all black has become a bit of a fashion trope, synonymous with the tyranny of so-called good taste (read: safe, restrained, maybe a bit boring). stories.title: Action needed to ensure groups aren't unduly 'de-banked' over terror risks: report
stories.summary: There’s “a near-total absence” of effective recourse for non-profit organizations and individuals whose banking services are cut off due to alleged ties to terrorist financing, a new report says.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — There’s “a near-total absence” of effective recourse for non-profit organizations and individuals whose banking services are cut off due to alleged ties to terrorist financing, a new report says.

The International Civil Liberties Monitoring Group report examines the phenomenon known as derisking or de-banking — ending or restricting access to financial services for clients or sectors in order to avoid perceived risks.

The Ottawa-based group includes dozens of non-governmental organizations, unions, professional associations, faith groups, environmental organizations, human rights and civil liberties advocates, and representatives of immigrant and refugee communities in Canada.

Its report says a lack of case-specific and evidence-based decision making by banks has resulted in “unjustified and discriminatory decisions” that affect their clients, including non-profits and charities.

It argues that the derisking of organizations — particularly those active in Muslim communities or carrying out humanitarian activities abroad — is not a series of isolated commercial decisions by individual banks but a predictable outcome of Canada’s anti-money laundering and anti-terrorist financing framework.

Charities and advocacy organizations are reporting episodes of service denial that appear to be based on risk avoidance rather than case-by-case assessment, raising “serious questions of discrimination, profiling, disproportionate impact and unintended consequences,” the report says.

Tim McSorley, the monitoring group’s national coordinator, said that while “any financial crime, including terrorist financing, needs to be addressed,” organizations with no extremist involvement face “penalties and harm because of overly broad and opaque anti-terror financing laws.”

That means millions of dollars intended for life-saving aid and international development are being cut off, McSorley said.

The organizations most affected by derisking include Muslim-led charities, international humanitarian and development NGOs and organizations linked to jurisdictions such as Syria, Palestine or Pakistan, the report says.

It says the consequences of derisking include abrupt account closures and service denials, exclusion from payment processors, disruption to humanitarian programs, individual derisking of employees, board members and their families, and lasting reputational harm.

In one case, a donation-processing platform notified a large, established humanitarian organization operating in Syria and other countries that it would be dropped within 15 to 30 days, after the platform’s new banking partner made a derisking decision, the report says.

“No explanation of the underlying risk was given.”

In another case outlined in the report, a charity’s application for credit card services was welcomed by account managers, only for the account and associated donation processing to be suspended without warning a week later.

The report says financial institutions are not legally required to provide a specific reason for closing an account. It adds that no independent body in Canada has the mandate to review whether a derisking decision was reasonable, non-discriminatory or evidence-based, and no authority systematically collects data on the scale or nature of derisking in Canada.

“The result is a system in which life-altering financial decisions are made behind closed doors, based on undisclosed criteria, without meaningful appeal,” the report says.

The monitoring group’s report follows a study earlier this year by University of Toronto law and history professor Anver Emon. It found strict measures to prevent terrorism financing are prompting Muslim charities in Canada to withdraw humanitarian assistance from countries in need because they fear losing access to banking services.

The monitoring group’s report says derisking is embedded across the financial system — not confined to a single institution or sector — and cannot be addressed without structural reform, transparency requirements and meaningful accountability mechanisms.

It makes a dozen recommendations to the federal government, supervisory bodies, financial institutions and payment processors.

The Canada Revenue Agency does not comment on third-party reports. The Finance Department and Public Safety Canada had no immediate comment on the recommendations.

Finance has said the federal government continues to engage with interested parties to ensure anti-terrorism financing measures remain effective, proportionate and responsive to emerging issues.

The monitoring group welcomes further engagement with the government but wants more than meetings and consultations, McSorley said.

“We need to see concrete policy changes.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 15, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Which stocks will win? Focus on profits
stories.summary: As contest approaches its second half, the standings suggest staying nimble is key
stories.author: Jon Erlichman
stories.content:
Well, hello! It’s time for another weekly edition of Trade Secrets, our newsletter tracking The Globe and Mail’s Trade Off stock market competition. Time certainly flies, when you consider we’re nearly midway through the contest.

Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Be sure to sign up to receive the Trade Secrets newsletter in your inbox.

If you haven’t reviewed your portfolio of late, now‘s a good time to think about your positioning for the second half. Let’s start with a look at the standings.

Our leaderboard reflects the fact that staying nimble matters. Between the trade war tensions and September’s seasonal weakness, many stocks have stumbled. Names that enjoyed momentum in the first half, such as MDA Space, have looked wobblier. Energy and gold stocks have been having a moment, but it’s a macro-driven rally and we know those trades can also twist and turn.

Since it’s tough to know which flavour will win, a top JPMorgan strategist is advising investors to just focus on profits. Mislav Matejka told clients in a note that if analyst earnings estimates continue to climb, that’s a good sign for stocks. And if the stocks you’re buying represent companies with solid profit growth, you should probably just take a deep breath.

I’m frequently asked about this, so I decided to ask a top tech analyst for his perspective. Gil Luria, head of technology research at U.S. investment firm D.A. Davidson, joined me on Ticker Take and said he does not believe we’re in a bubble. From his perspective, there’s been too much economic benefit from the AI boom to suggest we’re headed for a bust. Meanwhile, if you’re measuring it based on stock prices, he argues a lot of big tech companies are trading at valuations that are nowhere near some of their historic highs.

Now, that’s not to say Mr. Luria isn’t preparing for both a bullish and bearish scenario. He says if you believe the AI story has legs, stocks like Micron Technology may continue to shine. If you’re in the skeptics camp, he’d argue Apple and Meta are in good shape even if there’s a bust. Interestingly, Palantir is a name that he believes could win in both scenarios, partly because its success in combing through customer data gives it a sticky, fast-growing business.

That line was a response to a recent post of mine on X, where I looked at 15-year returns for companies that have been disruptors (including Nvidia, Tesla, Netflix and Amazon) compared with the incumbents. To me, it’s a reminder that new ideas can lead to big returns over the long term.

Speaking of big ideas, Prime Minister Mark Carney is hoping to spark some fresh thinking about Canada’s road ahead. Be sure to keep tabs on the The Globe and Mail’s coverage of the Canada Investment Summit, happening this week in Toronto alongside the Toronto International Film Festival.

Getting back to your investments, Rob Carrick recently reminded readers that if negative headlines spoil your retirement plans, you probably need to refresh how you think about retirement planning.

On a related note, if you want to find a financial adviser who fits with your approach, The Globe has a great tool to review many of the adviser options out there.

Happy trading!

Jon Erlichman is the founder of Ticker Take on YouTube and a contributor to BNN Bloomberg.

stories.title: Blue Jays’ Soriano untouchable until tenacious Tigers figure him out, rally to win 6-5
stories.summary: Dillon Dingler's RBI single cashed in Torres, then Max Clark had a two-run double. Spencer Torkelson drove Clark in with another double.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Jose Soriano was flirting with history for seven innings, but then he hit a wall.

Soriano pitched a perfect game for 5 1/3 innings and had a no-hitter going for another inning before giving up four runs and getting the hook as his Toronto Blue Jays eventually fell to the Detroit Tigers 6-5 on Monday.

Soriano said that his no-hit bid was undone because the Tigers figured him out as the game wore on.

“I think everything was working well, I was pounding the zone, that’s a big part of this in the first couple of innings,” said Soriano.

stories.title: Alberta NDP wins by-election in longtime Conservative riding
stories.summary: Unofficial results showed the Opposition party snatched up Calgary-Shaw
stories.content:
Naheed Nenshi’s NDP on Monday declared victory in a south Calgary by-election after unofficial results showed the Opposition party snatched up the longtime Conservative stronghold of Calgary-Shaw.

NDP candidate Kyle Campbell received 7,461 votes, and Mike Derry of Premier Danielle Smith’s governing United Conservative Party got 6,879.

Campbell’s win drew cheers, applause and shouts of “NDP, NDP” from supporters at a constituency watch party, who also sang We Are The Champions by the rock band Queen.

“This opportunity is a chance to live what I believe in my heart, which is that leadership is about service,” Campbell told supporters. “So thank you. Thank you.

“Let’s do it for Alberta. We’re in Canada forever.”

The by-election comes as the province prepares to vote Oct. 19 on whether to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on quitting the country.

The new legislature member for Calgary-Shaw and Alberta's NDP leader Naheed Nenshi say concerns about a referendum on separation next month helped their cause in Monday's by-election in Calgary Shaw. Unofficial results show NDP candidate Kyle Campbell defeated the United Conservative Party candidate by nearly 600 votes.

The Canadian Press

During the campaign, Nenshi said voters should choose his party and send a message to the premier that they don’t want a government that caters to separatists.

In a social media post Monday , Smith congratulated Campbell and said her government would work with him to meet the needs of his constituency.

Her post also thanked Derry for his work during the campaign.

“Our UCP government will continue to work every day to grow our province’s economy, strengthen our core social services and build a stronger Alberta,” Smith’s post said.

The riding, created in 1986, has long voted Conservative. The NDP won the seat only once in 2015 as part of the “orange wave” that brought former premier Rachel Notley into government.

The by-election was called after former United Conservative Party cabinet minister Rebecca Schulz – now an executive at a major oil and gas producer in Alberta – resigned in May.

Schulz was environment minister from 2023 to the end of 2025.

Meanwhile, Progressive Tory candidate Kyle Joseph came in third place in Monday’s by-election with 978 votes, while Liberal candidate John Roggeveen received 602.

Independent candidate Rolly Ashdown finished last with 82 votes.

Elections Alberta says an official count is scheduled for Sept. 24.

stories.title: Carney’s investment summit in Toronto draws protests by Indigenous leaders, eco groups, unions
stories.summary: The summit is expected to attract the heads of some of the world's largest asset managers, including BlackRock CEO and chairman Larry Fink.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Alessia Passafiume and Maan Alhmidi, The Canadian Press

Posted September 15, 2026 5:23 am.

Last Updated September 15, 2026 6:23 am.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s high-stakes pitch for foreign investment drew a diverse crowd of protesters to Toronto on Monday evening as Indigenous leaders, environmental groups, union leaders and others marched together in opposition of his agenda.

Hundreds of executives and global asset managers descended on the city for Canada’s first-ever national investment summit. Carney has set an ambitious goal of attracting $1 trillion in new investment over the next five years.

Protesters, including representatives of labour unions and climate and housing advocates , mobilized against the event at a downtown rally that grew bigger as demonstrators made their way to the summit’s opening gala at the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), where they were met by a police barrier.

Protesters said they reject the idea of leaving Canada’s economic future in the hands of CEOs and worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

“We’re here today because we represent young workers who want good jobs and a livable future,” said Hailey Asquin of the group Common Horizon.

Asquin said her peers are not against investments but are concerned about spending on artificial intelligence, the military and fossil fuels.

“We want to be part of building a Canada that we can be proud of, one that is a superpower in things like renewable energy and health care,” she said.

Demonstration: Nathan Phillips Square 7:05 pm -Demonstrators are marching Temporary Road Closures: -Closures will be intermittent -Currently Queen St W is Closed between Nathan Phillips Square & McCaul St #GO1933610 ^ma pic.twitter.com/asDnglbv9n — Toronto Police Operations (@TPSOperations) September 15, 2026

Tom Deadman, a teacher from Ottawa, said he takes issue with Carney inviting executives from American companies in the midst of a trade war with the United States.

“Our concern is that he is basically giving away massive parts of our public services to American CEOs,” he said.

Kakeka ThunderSky, a member of Poplar River First Nation, travelled from Winnipeg to join the protest out of concern about fast-tracked environmental assessments and government policies that affect First Nations’ land.

“I came here … to confront Carney’s CEO summit to let them know that our lands and our resources are not on the chopping block for their profit and their benefit,” ThunderSky said.

Speaking in Toronto earlier on Monday, Wet’suwet’en Hereditary Chief Na’Moks said Carney has used U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war to build momentum behind his major projects push.

“Canada is getting very good at blackmailing the public,” he said, citing the prime minister’s argument that Canada needs to build more major projects to protect itself from predatory U.S. trade policy.

“That’s their story. Their story is false, the same way that they think that these projects will go on without your support, without our support,” said Na’Moks, who has organized opposition to pipeline projects in B.C.

The summit is expected to attract the heads of some of the world’s largest asset managers, including BlackRock CEO and chairman Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray.

Kai Nagata, spokesperson for the environmental group Dogwood, said every piece of the country Carney sells off to American billionaires takes Canada closer to American annexation.

“We need investments in this country. That doesn’t mean running back into the arms of the same American billionaires who are bankrolling the Maga movement and advising their senile president,” said Nagata, Dogwood’s director of energy and democracy.

“Yes, we need jobs and we need projects in this country. But that doesn’t mean jobs overseas and projects that are owned by the same American billionaires that are trying to buy up our entire country.”

Nik Barry-Shaw of the Council of Canadians argued the investment summit is actually a privatization summit and he doesn’t think the outcome will be good for Canadians and the Indigenous communities whose lands will be affected.

“And unfortunately, it doesn’t seem like we are shareholders in this asset management enterprise that Carney is leading,” he said.

At a reception Sunday evening with Canadian business leaders and politicians, Carney said his government is working in partnership with Indigenous groups to get projects built.

Carney’s government faced some loud opposition from Indigenous leaders last year when it pushed through legislation to speed up major projects.

The tone has changed since then. Several Indigenous business leaders were invited to Sunday’s reception, including First Nations Bank president and CEO Bill Lomax, First Nations Major Projects Coalition CEO Mark Podlasly and First Nations Financial Management Board deputy CEO Scott Munro.

But many young people in Indigenous communities oppose Ottawa’s plans. A collective of Indigenous youth groups is hosting events in Toronto, Ottawa and other parts of the province this week to protest the major projects agenda they say threatens their lands and way of life.

Ramon Kataquapit, founder of the First Nations youth movement Okiniwak, said youth are looking to build solidarity through the events, which will feature keynote speakers and musical performances.

The Prime Minister’s Office says it invited the leaders of the three national Indigenous organizations to the reception Sunday, but only Métis National Council President Victoria Pruden attended.

Manitoba Métis Federation president David Chartrand, who has generally been receptive to Carney’s agenda, was also there, while the Assembly of First Nations sent a proxy on behalf of the national chief.

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak was expected to attend the opening gala Monday evening. So was Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami president Natan Obed.

On social media, Woodhouse Nepinak said her message to investors is that they can avoid costly legal battles by speaking directly to chiefs and First Nations about major projects before proceeding.

“Gone are the days of First Nations being only the bricklayers for big companies. Smart investments and forward thinking for the economy must include First Nations being owners and suppliers at every step of the way of any project,” she wrote.

“We cannot be left out anymore.”

stories.title: The office is back (at least in Canada’s financial hub)
stories.summary: Return-to-office mandates have driven office vacancy rates down
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland, Jason Kirby
stories.content:
Headlines about vacant office buildings and deserted downtowns is old news. The return to office , in downtown Toronto especially, is back on. Vacancy rates have plummeted, commute-fuelled traffic is up and businesses are scrambling to find more space for their workers.

Globe reporter Jason Kirby takes us behind the numbers, the return-to-office mandates and what this post-pandemic shift tells us about the future of work.

stories.title: A week of Mammon and muses
stories.summary: Toronto is putting on its best face for two big events, but let’s not overlook the real task
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
Toronto is enjoying a brief moment in the sun. Money men and money women from all over the world have descended on the city for the Canada Investment Summit, which the federal government is billing as a “first-of-its-kind gathering” aimed at “accelerating new investment into Canada” – luring billionaires, in other words. Producers, directors and actors from all over the world are in town for the Toronto International Film Festival , the annual movie-industry extravaganza.

The pair of big events – Mammon and the muses side by side – is a golden opportunity to show off the virtues of Canada and its leading city. We are making the best of it.

At a kick-off reception for the investment summit Sunday night at the Royal Ontario Museum, Prime Minister Mark Carney told the assembled suits that “we have what the world wants. The energy, the resources, the talent, the technology.”

The same evening, he appeared with his wife, Diana, at a Tiff gala, drawing big cheers from the crowd outside the Fairmont Royal York Hotel. This time, he boasted about the country’s vibrant arts.

“A confident country welcomes in culture from all around the world,” he said, speaking about the throng of industry folk who are in Toronto to make pitches, talk deals and parade on the red carpet. In Canada, he said, “we love our culture and we’ll always protect and promote our culture.”

It was a strong message, presented by a charming salesman against a brilliant backdrop. Toronto is putting on its best face for the events and the vibe is great.

Crowds of moviegoers strolled along Festival Street, the Tiff fan zone on a closed-to-traffic King Street West, grazing from food trucks, taking selfies and craning their necks for glimpses of movie stars. Lines of limousines queued outside the ROM and, the next night, the Art Gallery of Ontario to drop off and pick up a host of sleek summiteers. Big black cars and little black dresses were everywhere.

Toronto’s downtown has come roaring back from its pandemic ghost years. The streets are full again and the Path underground network is crowded with office workers at lunchtime.

Lots of other good things are happening. The once-neglected waterfront is reviving. The once-underbuilt transit system is filling out, with two new light-rail lines recently opened and a big subway project under construction.

The district around the Tiff headquarters on King has been utterly transformed in the past decade or two. Where once there were acres of parking lots, rail yards and warehouses, a new district of bristling skyscrapers has grown up.

But if the week of Mammon and the Muses puts the virtues of Toronto (and Canada) in the shop window, it also holds up a mirror to our shortcomings. Those who filtered out of the ROM reception where the Prime Minister spoke probably didn’t see the guy sitting on a bench with his knees pulled up to his chin and a hoodie pulled up over his head, sleeping it off. Nor did they see the intoxicated man swaying and singing to himself on the platform of the Bloor-Yonge subway station a few blocks away. Toronto, like many Canadian cities, has a big and increasingly visible population of people who suffer from homelessness, mental illness and drug addiction – often all three.

Its transit system, despite all the new investment, is looking down at heel. Some of the billions of dollars going to the new lines should have been spent on maintaining what already exists. Its parks are often scruffy. Just look at popular Trinity Bellwoods in the city’s west end, where some of this week’s visitors will go to hang out.

Its greatest cultural institutions, the ROM and the AGO, are undergoing the latest in a series of poorly thought-out renovations. Its highway system is in a miserable state of repair. The route that those black cars will follow from the airport to downtown looks like a goat track in places.

Invest in Canada, Mr. Carney says. What he doesn’t say is that, for all its strengths, this country also suffers from chronically low productivity, a cumbersome tax system, rising government debt, timorous corporate leadership, hidebound, needlessly bureaucratic banks, an aging population, a slowing birth rate and a host of interprovincial and international trade barriers that hinder its growth.

Canada is a wonderful country. Toronto is a wonderful city. Displaying their strengths to the world makes sense at a time when our best friend is running us down. But salesmanship won’t win the war. The main task before us is to make our cities and our country better places to live, work and build. Then the investors will come running.

stories.title: 'Associate member' or 'unique alliance,' Carney jets to EU in search of new and deeper ties
stories.summary: In effect it's just setting the table for a much bigger feast for the prime minister: a EU-Canada Summit in Montreal in late October.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Some have called it an “associate memberships.” Others, a historic deeper partnership. Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as a “unique alliance.”

No matter what it’s called, one thing is for certain: Carney is heading to the European Parliament this week with the intention of pitching a whole new relationship directly to elected representatives of the massive block of 27 European countries.

On Tuesday, Carney will leave Toronto and fly to Strasbourg, France, to hear EU President Ursula von der Leyen deliver her annual “State of the European Union” speech at the European Parliament on Wednesday. He will also make a quick in-and-out trip to the U.K. to meet new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

He will then deliver his own speech to EU representatives on Thursday, one a senior government official said will serve to deliver a message that Canada wants to “create a deeper alliance” on a range of files including trade, defence and “people-to-people” ties (culture, travel, etc.).

“I don’t expect any massive deliverables,” said the source, who requested anonymity to speak candidly. “If you’ve paid attention to anything the prime minister has been saying for the last 18 months, none of what he will say in his Strasbourg speech is going to be a surprise.”

While many expect Strasbourg to be a redux of Carney’s now-famous Davos speech last January, in effect it’s just setting the table for a much bigger feast for the prime minister: a EU-Canada Summit in Montreal in late October.

The summit is where Carney’s government is expected to start putting ink to paper, signing agreements that aim to facilitate travel mobility for Canadian workers, students and travellers to the EU, increase collaboration on artificial intelligence and get more Canadian energy to Europe.

Canada seeking 'unique alliance' with EU, not membership: Carney

Canadians are 'overwhelmingly open' to closer EU ties as Carney heads to Europe: poll

All of this happening amid the failure of trade talks and an escalating war of tariffs and words with U.S. President Donald Trump since last month.

As Carney told Bloomberg on Monday, the new relationship with the U.S. isn’t going to be “solved” in Strasbourg, but “it’s the start of a process, a high-ambition process” leading to the October summit.

As a sign of the importance of the summit to Carney, he put it in the hands of his “personal representative” to the European Union: John Hannaford, the former clerk of the privy council (the government’s top public servant).

“I think that’s where the formal announcements would be made,” said Senator Peter Boehm, a retired longtime Canadian diplomat and unofficial advisor to many in Carney’s government.

The Strasbourg speech Thursday, he noted, will allow the prime minister to impress a sense of urgency on the notoriously slow EU bureaucracy.

“I think in fact he has to do that because, if the level of ambition is to be realized, and the bureaucracy has to to operationalize that both in Brussels and in Ottawa, you’ve got to talk fairly loudly,” Boehm said.

Carney will also use it to spell out to Canadians what the government’s intentions are vis-à-vis the EU.

That’s exactly what Marc Camilleri, the co-founder of the Canada EU-Trade and Investment Association, hopes to hear from Carney at the European Parliament.

“What I’d like to see is really this flushing out of this idea of what does it mean to be a trusted partner in this new world of of economic uncertainty,” he told National Post.

The last Canada-EU summit in June 2025 “reoriented” the relationship between both countries, Camilleri said. It set the stage for the deepening alliance and launched negotiations for Canada to become the only non-EU to join the Security Action for Europe (Safe) agreement, a European defence procurement program.

What do we know as of now of Carney’s intentions for a deeper alliance with the EU, itself grappling with major issues such as mass migration, soaring energy costs, the looming threat of a Russian invasion and the rise of far-right populist parties?

On Saturday, the Wall Street Journal published an eye-popping scoop: Carney was seeking such a deep new alliance with the EU that there were talks of creating a new, “associate member” category for Canada.

Reaction online was swift, with some observers celebrating the novel move while critics, including Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, panned any talk of Canada becoming a member of the union.

“We will Never be the 51st U.S. state. And we will Never be the 28th EU state,” Poilievre wrote, accusing Carney once again of being out of touch.

If you've paid attention to anything the prime minister has been saying for the last 18 months, none of what he will say in his Strasbourg speech is going to be a surprise

Shortly after the Wall Street Journal report, the prime minister and his office swore up and down that talk of any form of EU membership is overblown.

“We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” Carney told quizzical reporters on the red carpet of Toronto’s International Film Festival (Tiff) Sunday evening.

“What we are looking, and will begin discussions for, (is) a unique alliance with the European Union,” he added.

Various sources say the idea of pushing for a new “associate member” position within the EU has been passed around the Prime Minister’s Office for months now, and even made its way briefly into the draft of at least one of his speeches in Europe this year. But with Carney’s comments at Tiff, that idea — or at least the branding — is likely dead.

So whether it’s as an “associate member,” a part of a “unique alliance” or a signatory to a “deeper” partnership with the EU, Carney promises that what is to come with the block of nations is “above and beyond” a trade deal.

Carney has spoken of increased collaboration on trade, energy, space, artificial intelligence, defence and improved mobility between Canada and the EU.

On the latter point, he’s specifically mentioned easing mobility for labour (facilitating workers’ movement between countries), students and researchers.

According to Boehm, that could mean that eventually Canadians are going through the same security gate at European airports as EU residents, for example.

But the possibility of increased labour mobility from the EU — a key irritant in the U.K.’s Brexit debate — raises hackles in Canada. For example, Conservatives said Carney “must be absolutely clear that he will not make matters worse by importing Europe’s immigration crisis.”

And what about full EU membership one day? On that, Boehm and Camilleri are categorical: no.

“Membership would not be in our our interest because of the tremendous regulatory burden that it would bring, and it would also circumscribe our ability to act in a sovereign way,” Boehm said.

stories.title: The trial that decided if an Ottawa man truly outwrestled a bear
stories.summary: When an Ottawa man wrestled a bear at Lansdowne Park in 1966, it took a courtroom to decide who was the definitive winner.
stories.author: Bruce Deachman
stories.content:
Before an Ottawa jury could decide whether John Szigeti had earned $3,000 by pinning a massive black bear in a wrestling match, his lawyer, Arthur Cogan, had to answer this fundamental question: Does a bear even have shoulders?

To understand why the question ever came up in an Ottawa courtroom, let’s back up a couple of years — to July 1966.

It was wrestling night in Ottawa — a Wednesday. The ring was set up at the middle of the football field at Lansdowne Park. The main event was a tag-team match pitting Lord Athol Layton and Edouard Carpentier against The Masked Yankees (No. 1 and No. 2) in a best-of-three-falls contest. Another bout on the card featured 82-pound Little Brutus against 91-pounder Jamaica Kid.

And there was Terrible Ted, a seven-foot black bear whose weight was billed as an improbably precise 692 pounds. Ted would fight his owner, Gene DuBois — the wrestling name of Dave McKigney — that night, along with anyone else who dared get in the ring with him. Event promoter Howard Darwin — he of Ottawa 67’s, London Knights and Ottawa Lynx fame — had offered a $3,000 reward — the equivalent today of almost $27,000 — to anyone who could pin Ted.

This was nothing new to Ted who, in an era when wrestling bears was considered entertainment, had his claws and teeth removed and was paraded across North American arenas where he routinely tossed men from wrestling rings with, in some cases, a single swipe of his paw. According to newspaper reports at the time, the Gaspé-born bear had previously faced some 1,500 men — beating them all, according to DuBois — before Szigeti entered the ring against him.

It was definitely Szigeti’s first match against a bear. But the 36-year-old, 220-pound Hungarian-born welder had wrestled large animals before. He’d worked in an abattoir in his native Hungary, and was familiar with fighting 400-pound pigs.

Besides, he desperately needed the money. His truck had recently been hit by lightning and needed replacing, an expense Szigeti could ill afford. So into the ring he went, incidentally just seconds after the previous challenger unceremoniously flew out of it.

You've likely never been inside Snider Park. Here's why | Opinion

Is Trump the greatest Canadian nation-builder of the 21st century?

The match lasted about four-and-a-half minutes. Szigeti later testified that he got his arms around Ted, lifted the bear slightly and twisted him off balance, bringing him onto his back. Szigeti ended up laying across Ted’s chest.

The promoter disagreed, and didn’t pay the $3,000.

The case landed with Cogan, the lawyer who thought he could win.

Which brought Cogan to the shoulders.

“If it was an athletic event,” he told me the other day, his memory uncanny for something that happened 60 years ago, “then I treat it as an athletic event.

And they deliberated.

Just before 9 p.m., they returned to tell the judge — Archibald M. Carter — that they couldn’t reach the five-to-one majority required for a verdict.

He sent them back.

Within weeks it was announced that Terrible Ted would return to Ottawa as part of the new Civic Centre’s inaugural wrestling card. And Darwin had an idea for an opponent: John Szigeti. “The long and the short of it,” he says, “is that Howard paid the $3,000.”

So Szigeti got his money, and Cogan got a story he’s been telling to other lawyers for nearly six decades.

stories.title: Quebec party leaders are set to spar in their first debate this evening
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec party leaders and voters alike are preparing for the first major campaign debate tonight.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette was the main target in the first debate of the provincial election campaign on Tuesday as the five main party leaders sparred over the economy, Quebec sovereignty and immigration.

From the first moments of the debate, Fréchette’s rivals criticized the last eight years of her party’s governance.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said his party would end years of “CAQ waste,” while Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said Fréchette’s party hadn’t taken care of the economy and businesses, and “doesn’t in any way represent the changes Quebecers need.”

Fréchette took no time in distancing herself from her predecessor and former premier.

“I am not François Legault. I am Christine Fréchette, and I come with my own way of doing things,” she said.

Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime and Québec solidaire’s Ruba Ghazal were also on the stage for the two-hour debate, hosted by Quebec’s TVA television network.

Host Paul Larocque urged the leaders to stay respectful as the debate got underway.

The debate focused on three main themes: the economy, taxes and public services, and the future of Quebec.

It also featured a head-to-head format, with two leaders being paired off to debate most of the questions.

St-Pierre Plamondon, Milliard and Duhaime accused the Coalition Avenir Québec government — and Fréchette as a minister and more recently premier — of having presided over ballooning state spending and a growing debt, as well as scandals around the now-defunct Northvolt electric battery plant project and cost overruns at the province’s auto insurance board.

Fréchette said her government could create stability and predictability, and touted deals such as the recent tentative energy agreement reached with Newfoundland and Labrador.

In one testy exchange, Fréchette said Duhaime’s plan to cut $47 billion in state spending over the next five years would hurt working mothers.

“It seems that for Mr. Duhaime, financial independence stops at women because he doesn’t actually want to increase the number of spots in (daycares),” she said.

Duhaime shot back, saying he was only proposing what amounted to a five per cent spending cut.

“Five per cent, people who are listening at home do that every week.”

St-Pierre Plamondon also faced criticism over his promising a sovereignty referendum in the next four years if his party forms government.

Fréchette said a Parti Québécois government would focus on sovereignty rather than other priorities such as health.

“We see that their priority, in fact, is to create a new Quebec currency, to create a Quebec army, and wait, a Quebec space agency. So I would like to say to Mr. Plamondon: come back down to earth and work on real priorities,” she said.

The Parti Québécois leader, in response, targeted Fréchette’s refusal to say whether she’d vote yes or no in a sovereignty referendum, and her attempts to distance herself from her party’s past.

“You can ridicule, Ms. Fréchette, if you want, the aspiration of a people to go toward more equality and more respect between people. Me, I’m in politics, I don’t hide my convictions, I don’t hide the name of my party,” he said.

Milliard also criticized Fréchette’s refusal to say how she’d vote in a referendum, saying she had people in her party supporting both sides of the sovereignty debate and describing her position as “unworthy” of leadership.

The leaders were also questioned on their stances on immigration. Ghazal criticized St-Pierre Plamondon for earlier comments linking immigration to overcrowded schools and the decline of the French language.

“This really touches me because I have six nieces and nephews who are second-generation Quebecers, and they aren’t the ones causing schools to overflow,” she said. “The reason our schools are overcrowded is underinvestment.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said Ghazal was twisting his words.

“You’re falsely implying that I blamed children. Obviously, I didn’t do that. I was talking about the CAQ’s immigration thresholds.”

Tuesday’s debate was the first of three involving the main party leaders. They return for a second debate Wednesday, and a third on Sept. 23.

Quebec voters go to the polls Oct. 5.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Carney to deliver remarks, hold press conference on day two of investment summit
stories.summary: Toronto — Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to deliver remarks and hold a press conference at his government's investment summit in Toronto today.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at Canada's national investment summit as Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic, left, and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe look on, in Toronto, ON Monday, Sept. 14, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Nathan Denette

By The Canadian Press staff

Posted September 15, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 15, 2026 5:23 am.

Toronto — Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to deliver remarks and hold a press conference at his government’s investment summit in Toronto today.

The prime minister is also scheduled to participate in a discussion with Deborah Orida, the CEO of PSP Investments which is one of Canada’s largest pension investors.

Hundreds of executives and global asset managers are in Toronto this week for Canada’s first-ever national investment summit and Carney has set an ambitious goal of attracting $1 trillion in new investment over the next five years.

Day one of the investment summit saw billion-dollar announcements and changes to Canada’s tax policy.

The federal government said investors putting $1 billion or more into Canada’s economy will get priority access to a program that offers binding decisions from the Canada Revenue Agency, while Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe announced an expansion of Bell’s AI data centre project in Saskatchewan.

The event has been criticized by some Indigenous leaders, environmental groups and union leaders who say they worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Carney wants private investors to run Canada’s four largest airports
stories.summary: Carney says he wants to see private investors operate Canada's four largest airports — Toronto Pearson, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he wants to see private investors take over operations at Canada’s four largest airports — Toronto Pearson, Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver.

In a keynote address at the investment summit in Toronto on Tuesday, the prime minister said the federal government would retain ownership of the land and assets.

Carney said the goal is to shift federal spending on major airports’ operating costs toward smaller regional airports.

“We will reinvest the tens of billions of dollars of capital that we raise into infrastructure that Canada needs for the next generation,” Carney said in his speech.

“That will mean investing in regional airports, providing better and more affordable regional and remote air connections. It will mean a better passenger experience.”

The prime minister said the proceeds from private investors taking over major airport operations would also go into both “nation-building” projects and local transportation infrastructure projects aimed at easing commutes.

During a fireside chat after his speech, Carney said he wants to hear from investors in airports like London’s Heathrow about how to transfer that model to Canada in a way that benefits both passengers and airport workers.

Deborah Orida, the CEO of PSP Investments — which owns seven airports around the world — asked Carney how he views privatization.

He said governments need to consider the “purpose” of a privatization deal.

“How is that going to make the experience of going to Pearson Airport, Calgary, Vancouver, Montreal, how is it going to make that experience better, safe, more efficient? How is it going to keep costs down?” Carney said.

Carney suggested privatizing operations at large airports could help the federal government cut travellers’ costs at smaller airports.

Carney added the government is looking for “concessions, not privatization” in these airport deals.

The overall goal of the investment summit is to attract $1 trillion in new investment in the Canadian economy over the next five years.

Carney told investors at the summit that Canada is positioning itself as a “safe harbour” for investment on a chaotic global stage.

The prime minister said in May the federal government was open to selling public assets if the proceeds could be used to fund other projects and singled out airports as a possibility.

stories.summary: Fredericton - A 25-year-old New Brunswick woman only a few months into her new job as a town crier is getting ready to compete at a world tournament of her peers — many of them twice her age.
stories.author: Eli Ridder The Canadian Press
stories.content:
FREDERICTON - A 25-year-old New Brunswick woman only a few months into her new job as a town crier is getting ready to compete at a world tournament of her peers — many of them twice her age.

Summer Gallant spent her early adult years travelling before she returned home to Riverview, N.B., where she channeled her theatre experience into a successful bid to land the town crier gig.

On a recent summer day, Gallant was wearing an ornate, red-and-blue jacket and tricorn hat when she turned toward the public gallery of Riverview’s town council chamber, rang a handheld bell and launched into a centuries-old tradition.

“Hear ye! Hear ye!” she bellowed as she opened a swearing-in ceremony for Riverview’s new council.

This week, Gallant will travel to the United Kingdom to compete against some of the world’s best town criers, starting Monday.

“I’m super excited because I collect unique experiences,” Gallant said in an interview with The Canadian Press. Her plan is to go “all in” as the youngest competitor at the World Town Crier Tournament in Chester, U.K.

Gallant’s predecessor, former town councillor Garry Forsythe, was Riverview’s unofficial town crier for about six years before he died last year. His daughter, Kelly Forsythe Preston, said he had a booming voice that could be heard from blocks away.

“No matter where he was, he was always heard before he was seen,” she said.

Forsythe Preston, who is now a councillor, said she was among a panel of judges who chose Gallant to replace her father. His traditional costume now belongs to Gallant.

“My dad’s spirit will be with her for sure,” Forsythe Preston said. “He’s almost in every seam of that garment.”

More than 20 criers from around the world will compete in various categories.

The ceremonial post is typically associated with fun municipal events, but some critics have suggested the position represents a dark symbol of colonialism.

The city of Duncan in British Columbia decided to retire its town crier in 2021, citing “a need to re-evaluate the practices and symbolism of the past.” Mayor Michelle Staples said the city would invite the Cowichan Tribes to participate in a process to pick a new ambassador for the community.

Daniel Richer dit LaFlèche, town crier for Ottawa and nearby Gatineau, Que., argues that virtually every country and ethnic group had some sort of town crier — a messenger who would travel from community to community to share information.

He cited the running messengers in ancient Greece, as well as the Roman heralds and the oral historians of West Africa, known as the griot.

“It is not an insult to go back to our roots, no matter what country you came from,” said Richer dit LaFlèche, a town crier for 45 year. “All of them should be represented at one point or another.” Still, he said Gallant has an opportunity to shape the future of the tradition. “There’s always room for evolution,” he said.

Aside from Gallant, several other Canadians are expected to compete in Chester.

Chris Whyman, town crier in Kingston, Ont., has won world titles in Chester three times. He said female criers are not as rare as some might think. They usually comprise between 10 and 20 per cent of crier guilds, he said.

As well, he said youth can be quite an asset because young criers are typically “fired up and ready to go.”

Liam Cragg of Alnwick-Haldimand in southern Ontario and James Stewart from New Glasgow, N.S., are also expected to belt it out in Chester, where the competition will last until Friday of next week.

Gallant says she’s in it to win.

“I write good cries,” she said. “I think I might have an edge on some other competitors.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 15, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta NDP wins byelection in dramatic vote: 'No safe conservative seat in Calgary,' Nenshi says
stories.summary: Kyle Campbell defeated the Ucp's Mike Derry by 582 votes in unofficial results posted late Monday night, 7,461 to 6,879.
stories.author: Hiren Mansukhani
stories.content:
Voters in the riding of Calgary-Shaw chose the Ndp’s Kyle Campbell in a tightly contested byelection that observers said would offer an early glimpse into the city’s political leanings ahead of next year’s provincial election.

Campbell defeated the Ucp’s Mike Derry by 582 votes in unofficial results posted late Monday night, 7,461 to 6,879.

“This is a political earthquake,” NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi told Postmedia late Monday. “This was considered to be one of the safest Conservative seats in the province. We lost it by 40 points in 2019, and this shows that there is no safe conservative seat in Calgary.”

Derry held a narrow lead before the final, late count of advance ballots swung the vote in favour of Campbell, an insurance and finance professional and, until recently, the president of the Somerset Residents’ Association.

Campbell took 51 per cent (3,560) of the 6,951 advance votes, compared to 2,705 for Derry.

Nenshi said he and his team were about to call off the watch party, so that everyone could go home and tend to their families, when the results were announced.

“I was standing in front of the cameras, I hear in the corner of the room people going, “Oh my God, we won!” Nenshi said. “It was quite a night.”

Campbell said he had almost given up on the prospect of winning as he saw UCP votes tick up.

“Even when we were behind, it was like this is still a great story that our hard work paid off,” he said. “This amazing sweep at the end was just tremendous.”

Nenshi ascribed his party’s performance at the advanced polls to their advocacy work.

“We (had) a ton of volunteers on the ground. We had hundreds of volunteers in this campaign,” he said. “A lot of folks just said, ‘You know what? I don’t want to take anything for granted. I don’t want it to be a snowstorm on election day. I want to take my kids on a weekend so they can see about voting, and we’re just going to get it in the bag.’

The byelection, triggered by former UCP cabinet minister Rebecca Schulz’s decision to step away from provincial politics earlier this year, was a test of support for the governing United Conservative Party’s track record, especially a little over a month before October’s referendum.

“This actually could be a really interesting race, even though a lot else is going on in Alberta politics at the same time,” Mount Royal University political science professor Lori Williams said in a recent Postmedia interview ahead of Monday’s byelection.

Schulz and the governing UCP handily won the riding in 2023 and 2019 following the Ndp’s surprise 101-vote victory in 2015.

“Normally, suburban ridings tend to lean a little bit more conservative, but this one was NDP in 2015,” Williams said. “There’s sort of a moderate, centrist character to voters in that riding, so it’ll be very interesting to see if someone who seems to be associated with far-right supporters and issues suffers as a result of that.”

Derry, who bested Ward 13 Coun. Dan McLean for the UCP nomination, thanked his volunteers and credited the work of Campbell’s team during the campaign.

“I think we’re fortunate for someone like Kyle that wants to do good for Calgary-Shaw,” he said. “So congratulations Kyle and Kyle’s team. It does truly take a team.”

Campbell, a first-time candidate said he was spurred to enter provincial politics after experiencing a Stage 4 cancer diagnosis three years ago, which led to him navigating the public health-care system.

He said that while he received incredible care, the experience showed him firsthand how strained Alberta’s health-care system has become.

“I spent many hours in a waiting room, and I remember thinking that no family should have to worry about whether the health-care system will be there when they need it,” Campbell told reporters, adding that his cancer has been in remission for two years.

“That experience changed me,” he said. “It reminded me how important it is to have the government focus on things that actually matter in people’s lives, because these issues are not abstract.”

Campbell has campaigned on investing in public health care and public education and opposing a separatist referendum.

Derry is a talent agency consultant who has previously worked at Telus and Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. His endorsements include Darrell Komick, a prominent Alberta separatist who ran for UCP board president last year as a pro-independence candidate.

Premier Danielle Smith said Derry “knows Calgary” and understands the challenges families and businesses are facing.

He campaigned on lowering taxes, building more schools and investing in healthcare. Alberta NDP recently cried foul over a UCP campaign video, which included footage of the new Evanston Heights School, which had not opened to the public at the time the video was posted.

Alberta NDP director Heather Wilson requested an investigation into whether the video footage constitutes a use of Government of Alberta resources by the campaign, which is prohibited by the Election Finances and Contributions Disclosure Act.

It was the debut election for Kyle Joseph and the newly formed Progressive Tory Party of Alberta. Joseph finished third in Monday night’s results with 978 votes.

John Roggeveen, leader of the Alberta Liberal Party, which lacks a seat in the legislature, finished fourth, with 602 votes.

“I think we’re fortunate for someone like Kyle that wants to do good for Calgary-Shaw,” he said. “So congratulations Kyle and Kyle’s team. It does truly take a team.”

Campbell, a first-time candidate said he was spurred to enter provincial politics after experiencing a Stage 4 cancer diagnosis three years ago, which led to him navigating the public health-care system.
He said that while he received incredible care, the experience showed him firsthand how strained Alberta’s health-care system has become.

“I spent many hours in a waiting room, and I remember thinking that no family should have to worry about whether the health-care system will be there when they need it,” Campbell told reporters, adding that his cancer has been in remission for two years.
“That experience changed me,” he said. “It reminded me how important it is to have the government focus on things that actually matter in people’s lives, because these issues are not abstract.”
Campbell has campaigned on investing in public health care and public education and opposing a separatist referendum.

Derry is a talent agency consultant who has previously worked at Telus and Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. His endorsements include Darrell Komick, a prominent Alberta separatist who ran for UCP board president last year as a pro-independence candidate.

content_blocks.text: Premier Danielle Smith said Derry “knows Calgary” and understands the challenges families and businesses are facing.

He campaigned on lowering taxes, building more schools and investing in healthcare. Alberta NDP recently cried foul over a UCP campaign video, which included footage of the new Evanston Heights School, which had not opened to the public at the time the video was posted.

Alberta NDP director Heather Wilson requested an investigation into whether the video footage constitutes a use of Government of Alberta resources by the campaign, which is prohibited by the Election Finances and Contributions Disclosure Act.
It was the debut election for Kyle Joseph and the newly formed Progressive Tory Party of Alberta. Joseph finished third in Monday night’s results with 978 votes.
John Roggeveen, leader of the Alberta Liberal Party, which lacks a seat in the legislature, finished fourth, with 602 votes.

stories.title: Mark Carney is squandering the Liberals’ advantage on climate change
stories.summary: This summer, polling from the Angus Reid Institute found some climate-conscious Liberal voters were migrating to the NDP. But with U.S. President Donald Trump threatening Canada, it’s clear Carney has an open road to diversify the Canadian economy as he wishes.
stories.author: Althia Raj
stories.content:
It’s been a brand-defining characteristic of the Liberal Party of Canada for more than a decade, a wedge issue successfully deployed against the Conservatives in four federal elections, and a useful tool to mobilize voters in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec specifically, but the Grits’ advantage on climate change is at risk of being squandered by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government.

Over the past year, Carney has scrapped the oil and gas cap, eliminated the electric vehicle mandate, and shown himself willing to override B.C.‘s long-standing oil tanker ban. In the spring, he delayed methane regulations, abandoned clean electricity regulations, and lowered industrial carbon pricing targets.

Over the summer, as forest fires raged, the prime minister announced a new West Coast pipeline backed by billions of taxpayers’ money. Then the government quietly signalled the project would be approved through a fast-track process, where politics tilts the scale over fulsome review.

World leaders need to understand that agree that human needs are based in buiology, and our legal, economic and political systems are destructive

In September, on the same day Environment and Climate Change Canada scientists publicly warned of sustained rising temperatures across Canada — of longer fire seasons, of droughts and flash floods becoming more frequent and more severe — the federal government quietly announced it was gutting its own legislation, what’s known as C-69, as the Conservatives long demanded.

“They called us knuckle draggers for saying we should get rid of C-69,” one Tory noted.

Through the Canada Gazette , Canadians learned the Impact Assessment Agency (IAA) was stripped of its mandate to review pipelines, midtier oilsands projects and natural gas-fired power generation facilities. Pipelines, offshore renewable energy and transmission lines will now be reviewed only by the Canada Energy Regulator (CER), while other projects won’t be subject to a federal review.

Julia Levin, the associate director for climate policy at Environmental Defence, called the move a “wrecking ball to Canada’s environmental safeguards and climate progress.”

“A lot of the things (Carney) has done is to give himself and his cabinet sweeping powers and avoid public oversight , ” she told the Star. “His whole major project agenda is ‘How can I keep American investors happy’ — because the largest contingent of people at this investment summit (in Toronto), 33 of the companies are American — so it’s still about keeping American investors happy while gutting environmental safeguards here.”

The IAA was set up by prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government in 2019 to assess the environmental, economic, health and social impacts of projects, as well as impacts on Indigenous Peoples. Trudeau argued natural resources projects were held up in court because reviews under his predecessor, Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper, weren’t adequately done. The IAA was intended to restore public trust, to offer a more credible and transparent process.

But that was then, and this is now.

Through the Gazette, the Carney government plainly acknowledged it is bowing to industry’s will, despite public concerns about potentially weakening independent environmental assessments, compressed timelines that reduce opportunities for public participation, as well as risks that projects could be approved without a full understanding of their environmental impacts, potentially leading to long-term ecological damage and higher remediation costs.

In Banff last week, Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for nearly everything of consequence, said the new west coast pipeline would go through the C-5 process — where cabinet can pick what laws to apply — but said the changes made allowed “more predictability” for other projects.

“We don’t accept at all that it’s weakening the environment reviews or the obligation to consult with Indigenous rights holders. It’s giving the proponents of those projects one competent, well-organized regulator with which that work can be done,” he said.

In Clive, Alta., Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson also defended the government’s decision to expand more fossil fuel production, suggesting that “done properly, it reduces overall global emissions.”

Those comments landed as a new report from the Canadian Climate Institute found Canada’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 is nowhere in sight. “At this rate, Canada would be lucky to hit its 2030 target in 2050 — 20 years behind schedule,” said the Institute’s President Rick Smith.

“Canada has proven we can cut emissions while growing the economy, but it won’t happen on its own. Specific government decisions are required,” he said.

If tough new actions are planned this fall, the government isn’t hinting at it. In a survey of Liberals, the Carney government asked which 30 measures it should prioritize this fall — serious action on climate change wasn’t one of the options.

“I’m very disappointed. I’m angry,” environmentalist David Suzuki told the Star, about the hope he’d placed in Carney.

This summer, polling from the Angus Reid Institute found some climate-conscious Liberal voters were migrating to the NDP. But with U.S. President Donald Trump threatening Canada, it’s clear Carney has an open road to diversify the Canadian economy as he wishes.

While some Liberals fear the turn toward more oil and gas development will prevent a credible swing back to environmental concerns when the voters demand it, and restrict the party’s voter coalition, political scientist Alex Marland suggests the Liberal brand will adapt.

“The core foundational element of what is the brand of the Liberal Party of Canada is electability,” he said.

stories.title: Trans inmate sues federal government. Guard at Ontario prison used slurs, tried to force strip-search by man, she claims
stories.summary: The inmate at Beaver Creek Institution in Gravenhurst alleged a male correctional officer used transphobic language while insisting she be strip-searched by a man.
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
A transgender woman is suing the federal government for $325,000 over allegations a correctional officer used transphobic language while insisting she be strip-searched by a man.

The incident occurred at Beaver Creek Institution in Gravenhurst early on the morning of Nov. 19, 2025, when inmate Sydnee Lines, 37, was returning from an emergency hospital visit, according to a statement of claim filed in Ontario Superior Court. Lines was serving a sentence for criminal harassment, uttering threats and failure to comply with probation.
