stories.title: There are costs for Mark Carney’s closer ties with Europe
stories.summary: There could be a political cost in addition to the financial price tag for Canada’s proposed “unique alliance” with the European Union.
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s cosying up to the European Union has been cast as a bid to control Canada’s destiny in a rapidly changing world.

But several countries that already have close ties to the EU have cited the desire for control and sovereignty as a reason to ultimately reject deeper integration or full-fledged membership in the 27-country bloc.

Most recently, in late August, voters in Iceland rejected a referendum question about restarting talks to formally join the EU.

The ‘No’ side won the day by warning EU membership could cost the country sovereign control over its lucrative fisheries, which accounts for 8 per cent of Iceland’s GDP and more than 40 per cent of its exports.

As Carney hits the European circuit, his critics and supporters believe it’s time to flesh out what his idea of deeper ties really looks like.

“For most Icelanders, this is where the conversation stops,” Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir, Iceland’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, wrote in an article published by the European Council on Foreign Relations . “It is out of the question.”

The impetus for Carney’s pivot toward Europe is to build closer bonds with new partners and diversify the trade in Canadian goods away from the United States, which under U.S. President Donald Trump has imposed stiff tariffs.

But there could be a political cost in addition to the financial price tag for securing closer ties to Europe.

Ottawa is already paying for access to EU programs like Erasmus Plus, a university exchange program; the research funding partnership known as Horizon Europe; and an EU defence procurement partnership, Security Action for Europe.

The contours of the deepening relationship are to be revealed this week in speeches by Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament.

In a Bloomberg interview Monday, the Prime Minister hinted that there could be closer co-operation in space programs, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and energy.

“There’s a huge opportunity for both of us to build our sovereignty (and build) prosperity for all.”

Carney has, however, denied a Wall Street Journal report that cited him as saying Canada could ultimately become an “associate member” of the European Union.

The report sparked a frenzy among opposition parties, with Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre writing in a social media post that there were just as many problems with Canada becoming the 28th EU member state as with becoming the 51st American state.

“Will European border policies apply in Canada, further overwhelming our immigration system while our youth can’t find homes? Will Canadian waitresses struggling with rent have to pay tax dollars to the bloated EU bureaucracy?” he asked.

Instead of EU membership in any form, Carney has said Canada would be forging a “unique alliance.”

“We share the same values. We have the same priorities. And we have very complementary strengths. We’re stronger together and this is at a time when the world is more dangerous and divided,” he said.

“Friends need to stick together at these times.”

The full-court Canadian press is welcome in Europe, where it is seen as giving a boost to the continent’s perpetually-challenged political project. A decade ago, the United Kingdom voted to leave the EU and Switzerland withdrew its bid for full membership.

Iceland’s most recent rejection comes with the rise of insular, far-right political parties in Germany and in France, where Marine Le Pen’s National Rally is leading in early presidential election polls.

Federal and provincial governments have squandered the last decade of opportunities. That needs to change

Against that context, Canada is being held up as a glittering counterpoint, said Petros Fassoulas, secretary general of European Movement International, a Brussels-based group that promotes democratic participation and co-operation.

“I think it demonstrates that there is indeed an appreciation of what European integration can offer a country,” he said.

There are several existing models that the emerging Canada-EU partnership could follow.

Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are part of the European Economic Area and Single Market, meaning that they have free movement and tariff-free trade into Europe, but maintain control of their borders and their trade agreements with other countries.

As part of the deal, they pay grants similar to Canadian equalization payments to fund poorer EU countries.

Turkey has a customs union with the EU that binds the country to adopt European tariff rates but does not include passport-free movement of people.

In both cases, the countries are obliged to adopt EU rules and regulations to secure the special market access but don’t get to vote or a say over the adoption of rules in the European Parliament.

Turkey and nine other countries — among them Ukraine, Georgia, Albania and Moldova — have been identified as candidates for future EU membership . However, their bids are hampered by concerns about respect for democratic norms, corruption and potential interference and repercussions from Russia.

Fassoulas said that EU enlargement has always ended up benefiting the bloc by increasing its economic and political clout.

“That’s why the argument is always in favour of enlargement among many EU officials. And certainly, when it comes to a country like Canada, that would be even more pronounced.”

Some argue that the EU needs to become even more creative in partnering with countries that lie outside of the European continent, including Canada, Japan and South Korea.

The conditions for such partnerships should be “geopolitical rather than geographical,” said Fabian Zuleeg, chief executive and chief economist at the European Policy Centre, writing in the Guardian this week .

“This relationship could ultimately amount to quasi-membership, with corresponding rights and obligations.”

In an interview, Zuleeg said such EU partnerships could send “an important signal” about the value of alliances and need to work co-operatively “in the absence of leadership from others.”

That’s not only a reference to Trump’s Washington, but to the World Trade Organization, the G7, the G20 and other international organizations that have had difficulty fulfilling their mandates of promoting global co-operation and stability.

“It is also signalling to the rest of the world that we are not just simply going to be on the menu, but that we are willing to work together to have that critical mass, to have that weight, that we need.”

Zuleeg believes that Canada should be among the first candidates for the new model of partnership with the EU, given Ottawa’s requirement for new friends on the world stage and Europe’s need for energy and critical minerals.

“Both sides will gain significantly from this,” he said, noting that there are “legal limits” in the EU constitution that would prevent Canada from becoming a full member.

And he added that there will be “certain costs” and obligations involved in such a partnership—conditions that have, for example, made it difficult to strike a new deal with the UK a decade after Brexit.

“If you work together in this kind of partnership, you will have to also bear certain costs together,” Zuleeg said. “The moment one of the partners is not willing to do that, then the co-operation does not work.”

But several countries that already have close ties to the EU have cited the desire for control and sovereignty as a reason to ultimately reject deeper integration or full-fledged membership in the 27-country bloc.
Most recently, in late August, voters in Iceland rejected a referendum question about restarting talks to formally join the EU.

The ‘No’ side won the day by warning EU membership could cost the country sovereign control over its lucrative fisheries, which accounts for 8 per cent of Iceland’s GDP and more than 40 per cent of its exports.
As Carney hits the European circuit, his critics and supporters believe it’s time to flesh out what his idea of deeper ties really looks like.

“For most Icelanders, this is where the conversation stops,” Thordis Kolbrun Gylfadottir, Iceland’s ambassador to the United Kingdom, wrote in an article published by the European Council on Foreign Relations . “It is out of the question.”

The impetus for Carney’s pivot toward Europe is to build closer bonds with new partners and diversify the trade in Canadian goods away from the United States, which under U.S. President Donald Trump has imposed stiff tariffs.
But there could be a political cost in addition to the financial price tag for securing closer ties to Europe.

Ottawa is already paying for access to EU programs like Erasmus Plus, a university exchange program; the research funding partnership known as Horizon Europe; and an EU defence procurement partnership, Security Action for Europe.
The contours of the deepening relationship are to be revealed this week in speeches by Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament.
In a Bloomberg interview Monday, the Prime Minister hinted that there could be closer co-operation in space programs, artificial intelligence, critical minerals and energy.
“There’s a huge opportunity for both of us to build our sovereignty (and build) prosperity for all.”

stories.title: Althia Raj: Mark Carney is squandering the Liberals’ advantage on climate change
stories.summary: This summer, polling from the Angus Reid Institute found some climate-conscious Liberal voters were migrating to the NDP. But with U.S. President Donald Trump threatening Canada, it’s clear Carney has an open road to diversify the Canadian economy as he wishes.
stories.author: Althia Raj
stories.content:
It’s been a brand-defining characteristic of the Liberal Party of Canada for more than a decade, a wedge issue successfully deployed against the Conservatives in four federal elections, and a useful tool to mobilize voters in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec specifically, but the Grits’ advantage on climate change is at risk of being squandered by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government.

Over the past year, Carney has scrapped the oil and gas cap, eliminated the electric vehicle mandate, and shown himself willing to override B.C.‘s long-standing oil tanker ban. In the spring, he delayed methane regulations, abandoned clean electricity regulations, and lowered industrial carbon pricing targets.

Over the summer, as forest fires raged, the prime minister announced a new West Coast pipeline backed by billions of taxpayers’ money. Then the government quietly signalled the project would be approved through a fast-track process, where politics tilts the scale over fulsome review.

World leaders need to understand that agree that human needs are based in buiology, and our legal, economic and political systems are destructive

In September, on the same day Environment and Climate Change Canada scientists publicly warned of sustained rising temperatures across Canada — of longer fire seasons, of droughts and flash floods becoming more frequent and more severe — the federal government quietly announced it was gutting its own legislation, what’s known as C-69, as the Conservatives long demanded.

“They called us knuckle draggers for saying we should get rid of C-69,” one Tory noted.

Through the Canada Gazette , Canadians learned the Impact Assessment Agency (IAA) was stripped of its mandate to review pipelines, midtier oilsands projects and natural gas-fired power generation facilities. Pipelines, offshore renewable energy and transmission lines will now be reviewed only by the Canada Energy Regulator (CER), while other projects won’t be subject to a federal review.

Julia Levin, the associate director for climate policy at Environmental Defence, called the move a “wrecking ball to Canada’s environmental safeguards and climate progress.”

“A lot of the things (Carney) has done is to give himself and his cabinet sweeping powers and avoid public oversight , ” she told the Star. “His whole major project agenda is ‘How can I keep American investors happy’ — because the largest contingent of people at this investment summit (in Toronto), 33 of the companies are American — so it’s still about keeping American investors happy while gutting environmental safeguards here.”

The IAA was set up by prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government in 2019 to assess the environmental, economic, health and social impacts of projects, as well as impacts on Indigenous Peoples. Trudeau argued natural resources projects were held up in court because reviews under his predecessor, Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper, weren’t adequately done. The IAA was intended to restore public trust, to offer a more credible and transparent process.

But that was then, and this is now.

Through the Gazette, the Carney government plainly acknowledged it is bowing to industry’s will, despite public concerns about potentially weakening independent environmental assessments, compressed timelines that reduce opportunities for public participation, as well as risks that projects could be approved without a full understanding of their environmental impacts, potentially leading to long-term ecological damage and higher remediation costs.

In Banff last week, Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for nearly everything of consequence, said the new west coast pipeline would go through the C-5 process — where cabinet can pick what laws to apply — but said the changes made allowed “more predictability” for other projects.

“We don’t accept at all that it’s weakening the environment reviews or the obligation to consult with Indigenous rights holders. It’s giving the proponents of those projects one competent, well-organized regulator with which that work can be done,” he said.

In Clive, Alta., Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson also defended the government’s decision to expand more fossil fuel production, suggesting that “done properly, it reduces overall global emissions.”

Those comments landed as a new report from the Canadian Climate Institute found Canada’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 is nowhere in sight. “At this rate, Canada would be lucky to hit its 2030 target in 2050 — 20 years behind schedule,” said the Institute’s President Rick Smith.

“Canada has proven we can cut emissions while growing the economy, but it won’t happen on its own. Specific government decisions are required,” he said.

If tough new actions are planned this fall, the government isn’t hinting at it. In a survey of Liberals, the Carney government asked which 30 measures it should prioritize this fall — serious action on climate change wasn’t one of the options.

“I’m very disappointed. I’m angry,” environmentalist David Suzuki told the Star, about the hope he’d placed in Carney.

This summer, polling from the Angus Reid Institute found some climate-conscious Liberal voters were migrating to the NDP. But with U.S. President Donald Trump threatening Canada, it’s clear Carney has an open road to diversify the Canadian economy as he wishes.

While some Liberals fear the turn toward more oil and gas development will prevent a credible swing back to environmental concerns when the voters demand it, and restrict the party’s voter coalition, political scientist Alex Marland suggests the Liberal brand will adapt.

“The core foundational element of what is the brand of the Liberal Party of Canada is electability,” he said.

“A lot of the things (Carney) has done is to give himself and his cabinet sweeping powers and avoid public oversight , ” she told the Star. “His whole major project agenda is ‘How can I keep American investors happy’ — because the largest contingent of people at this investment summit (in Toronto), 33 of the companies are American — so it’s still about keeping American investors happy while gutting environmental safeguards here.”

The IAA was set up by prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government in 2019 to assess the environmental, economic, health and social impacts of projects, as well as impacts on Indigenous Peoples. Trudeau argued natural resources projects were held up in court because reviews under his predecessor, Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper, weren’t adequately done. The IAA was intended to restore public trust, to offer a more credible and transparent process.
But that was then, and this is now.

Through the Gazette, the Carney government plainly acknowledged it is bowing to industry’s will, despite public concerns about potentially weakening independent environmental assessments, compressed timelines that reduce opportunities for public participation, as well as risks that projects could be approved without a full understanding of their environmental impacts, potentially leading to long-term ecological damage and higher remediation costs.

In Banff last week, Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for nearly everything of consequence, said the new west coast pipeline would go through the C-5 process — where cabinet can pick what laws to apply — but said the changes made allowed “more predictability” for other projects.

“We don’t accept at all that it’s weakening the environment reviews or the obligation to consult with Indigenous rights holders. It’s giving the proponents of those projects one competent, well-organized regulator with which that work can be done,” he said.

In Clive, Alta., Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson also defended the government’s decision to expand more fossil fuel production, suggesting that “done properly, it reduces overall global emissions.”

Those comments landed as a new report from the Canadian Climate Institute found Canada’s goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 is nowhere in sight. “At this rate, Canada would be lucky to hit its 2030 target in 2050 — 20 years behind schedule,” said the Institute’s President Rick Smith.
“Canada has proven we can cut emissions while growing the economy, but it won’t happen on its own. Specific government decisions are required,” he said.

If tough new actions are planned this fall, the government isn’t hinting at it. In a survey of Liberals, the Carney government asked which 30 measures it should prioritize this fall — serious action on climate change wasn’t one of the options.
“I’m very disappointed. I’m angry,” environmentalist David Suzuki told the Star, about the hope he’d placed in Carney.

This summer, polling from the Angus Reid Institute found some climate-conscious Liberal voters were migrating to the NDP. But with U.S. President Donald Trump threatening Canada, it’s clear Carney has an open road to diversify the Canadian economy as he wishes.

While some Liberals fear the turn toward more oil and gas development will prevent a credible swing back to environmental concerns when the voters demand it, and restrict the party’s voter coalition, political scientist Alex Marland suggests the Liberal brand will adapt.
“The core foundational element of what is the brand of the Liberal Party of Canada is electability,” he said.

Tuesday, September 15, 2026

The City of London is pleased to announce that Moody’s Investors Service has maintained the City’s Aaa credit rating and stable outlook. This year marks the 50th consecutive year that the City of London has received a top-tier Aaa credit rating, which is the highest rating possible, reflecting the City’s longstanding commitment to strong financial management, fiscal responsibility and sustainable financial planning.

“Reaching 50 consecutive years with an Aaa credit rating is an extraordinary achievement for London and a reflection of the strong financial foundation that Council and staff have built over generations,” says Sandra Datars Bere, City Manager. “I’m proud of the work of our financial leadership and staff who continue to uphold the high standards behind this achievement.”

In assigning this rating, Moody’s noted that the City’s excellent governance and management, low reliance on debt and high levels of cash and investments provide increased bondholder security.While an upward pressure on debt levels from growth related capital projects is anticipated, Moody’s does not see this as a change in the City’s strong debt management policies.

“Maintaining this top rating for 50 consecutive years speaks to the strength and consistency of London’s financial management,” says Anna Lisa Barbon, Deputy City Manager, Finance Supports and City Treasurer. “Our long-term approach to financial planning helps us navigate the opportunities and pressures that come with growth, while continuing to make thoughtful investments in the services and infrastructure our community relies on. This milestone reflects the financial practices across many Council terms that have helped position London for continued success.”

Moody’s, a leading provider of credit ratings, research, and risk analysis, typically reviews the City’s credit worthiness annually, then assigns a credit rating. This includes a review of the City’s most recent audited financial statements, the most recent Multi-Year Budget and applicable annual updates, forecasts, meeting with City administration and mayor, and other independent research.

Tuesday, September 15, 2026

The City of London is pleased to announce that Moody’s Investors Service has maintained the City’s Aaa credit rating and stable outlook. This year marks the 50th consecutive year that the City of London has received a top-tier Aaa credit rating, which is the highest rating possible, reflecting the City’s longstanding commitment to strong financial management, fiscal responsibility and sustainable financial planning.

“Reaching 50 consecutive years with an Aaa credit rating is an extraordinary achievement for London and a reflection of the strong financial foundation that Council and staff have built over generations,” says Sandra Datars Bere, City Manager. “I’m proud of the work of our financial leadership and staff who continue to uphold the high standards behind this achievement.”

In assigning this rating, Moody’s noted that the City’s excellent governance and management, low reliance on debt and high levels of cash and investments provide increased bondholder security.While an upward pressure on debt levels from growth related capital projects is anticipated, Moody’s does not see this as a change in the City’s strong debt management policies.

“Maintaining this top rating for 50 consecutive years speaks to the strength and consistency of London’s financial management,” says Anna Lisa Barbon, Deputy City Manager, Finance Supports and City Treasurer. “Our long-term approach to financial planning helps us navigate the opportunities and pressures that come with growth, while continuing to make thoughtful investments in the services and infrastructure our community relies on. This milestone reflects the financial practices across many Council terms that have helped position London for continued success.”

Moody’s, a leading provider of credit ratings, research, and risk analysis, typically reviews the City’s credit worthiness annually, then assigns a credit rating. This includes a review of the City’s most recent audited financial statements, the most recent Multi-Year Budget and applicable annual updates, forecasts, meeting with City administration and mayor, and other independent research.

stories.title: Temporary overnight closure of Highbury Avenue over Highway 401
stories.summary: Highbury Avenue over Highway 401, as well as Highway 401 itself, will be closed overnight on Wedn
stories.content:
Highbury Avenue over Highway 401, as well as Highway 401 itself, will be closed overnight on Wednesday, September 16, from 7 p.m. to 5 a.m. to allow crews to install large structural beams, known as girders, that will support the new bridge.

During the closure, motorists will not be able to cross Highway 401 using Highbury Avenue. A signed detour will be in place for the northbound and southbound traffic that will require drivers to use Pond Mills Road via Bradley Avenue and Wilton Grove Road.

Motorists are encouraged to plan ahead, follow posted detour signs and allow additional time when travelling through the area.

The overnight closure is weather dependent and May be rescheduled if required.

The overnight closure is a part of the Ministry of Transportation’s (MTO) Highbury Avenue South underpass bridge replacement and interchange rehabilitation project.

The MTO project includes replacing the Highbury Avenue bridge over Highway 401 and making improvements to the Highway 401 interchange.

The work is now at the stage where crews are installing the structural beams or girders for the new bridge.

At the same time, the City of London is completing a separate rehabilitation project on Highbury Avenue South.

The City is reconstructing Highbury Avenue South and making improvements to the stormwater system. The project also includes repairs to the Commissioners Road and Bradley Avenue underpasses and the signalized intersection on Commissioners Road, west of Highbury Avenue South.

While the two projects are separate, they are taking place in the same area and May affect travel through Highbury Avenue South and the Highway 401 interchange.

For information about the City of London’s Highbury Avenue South rehabilitation project , including construction updates, project timelines, visit the City’s Get Involved webpage.

For information about the MTO project, including construction updates, project details and traffic impacts, visit the MTO project website.

stories.title: Sally Field shouts out Canada at Emmy Awards as Hollywood honours Catherine O’Hara
stories.summary: Canada's relationship with the United States made its way to the Emmy Awards on Monday, as Sally Field took the stage to accept a top prize.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Aaron Sousa, The Canadian Press

Posted September 14, 2026 11:10 pm.

Last Updated September 15, 2026 6:19 am.

Canada’s rocky relationship with the United States made its way to Hollywood on Monday night as Sally Field accepted a top prize at the Emmy Awards, while actors also paid tribute to the late Catherine O’Hara.

Field took home the trophy for best actress in a limited or anthology series or TV movie for her role in the Netflix drama “Remarkably Bright Creatures.” At 79, she became the oldest Emmy winner in the category.

The movie, based on Shelby Van Pelt’s 2022 novel by the same name, follows the deep bond formed between a widowed aquarium worker and a young aspiring musician played by Lewis Pullman.

The movie was filmed in Deep Cove, B.C., including some scenes at the Vancouver Aquarium.

Field name-dropped Canada during her acceptance speech.

“Blessed Canada, our neighbours, our friends,” she said, drawing applause and cheers from the audience at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

Sally Field wins the #Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for “Remarkably Bright Creatures” ✨ pic.twitter.com/BnfriPZVfP — Television Academy (@TelevisionAcad) September 15, 2026

The awards come amid an ever-evolving trade war between Canada and the U.S., and as President Donald Trump pushes for Hollywood to shoot movies domestically rather than outsource filming to other countries, including Canada.

Also honoured was Edmonton-born actor and director Michael J. Fox, who was introduced as a “proud son of Canada” before accepting the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award for his advocacy for a cure for Parkinson’s disease.

The actor was diagnosed with Parkinson’s in 1991 when he was 29 years old. In 2000, he founded the Michael J. Fox Foundation, which funds research and spreads awareness.

Monday’s ceremony also saw Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy pay tribute to Canadian actor and comedian Catherine O’Hara, who died Jan. 30 at age 71.

O’Hara died from a pulmonary clot, with rectal cancer listed as the underlying cause. Her career spanned decades, from the sketch series “Sctv” and the “Home Alone” movies to her work as Moira Rose on “Schitt’s Creek.”

Levy, who co-wrote and acted in Canadian TV comedy “Schitt’s Creek,” said O’Hara taught him to never say no — namely, to her creative instincts.

“Say yes to her dinner invites and her stories and her wisdom and her generosity,” he said. “Those are the things you will hold on to the tightest. Always say yes to any opportunity to revel in the presence of greatness.”

Murphy, who played O’Hara’s daughter Alexis Rose on “Schitt’s Creek,” remembered her co-star’s unmistakable laugh and the joy she brought to audiences.

She also talked about the memories people shared with her after O’Hara’s death.

“I was passed a note on an Air Canada flight that said, ‘She was so special. I hope you’re doing OK,'” she said.

“On a drive up north, I was hugged by an extremely gruff gas station attendant … while buying wine at the Lcbo, I was treated to a very lively Catherine (impression).”

And Culkin, who played the young son O’Hara left behind in the “Home Alone” movie series, said there were many words he could use to describe his former co-star.

“She was encouraging, she was warm, she was funny. But the word that I think of is mama,” he said. “She always showed up when I asked her to — because that was Catherine. That’s what she did. She showed up.

“And this is the best we can do for her tonight. We’re showing up for her. So she May have forgotten me — twice — but we will always remember her.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

Aaron Sousa, The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. adds $450-million to record deficit following math error, expensive wildfire season
stories.summary: Overall 2026 budget debt is now seen at $13.8-billion for the fiscal year
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
British Columbia’s record budget deficit is now seen to be $450-million higher than previous estimates, and Finance Minister Josie Osborne chalked it up to factors including a math error that resulted in an earlier overestimation of natural-gas revenue and an expensive wildfire season.

The additional $450-million brings the 2026 budget’s overall deficit to $13.8-billion for the fiscal year that began in April, according to Monday’s fall update from Ms. Osborne, who took over the portfolio last month.

Her ministry estimates $887-million more in income tax revenue will come in over the course of this budget year. But that was offset by the “serious mistake” the government first admitted to making last month when it miscalculated the amount of natural gas royalties by $306-million this year and in the next four fiscal years for a total of $1.46-billion.

Plus, Ms. Osborne said, wildfire fighting costs are projected to be $614-million more this year and refundable tax credits for business and renters rose by $458-million.

She did not provide a timeline as to when the province May return to balancing its budgets as Premier David Eby promised before getting re-elected two years ago.

“What’s different today then right after the 2024 election is the situation that we see ourselves in with respect to Trump and his administration and the unjustified actions that he has taken engaging in a trade war with Canada,” Ms. Osborne said. “This is not a situation we expected to see ourselves in, and it is one that requires government to staunchly defend and protect the services that people rely on – especially at a time of such economic uncertainty.”

Mr. Eby inherited an almost $6-billion surplus from former premier John Horgan in 2022, but has since run deficits, leading to multiple bond rating agencies issuing downgrades to B.C.’s credit rating.

Despite the turmoil, the provincial Finance Ministry said businesses are adapting to changes in global trade, with exports rising by 16 per cent year-over-year to destinations like China, South Korea and India.

Gavin Dew, the Opposition BC Conservatives’ finance critic, said the update does not engender confidence, noting his party is still calling on the NDP government to explain what Mr. Eby knew about the natural-gas accounting issue and when he first learned about it.

Before the trade tensions with the U.S. escalated this summer, other provinces had warned of coming budgets drenched in red ink. Ontario’s fiscal watchdog said in the spring that the province is not on track to deliver its promised balanced budget by 2027. And Quebec announced an estimated deficit of $8.6-billion this year.

Alberta initially projected $9.4-billion deficit for this year, but last month its first-quarter update showed it now projects a surplus of $2-billion, thanks to oil prices, which have surged because of the U.S. conflict with Iran.

B.C. isn’t as lucky, Ms. Osborne noted, but her ministry reported the overall value of B.C. exports increased 4.2 per cent until July, 2026, mostly due to a strong demand for copper. Plus, she said, the province stands to benefit from the influx of federal funding for several major projects.

Meanwhile, B.C. has also been hit by lower revenues from the property transfer tax it places on home sales because more and more people have been postponing the purchase of a new home over the past year, according to Bryan Yu, chief economist for Central 1, a payments and treasury company owned by credit unions from across B.C. and Ontario.

Plus, he added, real estate prices have dipped, which means the resulting property transfer taxes have also been lower than in past frothier markets. For example, he said, the province took in $3.3-billion in these taxes in the 2021 fiscal year compared to $1.6-billion in this budget update, which was down nearly $300-million from the initial spring estimates.

“It wouldn’t be necessarily that bad if prices were declining if there was still kind of some movement, but having that coupled with the lack of sales really is hurting the bottom line here,” Mr. Yu said.

Her ministry estimates $887-million more in income tax revenue will come in over the course of this budget year. But that was offset by the “serious mistake” the government first admitted to making last month when it miscalculated the amount of natural gas royalties by $306-million this year and in the next four fiscal years for a total of $1.46-billion.

stories.title: Ottawa to announce steps toward opening up airports to more private investment, sources say
stories.summary: Two Liberal MPs briefed on the plans said the Transport Minister referenced opening up Canada’s four major airports to foreign investment
stories.author: Bill Curry, Stephanie Levitz, James Bradshaw
stories.content:
The Carney government will announce next steps on Tuesday toward opening up Canada’s airports to more private investment as it continues its two-day investor summit in Toronto, four MPs told The Globe and Mail.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon briefed Liberal MPs Monday on the plans in a late-day call, the four MPs said.

Two of the MPs, both of whom were on the call, said Mr. MacKinnon referenced opening up Canada’s four major international airports – Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Montreal – to foreign or other private investment.

Two government officials confirmed the call took place and said Mr. MacKinnon spoke to MPs about airport modernization. They said more details will be made public tomorrow.

A separate source from the private sector said they believe the government will lay out Tuesday morning the beginning of the process of opening up stakes in major airports to private investors.

The Globe is not naming the sources, because they were not authorized to disclose private discussions.

Mr. MacKinnon’s office declined to comment.

The federal government currently delegates management of major airports to not-for-profit airport authorities through long-term ground leases.

The government had signalled in its 2025 budget that it would “consider options for the privatization of airports,” and revisited the issue in the spring economic update with few details.

The bill to implement elements of that update contained new measures that give the government more power to obtain financial information from airports.

Canada’s large airports were not mentioned in a 66-page “prospectus” booklet circulated among summit participants. The event began on Monday.

A survey of 3,000 Canadians, commissioned by Australian asset manager IFM Investors ahead of the investment summit, found that 79 per cent of respondents said additional investment in airports is important or needed.

IFM is one of several pension-fund investors that have signalled their interest in investing in Canada’s airports if they are opened to private capital.

One model that Ottawa is believed to have studied closely is Australia’s own experience with privatization. Under that country’s model, the government maintains ownership of major airports , but signs long-term leases with private-sector investors.

Law firm Gowling WLG reported in an article published Monday that as of last year, more than 850 airports across more than 90 countries involve some form of private-sector participation.

Europe leads with roughly 75 per cent of global air traffic to airports with private involvement; North America stands at just 1 per cent.

But the Canadian Labour Congress has urged Ottawa not to include airports on the agenda at this week’s summit. It released a report on Friday outlining economic arguments against airport privatization.

stories.title: 200 trees planted in London to mark city’s bicentennial
stories.summary: Two hundred trees were planted in London’s Soho neighbourhood over the weekend to mark the city’s 200th anniversary.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Two hundred trees were planted in London’s Soho neighbourhood over the weekend to mark the city’s 200th anniversary.

The bicentennial tree planting was held along a new path between Wellington and Maitland streets, recognizing London distinction as the forest city.

London mayor Josh Morgan said the bicentennial is an opportunity to reflect on the city’s history, but also the city’s future.

“When I think about the soho neighborhood, you know, ON the southern edge of downtown in our city and how it has transformed over the last number of years, you know, this is really about the future of our city,” said Morgan.

stories.title: Bilaterals and billboards: How provinces are seeking to capitalize on Carney’s investment summit
stories.summary: Premiers are carting around lists of specific projects to make a more personal case for direct investment
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz, Bill Curry
stories.content:
Provincial premiers hustled to capitalize on Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto, holding a flurry of back-to-back meetings ahead of the event’s formal start in a bid to court capital for projects.

For New Brunswick and British Columbia, the effort went beyond bilateral talks.

Both provinces have mobile promotional billboards circling Toronto’s exclusive Yorkville neighbourhood. There, hotel rooms, coffee shops, restaurants and even park benches are sites of high-stakes discussions between investment bankers, sovereign wealth fund leaders, venture capitalists, Canadian executives, politicians, civil servants and others trying to unleash a flow of private capital into Canada.

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt and her Natural Resources Minister, John Herron, are in Toronto to promote what the province described as more than $30-billion in capital investment opportunities.

Some of the plans the province listed in a news release include mining projects, a Belledune port expansion and a Lorneville data centre.

Saskatchewan hosted its own booster event on Monday, with Premier Scott Moe thanking Mr. Carney for giving the country a chance to show off.

“We are at a time when the world is so very uncertain,” he said. “Canada and Saskatchewan are not.”

At the Invest in Saskatchewan Forum, Mr. Moe and BCE Inc. announced plans to quadruple the company’s investment in artificial-intelligence data centres in the province. The Premier said the days ahead will showcase more opportunities to invest in Saskatchewan.

Though the officials organizing the summit have pulled together a prospectus of more than 160 projects in various stages of development that are open for investment, premiers are carting around lists specific to their backyards to make a more personal case for direct investment.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew pitched investors on plans for a major expansion of the Port of Churchill. He spoke to the Canadian Global Growth Forum, a side event Monday organized by the Canadian Venture Capital and Private Equity Association.

In his brief speech, Mr. Kinew said Manitoba will offer a provincial sales tax exemption on major capital investments related to what his government calls the Port of Churchill Plus project.

“We’re willing to do the deal-making to make this thing happen,” he said.

Given the shortened shipping season in the north, the proposed expansion of the existing port would require the use of icebreakers in Hudson Bay to extend the season, as well as an upgraded rail line and a new energy corridor.

In February, the federal government announced a market-sounding study to gather industry input on the project’s potential.

A copy of British Columbia’s deal book viewed by The Globe and Mail largely covers the same projects as the broader federal package, including the Ksi Lisims LNG project, port infrastructure, and gold and copper mines.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford did not speak publicly on Monday at any of the various events in his province’s capital city.

But his government released its own list of 15 priority projects just ahead of the summit. The list highlights several nuclear energy expansion projects as well as mining opportunities in Ontario’s northern Ring of Fire region. It also includes investment in Toronto-based AI company Cohere Inc.

Quebec, whose current government is at risk of losing power in next month’s provincial election, is taking a less promotional approach at the summit.

Premier and Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette took a pass on the event in order to prepare for the campaign’s first debate on Tuesday.

Finance Minister Eric Girard is representing Quebec in Toronto this week. In an interview, he said Quebec supports the calls for more private-sector investment, but he will not be endorsing specific projects.

“Maybe because I’m not premier, maybe because there’s an election, I’m not taking the same posture that the Premier of Manitoba is taking,” he said, adding that he was filling ”more of a quiet, efficient role.”

While the federal government’s prospectus includes several projects in Quebec, Mr. Girard said that doesn’t mean that they all have the province’s support.

“These are private projects, with private promoters, that are being pitched to international investors,” he said.

At the Invest in Saskatchewan Forum, Mr. Moe and BCE Inc. announced plans to quadruple the company’s investment in artificial-intelligence data centres in the province. The Premier said the days ahead will showcase more opportunities to invest in Saskatchewan.

Though the officials organizing the summit have pulled together a prospectus of more than 160 projects in various stages of development that are open for investment, premiers are carting around lists specific to their backyards to make a more personal case for direct investment.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew pitched investors on plans for a major expansion of the Port of Churchill. He spoke to the Canadian Global Growth Forum, a side event Monday organized by the Canadian Venture Capital and Private Equity Association.
In his brief speech, Mr. Kinew said Manitoba will offer a provincial sales tax exemption on major capital investments related to what his government calls the Port of Churchill Plus project.
“We’re willing to do the deal-making to make this thing happen,” he said.

Given the shortened shipping season in the north, the proposed expansion of the existing port would require the use of icebreakers in Hudson Bay to extend the season, as well as an upgraded rail line and a new energy corridor.
In February, the federal government announced a market-sounding study to gather industry input on the project’s potential.

A copy of British Columbia’s deal book viewed by The Globe and Mail largely covers the same projects as the broader federal package, including the Ksi Lisims LNG project, port infrastructure, and gold and copper mines.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford did not speak publicly on Monday at any of the various events in his province’s capital city.

But his government released its own list of 15 priority projects just ahead of the summit. The list highlights several nuclear energy expansion projects as well as mining opportunities in Ontario’s northern Ring of Fire region. It also includes investment in Toronto-based AI company Cohere Inc.
Quebec, whose current government is at risk of losing power in next month’s provincial election, is taking a less promotional approach at the summit.
Premier and Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette took a pass on the event in order to prepare for the campaign’s first debate on Tuesday.

Finance Minister Eric Girard is representing Quebec in Toronto this week. In an interview, he said Quebec supports the calls for more private-sector investment, but he will not be endorsing specific projects.

“Maybe because I’m not premier, maybe because there’s an election, I’m not taking the same posture that the Premier of Manitoba is taking,” he said, adding that he was filling ”more of a quiet, efficient role.”
While the federal government’s prospectus includes several projects in Quebec, Mr. Girard said that doesn’t mean that they all have the province’s support.
“These are private projects, with private promoters, that are being pitched to international investors,” he said.

stories.title: Two more plea deals reached in case of Penticton man killed in 2021
stories.summary: On Sept. 4, one of those accused pleaded guilty to manslaughter as part of a plea agreement. Now, the other two minors have also reached similar plea deals.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
The family of Taig Savage is facing another difficult development in the case of the 22-year-old Penticton man who was killed five years ago.

“It’s shocking. It’s really shocking,” Taig’s mom Tracey Savage said Monday after learning that two more accused have reached plea agreements in the case.

The developments come just a week and a half after another accused pleaded guilty to manslaughter in a plea deal.

Savage’s lifeless body was found on the track field at Penticton Secondary School in September 2021.

Four people were charged with second-degree murder two years later.

Three of the accused were minors at the time of the killing.

On Sept. 4, one of those accused pleaded guilty to manslaughter as part of a plea agreement.

Now, the other two minors have also reached similar plea deals.

Tracey Savage said the family feels like there is no justice for Taig.

“I held my granddaughter just recently, and I realized that my son will never meet her,” she said as she tried holding back tears. “It’s not the way we wanted things, but as I learned today, nothing, or most things in life, are not fair and this will never be fair.”

Under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, the maximum sentence for manslaughter is three years, compared to seven years for second-degree murder.

“When it comes to second-degree murder versus manslaughter, the big hurdle for the Crown to prove secondary murder is that they have to prove that the accused actually intended to cause the death of the victim,” said Rob Dhanu, a former criminal crown prosecutor.

Dhanu added that murder cases are extremely complicated, even more so when multiple people are accused of the crime.

“What the Crown has to do they have to prove not only who did what but who intended to do what, Dhanu said. “The Crown May have felt that in this case it was better to go with the bird in hand rather than the two in the bush and plead to a lesser included offense where they get the conviction.”

A publication ban prevents the reporting of the circumstances revealed in court because Isaac Jack, the only adult accused in this case, has yet to be tried.

Jack’s trial is scheduled for this spring, but Tracey Savage wonders if that trial will go forward after the three plea deals.

“I hope that we are not sitting here another year from now in May 2027 when this court case gets rolling with the same expression and same face that I have today,” she said. “It’s a very sad day.”

stories.title: The deals and dealmakers to watch at the Canada Investment Summit
stories.summary: Ottawa has identified scores of projects to showcase during the event
stories.author: Jason Kirby
stories.content:
This week investors from around the world have descended on Toronto for the Canada Investment Summit, Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s effort to show the world the country is ready to build big things again.

As part of that, Ottawa has identified scores of projects to showcase during the event, which 120 Canadian and international funds and investment companies with roughly $120-trillion in combined assets under management are expected to attend.

Here’s a look at possible candidates for deals and some of the big-name investors set to show up for the summit.

Ahead of the summit, the federal government identified more than 160 projects that are open for development, which it compiled into a “prospectus” that was shared with attendees.

Some of the projects are well underway, with permits in hand and construction already started.

Many others are, at best, a twinkle in an entrepreneur’s eye.

The prospectus grouped the projects into eight sectors and included details on the current state of each project and the estimated capital spending (capex) required to bring them to fruition.

All told, the prospectus included projects with capex needs of roughly US$620-billion.

Mr. Carney has said he wants to attract $1-trillion in new investment over the next five years by slashing red tape and developing mining, energy, infrastructure and other projects.

Landing deals on any of these projects would help meet that ambitious target.

Telesat Lightspeed low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation

Company: Telesat Corp. Tsat-T

Project capex: US$5.2-billion

Publicly traded Telesat’s Lightspeed aims to build a communications network of 225 low-Earth-orbit satellites. It’s one of four space-related projects on the summit prospectus.

While the Lightspeed network is already fully funded, Telesat is offering minority stakes either in the company itself or in the Lightspeed program. In return, sovereign investors would score dedicated capacity on the network for their home countries once the service is up and running in the first quarter of 2028.

Red Leaf Pulp Ltd., a Regina-based alternative fibre company, is pitching a US$860-million biorefinery to convert cereal straw into pulp.

Saskatoon-based CellCore Technologies Inc. bills itself as Canada’s first Indigenous-owned manufacturer of nitrocellulose, a highly flammable material, and it is developing a US$220-million facility to produce military-grade propellant products.

A long shot: Project Arrow Defence Industries, a joint venture between the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association and South Korea’s Hanwha, plans to build specialty industrial vehicles using Canadian steel and aluminum, though the $1-billion project is still in the development phase.

Nova Scotia renewable energy park

Company: Octopus Energy Generation Ltd.

Project capex: US$4.5-billion

Nova Sustainable Fuels, a company backed by U.K.-based Octopus, is developing a facility to produce sustainable aviation fuel and other products near Goldboro, N.S.

While the project is still relatively early in its development, preliminary engineering is complete, and last December, the project received environmental approval from the province.

Elemental Clean Fuels, a New York-based clean energy company, has proposed a $1.3-billion biofuels facility near Prince Rupert, B.C., ON the site of the former Skeena Pulp Mill.

The US$800-million Alberta Industrial Heartland 1.0 project would convert municipal solid waste from the City of Edmonton into electrical power with carbon capture. The project has been greenlit by the Alberta Utilities Commission.

A long shot: The New Brunswick government has proposed expanding nuclear capacity at its Point Lepreau facility, though the concept is still at the initial project design stage.

Ksi Lisims liquefied natural gas terminal

Company: Ksi Lisims

Project capex: US$28.5-billion

The Ksi Lisims LNG project, backed by the Nisga’a Nation along with Rockies LNG and Western LNG, received regulatory approval last year, with a goal of exporting LNG to Asia from northwest B.C. starting in 2029.

The project has received the backing of five First Nations, which have signed benefits agreements with Ksi Lisims. The final investment decision on whether to proceed is slated for next year.

South Bow Canada Services Ltd.’s Sobo-T Prairie Connector is a proposed US$2.1-billion pipeline expansion to connect Hardisty, Alta., to the Canada-U.S. border, with a final decision due in mid-2027.

CSV Midstream Solutions Corp.’s US$1-billion Gold Creek Industrial Complex bills itself as a “shovel-ready” natural gas processing hub in northeastern B.C.

A long shot: The US$440-million Blue and Turquoise Hydrogen and Methanol Modular Processing Plant is an Alberta project proposed by Bolton, Ont.-based Enervoxa, though the company’s website makes no mention of the project.

AI Hub of Innovation

Company: Havenz Corp

Project capex: $2.7-billion to $3.2-billion

One of several data centre-related developments on the government’s prospectus, the project, featuring an on-site power energy centre, is located near Red Deer, Alta.

The centre, designed to be a large-scale AI and innovation hub, is currently under construction on 119 acres, with the potential to expand to more than 500 acres.

The Redcliff AI data centre campus, a $14.5-billion project proposed by Norway’s BW Velora, would be located near Medicine Hat, Alta., though the permitting process is still continuing.

The US$620-million Leif Erikson transatlantic fibre system, proposed by Norway’s Bulk Infrastructure Group AS, would connect Atlantic Canada to Norway and bills itself as “execution ready.”

A long shot: Xanadu Quantum Technologies Xndu-T , which went public in March, is developing a photonic quantum computer. The prospectus acknowledges the $1.3-billion “Project Optimism” has a “long-term development horizon, with full realization targeted for 2040.″

Port of Churchill Plus

Proponent: Manitoba government

Project capex: US$57-billion

The Port of Churchill expansion, the largest project on the prospectus, had a home-province booster at the summit on Monday in Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who announced the project would receive an exemption from the province’s 7-per-cent retail sales tax.

The goal of the expansion is to transform the port into a four-season gateway through rail upgrades, a port modernization project and the construction of all-weather road access.

With all permits secured, the US$350-million Qikiqtarjuaq Deep Sea Port (Qik Port) project bills itself as a shovel-ready deep-water Arctic port, located on the Western shore of Broughton Island, in Nunavut.

The US$357-million Melford International Terminal is also considered shovel-ready for a fully permitted deep-water terminal and rail hub in Nova Scotia.

A long shot: Port Saint John has pitched a brownfield expansion to upgrade warehouses and a new Canada Border Services Agency container examination facility, but it remains at the planning stage with no capex estimate.

Rook 1 uranium project

Company: NexGen Energy Ltd. NXE-T

Project capex: $1.6-billion

Construction is under way on the uranium project in northern Saskatchewan, located roughly 155 kilometres north of the town of La Loche, with NexGen arguing it could become one of the largest new sources of uranium in the world.

The publicly traded company estimates the mine could produce 30 million pounds of uranium each year when it is fully constructed, and is seeking institutional investors to support its capital needs.

The US$2-billion Crawford nickel mine, north of Timmins, Ont., is in the preconstruction phase but Canada Nickel Company CNC-X , which is backing the project, expects it to produce more than 1.6 million tonnes over its 40-year life.

The US$881-million Prairie Lithium project in southeast Saskatchewan is under construction.

A long shot: An Alberta critical minerals and rare earth refining complex, budgeted at between US$216-million and US$360-million, is the second Enervoxa-backed project on the prospectus, which says a scoping study will be completed this year.

Marguerite Lake Energy Storage

Company: Cache Power Corp.

Project capex: $790-million

The project is a large-scale energy storage facility that works by compressing excess grid electricity into underground salt caverns, then releasing it through turbines to generate power on demand.

Last December, EllisDon, a large construction services company, partnered with Cache Power to develop the project, which would be capable of storing up to 48 hours of energy once completed.

The Mactaquac Generating Station in New Brunswick is embarking on a US$5.1-billion to US$6.6-billion project to ensure the station operates for its intended lifespan out to 2068.

The $3.4-billion Inuit-led Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link would connect Nunavut to the North American electricity grid and fibre-optic network for the first time.

A long shot: While Novatron Energy’s onshore and offshore wind project carries one of the largest price tags in the prospectus, at US$36-billion, the project is still in its early stages.

Company: Thompson Regional Airport

Project capex: US$178-million

Area 55 is a cold-weather research and testing facility at the Thompson Regional Airport in northern Manitoba. It gets its name from the 55th parallel and was formerly operated by Ford Motor Company.

The facility is in the midst of expansion and the prospectus says it would be the first Indigenous-owned northern research and innovation centre. When completed, it would also provide testing for emerging technologies such as drones, robotics and automated vehicles.

The future of Halifax’s aging A. Murray MacKay Bridge is up in the air, with the Nova Scotia government launching a business case study in July for the project, which would exceed $3-billion.

A (pair of) long shots: In Canada’s long-delayed quest for high-speed rail, the prospectus includes two competing high-speed rail lines that would eventually link Calgary and Edmonton: the $10.9-billion Prairie Link High Speed Rail project, and the $22-billion TransPod Alberta ultrahigh-speed corridor.

For Canada to meet Mr. Carney’s sky-high investment goals, the Prime Minister reached into his contact list to tap the heads of some of the largest money managers in the world – individuals he has rubbed elbows with many times over the years in his previous careers.

The scores of big names expected in Toronto this week include:

Mr. Fink built BlackRock BLK-N into the world’s largest asset management company, overseeing more than US$15-trillion of investments. The company was a founding member of the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (Gfanz), which Mr. Carney co-chaired from 2021 to 2024. Before that, Mr. Carney, in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board from 2011 to 2018, monitored asset managers like BlackRock.

With Mr. Gray as president since 2018, Blackstone BX-N expanded its assets under management to more than US$1-trillion. On Tuesday morning, Mr. Gray is expected to join Mr. Fink, Annette Mosman, the CEO of APG Group, a large Dutch pension provider, and Dilhan Pillay, the CEO of Singapore’s state-owned Temasek Holdings, in a panel discussion about Canada as an international investment destination.

Ms. Mosman has been the head of APG Group, one of the Netherland’s largest pension funds overseeing US$700-billion in assets, since 2021. That year, APG formally signed on to the Net Zero Asset Managers initiative, one of the alliances under Gfanz, while Mr. Carney was co-chair.

Ms. Languille has served as the co-head of private equity at the US$385-billion Abu Dhabi state-owned investment fund since 2013. In November, 2025, Mr. Carney met with Mubadala’s leadership as part of talks on an investment pact between Canada and the United Arab Emirates, which led to a pledge by the UAE to invest $70-billion in Canada.

Temasek Holdings is a Singapore state-owned investment company with roughly US$400-billion in assets under management. In 2021, Temasek was a founding investment partner when Brookfield Asset Management launched its Global Transition Fund, of which Mr. Carney was co-head. He and Mr. Pillay also worked together at Gfanz.

Editor’s note: The map has been updated to correct the location of the Spruce Lake Data Center Hub in New Brunswick.

Some of the projects are well underway, with permits in hand and construction already started.
Many others are, at best, a twinkle in an entrepreneur’s eye.
The prospectus grouped the projects into eight sectors and included details on the current state of each project and the estimated capital spending (capex) required to bring them to fruition.
All told, the prospectus included projects with capex needs of roughly US$620-billion.
Mr. Carney has said he wants to attract $1-trillion in new investment over the next five years by slashing red tape and developing mining, energy, infrastructure and other projects.
Landing deals on any of these projects would help meet that ambitious target.
Telesat Lightspeed low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation
Company: Telesat Corp. Tsat-T
Project capex: US$5.2-billion
Publicly traded Telesat’s Lightspeed aims to build a communications network of 225 low-Earth-orbit satellites. It’s one of four space-related projects on the summit prospectus.

While the Lightspeed network is already fully funded, Telesat is offering minority stakes either in the company itself or in the Lightspeed program. In return, sovereign investors would score dedicated capacity on the network for their home countries once the service is up and running in the first quarter of 2028.
Red Leaf Pulp Ltd., a Regina-based alternative fibre company, is pitching a US$860-million biorefinery to convert cereal straw into pulp.

Saskatoon-based CellCore Technologies Inc. bills itself as Canada’s first Indigenous-owned manufacturer of nitrocellulose, a highly flammable material, and it is developing a US$220-million facility to produce military-grade propellant products.

A long shot: Project Arrow Defence Industries, a joint venture between the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association and South Korea’s Hanwha, plans to build specialty industrial vehicles using Canadian steel and aluminum, though the $1-billion project is still in the development phase.
Nova Scotia renewable energy park
Company: Octopus Energy Generation Ltd.
Project capex: US$4.5-billion
Nova Sustainable Fuels, a company backed by U.K.-based Octopus, is developing a facility to produce sustainable aviation fuel and other products near Goldboro, N.S.
While the project is still relatively early in its development, preliminary engineering is complete, and last December, the project received environmental approval from the province.
Elemental Clean Fuels, a New York-based clean energy company, has proposed a $1.3-billion biofuels facility near Prince Rupert, B.C., ON the site of the former Skeena Pulp Mill.

The US$800-million Alberta Industrial Heartland 1.0 project would convert municipal solid waste from the City of Edmonton into electrical power with carbon capture. The project has been greenlit by the Alberta Utilities Commission.
A long shot: The New Brunswick government has proposed expanding nuclear capacity at its Point Lepreau facility, though the concept is still at the initial project design stage.
Ksi Lisims liquefied natural gas terminal
Company: Ksi Lisims
Project capex: US$28.5-billion

The Ksi Lisims LNG project, backed by the Nisga’a Nation along with Rockies LNG and Western LNG, received regulatory approval last year, with a goal of exporting LNG to Asia from northwest B.C. starting in 2029.
The project has received the backing of five First Nations, which have signed benefits agreements with Ksi Lisims. The final investment decision on whether to proceed is slated for next year.
South Bow Canada Services Ltd.’s Sobo-T Prairie Connector is a proposed US$2.1-billion pipeline expansion to connect Hardisty, Alta., to the Canada-U.S. border, with a final decision due in mid-2027.
CSV Midstream Solutions Corp.’s US$1-billion Gold Creek Industrial Complex bills itself as a “shovel-ready” natural gas processing hub in northeastern B.C.

A long shot: The US$440-million Blue and Turquoise Hydrogen and Methanol Modular Processing Plant is an Alberta project proposed by Bolton, Ont.-based Enervoxa, though the company’s website makes no mention of the project.
AI Hub of Innovation
Company: Havenz Corp
Project capex: $2.7-billion to $3.2-billion
One of several data centre-related developments on the government’s prospectus, the project, featuring an on-site power energy centre, is located near Red Deer, Alta.
The centre, designed to be a large-scale AI and innovation hub, is currently under construction on 119 acres, with the potential to expand to more than 500 acres.
The Redcliff AI data centre campus, a $14.5-billion project proposed by Norway’s BW Velora, would be located near Medicine Hat, Alta., though the permitting process is still continuing.
The US$620-million Leif Erikson transatlantic fibre system, proposed by Norway’s Bulk Infrastructure Group AS, would connect Atlantic Canada to Norway and bills itself as “execution ready.”

A long shot: Xanadu Quantum Technologies Xndu-T , which went public in March, is developing a photonic quantum computer. The prospectus acknowledges the $1.3-billion “Project Optimism” has a “long-term development horizon, with full realization targeted for 2040.″
Port of Churchill Plus
Proponent: Manitoba government
Project capex: US$57-billion

The Port of Churchill expansion, the largest project on the prospectus, had a home-province booster at the summit on Monday in Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who announced the project would receive an exemption from the province’s 7-per-cent retail sales tax.
The goal of the expansion is to transform the port into a four-season gateway through rail upgrades, a port modernization project and the construction of all-weather road access.

With all permits secured, the US$350-million Qikiqtarjuaq Deep Sea Port (Qik Port) project bills itself as a shovel-ready deep-water Arctic port, located on the Western shore of Broughton Island, in Nunavut.
The US$357-million Melford International Terminal is also considered shovel-ready for a fully permitted deep-water terminal and rail hub in Nova Scotia.

A long shot: Port Saint John has pitched a brownfield expansion to upgrade warehouses and a new Canada Border Services Agency container examination facility, but it remains at the planning stage with no capex estimate.
Rook 1 uranium project
Company: NexGen Energy Ltd. NXE-T
Project capex: $1.6-billion

Construction is under way on the uranium project in northern Saskatchewan, located roughly 155 kilometres north of the town of La Loche, with NexGen arguing it could become one of the largest new sources of uranium in the world.
The publicly traded company estimates the mine could produce 30 million pounds of uranium each year when it is fully constructed, and is seeking institutional investors to support its capital needs.

The US$2-billion Crawford nickel mine, north of Timmins, Ont., is in the preconstruction phase but Canada Nickel Company CNC-X , which is backing the project, expects it to produce more than 1.6 million tonnes over its 40-year life.
The US$881-million Prairie Lithium project in southeast Saskatchewan is under construction.

A long shot: An Alberta critical minerals and rare earth refining complex, budgeted at between US$216-million and US$360-million, is the second Enervoxa-backed project on the prospectus, which says a scoping study will be completed this year.
Marguerite Lake Energy Storage
Company: Cache Power Corp.
Project capex: $790-million
The project is a large-scale energy storage facility that works by compressing excess grid electricity into underground salt caverns, then releasing it through turbines to generate power on demand.
Last December, EllisDon, a large construction services company, partnered with Cache Power to develop the project, which would be capable of storing up to 48 hours of energy once completed.
The Mactaquac Generating Station in New Brunswick is embarking on a US$5.1-billion to US$6.6-billion project to ensure the station operates for its intended lifespan out to 2068.
The $3.4-billion Inuit-led Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link would connect Nunavut to the North American electricity grid and fibre-optic network for the first time.
A long shot: While Novatron Energy’s onshore and offshore wind project carries one of the largest price tags in the prospectus, at US$36-billion, the project is still in its early stages.
Company: Thompson Regional Airport
Project capex: US$178-million
Area 55 is a cold-weather research and testing facility at the Thompson Regional Airport in northern Manitoba. It gets its name from the 55th parallel and was formerly operated by Ford Motor Company.

The facility is in the midst of expansion and the prospectus says it would be the first Indigenous-owned northern research and innovation centre. When completed, it would also provide testing for emerging technologies such as drones, robotics and automated vehicles.
The future of Halifax’s aging A. Murray MacKay Bridge is up in the air, with the Nova Scotia government launching a business case study in July for the project, which would exceed $3-billion.

A (pair of) long shots: In Canada’s long-delayed quest for high-speed rail, the prospectus includes two competing high-speed rail lines that would eventually link Calgary and Edmonton: the $10.9-billion Prairie Link High Speed Rail project, and the $22-billion TransPod Alberta ultrahigh-speed corridor.

For Canada to meet Mr. Carney’s sky-high investment goals, the Prime Minister reached into his contact list to tap the heads of some of the largest money managers in the world – individuals he has rubbed elbows with many times over the years in his previous careers.
The scores of big names expected in Toronto this week include:

Mr. Fink built BlackRock BLK-N into the world’s largest asset management company, overseeing more than US$15-trillion of investments. The company was a founding member of the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero (Gfanz), which Mr. Carney co-chaired from 2021 to 2024. Before that, Mr. Carney, in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board from 2011 to 2018, monitored asset managers like BlackRock.

With Mr. Gray as president since 2018, Blackstone BX-N expanded its assets under management to more than US$1-trillion. On Tuesday morning, Mr. Gray is expected to join Mr. Fink, Annette Mosman, the CEO of APG Group, a large Dutch pension provider, and Dilhan Pillay, the CEO of Singapore’s state-owned Temasek Holdings, in a panel discussion about Canada as an international investment destination.

Ms. Mosman has been the head of APG Group, one of the Netherland’s largest pension funds overseeing US$700-billion in assets, since 2021. That year, APG formally signed on to the Net Zero Asset Managers initiative, one of the alliances under Gfanz, while Mr. Carney was co-chair.

Ms. Languille has served as the co-head of private equity at the US$385-billion Abu Dhabi state-owned investment fund since 2013. In November, 2025, Mr. Carney met with Mubadala’s leadership as part of talks on an investment pact between Canada and the United Arab Emirates, which led to a pledge by the UAE to invest $70-billion in Canada.

Temasek Holdings is a Singapore state-owned investment company with roughly US$400-billion in assets under management. In 2021, Temasek was a founding investment partner when Brookfield Asset Management launched its Global Transition Fund, of which Mr. Carney was co-head. He and Mr. Pillay also worked together at Gfanz.
Editor’s note: The map has been updated to correct the location of the Spruce Lake Data Center Hub in New Brunswick.

stories.title: First Nations leaders, family demand answers for woman’s death after being denied medical travel
stories.summary: After being denied by the Non-Insured Health Benefits program following open heart surgery, the 31-year-old missed four appointments outside her community
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
A couple of weeks before she died, Miranda Mamakwa described feeling abandoned by a federal agency that was supposed to help her get to crucial health appointments.

Ms. Mamakwa, 31 and a member of Fort Severn First Nation in Northern Ontario, had open-heart surgery in April.

She wrote on Facebook in August that the federal Non-Insured Health Benefits program failed her by denying her medical travel for follow-up care, only available outside of her community.

She had missed four appointments - on May 28, June 11, July 2 and Aug. 6.

The mother of three young children also made a haunting request: If she died, she wanted others to “go after” the Nihb, to seek accountability.

Ms. Mamakwa’s health deteriorated to the point where she could no longer wait for medical care. She went to her community’s nursing station for help and was airlifted by an Ornge helicopter from Fort Severn First Nation, a fly-in-only community located near Hudson’s Bay, to Thunder Bay Regional Health Services Centre.

She died last Tuesday.

Following her death, Ms. Mamakwa’s family is working with First Nations leaders and the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority, which delivers health programs and services to First Nations across Northwestern Ontario, to demand answers.

“We will honour her dying wish by demanding full accountability,” said Alvin Fiddler, Grand Chief of Nishnawbe Aski Nation.

NAN, representing 49 First Nations in Northern Ontario, says that the Nihb failed to arrange medical travel for Ms. Mamakwa’s four follow-up appointments.

“It is outrageous that Miranda’s travel was denied,” Mr. Fiddler said.

“There is no doubt in my mind that her life May have been saved if she had been allowed to travel to her appointments.”

Federal Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty on Friday called for a review to learn what happened with Ms. Mamakwa’s requests for medical travel.

“I have instructed Indigenous Services Canada officials to urgently establish the facts surrounding Miranda’s death and the circumstances that led to it,” she wrote in a statement released on X.

Ms. Gull-Masty said she would meet with the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority and NAN to discuss what needs to happen next. A date has not been announced.

The Nihb covers the cost of travel and accompanying expenses, including meals and hotel stays, when medically necessary care is not available in a First Nations or Inuit community.

The federal program, offered through Indigenous Services Canada, has been criticized by First Nations leaders, who have raised concerns about the bureaucratic red tape that makes it more difficult for Indigenous people to receive timely services.

Sonia Isaac-Mann, president and chief executive officer of the Sioux Lookout First Nations Health Authority, said Ms. Mamakwa’s death underscores much wider issues of system failures.

The health authority and NAN say they have spent years warning the federal government about how delays and administrative failures put lives at risk.

The organizations say Ms. Mamakwa’s death is the “clearest and most devastating proof yet” these were not exaggerated warnings.

Sol Mamakwa, the deputy leader of the Ontario NDP who is not related to Ms. Mamakwa, issued a recent statement that echoed the health authority and Nan’s call for accountability.

“Miranda deserved so much better,” he said.

He also noted how demonstrators held a rally in June in Sioux Lookout, urging Ottawa fix the Nihb program.

“Miranda’s death was not an accident, but a result of both individual decisions and systemic failures that continue to compromise the lives of First Nations people in this province,” he said.

“It’s time the Nihb program and the federal government take accountability in Miranda’s death and acts to ensure that no more lives are lost because of the program’s failures.”
