stories.title: Transition committees for conservation authorities directed to sign NDAs and keep public info confidential: Utrca Chair
stories.summary: The chair of the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority (Utrca) is raising concerns over what he believes is a lack of public transparency in the province’s plan to consolidate conservation authorities.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
The chair of the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority (Utrca) is raising concerns over what he believes is a lack of public transparency in the province’s plan to consolidate conservation authorities.

“We want to be at the table to make sure our voices are being heard, but we want to be able to do that in an open and transparent way,” said Brian Petrie, Utrca Chair and mayor of Ingersoll.

Petrie says he’s uncomfortable with rules handed down by the province to transition committees, those appointed to oversee the amalgamation of Conservation Authorities (CAs). Petrie says the Terms of Reference make all business of these committees confidential, with no public oversight. Further, Petrie says members have been directed to sign non-disclosure agreements.

“It’s something I’m not comfortable with. We are open. We are required by the Municipal Act to be open as much as possible. There’s certainly circumstances where you need to take things behind closed doors to make sure peoples’ identities and confidential information is kept quiet, but it’s one of those things where it’s certainly not the norm,” Petrie said.

Ontario’s 36 CAs will be down to nine regional groups as of February of 2027. Utrca will join three other CAs in becoming part of the Western Lake Erie Regional Conservation Authority.

Oxford County Warden Marcus Ryan says for municipalities, it means minimal input for major decisions.

“The challenge then is, that as it gets larger and larger and larger, that proportional representation is less and less meaningful, right? You got your two people, or whatever it is, but they’re in such a large group, is it meaningful? Can you actually change direction,” he questioned.

Alexandru Cioban, spokesperson for Todd McCarthy, Minister of Environment, Conservation and Parks issued a statement to CTV News, which says, in part:

Throughout this process, conservation authorities remain municipally governed, and budget decisions continue to be made by conservation authority boards, which consist of representatives appointed by participating municipalities.

Confidentiality expectations are routine and regularly employed by municipalities when individuals have access to sensitive and confidential information, including financial, legal and human resources records.

In the meantime, Petrie has called an emergency meeting of the Utrca Board, where concerns over confidentiality and public accountability are expected to be discussed. Petrie will also seek direction from his board before signing an NDA, or agreeing to take part in the transition committee for this region.

That meeting is set for Tuesday morning.

stories.title: London police looking into overnight heist by masked men robbing safe
stories.summary: The video obtained by CTV News London showed masked individuals pulling into the parking lot in what is believed to be a stolen SUV and then within seconds they are seen breaking into the store using a crowbar and large screwdrivers.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The surveillance camera outside of Berries Market on Wharncliffe Road South captures it all.

The video obtained by CTV News London showed masked individuals pulling into the parking lot in what is believed to be a stolen SUV and then within seconds they are seen breaking into the store using a crowbar and large screwdrivers.

Once inside they are seen rummaging through an office. Then moments later the camera shows the four individuals finding a safe that the store’s accounts manager Mostafa Al Hallak says contained a substantial amount of money.

Then the individuals are seen putting the safe on a cart and wheel it off.

When workers showed up Monday morning, Al Hallak says there was a mess, “They threw papers all over the floor and broke the doors.”

stories.title: Trump scoffs at AI danger warnings as Carney calls for global tech body to strengthen guardrails
stories.summary: Trump's pushback -- arriving over six social media posts Monday -- comes amid growing international alarm about AI that sent stocks falling.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Trump's pushback -- in a screed of six social media posts on Monday -- comes amid growing international alarm about AI that sent stocks falling

Author of the article:

Canada wants to see the creation of a global “technology stability” body to help oversee artificial intelligence and ensure it is safe, Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

“There’s a need for coordination,” Carney said in an interview with Bloomberg News on Monday. “Ultimately, a technology stability board, in our view, along the lines of the Financial Stability Board would make sense.”

“It’s an opportunity — and I think ultimately what it’s going to mean is greater value creation and greater value delivery to people.”

The leaders of major AI labs, including Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei, have said development of the most advanced systems must be slowed in order to prevent AI slipping beyond human control and inflicting catastrophic harm. Other AI industry leaders, including OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, concurred with Amodei’s calls for a slowdown.

But U.S. President Donald Trump dismissed calls for artificial intelligence guardrails and slammed Amodei for urging a slowdown in the technology’s development.

In a Monday social media post, Trump blamed a “Sick conspiracy” for voter backlash on AI data centres and increased concern about frontier models, adding that “the only one that is happy about it is China.”

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a Strong AND Smart (High IQ!) President, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump posted. “We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so. Conspiracy Theorists, Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers, Beware!”

Trump said in a subsequent post that the idea that AI would destroy humanity is a “Hoax” and that the development of the technology “will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President Donald J. Trump.”

Trump’s comments went a step further from remarks he made over the weekend, when he acknowledged the need for some regulation. The president, however, has consistently dismissed warnings about AI safety risks and has emphasized the importance of developing the technology to stay ahead of China.

The president even opened a new line of attack on Alphabet Inc.’s Google over its decision to spend 13 billion euros ($20.9 billion) on AI infrastructure in Finland. “I am not happy about this, and want them to change their thinking,” he posted.

Aidan Gomez, CEO of Canada’s Cohere Inc., said he was concerned by Amodei’s call for temporary waivers of antitrust laws to allow for safety-related discussions between competitors. These laws “were set up to prevent the formation of cartels,” Gomez pointed out at a Milken Institute event in Toronto.

“That should raise a huge red flag in terms of what some of the incentives behind this might be,” he said, while adding he didn’t want to downplay the risks of the “incredibly potent” technology.

“What we need is a process by which to come up with the right regulation, and that should include things like testing of these models in advance and an independent third party that isn’t isolated to any one country and isn’t dominated by any one industry player.”

The people that say AI is going to destroy the World, and that Data Centers are bad for your neighborhood, are the same people that said, just a short time ago, that the World would be extinguished by “Climate Change.” That Hoax never worked out for them, and now they’re on to… pic.twitter.com/OAhpcD2fac — Commentary Donald J. Trump Truth Social Posts On X (@TrumpTruthOnX) September 14, 2026

stories.title: Carney sees chance to tap into Asian, European markets at investment summit
stories.summary: Prime Minister says the event is part of a strategy to line up foreign capital behind Canada’s manufacturing sector
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an interview Monday that his government’s investment summit is part of a strategy to line up foreign capital behind Canada’s manufacturing sector while boosting trade with Asia and Europe.

The summit, taking place Monday and Tuesday at the Four Seasons in Toronto, has drawn global investors and is being watched closely by a domestic audience waiting to see Mr. Carney’s next move in the trade war with the United States.

On the first day of the event, which welcomed roughly 300 executives, among them many of the world’s largest asset managers, Mr. Carney said capital is just one of many ingredients required to boost Canada’s economy.

“You need capital, you need deals, you need projects, you need the proper regulatory environment, you need a competitive tax environment, and you need ambition and action,” Mr. Carney said. He said the summit is meant to bring all these factors together, to the benefit of all Canadians, not just business leaders.

“We are launching the investment supercycle that the country needs,” he added, perched on the edge of a Four Seasons hotel chair and occasionally jabbing a finger in the air to drive home his point.

“There is a massive opportunity for Canada both in Europe and Asia,” said the Prime Minister. “It’s safe to say we haven’t realized our potential in those markets.”

In sectors where Canada is a powerhouse, such as energy and critical minerals, the country has an opportunity to strengthen relationships that have become both economic and strategic. “It’s the strategic benefits that make Europe, Korea and other countries interested in doing more with us,” the Prime Minister said.

“Our reputation, hard-earned over decades by Canadians, is for being reliable and trustworthy, we honour what we sign,” said Mr. Carney. “Canada is a low-risk jurisdiction, and that works to our advantage.”

The federal government’s data show Europe is the largest untapped market for Canadian goods and services, particularly for small- to-medium-sized business. Mr. Carney said while Canada has a free trade agreement with the EU, “we are not fully utilizing it.”

After the Toronto summit concludes on Tuesday, Mr. Carney is scheduled to fly to Europe and address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. The Prime Minister said his goal is to strike a “unique alliance” between Canada and the European Union.

Speaking of U.S. President Donald Trump’s second term in office, Mr. Carney said, “one of the lessons people are taking for the rupture, if I May use that term, is that economic integration can be weaponized.”

Last month, Canadian negotiators walked away from trade talks with the U.S. government, in part over the Trump administration’s attempts to repatriate truck manufacturing.

“We don’t want to lock in a competitive disadvantage for the Canadian auto sector,” said the Prime Minister. “That is not in the interest of U.S.-based auto firms. It is certainly not in best interest of the Canadian auto sector.”

Mr. Carney said he is confident the government can negotiate a “uniquely Canadian solution” that ensures a “vibrant, competitive auto sector” tied to U.S., Chinese and European manufacturers. He added trade negotiations with the U.S. are complicated by the fact that the auto industry is going through a period of transformation.

Canada’s focus in negotiating global trade alliances is on being a player in the auto sector that is “electric and connected,” Mr. Carney said, emerging areas where he said Canada has built expertise. While he never said Donald Trump’s name in the course of a 20-minute conversation, Mr. Carney did point out that two days ago the “U.S. President” spoke approvingly of Chinese automakers building U.S. plants.

Since taking office in March, 2025, the Prime Minister has met twice with China’s President Xi Jinping. Mr. Carney said those face-to-face sessions and the government’s diplomatic outreach have resulted in setting the “guardrails” needed to boost trade with the world’s second-largest economy while navigating issues such as security.

“We have taken the first steps in resetting our relationship,” Mr. Carney said.

“We can go deeper in agriculture with China, deeper in fish exports, energy exports and financial services, a sector in China that will ultimately open up.”

Executives from several Chinese asset managers, including the chief strategy officer from the US$1.6-trillion China Investment Corp., are at the Toronto summit this week.

As CEOs from Canada’s largest companies join federal and provincial politicians in Toronto to pitch the country as a place to invest, Mr. Carney said the key to the event’s success will be landing both cash and expertise from global fund managers, such as Singapore-based Temasek Partners, a US$400-billion fund that ranks among the world’s largest infrastructure investors.

“Investors like Temasek bring capital, and they catalyze change,” Mr. Carney said. “That makes a decisive difference when combined with the ambitions of Canadians up and down this country.”

Mr. Carney said his government is hoping to lure such investors in part by making significant changes to Canada’s tax regime.

“We need to extend corporate tax advantages to make Canada more attractive,” the Prime Minister said, suggesting Ottawa is developing tax measures meant to boost corporate investment in companies and incentivize entrepreneurs to scale-up business.

On Monday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced a new federal program to offer “advance tax rulings” for investments of $1-billion or more . That would give investors a binding decision from the Canada Revenue Agency on how Canadian tax law will apply to a transaction before they commit capital, giving them more certainty.

Mr. Carney said: “We’ve got more to do, above and beyond the advance tax ruling, so watch this space.”

The Prime Minister said the government also remains committed to streamlining the regulatory process to ensure a “one project, one review, one year” outcome for every initiative that requires federal sign-off, not just proposals selected by the Major Projects Office the government launched in August, 2025.

stories.title: Structural fire reported after black smoke seen in London
stories.summary: After multiple 911 callers reported black smoke in the area, crews responded to 900 block of Lorne Avenue.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe, Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London Fire respond to a structural fire in London after multiple 911 callers reported black smoke in the area.

Fire crews responded to 900 block of Lorne Avenue.

On arrival a working fire in a home was confirmed, crews quickly deployed a hose line, conducted a primary and secondary search and are checking for extension.

It is reported the fire started in the rear deck area and there is extensive damage to rear of the house.

The cause of the fire is yet to be determined.

Everyone had gotten out of the house by the time fire crews arrived. No injuries are reported at this time.

The fire is under control, crews are still working to fully stop the fire.

Lorne Ave is a narrow street. Fire crews say to avoid the area to allow them to work safely.

stories.title: B.C.'s deficit forecast up $450M to $13.8B after calculation errors on gas royalties
stories.summary: Victoria - The British Columbia deficit forecast has grown by $450 million to a record-setting $13.8 billion, largely because of a "calculation error" on natural gas royalties, in a situation one critic describes as a state of "fiscal crisis."
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VICTORIA - The British Columbia deficit forecast has grown by $450 million to a record-setting $13.8 billion, largely because of a “calculation error” on natural gas royalties, in a situation one critic describes as a state of “fiscal crisis.”

Finance Minister Josie Osborne, who just took over the finance portfolio last month, released the first quarterly report Monday that shows almost $800 million more in revenue, but spending is also up.

The added revenue comes from income and sales taxes, but wildfire fighting costs are projected to be $614 million more.

“If we backed out the 614 million extra dollars for wildfire recovery, (if) we had a different wildfire season, then we would have seen a different number for the final deficit,” she said. “But of course, British Columbians will always expect us, and we will always be there, to defend them and their properties in the time of wildfire.”

The minister said refundable tax credits for business and renters also rose by $458 million.

What fell by $531 million were projected royalties from natural gas. The Ministry of Finance said the lower forecast reflects lower prices, but also a $306 million error from the price forecast in Budget 2026, which the government earlier called a “serious mistake” in the calculation of the natural gas price.

Osborne said steps are underway to ensure that mistake will never happen again.

”(I) don’t want in any way to diminish the seriousness of this,” she said.

British Columbians need to have trust and confidence in the numbers that are before them, Osborne added.

Peter Milobar, the former finance critic for the B.C. Conservatives and interim leader of a new break-away party, told reporters in Vancouver that the figures clearly demonstrate that government has no control over the provincial finances.

“It, very much, points to a province in a fiscal crisis, and the changing of the finance minister really won’t help that any,” he said.

Osborne replaced Brenda Bailey after she was diagnosed with an early-stage cancer.

Milobar said there is a path toward balancing the budget, but it would require meaningful and serious private-sector growth and development.

“It means the government has to not just talk about trying to attract large projects and get the private sector economy going, but they actually, truly need to get out of the way.”

B.C. Conservative finance critic Gavin Dew said in a statement that the fiscal update shows the NDP government has a spending and math problem.

“The government is collecting more tax revenue and still can’t keep the books under control,” he said.

Bridgitte Anderson, president of the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade, said the update makes it clear that B.C.’s finances are out of balance.

“Repeated warnings about the state of provincial finances (have) not been heeded and spending is still growing faster than the economy that pays for it,” she said in a statement.

Osborne said the province will continue to make responsible and prudent decisions for British Columbians.

“We still have work to do, and we will stay focused on protecting the services for people, while we grow the economy, diversify the economy, and make sure that we are investing in good jobs for British Columbians.”

When asked about Premier David Eby’s election promise in 2024 about “steadily declining deficits” and a “return to balance,” Osborne said government was not expecting to be in an unjustified trade war.

“I think that requires government to staunchly defend and protect the services that people rely on, especially at a time of such economic uncertainty.”

She added that it is too early to talk about future budgets, including next year’s deficit and any future budget measures.

The finance minister said the province faces “significant headwinds” because of current trade issues, but the provincial economy remains resilient and is poised to grow, as it develops new markets other than the United States.

The Finance Ministry said businesses are adapting to changes in global trade, with exports rising by 16 per cent to destinations like China, South Korea and India.

It said the overall value of B.C. exports increased 4.2 per cent until July 2026, mostly due to a strong demand for copper.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Politics Insider: Carney hosts investment summit to show the world ‘what we can do, what we can build’
stories.summary: Event includes an address by former prime minister Stephen Harper
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Business leaders from around the world are in Toronto for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s long-awaited Canada Investment Summit, set to kick into high gear Tuesday with events that include an address by former prime minister Stephen Harper.

Harper, a Conservative, is to deliver a speech titled Capturing Canada’s Moment, concluding an event central to the policies of his successor, a Liberal.

(In 2007, Harper, then prime minister, appointed Carney governor of the Bank of Canada. He later said Carney had been a “valued partner” as his government worked to steer Canada away from the worst impacts of the 2008 financial crisis.)

“The world’s come to Canada this week to see what we can do, what we can build and to partner with us,” Carney told an event today announcing that BCE Inc. will expand its artificial-intelligence data centre operations in Saskatchewan.

The company plans to quadruple the capacity of those operations, with ambitions to provide as much as 1.2 gigawatts of compute power across three new facilities with a series of investments that could top $5-billion.

Irene Galea reports that the company made the announcement at the Invest in Saskatchewan Forum in Toronto with chief executive officer Mirko Bibic, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and Carney.

There are live updates here on events ahead of the summit, which has an opening-night gala dinner today.

Tuesday’s events include an opening keynote address by Carney, followed by a fireside chat.

This afternoon, the Prime Minister’s Office released a list of six power brokers Carney met with today ahead of the conference.

They included Larry Fink , the CEO of American multinational investment corporation BlackRock; Shemara Wikramanayake, the managing director and CEO of the Macquarie Group Ltd., an Australian investment banking and financial services group; Jonathan Gray , the president and chief operating officer of the New York-based alternative asset manager Blackstone Group; and Sheikh Saoud Salem Abdulaziz Al-Sabah , a board member and managing director of the Kuwait Investment Authority.

Capital Power CEO Avik Dey cautioned that transforming the enthusiasm of business and political leaders into final investment decisions will be the real challenge at the summit.

Emma Graney reports that Dey said the business community is on board with Carney’s ambition to broaden Canada’s economic ties in order to reduce its dependence on trade with the United States.

But he noted that catalyzing it into shovels in the ground means busting through Canada’s multiple layers of bureaucracy and regulation.

This is the daily Politics Insider newsletter, curated by

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

European Parliament to open office in Ottawa: Roberta Metsola, president of the European Parliament, says a new office in Ottawa will help facilitate exchanges with Canadian MPs and senators.

Online harms place substantial cost on Canada’s health and justice systems, report says: The cost could be as high as $4.8-billion per year, according to an analysis compiled by a policy consultancy run by Tyler Meredith, a senior fellow at the Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy.

Former B.C. Conservative joins Milobar’s new party: The new party led by former B.C. Conservative legislator Peter Milobar has gained a seventh member. Donegal Wilson announced her move today after discussions with residents of her riding.

Defence Investment Agency head informs staff he’s staying: Former banker Doug Guzman told staff in a mass e-mail Sunday that he remains chief executive officer of the agency and has no intention of quitting, despite reports he was frustrated and ready to leave.

Quebec party leaders prepare for two debates this week: The first debate, hosted by TVA, is scheduled for Tuesday evening. The second, held by Noovo and Crave, is set for Wednesday.

At TIFF, and in Washington, Quebec’s film industry finds itself in the hot seat: It is an industry that thrives inside its own provincial borders, rarely makes a dent outside of them and has now become crucial to the tremulous, fraught and existential battle for Canadian cultural sovereignty writ large.

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney is in Toronto for his government’s investment summit, which begins with a gala dinner tonight and runs through Tuesday. Today, he held an event on data sovereignty with Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe.

Carney’s office has announced he will travel to France and the United Kingdom from Tuesday through Thursday. In Strasbourg, he will address the European Parliament and attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union. In Liverpool, Carney will meet with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the first time.

The Prime Minister will also be visiting Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon on Sept. 20 to meet with French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss deepening the Canada-France partnership in strategic sectors. Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon is a French overseas collectivity located approximately 25 kilometres off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Party Leaders: Green Party Leader Elizabeth May attended a community meeting on Pender Island in British Columbia. No schedules available for other party leaders.

Ministers on the Road:

In Mississauga, Rechie Valdez, the Minister for Women and Gender Equality, announced a $60-million investment advancing menstrual equity and improving affordability through access to essential menstrual products across Canada.

In Toronto, Canadian Identity Minister Marc Miller, with representatives from Great Britain and Spain, signed modernized audiovisual co-production treaties with representatives of the governments of the United Kingdom, Northern Ireland and Spain to make it easier for Canadian producers to collaborate with British and Spanish producers.

In London, Ont., Agriculture Minister Heath MacDonald announced the launch of Farm Credit Canada’s $1-billion Agri‑food Project Finance Fund and $150-million to Velocity Agri-Capital Partners through FCC Capital’s $2-billion investment commitment.

“I’m shrinking in this role.” - Mark Carney to Dilhan Pillay, the CEO of Singapore-based Temasek Holdings, a multinational investment firm, as the two posed for the media before meeting in Toronto. Carney had remarked that Pillay seemed taller than in past.

Prime Minister Mark Carney will be visiting the French overseas collectivity of Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, on Sept. 20. Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon is said to be the only location in North America where a particular form of capital punishment was used in a case that inspired a feature film in 2000. What was the form of punishment?

On Oct. 19, every separatist in the province is going to get down to their local polling station and vote. This is a do-or-die moment for them. They need a win in order to force a second vote on the question they really want asked, which is a clear yes-or-no question on secession. And while they’re not performing too well in the polls, they’re passionate, they’re engaged and they’re going to make sure their votes count. — Tyler Dawson, Content Editor, Opinion

We’re selling Canada to big foreign investors. Why not sell to Canadians, too?

But the summit also gives Ottawa considerable leverage over what gets built and how. If taxpayers are going to help finance the next generation of Canadian businesses, we should think about whether they should have the opportunity to own them. — Darcy Morris is chief executive and co-founder of Ewing Morris & Co. Investment Partners Ltd.

But no prime minister makes historical allusions without calculation, and invoking Sir John A.’s name was a bold move with a message beyond railways and the National Policy. Mr. Carney was telling Canadians that we are a country mature enough to be able to recognize that historical achievements have a role to play in the success of a nation, even if they happened a long time ago and were accomplished by leaders whose actions may not always have aligned with the values we hold today. — J.D.M. paragraphs: Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Business leaders from around the world are in Toronto for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s long-awaited Canada Investment Summit, set to kick into high gear Tuesday with events that include an address by former prime minister Stephen Harper.
Harper, a Conservative, is to deliver a speech titled Capturing Canada’s Moment, concluding an event central to the policies of his successor, a Liberal.

(In 2007, Harper, then prime minister, appointed Carney governor of the Bank of Canada. He later said Carney had been a “valued partner” as his government worked to steer Canada away from the worst impacts of the 2008 financial crisis.)

“The world’s come to Canada this week to see what we can do, what we can build and to partner with us,” Carney told an event today announcing that BCE Inc. will expand its artificial-intelligence data centre operations in Saskatchewan.

The company plans to quadruple the capacity of those operations, with ambitions to provide as much as 1.2 gigawatts of compute power across three new facilities with a series of investments that could top $5-billion.
Irene Galea reports that the company made the announcement at the Invest in Saskatchewan Forum in Toronto with chief executive officer Mirko Bibic, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and Carney.
There are live updates here on events ahead of the summit, which has an opening-night gala dinner today.
Tuesday’s events include an opening keynote address by Carney, followed by a fireside chat.
This afternoon, the Prime Minister’s Office released a list of six power brokers Carney met with today ahead of the conference.

They included Larry Fink , the CEO of American multinational investment corporation BlackRock; Shemara Wikramanayake, the managing director and CEO of the Macquarie Group Ltd., an Australian investment banking and financial services group; Jonathan Gray , the president and chief operating officer of the New York-based alternative asset manager Blackstone Group; and Sheikh Saoud Salem Abdulaziz Al-Sabah , a board member and managing director of the Kuwait Investment Authority.
Capital Power CEO Avik Dey cautioned that transforming the enthusiasm of business and political leaders into final investment decisions will be the real challenge at the summit.
Emma Graney reports that Dey said the business community is on board with Carney’s ambition to broaden Canada’s economic ties in order to reduce its dependence on trade with the United States.
But he noted that catalyzing it into shovels in the ground means busting through Canada’s multiple layers of bureaucracy and regulation.

European Parliament to open office in Ottawa: Roberta Metsola, president of the European Parliament, says a new office in Ottawa will help facilitate exchanges with Canadian MPs and senators.

Online harms place substantial cost on Canada’s health and justice systems, report says: The cost could be as high as $4.8-billion per year, according to an analysis compiled by a policy consultancy run by Tyler Meredith, a senior fellow at the Munk School of Global Affairs & Public Policy.

Former B.C. Conservative joins Milobar’s new party: The new party led by former B.C. Conservative legislator Peter Milobar has gained a seventh member. Donegal Wilson announced her move today after discussions with residents of her riding.

Defence Investment Agency head informs staff he’s staying: Former banker Doug Guzman told staff in a mass e-mail Sunday that he remains chief executive officer of the agency and has no intention of quitting, despite reports he was frustrated and ready to leave.
Quebec party leaders prepare for two debates this week: The first debate, hosted by TVA, is scheduled for Tuesday evening. The second, held by Noovo and Crave, is set for Wednesday.

At TIFF, and in Washington, Quebec’s film industry finds itself in the hot seat: It is an industry that thrives inside its own provincial borders, rarely makes a dent outside of them and has now become crucial to the tremulous, fraught and existential battle for Canadian cultural sovereignty writ large.

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney is in Toronto for his government’s investment summit, which begins with a gala dinner tonight and runs through Tuesday. Today, he held an event on data sovereignty with Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe.

Carney’s office has announced he will travel to France and the United Kingdom from Tuesday through Thursday. In Strasbourg, he will address the European Parliament and attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union. In Liverpool, Carney will meet with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham for the first time.

stories.title: Canadian cities brace for tariff pain as trade war escalates
stories.summary: Candidates for local government, expecting turmoil, are turning to trade as a campaign issue in approaching municipal elections
stories.author: Matthew Scace, Temur Durrani, Laura Stone
stories.content:
In Calgary, city officials are projecting new tariff costs reaching close to half a billion dollars. Other cities across the country are anticipating economic pain in their communities. Candidates for local government, expecting turmoil, are turning to trade as a campaign issue in approaching municipal elections.

Canada’s trade war with the United States is beginning to hit home for municipalities. And with the possibility of tariffs and countertariffs lasting months or years, cities are starting to look into how the trade war could blow holes in their budgets.

“Municipalities are bracing for this,” Tim Tierney, president of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, said in an interview. Local governments are on the front lines of the trade war, but many of them don’t have extra money to spare for spiralling costs.

“Municipalities need the money. We can’t simply talk about it and plan for the future and do it in future budgets. The money is needed now.”

On Sept. 8, administrators with the City of Calgary estimated the latest tariffs and retaliatory measures by the U.S. and Canadian governments could cost the city between $315-million and $466-million on the remaining lifespan of existing contracts.

Calgary’s financial projections underscore the challenges ahead for municipalities if the trade war continues in the longer term, a reality for which Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the country should prepare.

Most municipalities across Canada haven’t assessed the extra costs that tariffs will inflict on their budgets but are preparing for deep economic wounds. The issue is becoming an increasingly important factor for voters in the lead up to municipal elections in Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island.

In Calgary, even though 95 per cent of the city’s contracts come from Canadian suppliers, many of those contractors are exposed to tariffs because they source materials from the U.S., Bill Black, chief executive officer of the Calgary Construction Association, said in an interview.

Calgary’s estimates show the city’s transit system is now likely to face $84-million in tariff costs on top of $535-million in future spending that city hall has already committed to its transportation network. Scotia Place, the glitzy $800-million arena scheduled to open at the beginning of the Calgary Flames’ 2027-28 season, is expected to face an extra $30-million in tariff costs, and projects for Calgary’s aging water infrastructure will feel the bite of an additional $21-million price tag.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said the extra costs would be equal to an annual property-tax hike of between 12 per cent and 18 per cent. His office said he is proposing for the federal government and Canada’s big-city mayors to find ways that will ensure cities aren’t at the losing end of a tariff fight.

The Globe and Mail reached out to more than a dozen municipalities across the country. The City of Brampton in Ontario was the only municipality apart from Calgary to outline the tariffs’ estimated impact, pegging its potential capital cost exposure at between $100-million and $150-million.

An official for the federal Department of Finance said in an e-mailed statement that municipalities can ask Ottawa for financial relief on tariffed products. However, municipalities typically recoup that money through their contractors, who are often responsible for paying the duties in the first place.

John Fragos, a spokesperson for Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said that Ottawa is always looking at ways to better support municipalities.

Evan Robinson, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli, pointed to a $40-million fund for “trade-impacted communities” to reshore critical supply chains, attract new investment and diversify economies.

Hamilton’s incumbent mayoral candidate, Andrea Horwath, said there is a sense of “concern and foreboding” in her Ontario city, which employs about 28,000 people in steel, manufacturing and food processing.

“People are really uncertain about the future,” she said in an interview. “There’s no doubt that Hamiltonians feel like we are specifically under attack.”

Marianne Meed Ward, the incumbent mayoral candidate in Burlington, who chairs Ontario’s big-city mayors’ group, said the tariffs will force cities to defer costs that will only become more expensive in the future. She said 43 per cent of Burlington’s businesses are directly affected by tariffs or countertariffs, representing about half the city’s jobs.

“It’s quite staggering, and very eye-opening,” she said.

The trade war has particularly animated Toronto’s mayoral race, where incumbent Olivia Chow and her main challenger, councillor Brad Bradford, are presenting different visions for how they would handle the issue in office. Election day is Oct. 26.

In a statement, Ms. Chow’s campaign defended her response so far, pointing to an economic action plan released in March, 2025, with the goal of diversifying Toronto’s trade and buying local. More than 98 per cent of the city’s spending now goes to Canadian companies, her campaign said. She has also launched a grant program for businesses and introduced a new industrial property tax deferral program.

Mr. Bradford, meanwhile, suggested the city’s tariff response has been inadequate. He has floated numerous proposals, including establishing a permanent tariff-response group, speeding up permit approvals for companies and tax relief. Mr. Bradford said he fully supports Mr. Carney’s efforts in the trade fight but added that cities such as Toronto are absorbing the costs.

“Every month this drags on is more pressure on a municipal budget that’s already stretched thin. It’s crucial for Ottawa to step up and provide tariff relief so cities aren’t left carrying this cost alone while Washington keeps moving the goalposts,” he said in a statement.

Elsewhere, other cities say they have either been able to withstand the effects of the tariffs so far or haven’t yet measured the repercussions on local budgets.

The issue has bubbled to the surface in Vancouver, where candidates are gearing up for the city’s Oct. 17 municipal vote.

Late last month, Vancouver councillor Lucy Maloney, who is running for re-election, called for a special meeting to push incumbent mayoral candidate Ken Sim to take urgent measures on U.S. tariffs. Mr. Sim declined Ms. Maloney’s plea, calling tariffs a national matter and stating that he is planning to support Ottawa “without adding unnecessary noise to the process.”

The City of Vancouver said it hasn’t conducted modelling similar to Calgary’s yet.

On the Prairies, where Manitoba is holding municipal elections this fall, City of Winnipeg spokesperson Adam Campbell said the city’s public service department is reviewing U.S. supplier arrangements to analyze “the potential economic impact of the tariffs.”

For Brandon, Man., incumbent Jeff Fawcett said his larger concern as mayor had been tariffs from China before they were rolled back earlier this year, as the levies directly affected the agriculture sector in and around what is colloquially dubbed the Wheat City. “The U.S. tariffs haven’t necessarily been as big of a problem for us,” Mr. Fawcett said in an interview.

One province over, in Saskatoon, chief financial officer Clae Hack said the city hasn’t yet calculated the impact, noting that it’s hard to examine how much costs will be passed on to the municipality.

A majority of East Coast cities – including Halifax, St. John’s and Charlottetown – say they are less vulnerable to tariffs compared to the rest of Canada, in large part because of diversified trade initiatives with Europe. Over the years, the Atlantic provinces have worked collectively toward solidifying export and sales pathways with countries such as Britain and Spain, which have particularly benefited the seafood and energy industries.

Still, the U.S. is Atlantic Canada’s largest international export market by a wide margin. Continued tariffs “will have impacts” on those local economies, including on Prince Edward Island, said City of Charlottetown spokesperson Jessica Bradley.

The situation, however, is more dire in New Brunswick. Last year, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce designated Saint John as the most tariff-vulnerable municipality in the country. Its exposure to risk is vastly higher because of southbound exports to the U.S., particularly in the energy and forestry sectors.

The seaport city, home to roughly 78,000 people, hasn’t yet run the numbers, said Lisa Kennedy, Saint John’s director of external relations.

“At this point, there is still too much uncertainty to put a firm number on the impact.”

Canada’s trade war with the United States is beginning to hit home for municipalities. And with the possibility of tariffs and countertariffs lasting months or years, cities are starting to look into how the trade war could blow holes in their budgets.

“Municipalities are bracing for this,” Tim Tierney, president of the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, said in an interview. Local governments are on the front lines of the trade war, but many of them don’t have extra money to spare for spiralling costs.
“Municipalities need the money. We can’t simply talk about it and plan for the future and do it in future budgets. The money is needed now.”

On Sept. 8, administrators with the City of Calgary estimated the latest tariffs and retaliatory measures by the U.S. and Canadian governments could cost the city between $315-million and $466-million on the remaining lifespan of existing contracts.

Calgary’s financial projections underscore the challenges ahead for municipalities if the trade war continues in the longer term, a reality for which Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the country should prepare.

Most municipalities across Canada haven’t assessed the extra costs that tariffs will inflict on their budgets but are preparing for deep economic wounds. The issue is becoming an increasingly important factor for voters in the lead up to municipal elections in Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba and Prince Edward Island.

stories.title: The Globe and Mail nominated for eight Jack Webster Awards
stories.summary: Nathan VanderKlippe, Justine Hunter, Andrea Woo, Marsha Lederman and David Ebner among the journalists recognized for their reporting
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
The Globe and Mail led nominations for British Columbia’s prestigious Jack Webster Awards, with judges noting work on the Tumbler Ridge school shooting and on the impact of the B.C. Supreme Court’s decision in the Cowichan case, among other work.

In all, Globe journalists received eight nominations, while the CBC received seven and The Tyee and the Investigative Journalism Foundation were named in four each.

Canadian newsrooms do not have the same amount of experience as their U.S. counterparts in responding to deadly gun violence in schools. Last February, when violence erupted in Tumbler Ridge, The Globe had to develop a plan quickly.

The Globe’s newsroom mobilized immediately, drawing in every one of its news reporters in British Columbia, as well as journalists from Calgary, Edmonton and Toronto. The coverage included a story published just hours after the shooting occurred with vivid language and meticulous reporting. Nathan VanderKlippe reported on a conversation with a 12-year-old student who, only hours earlier, had been comforted while hiding in a closet with classmates.

A day later, The Globe exclusively reported that the shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, had suffered mental health challenges so significant that she had once set fire to a bed in her family home while under the influence of psychedelic mushrooms.

The story included important context about the struggles the family was having in getting the shooter psychological help, and it revealed disturbing social media messages linked to the shooter that foreshadowed what was to come. All the information derived from social media posts was meticulously cross-referenced.

The Globe’s work on the Tumbler Ridge shooting was also nominated for the international Online Journalism Award.

Legislative reporter Justine Hunter led The Globe’s coverage of the explosive B.C. Supreme Court ruling in the Cowichan Indigenous land rights case, work that was awarded a Webster nomination in the news category.

Ms. Hunter’s collaboration with city reporter Frances Bula revealed for the first time the long reach of the decision, including its effects on other court cases and treaty negotiations, and its implications for municipalities, whose ability to levy taxes on urban land declared to be under Aboriginal title was thrown into question.

Ms. Hunter also received nominations for her interactive look at the dangers of navigating the Hecate Strait and for a feature retracing the steps of the plucky 20-year-old woman who helped map Strathcona Park in the summer of 1910.

Andrea Woo was also nominated in the feature category, for an in-depth piece on the exacting science, money and labour behind creating a playing field for the 2026 Fifa World Cup.

The reporting went behind the scenes to explore the massive, largely invisible effort required to build pitches capable of performing identically across 16 stadiums, three countries and radically different climates.

Opinion columnist Marsha Lederman received her third consecutive Webster nomination this year, this time for her thoughtful look back at how the reputation of popular author Steven Galloway disintegrated over explosive allegations of sexual misconduct. Lederman looked at the 10 years of lawsuits and conflict within Canada’s literary community left in the scandal’s wake.

Legal affairs reporter David Ebner received a nomination in the legal category for a piece examining Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pledge to bring in stricter bail rules .

Photographer and reporter Jesse Winter was among the first nominees in the new picture category for a photo of a Squamish-area resident packing their belongings as they prepared to evacuate their home while a wildfire burned in the forests above.

The Jack Webster Foundation was created in 1986 after the retirement of its namesake. Mr. Webster was a well known, influential reporter in Western Canada, and the organization says the awards are meant to create a community where B.C. journalism thrives.
paragraphs: The Globe and Mail led nominations for British Columbia’s prestigious Jack Webster Awards, with judges noting work on the Tumbler Ridge school shooting and on the impact of the B.C. Supreme Court’s decision in the Cowichan case, among other work.
In all, Globe journalists received eight nominations, while the CBC received seven and The Tyee and the Investigative Journalism Foundation were named in four each.

Canadian newsrooms do not have the same amount of experience as their U.S. counterparts in responding to deadly gun violence in schools. Last February, when violence erupted in Tumbler Ridge, The Globe had to develop a plan quickly.

The Globe’s newsroom mobilized immediately, drawing in every one of its news reporters in British Columbia, as well as journalists from Calgary, Edmonton and Toronto. The coverage included a story published just hours after the shooting occurred with vivid language and meticulous reporting. Nathan VanderKlippe reported on a conversation with a 12-year-old student who, only hours earlier, had been comforted while hiding in a closet with classmates.

A day later, The Globe exclusively reported that the shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, had suffered mental health challenges so significant that she had once set fire to a bed in her family home while under the influence of psychedelic mushrooms.

The story included important context about the struggles the family was having in getting the shooter psychological help, and it revealed disturbing social media messages linked to the shooter that foreshadowed what was to come. All the information derived from social media posts was meticulously cross-referenced.
The Globe’s work on the Tumbler Ridge shooting was also nominated for the international Online Journalism Award.

Legislative reporter Justine Hunter led The Globe’s coverage of the explosive B.C. Supreme Court ruling in the Cowichan Indigenous land rights case, work that was awarded a Webster nomination in the news category.

Ms. Hunter’s collaboration with city reporter Frances Bula revealed for the first time the long reach of the decision, including its effects on other court cases and treaty negotiations, and its implications for municipalities, whose ability to levy taxes on urban land declared to be under Aboriginal title was thrown into question.

Ms. Hunter also received nominations for her interactive look at the dangers of navigating the Hecate Strait and for a feature retracing the steps of the plucky 20-year-old woman who helped map Strathcona Park in the summer of 1910.
Andrea Woo was also nominated in the feature category, for an in-depth piece on the exacting science, money and labour behind creating a playing field for the 2026 Fifa World Cup.

The reporting went behind the scenes to explore the massive, largely invisible effort required to build pitches capable of performing identically across 16 stadiums, three countries and radically different climates.

Opinion columnist Marsha Lederman received her third consecutive Webster nomination this year, this time for her thoughtful look back at how the reputation of popular author Steven Galloway disintegrated over explosive allegations of sexual misconduct. Lederman looked at the 10 years of lawsuits and conflict within Canada’s literary community left in the scandal’s wake.

stories.title: Canadian agri-food industry gets $1B federal funding boost for domestic production projects
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 14, 2026 10:22 PM | Last Updated: 18 hours ago
stories.author: Jack Sutton
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 14, 2026 10:22 PM | Last Updated: 18 hours ago
The new Agri-Food Project Finance Fund will be delivered by Farm Credit Canada

The federal government has announced $1 billion in new funding for agri-food processing and manufacturing projects across Canada in an effort to have more value-added agricultural products produced at home.
Agriculture and Agri-Food Minister Heath MacDonald was at Arva Flour Mills north of London, Ont., ON Monday afternoon to make the announcement.
MacDonald said many Canadian agricultural products are sent for processing in other countries, only for those value-added products to be imported and sold in Canadian grocery stores.
"We would like to keep those products to be able to process them here," he said.
"If we can do that, we take some of the cost away for logistics purposes, which entails possibly a lesser cost on the grocery shelves."
Part of the government's $3.2-billion

National Food Security Strategy , the new $1-billion Agri-Food Project Finance Fund aims to help kickstart projects that will expand Canada's processing capacity, he said, adding it would help companies overcome financial barriers that May be deemed "too complex for traditional lenders or investors."

Farm Credit Canada (FCC), the country's leading agricultural term lender and creator of the fund, launched a 60-day expression of interest process on Monday for businesses to apply for consideration .
The new fund is a "major step forward for Canada's food system," according to Justine Hendricks, Fcc's president and chief executive officer.
Hendricks said the intended recipients are mid-market projects, typically those with total capital costs between $25 million and $500 million.
Such projects are often too large or complex for conventional lending, Hendricks added, but too specialized for traditional investors.
"That's the gap we are here to fill. It's financing built to unlock projects and bring other lenders and investors alongside us.
"So, definitely to be done in partnership, and our goal is to make high-value projects more financeable so more of them get built here in Canada."

The expression of interest period is just the first phase of the fund, she said, noting that it isn't a guarantee of funding. Rather, it will help FCC "identify the strongest opportunities and understand where FCC can have the greatest impact."
Alongside the $1-billion fund, MacDonald also announced $150 million to Velocity Agri-Capital Partners, through Fcc's commitment to provide $2 billion to Canadian food and agriculture by 2030.
Headed by Canadian entrepreneur Arlene Dickinson, Velocity aims to support and invest in mid-sized agri-food businesses and help them reach export markets in Southeast Asia.
The $150 million for Velocity will be combined with $350 million that it intends to raise from domestic and international investors.
"When we bring public and private investment together, we can unlock more capital, accelerate innovation and create new opportunities for Canadian businesses," MacDonald said.

stories.title: Spanish parent company of Grifols takes full ownership of Canadian operations
stories.summary: Company’s plasma collection sites have been closed to donors since Aug. 14, two days after Health Canada delivered its most recent critical review
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
The Spanish parent company of the Grifols chain of private plasma collection centres has taken over full ownership of its Canadian operations, according to corporate documents.

The disclosures shed light on internal changes the company is making as it works to address concerns from Health Canada since announcing a temporary closure last month, including parting ways with a director who started many of the company’s Canadian collection centres.

Grifols is the country’s only major commercial collector of plasma, a golden-coloured fluid found in blood that is used to make medicine.

The company operates in Canada as part of an agreement signed with Canadian Blood Services in 2022. CBS relies on volunteers for blood and plasma donations, while Grifols pays donors. CBS spends more than $1-billion per year on supplying hospitals with drugs made from plasma and other related products.

Grifols has been the target of scrutiny in recent months after the deaths of two donors in Winnipeg. The company’s locations, including its head office, have received multiple “non-compliant” ratings from Health Canada inspectors in the past year.

The company’s plasma collection sites have been closed to donors since Aug. 14, two days after Health Canada delivered its most recent critical review.

Grifols said it would use the temporary closure to retrain staff and work with Health Canada and CBS to improve its operations.

Recent corporate disclosures show the company has also used the time to revamp some of its internal leadership.

Grifols owns 17 collection centres across six provinces, as well as a pharmaceutical factory in Montreal. Most of those collection sites were started by other companies before Grifols bought them.

Ten of those centres were started by a company called Canadian Plasma Resources (CPR), whose co-founder and chief executive officer was Barzin Bahardoust. Grifols announced in the summer of 2023, after reaching its agreement with Canadian Blood Services, that it intended to acquire CPR.

According to financial statements and an interim directors’ report released on July 28, the publicly traded Grifols S.A. and its subsidiaries acquired 50.1 per cent of CPR two years later, ON Nov. 1, 2025, and renamed the company to “Grifols Canada Plasma Corporation.” The transaction was worth $27-million, paid in shares, which included transaction costs.

But even with a majority ownership, the documents said “the governance structure and the contractual arrangements in place restrict Grifols’ ability to control Grifols Canada Plasma Corporation.”

The documents continue that the “management and direction” of the company’s activities correspond to its “Sole Director,” who “holds full decision-making authority over operating activities − including the approval of the business plan, the annual budget, the dividend policy, and the direction of operations − without any contractual mechanisms requiring such decisions to be submitted to Grifols for approval."

The financial documents said Grifols and its subsidiaries had an agreement to purchase the remaining shares of the Canadian operation starting in January of 2027. The final price would be determined by a formula that included the volume of plasma collected by the Canadian operations.

Canadian corporate records show that as of late July the only director listed for Grifols Canada Plasma Corporation was Mr. Bahardoust, the former chief executive officer of CPR.

But on Sept. 1, Grifols changed the directors of the Canadian corporation to remove Mr. Bahardoust and replace him with three Grifols executives, one based in Canada, one based in the United States and one based in Spain.

Grifols told The Globe and Mail in an unsigned statement that it is now the sole shareholder of the Canadian corporation.

“In connection with this transition, Mr. Bahardoust is no longer a corporate director nor is he currently employed by or contracted by Grifols,” the company said.

Mr. Bahardoust did not respond to a request for comment.

Grifols said it has been a long-time supplier of plasma-derived drugs to Canadians and has invested more than $1-billion in its Canadian operations, including the construction of the drug manufacturing facility in Montreal.

Grifols’ agreement with CBS calls for it to collect 600,000 litres of plasma per year in Canada. The company said it collected about 400,000 litres in 2025.

The company did not say when it expects to start collecting plasma again in Canada.

“Collection activities are expected to resume as soon as feasible, in agreement with Health Canada on the requirements and conditions for reopening,” Grifols said.

Alexandre Bergeron, spokesperson for federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel, said Health Canada was continuing to work with the company on corrective active plans for its locations.
